4.8 宗祠里的祭祀
Section 8

八、宗祠的建筑 宗祠是一种严肃的礼制建筑。它核心部分的型制从住宅演化而来，住宅在生活中由于种种条件而千变万化，同样，作为崇祀建筑，有些庙宇在山区，在水边，都有极丰富的形体变化。

宗祠虽然也有变化，但变化不大，保持着一副由于功能而程式化的主要空间组合和一种庄重、整齐的格调。宗祠是举行祭祀的场所，祠祭要严格按照《朱文正公家礼》规定的程序进行，以致宗祠建筑本身，尤其是它的中央主体部分，是有一定程式的。

大多数宗祠，主要有三部分，从前到后，一是大门门屋；二是拜殿，或者叫享堂，是举行祭拜仪式的地方；三是寝室，是从《礼记·王制》里说的那个"庶人祭于寝"的"寝"字引发出来的名称，专为供奉祖先神位。《光绪合肥邢氏家谱》道："家庙者，祖宗之宫室也，制度即隘，亦少不得三进两庑：前门户，中厅事，后寝室。

"江西省婺源县黄村的经义堂和汪口村的仁本堂以及安徽、浙江大量的宗祠都是很标准的这种格局。局面小一点的宗祠，不另建寝室，而把神牌就供奉在拜殿后墙前的神龛里。

如不够，便在山墙前也设神龛；再不够，则合并神主，在一方神主牌上写一二十个祖先名讳，这合并的措施叫"祧"。

四川《云阳涂氏族谱·祠堂碑记》清楚地说："上建龛堂，所以安神主而序昭穆也；中树厅事，所以齐子孙而肃跪拜也；前列回楼，所以接宾朋而讲圣旨也；左右两庑，所以进子弟而习诗书也。"它把各部分的功用都说齐了，左右两庑的使用很有历史的特色。龛堂就是寝室，它的地坪往往比享堂的高出不少，回楼即倒座门楼。

这说的是一般规模的祠堂，稍大一点的则在这里建戏台。三进房子之间是两个院落，院落左右有廊庑。有的把后院廊庑发展成厢房，也用作"寝室"，分"左昭右穆"，恭奉先人牌位，前院廊庑分隔成小间，或作宗族办事用房，如谱房、账房或长老们的议事室。而《云阳涂氏族谱》里则规定它的用途为书塾。

凡大宗祠和房祠，都必需有一个宽敞的厨房，以烹制祭祀用的各种食品，如胙肉。大而富的宗族，宗祠有多种公共功能，因而宗祠便也比较复杂。除了核心部分之外，附属于宗祠建筑的常有后花园、书塾、义仓、义厝等等，少数的如浙江省武义县俞源村的俞氏宗祠甚至更附有孤儿院、养老院等等。

最简单的氏级别祠堂，只有大门和拜殿，把祖先神位供奉在拜殿里紧贴后墙的神橱里，免去专门的寝室，甚至没有前进和两庑。广东省珠江三角洲各地的宗族分支很早，所以宗祠多是这种小型的。

规模较大一点的宗祠，在门屋里造一个戏台，面对拜殿，前院和它两侧的廊庑成了看戏人的所在位置，甚至设楼，楼上为女眷的观戏厅。楼下在演戏时由小贩摆各种食品摊。江西省乐安县流坑村，相传为汉儒董仲舒后人的聚落，董氏大宗祠是一座少有的大型祠堂，建于村北的陌兰洲，距村落住宅区约二百米。

坐北朝南，面对村落，背靠自南而北再向西转弯的乌江。从大宗祠入村要通过寨墙上的拱宸门。

大宗祠建于村外，背对村落的朝山，任乌江在后面流过，这种布局不合堪舆术常见的教条，在非常重视堪舆之说的江西省（杨筠松即江西人），流坑董氏大宗祠的这个位置可能有一些说法，但没有留下记载。

董氏大宗祠和一左一右的另外两座房祠形成建筑群，三幢建筑并列，东西宽九十米，南北纵深七十多米，共占地七千平方米。大宗祠位于中央，东侧是桂林祠，祀董氏十六世祖董季敏。西为桂岩祠（后改为文馆，祀孔子和文昌帝君）。有子弟备考科举的小小读书室。三祠前有一个共有的公共空间，形成宽敞的横向院落。院中央有一口长方形的"墨池"。

院子东西端均有三开间砖坊一座，西坊书"优入贤关"（外）和"簪缨世第"（内），东坊书"理学名贤"（内）和"科甲联芳"（外）。这两座砖坊初建于康熙年间（1662—1722）。大宗祠前为三间牌坊式砖门，重檐，中央一匾正面书"厚德流光"，背面匾上书"文献世家"。次间各有石狮子一座。门前有墨池，池南有坊名"追远"，表示对祖先的怀念。

池东西各有一座木坊相对，和外墙上"优入贤关"、"科甲联芳"两座砖坊在一条直线上。东木坊书"累朝师保"，西木坊书"奕世科名"，炫耀仕宦和功名的成就。院正面南墙有影壁，书"累朝世家"四个大字。

进入"厚德流光"门，在前院的左右还有钟、鼓楼各一座。大宗祠共三进，第一进为"育贤楼"大厅，三开间重檐，中央一间额"宋赠大司徒董公大宗祠"，东间额"祖孙台部"，西间额"三世尚书"。

第二进大厅为"敦睦堂"，三开间重檐，匾额书"万殊一本"。第三进为五开间，中央三开间为两层，上层额"敕书阁"。下层明间有匾额书"孝敬堂"，左右按昭穆次序为"彰义堂"、"报功堂"、"宗原堂"、"道原堂"，均有额。

育贤楼和敦睦堂两侧有厢房，东侧祀"忠"、"廉"，西侧祀"孝"、"节"。按昭穆次序应是忠、孝、廉、节。宗祠犹如一座家族忠臣义士节妇贞女的纪念馆。孝敬、彰义、报功三堂先落成于嘉靖四十年（1565年）。

明人董燧写《彰义堂记》说，"中题曰孝敬堂，所以祀爵也；左题曰彰义堂，所以祀义也；右题曰报功堂，所以祀功也。三堂之外，总题曰敦睦堂，所以序昭穆也。"孝敬堂祀仕宦，报功堂祀堪舆家杨筠松、曾文辿和廖瑀。董氏宗族一直认为本族的发达全由于这几位风水"大师"给祖坟和聚落寻了好风水。

"彰义堂"是专祀那些捐钱捐田助建宗祠和助祭的族人的，标准是十两银子一位，钱多就有好位置。敦睦堂祀合族历代祖先。宗原堂和道原堂后建，万历九年（1581年）董燧在《宗原道原两堂簿引》中写道："道原堂特祀仲舒公，溯吾董道学之原也。……宗原堂特祀清然公列祖……重其始也。"仲舒公是汉代的董仲舒，被尊为董姓始祖；清然公是董姓迁江西省宜黄县的始祖。

大宗祠因此又是一座家族传统教育的展览厅，纪念和教育，都与流坑的历史特点相符合。敦睦堂有一副对联： 以祖宗之心为心，自求多福； 若先王之法不法，入此何颜。更揭示出宗祠的教化作用。但特别值得注意的是"彰义堂"，它所说的"义"，就是向宗族捐款，捐田。

彰义堂里供奉的就是些这样的大商人或大地主，就像不必读书应考，靠捐纳便得到什么"大夫"、"司马"的虚衔一样，靠捐纳也可以进入专祠，永享殊荣。这情况反映着明代晚期长江中下游地区商业经济发达的历史性变化，这变化在意识形态上的表现之一，便是这样突破了封建宗法制度的伦理观念。明代晚期，流坑村不少人就因经营漕运和木材而致大富。

宗祠作为庄严的礼仪建筑，格局变化少，但也有些变体。广州市的陈氏宗祠除中轴上的一路五开间厅堂和院落以外，左右还各有一路院落和厅堂，每路三进，一共九厅六院。三路之间只以敞廊相隔，最外侧处才有厢间。

厅堂、厢房和斋房一共十八座，总面积竟达一万三千二百平米，这座宗祠的空阔开敞是少有其匹。浙江省永嘉县岩头村的桂林公祠，由书院改成，享堂前有大水池，中央立方亭一座，由一道桥从仪门经方亭再到享堂。仪门外又是一座水池，进大门后，绕水池方得抵仪门。这布局很有个性。

华北地区历来多战乱，稳定有力的宗族少，所以村落多为杂性，有些人口不多的小宗族。因此也就少宗祠，尤其少大型宗祠。村落的管理多由地缘性或行业性的"社"担当。公共活动在庙宇里举行。

最小的宗祠无非是仅能容身的小屋一间，四周墙上写满了祖先名讳就罢了，屋中央立一个小小的香火架，例如河北省蔚县宋家庄的苏氏宗祠，只有小小一间。大宗祠门屋里一般都有戏台。

有些富裕村落，房祠和支祠也有戏台。

门屋里的戏台主要有三种，一种全部都在门屋的明间里面；一种有一半向祠内凸出于明间之外；第三种则是全部凸出，前面高高翘起一对翼角，而后台则在门屋明间里。

第三种做法，观众可从戏台三面看戏，台上台下的隔阂比较小。

第一种做法，戏台挡住了宗祠的大门，平日，包括演戏的日子，只开左右次间的侧门，特殊的日子，例如祭祖，例如奉安神主，便把戏台中央一溜活动台板移开，空出一条通道来。

第二、第三种做法，在中央正门进入门屋，分左右绕过戏台再向拜殿。化妆室通常设在门屋次间的夹层里，有小木楼梯从戏台太师壁后的候场处上下。

候场处与前台之间设一道板壁，太师壁，叫"守旧"，正面大多画一幅《唐明皇游月宫》图。唐明皇就是唐玄宗，他精通音律，好歌舞，曾亲自在宫中梨园里训练戏班子，所以被戏剧行业奉为祖师爷，叫"老郎神"。唐明皇游月宫是一则很浪漫的故事，白居易有诗叙述明皇因"安史之乱"仓皇出逃四川，中途杨贵妃在六军逼迫下自尽，"君王掩面救不得，回首血泪相和流"。乱平返都，明皇日夜思念贵妃。道士叶法善便作法引导明皇到月宫里去，和已经升仙住在月宫里的杨贵妃会面。

二人相誓"在天愿作比翼鸟，在地愿为连理枝"。明皇游月宫的情节极富戏剧性，所以经常用来画在这个"守旧"板壁上。"守旧"的上方挂一块横匾，大都是赞扬演出的，不出"金声玉振"、"作古振今"、"翻风弄月"之类，以套话为多。"守旧"的两侧是上场门和下场门，门额上大多各写"出将"、"入相"两个字。也有的写得花巧些，但意思不变。台子左右和前沿，有纤小的高仅盈尺的栏杆，保护演员。

栏杆小柱头上蹲着木雕的麒麟等等瑞兽。有些宗祠，如浙江省永嘉县芙蓉村的"陈氏宗祠"，在戏台左后侧附一个小小的台子，给乐队专用。

戏台往往是小木作、木雕和彩画作的精品。首先是戏台上方为拔音（或称拢音）而多用深藻井，藻井的样式极多，木工师傅们争奇斗巧，别出心裁地进行创作，频出精品。

如浙江省永嘉县各村宗祠的戏台常用八角覆斗形藻井，溜金斗拱沿八个阴角线和八面中线层层上挑，长拱如流云，如灵芝，宛转曲伸，非常生动。

浙江省宁海县农村，戏台的藻井各式各样，变化很多，最生动的叫"百鸟朝凤"（民间叫"鸡笼顶"），图案呈螺旋形上腾，蓬勃的动势和戏剧的热烈相呼应，珠联璧合。有些藻井整个覆满鲜艳的彩画，"开光盒子"里的戏剧场景画得很精致逼真。

其次是戏台台面前沿，大木枋子前贴着一条通长的木雕，雕刻的题材都是戏剧情节。这幅雕刻是雕花匠大展身手的地方。四川省各地把这幅长长的雕花板叫做"照面枋"，意思就是说它面对观众。照面枋专供大家品评，所以制作格外精心。

江西省乐平县，村村祠堂有戏台，甚至有些村几个祠堂都有戏台，全县在"文化大革命"后保存下来的戏台还有三百多座。

乐平戏台的型制大多有些特殊，而且雕梁画栋，穷极艳丽，几乎是无处不雕，无雕不贴金箔，一派耀眼的灿灿金光。

戏台前檐的一对柱子，叫"台柱"，台柱上必挂楹联，有一些是即景而写的，比较浅显直露，如"看去俨然如是，想来或者有之"；有一些带有感慨，如： 一曲商音，演成千古兴亡胜负； 数声越调，点出百年离合悲欢。又如： 移步换形，漫说炎凉都是假； 描眉画角，须知喜怒皆成真。台口上方也有横匾，大多书"普天同庆"、"盛世纶音"之类的喜兴话。

看戏的观众，按祠堂里规矩，一般是男的在院子里，女的在拜殿前檐下，自带凳子。院子两侧的廊庑里也是妇女们看戏的场所。山西、江西和四川等诸省有些祠堂，厢廊上有看楼，左为"男居楼"，右为"女居楼"，专为"有身份人家"使用。明清两代有些道学腐儒，认为演戏有伤风化，如明代劳宜斋在《瓯江逸志》里批评道：每逢演戏，"十余日昼夜游观，男女杂乱"。清代道光、咸丰年间（1821—1861）永嘉县令汤成烈在《县志稿》里也写道："报赛侈鬼神之会……士女游观，靓妆华服，阗城溢郭，有司莫之能禁。"想禁又禁不住，很不满意。

社会上层的这种保守意识，当然会影响到村子里的主事人物，所以祠堂里演戏要划分男女观众的位置，并且有几个六十岁以上的老人家在观众群里巡视，用长长的旱烟杆敲打眼光不老实的小后生。一般村落，戏台大多只建在大宗祠（总祠）门屋里，面对享堂。

但也有一些村落把戏台造在宗祠大门外的广场上，面对宗祠。有些村落，如福建省连城培田村，戏台的位置和朝向就不很规矩。其实是连大门的位置都不很规矩。

每逢演戏，邻村的人都会来看，而且四方小贩，卖小吃食的、卖零杂货的，也都会赶来在祠堂前或戏台前两侧廊庑里摆摊，形成临时的闹市。为了保护村落内部的安全和宁静，是大多村落把总祠建在村边而不建在村子核心区的原因之一。也有少数宗祠门厅里的戏台是可以拆卸的，如江西省婺源县黄村的总祠经义堂。

浙江省建德县新叶村智字房的崇仁堂，它的戏台也是可拆卸的，木架构件平时收在祠堂里，用时取出搭在大门前泮池的水面上。这种活动戏台叫"雨台"或"露台"。

号称水乡的浙江省绍兴市有一种戏台，搭在宗祠前的水面上，距岸比较远，四乡的人驾船来看戏，船就停在戏台前。从开戏到戏散，一直乱而不清，但"看戏"的乡民倒更增添不少趣味。冬烘先生们认为，妇女坐在自家的小船里看戏有利于保护风化。

山西省有些县里，庙内并肩建两三座戏台，且相距不远，看戏大受干扰，但很得村民欢喜。看戏其实以热闹为第一。南方多雨，有些戏台前建大堂或敞厅为观众遮雨。如江西省抚州市的万寿宫，一座大堂占满了院子。

浙江省宁海县有些宗祠，戏台前的院子里建高大的敞厅，沿院子中央纵向延长，少的两间，多的三间，每间顶上做一个藻井，非常精致细巧。祠堂的第二进是拜殿，或者叫享堂。庶民的祠堂，拜殿一般遵制是三开间，但五开间的也有。特殊人物如列入朝廷祀典的诸葛亮的祠堂为五开间。

安徽省歙县呈坎村东舒祠的享堂也是五开间，总面宽26.5米，进深22.5米，非常宏敞。在南方地区，拜殿的前檐完全敞开。这里是举行祭祀仪式的地方，也是最要壮观的地方。大堂高爽，木构架都很粗大，而且以雕刻装饰。拜殿其实是宗族历史成就和荣誉的陈列室，是促成宗族团结和发展的纪念堂。

它的梁枋上挂满了大匾，内容都是歌颂族人的功名、德行、寿考等等的。如"贡元"、"进士"、"叙伦"、"乡贤"、"父子柱史"、"宗德流芳"、"厚德载福"、"承天宠锡"、"耆英厚望"、"祖泽缉熙"等等，都是炫显可以"光宗耀祖"的人物或事件的，色彩灿烂辉煌，引得來祭祀的族人十分振奋。柱身上都有楹联，内容比较驳杂。

凡家世显赫的宗姓，必有一副长联，上联统叙历祖历宗的功业、懿德、声名，下联颂扬从始祖播迁以来到落根本地的经过等等。如浙江省兰溪市诸葛村大公堂的楹联： 溯汉室以来，祀文庙，祀乡贤，祀名宦，祀忠孝义烈，不少传人，自有史书标姓氏； 迁浙江而后，历绍兴，历寿昌，历常村，历南塘水阁，于兹启宇，可从谱谍证渊源。

浙江省永嘉县鹤垟村谢灵运后人宗祠叙伦堂的楹联： 江左溯家声、淝水捷书，勋绩于今照史册； 瓯东绵世泽，池塘春草，诗才亘古重儒林。没有显赫的历史人物的宗姓，便写些颂扬宗族搬迁过程，如今的繁荣、富足，村子祥和、有序等等的闲话，如浙江省建德市新叶村有序堂的楹联： 迁移自杭睦寿而来，氏族清嘉，斯地奠安称梓里； 裔嗣绳宋元明以后，诗书启绍，先人腾达颂玉华。

又如湖南省会同县高椅村大宗祠的主联： 祖德启鸿图，念先人伯仲营迁分两甲； 孙谋贻燕翼，裕后嗣子孙螽羽绍千秋。享堂明间的后金柱之间大多有樘板，可以启闭如门扉，在恭请祖先神主或奉安祖先神主的时候因为要出入后院的寝室，就把樘板打开。

每逢祭祀则关闭樘板，在樘板上悬挂始祖和杰出祖先的画像，有些地方称为"祖容"，北方则称为"图"。樘板上方多挂祠堂的堂号匾，如"敦睦堂"、"崇恩堂"、"德馨堂"之类。那副主题性的长联便悬挂在樘板左右的后金柱上。那里光线暗淡，联、匾以黑色打底，文字贴了金箔，闪闪发亮，非常庄重肃穆。

浙江省和江西省有些大宗祠拜殿明间的前后两对金柱分别用柏、梓、桐、椿四种木材制作，谐音"百子同春"，讨个子孙繁衍发达的吉祥，这是被供奉着的祖先最关心的事。江西省婺源县黄村黄氏大宗祠明间左右前金柱下分别用青石和白石做磉墩，象征"左青龙、右白虎"，这做法殊不多见，但也并非孤例。

拜殿的两个次间，前金柱和前檐柱之间的轩顶下，架着钟鼓。左钟右鼓，在祭祀时应仪式而敲响。

也有些祠堂，如江西省婺源县汪口村的俞氏宗祠，把拜殿两侧次间前檐局部向前扩大一点，分别悬挂钟、鼓，再向前便与廊庑相接，有一只檐角向侧前方挑出。

浙江省兰溪市诸葛村"敕建"的名臣诸葛亮的祠堂则在寝殿左右末间前各建敞开的一小间为钟鼓楼，上覆卷棚顶，外侧面用拉弓式硬山封火墙。

江西省乐安县流坑村的董氏大宗祠在大门内两侧分别建造了独立的钟鼓楼。这种独立的钟鼓楼有些重在祠内观赏，有的则为宗祠的外观增添了极强的表情，但实例很少。

浙江省旧兰溪市境内，流行一种很独特的拜殿型制，叫"中庭"，专建于村内宗族的总祠（大宗祠）内。

这就是把大宗祠的拜殿建成一个面阔、进深都是三开间的近于正方的建筑，几乎满满地塞在大院子里，四面却与其他建筑如前面的门屋、后面的寝室以及两侧的廊庑都没有连接，而且不置樘板，开敞如亭。

例如诸葛村的丞相祠堂，里叶村、新叶村的叶氏大宗祠（西山祠堂），上唐村的李氏大宗祠，洞源村的赵氏大宗祠，西姜村的姜氏大宗祠等。

这种中庭式的拜殿只供举行隆重的祭祀仪式，不设神橱，所以必有第三进寝室，正所谓"前庭后寝"。通用的拜殿后檐墙为砖砌，中央明间设后门。从拜殿樘板两端下金柱后面的"耳门"可以达到樘板后面，再从后门出去通向后院。后院的正面是"寝室"，专供祖先神主。

为了保护神主的绝对安全，有些宗祠在后院中央砌一道高高的横墙，隔开前后，为的是防火。例如江西婺源黄村的经义堂，它的寝室与拜殿之间相距有十一米左右，并隔一道高而且厚的砖墙。放神主的神橱往往是小木作的精品，花格细巧，雕刻生动。

神橱的上方正中经常挂匾额，写"彝伦攸叙"、"祖德流芳"之类的颂词，金光灿烂。神橱前置香案，上陈烛台、香炉。香案前放些拜垫在地上，气氛肃穆庄严。神橱有门或无门，正中坐始迁祖的大神主牌，上雕二龙戏珠，左右雕升降龙镶边。

在它左右，恭陈历代功宗德祖的神主。两个次间有几层台子供历代祖先神位，有时也建神橱加以装饰。神主多了，就在两侧的山墙前建台。再多，则把前院两厢都改做寝室，如浙江省兰溪市诸葛村的大宗祠。

一个宗族在一处定居很久，历代人丁兴旺，就会有许多神主，这种情况下每隔若干年就要把晚近几代的神主改写，合并十位左右先人在一块神主牌上，以减少神主牌总数。这个仪式叫做"祧"，和各家各户把高祖以上的神主送进宗祠合并统祭一样。

绝大多数的大宗祠，始迁祖神主左右合族祖先的神主都按昭穆次序排列。少数大宗祠，如福建省福安县楼下村的刘氏大宗，则沿两边山墙按房派分建神橱安置各房祖先神主，一房一个，不另外建房祠。

福建连城县培田村的吴氏宗祠报德堂和敬承堂等，始祖神主右侧供奉"杨公先师"即江西派风水祖师杨筠松的神主。

更特殊的是江西省乐安县流坑村，董氏大宗祠五间正寝里竟以西次间为"报功堂"，专门用来设龛奉祀杨筠松、曾文辿和廖瑀三位风水祖师的神主，地位在一般本族祖先之上。按照万历年间（1573—1620）董氏宗谱的记载，流坑村董氏的发达，首先是因为杨、曾二人给老祖宗选了上好坟地和上好村址。

对风水师的礼敬感恩，这可能是规格最高的了。神主多了，寝室容不下时，除了采用"祧"的办法外，还有些宗祠建两层楼的寝室，如江西省婺源县黄村的黄氏大宗祠"经义堂"，安徽歙县呈坎村东舒祠的宝纶阁。

有的在两侧附建小院，如浙江省兰溪市桐山后金村的仁山书院（原为金氏大宗祠），跨院门上分别嵌石匾阴刻"左昭"、"右穆"额。江西省乐安县流坑村，董氏大宗祠寝室楼上有"敕书阁"，恭存皇帝御书。董氏在宋代出过三十名进士，并有一名状元，御赐敕书当不在少数。

小一点的宗祠，例如普通的房祠、支祠，大都不建寝室，而在第二进拜殿里建神橱。不足时再扩大到厢间里。最小的宗祠则整个只有堂屋一间而已。有极少数宗祠，在拜殿和寝室间沿中轴建一个宽宽的廊厅，使二者连接呈工字形。

如浙江省建德市新叶村的崇仁堂和相距不远的永康县的一些宗祠。距新叶村数里的桐山后金村有两座金氏房祠型制极特别，拜殿和寝室连接成一个纵向的大厅，梁架和中轴线相垂直，完全与中国建筑内部为横向空间的传统相异，连村里《金氏宗谱》都写上一笔，表示不理解。

大宗祠大多在拜殿或寝室一侧有宽敞的厨房以便春秋大祭时烹煮祭品。厨房近才能保持祭品的洁净。在南方各省，宗祠是村落里建筑艺术的亮点。就正立面说，比较简单的一种是三开间的明柱门屋，平稳而深沉。脊檩下设樘板，当心间开门，门枕石上立抱鼓石一对。

前檐廊简洁明快，平脊明柱，也有一些在前檐柱间设签子门和签子栏杆，如江西省婺源县洪村的洪氏大宗祠。又一种是砖牌楼式，有单开间的，也有三间三楼式的。用水磨砖贴在大门正面的砖墙上，大多仿木构做法，如浙江省兰溪市诸葛村的雍睦堂和"乡会两魁"祠。不但梁枋齐全，而且节点上麻叶头、雀替之类也一个不缺。

柱子上部、枋子、垫板等处都布满浅浮雕，图案基本上仿彩画，把彩画浮雕化。檐下做细巧的砖雕斗拱或者多层镂空的细线脚，简单一点的做冰盘线，也有用四十五度斜出的砖砌成"狼牙"线脚的。江西省抚州地区，这种狼牙线可重叠三四层，有些门上，"狼牙"变形为曲面饱满的莲瓣形，显得很丰满。

在江西省乐安县湖坪村和流坑村，有些砖牌楼用木材做斗拱，工艺上比较简易合理。复杂的纯装饰性斗拱大多交叉如网状，村人爱说，这种砖仿木式牌楼的祠堂大门是族里出了有大功名的人物的标志，所以中央有"恩荣"二字竖匾，上下枋之间书"荷宠凝庥"之类的谀辞。不过大多其实并没有这种"圣眷"的荣耀，为虚荣而假冒，反正也没有人来查处。

更加华丽辉煌的一种是木牌楼式的大门，一般为三间三楼或五楼式，也有更复杂的。木牌楼形式上是独立的，其实却和门屋连成一体。比较复杂的有江西省婺源县汪口村俞氏宗祠的牌楼式大门，三重屋顶，上两重为歇山式，最下一层为硬山式。它的网式斗拱斜出五跳。

木构架上布满了浮雕和彩画，大多用说部或戏剧中的慈孝忠义情节为题材。檐柱间也设签子栏杆。婺源县黄村黄氏宗祠经义堂则正门柱子为石质，以上全部为木料，比例非常清秀。安徽省黟县南屏村叶氏宗祠有一个三间三楼式的木构牌楼门。

门道左右有抱鼓石一对，门扉上绘全身屹立的武门神。浙江省兰溪市诸葛村诸葛亮的专祠"大公堂"的门屋，在明间由两棵柱子架起一个歇山顶和两只翼角，檐牙高啄，非常生动。

更庄重古朴的木牌楼式的大门是浙江省永嘉县花坦村朱氏雍睦堂（即"乌府"）的大门，三开间，五楼式木架，斗拱十分雄健，真昂真拱，做法与宋代《营造法式》的相似。小型祠堂，如广东省东莞市南社村的一些，它们只有门屋和正堂。

三开间门屋的前檐大多用石质的明柱和梁架，但明间没有随梁。又有一些小型祠堂的大门，是个随墙门，上面略加一道砖门楣罢了，不过雕饰极为华丽，尤其在正脊上。进了随墙门，里面有个木架雨篷。这是当地气候的表现。

宗族里每出一位举人、进士，就在大宗祠大门前立一对木杆，叫做"桅"。桅杆上装"斗"，举人每杆一只，进士每杆两只。

有些宗祠大门前隔不宽的前院有长长的照壁，这种情况下，桅杆会靠照壁内侧而立，如江西省婺源县洪村洪氏大宗祠光裕堂有七对桅杆，六对贴照壁，一对在前院西门前。

不过它们的夹杆石上刻的多是奉政大夫、朝议大夫之类靠捐纳得来的虚衔，只有一对是恩科进士的，地位也不高。有些大宗祠大门前布局十分辉煌。

如江西省乐安县流坑村董氏大宗祠，在重檐歇山顶的三开间门屋之前有一个长方形的水池，叫墨池，池对岸有三间三楼式砖照壁（坊）一座。池的左右岸各有一座三间三楼式木牌楼。它们的外侧又各有一座三楼式砖牌坊。

门屋和这五座牌楼（坊）形成大宗祠前的广场，排满了将近一百对桅杆，仅进士的便有三十对出头，读书郎真正是"光宗耀祖"了。

门屋内侧又有钟鼓楼一对。这个大门建筑群层次多，轮廓丰富，彩色灿烂，形体变化大而和谐，在农村中极少见。

浙江省青田县南田镇的明代开国功臣刘伯温专祠"文成庙"，庙门正对一座很长的影壁，形成一个横长的、略略封闭的小广场，广场左右作为入口各有一座三间三楼式木牌楼，东边的嵌《帝师》额，西边的嵌《王佐》额，牌楼高大，出檐深远，风格很凝重生严，显耀刘伯温的身份地位。

8.Architecture of Ancestral Halls The ancestral hall is a solemn ritual building.Its core typology evolved from residences.

Residences vary endlessly due to living conditions; similarly, temples in mountains or by water have rich formal variation.

Ancestral halls, while varying, change little—maintaining a functional, formulaic spatial composition and a dignified, orderly character.Ancestral halls are venues for sacrifice.

Hall rituals strictly follow procedures in 《朱文正公家礼》 (Zhu Wenzheng's Family Rituals), so the building itself—especially its central main part—follows a formula.

Most halls have three parts, front to back: (1) gatehouse (大门门屋); (2) worship hall (拜殿/享堂), where sacrifice rituals occur; (3) sleeping chamber (寝室), named from "commoners sacrifice in the chamber" in 《礼记·王制》, dedicated to ancestral spirit tablets.

《光绪合肥邢氏家谱》 says: "The family temple is the ancestors' palace; even if modest, it must have three bays and two side wings: front gate, middle hall, rear chamber.

" Wuyuan Huang Village's Jingyi Hall and Wangkou Village's Renben Hall, plus many Anhui/Zhejiang halls, follow this standard layout.

Smaller halls skip a separate chamber, placing spirit tablets in a shrine against the worship hall's rear wall.

If insufficient, shrines are added before gable walls; if still insufficient, spirit tablets are merged—writing 10–20 ancestor names on one tablet, called "祧" (tiao).

Sichuan 《云阳涂氏族谱·祠堂碑记》 clearly states: "Above, shrine hall for spirit tablets and zhao-mu order; middle, hall for descendants' reverent kneeling; front, reversed tower for receiving guests and reading imperial edicts; left/right wings for children studying.

" It enumerates all parts' functions.The shrine hall is the chamber, often with floor higher than the worship hall; the reversed tower is the gatehouse.This describes average-sized halls; larger ones build stages here.

Between the three bays are two courtyards with side corridors (廊庑).Some develop rear corridors into wing rooms also used as "chambers," divided into "left zhao, right mu" (左昭右穆) for ancestral tablets.

Front corridors are partitioned into small rooms for clan administration—genealogy room, account room, elders' meeting room.《云阳涂氏族谱》 stipulates their use as schools.

All main and branch halls need a spacious kitchen for sacrificial food like sacrificial meat (胙肉).Large, wealthy clans have halls with multiple public functions, making them complex.

Beyond the core, attached buildings often include rear gardens, schools, charitable granaries (义仓), charitable mortuaries (义厝).A few, like Wuyi Yu源 Village's Yu clan hall, even attach orphanages and old-age homes.

The simplest branch-level halls have only gate and worship hall, with ancestral tablets in a shrine against the rear wall—no separate chamber, no front bay or side wings.

Guangdong Pearl River Delta clans branched early, so halls are often this small type.

Larger halls build a stage in the gatehouse facing the worship hall; the front courtyard and side corridors become audience seating, sometimes with upper floors for women's viewing.Below, vendors set up food stalls during performances.

Le'an Liukeng Village (Jiangxi), said to be descendants of Han Confucian Dong Zhongshu, has the Dong main hall—a rare large hall built on Molan Isle north of the village, about 200m from the residential area.

Facing south toward the village, backed by the Wujiang River flowing south-to-north then west.Entering the village from the hall passes through the Gongchen Gate on the village wall.

Built outside the village,背对 the village's facing mountain with the river behind—this layout violates common fengshui doctrine.

In fengshui-venerating Jiangxi (Yang Yunsong was Jiangxi native), the Dong hall's position may have had explanations, but none were recorded.

The Dong main hall plus two branch halls (left/right) form a complex: three buildings side by side, 90m east-west, 70+m north-south, 7,000 sqm total.

The main hall is central; east is Guilin Hall (worshiping 16th-generation ancestor Dong Jimin); west is Guiyan Hall (later converted to literary school worshiping Confucius and Wenchang Emperor), with small study rooms for exam-preparing children.

Before the three halls is shared public space forming a wide transverse courtyard.Center has a rectangular "ink pond" (墨池).

East/west ends each have a three-bay brick archway: west arch "优入贤关" (outer) / "簪缨世第" (inner); east arch "理学名贤" (inner) / "科甲联芳" (outer).Both built in Kangxi era (1662–1722).

Before the main hall is a three-bay archway-style brick gate with double eaves; central plaque front "厚德流光", back "文献世家".Side bays each have stone lions.

Before the gate is the ink pond; south of pond is "追远" arch (commemorating ancestors).East/west of pond each have a wooden arch aligned with the brick arches: east "累朝师保", west "奕世科名"—showing off official and exam success.

South wall has a screen wall with "累朝世家" in large characters.Entering the "厚德流光" gate, left/right front courtyard have bell and drum towers.

The main hall has three bays: first "育贤楼" hall (three-bay double-eave), central plaque "宋赠大司徒董公大宗祠", east "祖孙台部", west "三世尚书".

Second "敦睦堂" (three-bay double-eave), plaque "万殊一本".

Third five-bay: central three bays two-story, upper "敕书阁"; lower central "孝敬堂", left/right by zhao-mu order "彰义堂", "报功堂", "宗原堂", "道原堂"—all with plaques.

Yuxian and Dunmu halls have side wings: east worshiping "loyalty" (忠), "integrity" (廉); west "filial piety" (孝), "chastity" (节).By zhao-mu order: loyalty, filial piety, integrity, chastity.

The hall is like a memorial to loyal ministers, righteous scholars, chaste women.Xiaojing, Zhangyi, Baogong halls first completed in Jiajing 40 (1565).

Ming Dong Sui wrote 《彰义堂记》: "Central Xiaojing Hall worships official rank; left Zhangyi Hall worships righteousness; right Baogong Hall worships merit.Beyond these three, overall Dunmu Hall orders zhao-mu.

" Xiaojing worships officials; Baogong worships fengshui masters Yang Yunsong, Zeng Wenchan, Liao Yu.

The Dong clan believed its prosperity came from these fengshui "masters" finding good grave and village sites.

Zhangyi Hall specially worships clansmen who donated money/land for hall construction and sacrifices—standard: 10 taels per person, more money = better position.Dunmu worships all clan ancestors.

Zongyuan and Daoyuan halls built later; Wanli 9 (1581) Dong Sui wrote: "Daoyuan Hall specially worships Dong Zhongshu, tracing our Dong clan's Confucian origin...Zongyuan Hall specially worships Qingran-gong ancestors...honoring the beginning.

" Dong Zhongshu (Han dynasty) is revered as Dong surname ancestor; Qingran-gong is the ancestor who moved to Yihuang, Jiangxi.

Thus the main hall is also a clan tradition education exhibition hall—commemoration and education matching Liukeng's historical character.

Dunmu Hall has a couplet: With ancestors' heart as heart, seek fortune yourself; If not following ancient kings' laws, what face to enter here.This reveals the hall's educational function.

Notably, "righteousness" in Zhangyi Hall means donating money/land to the clan.

Those worshiped are large merchants or landlords—just as one can obtain empty titles like "大夫" or "司马" through donation without exams, one can enter a special hall through donation and enjoy eternal honor.

This reflects late-Ming commercial economic development in the middle-lower Yangtze; one ideological manifestation was breaking through feudal clan ethics.Late Ming, many Liukeng villagers grew wealthy through grain transport and timber.

As solemn ritual buildings, halls have little layout variation, but variants exist.

Guangzhou Chen clan hall: beyond the central axis's five-bay halls and courtyards, left/right each have a courtyard-hall route, three bays each—total nine halls, six courtyards.

Three routes separated only by open corridors; outermost have side rooms.Eighteen buildings total (halls, wings, study rooms), 13,200 sqm—rarely matched in spacious openness.

Yongjia Yantou Village's Guilin Gong Hall, converted from an academy, has a large pond before the worship hall with a central square pavilion; a bridge from the ceremonial gate (仪门) through the pavilion to the worship hall.

Outside the ceremonial gate is another pond; after entering the main gate, one circles the pond to reach the ceremonial gate.Very individual layout.

North China historically had frequent warfare, few stable powerful clans—so villages are mostly mixed-surname, some small clans with few people.Hence few ancestral halls, especially large ones.

Village management often by geographic or trade-based "associations" (社).Public activities held in temples.

The smallest halls are merely one small room with ancestor names written on walls and a small incense stand in the center—e.g., Yu County Songjiazhuang's Su clan hall, just one tiny room.Main hall gatehouses generally have stages.

Wealthy villages' branch and sub-branch halls also have stages.

Gatehouse stages have three main types: (1) entirely within the gatehouse's central bay; (2) half protruding into the hall beyond the central bay; (3) fully protruding with high upturned wing corners in front, backstage in the gatehouse central bay.

Type 3 allows viewing from three sides, less stage-audience separation.

Type 1 blocks the main gate—on ordinary days and performance days, only side doors open; on special days (ancestor worship, spirit tablet installation), the central movable stage planks are removed for passage.

Types 2 and 3: enter through central main gate, go left/right around the stage to the worship hall.

Dressing rooms usually in the gatehouse side bays' mezzanine, with small wooden stairs from the waiting area behind the stage's taishi wall.

Between waiting area and front stage is a board wall (taishi wall) called "守旧" (shoujiu), usually painted with 《唐明皇游月宫》 (Emperor Minghuang Visiting the Moon Palace).

Emperor Minghuang (Tang Xuanzong) mastered music, loved song and dance, personally trained opera troupes in the palace Pear Garden—hence revered as opera's patron god, "老郎神" (Old Master God).

The Moon Palace story is romantic: Bai Juyi's poem recounts Minghuang fleeing Sichuan during An Lushan rebellion; Yang Guifei forced to suicide by the army—"the emperor covered his face, could not save, turned back, tears and blood flowing together.

" After peace, Minghuang missed her day and night.Daoist Ye Fashan conjured him to the Moon Palace to meet the immortalized Yang Guifei.

They vowed: "In heaven,愿 be birds flying wing to wing; on earth,愿 be trees with branches intertwined." Highly dramatic, hence often painted on the "守旧" wall.

Above "守旧" hangs a horizontal plaque praising performances—usually "金声玉振", "作古振今", "翻风弄月"—formulaic."守旧" sides are entrance and exit doors, plaques usually "出将" (generals emerge) and "入相" (ministers enter).

Some more ornate but same meaning.Stage sides and front edge have tiny one-foot-high railings protecting actors; railing post tops have carved qilin and other auspicious beasts.Some halls, e.g.

, Yongjia Furong Village's Chen clan hall, attach a small platform left-rear of the stage for the orchestra.Stages are often masterpieces of small woodwork, carving, and painting.

First, above the stage, deep caissons (藻井) for acoustics (拔音/拢音)—caisson styles abound, carpenters competing in creativity.

Yongjia village halls often use octagonal inverted-pyramid caissons with golden-flowing bracket sets (溜金斗拱) rising along eight internal corners and eight center lines—long brackets like flowing clouds, lingzhi mushrooms, gracefully curving.

Ninghai rural stages have varied caissons; most vivid is "百鸟朝凤" (folk: "鸡笼顶"/chicken-cage top), spiral upward pattern—vital momentum echoing theatrical excitement.

Some caissons fully covered in bright paintings, "开光盒子" theatrical scenes exquisitely realistic.

Second, stage front edge: a long wood carving on the main beam, themes all theatrical plots—this carving is where master carvers shine.

Sichuan calls this long carved board "照面枋" (face-facing beam)—facing the audience, hence specially crafted for public appraisal.

Leping County (Jiangxi): every village hall has a stage, some villages several; over 300 stages survived the Cultural Revolution.

Leping stages have distinctive typologies, carved beams and painted pillars, extremely ornate—almost everywhere carved, every carving gilded—dazzling golden light.Stage front-eave pillars, "台柱" (stage pillars), always bear couplets.

Some situational and plain: "Watching, it seems so; thinking, perhaps so." Some reflective: One tune of Shang music, performing millennia of rise and fall; Several notes of Yue melody, revealing a century of parting and reunion.

Another: Steps change form, don't say favor and disgrace are all false; Brows painted, corners drawn—know joy and anger are all real.

Above the stage mouth, horizontal plaques usually "普天同庆" (universal celebration), "盛世纶音" (prosperous era's edict)—festive phrases.

Audience positions per hall rules: men in courtyard, women under worship hall front eaves, bringing stools.Side corridors also women's viewing.

Some Shanxi/Jiangxi/Sichuan halls have viewing towers on side corridors: left "men's tower", right "women's tower"—for "respectable families." Ming-Qing pedantic Confucians considered performances harmful to morals.

Ming Lao Yizhai in 《瓯江逸志》 criticized: during performances, "ten+ days day/night viewing, men and women mixed." Qing Daoguang-Xianfeng (1821–1861) Yongjia magistrate Tang Chenglie in 《县志稿》: "festivals lavish on gods...

men and women viewing, ornate dress, filling city and suburbs, officials cannot ban." Wanting to ban but unable, dissatisfied.

This elite conservatism influenced village leaders—hence gender-segregated viewing, with 60+ elders patrolling the audience, rapping disrespectful young men with long tobacco pipes.

Most villages build stages only in main hall gatehouses facing the worship hall.But some build stages in the square outside the hall gate, facing the hall.Some villages, e.g.

, Liancheng Peitian (Fujian), stage position/orientation are irregular—even the gate position is irregular.

During performances, neighboring villagers come; vendors of snacks and sundries set up stalls before the hall or stage side corridors, forming a temporary market.

Protecting village internal safety and tranquility is one reason most villages build the main hall at the village edge rather than the core.A few halls have detachable stages—e.g., Wuyuan Huang Village's Jingyi Hall.

Jiande Xinye Village's Chongren Hall (Zhi-zi branch) also has a detachable stage; wooden components stored in the hall, assembled on the pond surface before the gate when needed.Called "雨台" (rain stage) or "露台" (open terrace).

Water-town Shaoxing (Zhejiang) has stages built on water before the hall, far from shore; villagers arrive by boat, boats moored before the stage.From start to end, chaotic but lively—villagers enjoy it more.

Pedantic scholars believed women watching from their own boats helped protect morals.Some Shanxi counties build 2–3 stages side by side in temples, close together—viewing greatly interfered, but villagers love it.

Viewing is ultimately about excitement.South is rainy; some stages have large halls or open pavilions for audience rain shelter.E.g., Fuzhou Wanshou Palace (Jiangxi): one large hall fills the courtyard.

Some Ninghai halls build tall open pavilions in the stage-front courtyard, extending longitudinally along the center—2 to 3 bays, each with a caisson on top, exquisitely detailed.

The hall's second bay is the worship hall (拜殿/享堂).Commoners' halls: worship hall generally three bays per regulation, but five-bay exists.

Special figures like Zhuge Liang (in state sacrificial canon) have five-bay halls.Shexian Chengkan Village's Dongshu Hall worship hall is also five-bay: 26.5m wide, 22.5m deep—very spacious.

In the south, the worship hall's front eaves are fully open.This is where sacrifice rituals occur—the most spectacular space.High and bright, with massive timber frames and carved decoration.

The worship hall is actually a display room of clan historical achievements and honors, a memorial hall promoting clan unity and development.

Its beams are covered with large plaques praising clansmen's exam success, virtue, longevity—e.g.

, "贡元", "进士", "叙伦", "乡贤", "父子柱史", "宗德流芳", "厚德载福", "承天宠锡", "耆英厚望", "祖泽缉熙"—all showing off "glorifying ancestors" figures/events, brilliant colors inspiring worshiping clansmen.Pillars bear couplets of varied content.

Illustrious clans always have a long couplet: upper line recounts ancestors' merits, virtue, fame; lower line praises migration from founding ancestor to settlement.E.g.

, Lanxi Zhuge Village's Dagong Hall: Since Han dynasty, worshiped in Confucian temple, as village worthy, as famous official, as loyal/filial/righteous/chaste—many transmitters, history records our surname; After moving to Zhejiang, through Shaoxing, Shouchang, Changcun, Nantang Water Pavilion—here established, genealogy proves our origin.

Yongjia Heyang Village (Xie Lingyun descendants) Xulun Hall: Jiangzuo traces family fame, Feishui victory, achievements still illuminate history; Oudong continues generation grace, pond spring grass, poetic talent eternally valued in Confucian circles.

Clans without illustrious historical figures write about migration process, current prosperity, village harmony/order—e.g.

, Jiande Xinye Village's Youxu Hall: Migrated from Hangzhou/Muzhou/Shouchou, clan pure and auspicious, this land settled as homeland; Descendants through Song/Yuan/Ming, books and poetry continue, ancestors' success praised at Yuhua.

Hunan Huitong Gaoyi Village main hall main couplet: Ancestor virtue opens grand plan, recalling ancestors' brothers migrating to two districts; Descendants' plans bless, future generations multiply through millennia.

The worship hall's central bay rear golden pillars usually have a "tang board" (樘板) that opens/closes like doors.

When inviting or installing ancestral spirit tablets (needing access to the rear chamber), the board is opened.

During sacrifice, it's closed; on it hang portraits of the founding ancestor and distinguished ancestors—called "祖容" (ancestor countenance) in some places, "图" (picture) in the north.

Above the tang board usually hangs the hall name plaque—"敦睦堂", "崇恩堂", "德馨堂", etc.The thematic long couplet hangs on the rear golden pillars flanking the tang board.

There, light is dim; couplets and plaques have black backgrounds with gold-leaf text, gleaming—very solemn.

Some Zhejiang/Jiangxi main halls use four wood types for the worship hall's front/rear golden pillar pairs: cypress (柏), catalpa (梓), tung (桐), toon (椿)—homophone "百子同春" (hundreds of children, same spring), auspicious for descendant prosperity—what worshiped ancestors care most about.

Wuyuan Huang Village's Huang main hall uses bluestone and white stone plinths under left/right front golden pillars, symbolizing "left azure dragon, right white tiger"—rare but not unique.

In the worship hall's two side bays, under the xu ceiling between front golden and front eave pillars, hang bell and drum.

Left bell, right drum—struck during sacrifice rituals.Some halls, e.g.

, Wuyuan Wangkou Yu clan hall, slightly extend the side-bay front eaves forward to hang bell/drum, then connect to corridors with one eave corner projecting side-forward.

Lanxi Zhuge Village's "imperially built" Zhuge Liang hall builds open small rooms as bell/drum towers before the寝殿's end bays, with curved-roof (卷棚顶) tops and bow-style gable fire walls on outer sides.

Le'an Liukeng Dong main hall builds independent bell/drum towers inside the gate's two sides.

Some independent towers focus on interior viewing; others strongly enhance the hall's exterior appearance—but examples are few.

Old Lanxi (Zhejiang) area has a unique worship hall typology called "中庭" (central courtyard), built only in village main halls.

The worship hall is built as a near-square building (three bays wide × three bays deep), almost filling the large courtyard, but disconnected from all other buildings (front gatehouse, rear chamber, side corridors)—no tang board, open like a pavilion.

Examples: Zhuge Village's Prime Minister Hall, Liye/Xinye Ye main hall (Xishan Hall), Shangtang Li main hall, Dongyuan Zhao main hall, Xijiang Jiang main hall.

This "central-courtyard" worship hall only hosts grand sacrifice rituals, no shrine—hence must have a third-bay chamber, so-called "front court, rear chamber.

" The standard worship hall's rear eave wall is brick, central bay has rear door.

From "ear doors" behind the tang board's lower golden pillars, one reaches behind the tang board, exits through the rear door to the back courtyard.The courtyard's front is the "chamber" (寝室) for ancestral spirit tablets.

To protect tablets' absolute safety, some halls build a high transverse wall in the back courtyard separating front/rear—for fire prevention.E.g.

, Wuyuan Huang Village's Jingyi Hall: chamber and worship hall ~11m apart, separated by a high thick brick wall.Spirit tablet shrines (神橱) are often small-woodwork masterpieces—delicate lattice, vivid carving.

Above the shrine center usually hangs a plaque: "彝伦攸叙", "祖德流芳"—golden and brilliant.

Before the shrine: incense table with candlesticks and incense burner.Before the table: kneeling cushions on the floor—solemn atmosphere.

Shrines may have doors or not; center holds the founding ancestor's large spirit tablet, carved with two dragons playing a pearl, flanked by ascending/descending dragon borders.

Beside it: reverently placed tablets of meritorious ancestors.Two side bays have tiered platforms for ancestral tablets, sometimes with shrines.

More tablets， platforms before side gable walls.Even more， convert front courtyard's two wings to chambers, e.g., Lanxi Zhuge Village's main hall.

A clan settled long with prosperous generations accumulates many tablets; every several years, recent generations' tablets are rewritten, merging ~10 ancestors per tablet to reduce total.

This ritual is "祧" (tiao)—same as households sending great-great-grandfather+ tablets to the hall for merged collective worship.Most main halls arrange founding ancestor and all clan ancestors' tablets by zhao-mu order.A few, e.g.

, Fu'an Louxia Village's Liu main hall, build separate shrines along both gable walls by branch—one per branch, no separate branch halls.

Liancheng Peitian Village's Wu clan halls (Baode, Jingcheng) place "Yang Gong Xianshi" (Jiangxi fengshui founder Yang Yunsong) tablet to the right of the founding ancestor.

Most special: Le'an Liukeng Dong main hall's five-bay chamber uses the west side bay as "报功堂" (Merit-Reporting Hall), with shrines worshiping fengshui founders Yang Yunsong, Zeng Wenchan, Liao Yu—status above ordinary clan ancestors.

Per Wanli-era (1573–1620) Dong genealogy: Liukeng Dong's prosperity first came from Yang and Zeng selecting excellent grave and village sites for ancestors.

Reverence and gratitude to fengshui masters—possibly the highest规格.When tablets exceed chamber capacity, besides "祧", some halls build two-story chambers—e.g.

, Wuyuan Huang Village's "经义堂", Shexian Chengkan Dongshu Hall's Baolun Pavilion.Some attach side courtyards—e.g.

, Lanxi Tongshan Houjin Village's Renshan Academy (formerly Jin main hall), with stone plaques "左昭" and "右穆" on cross-courtyard gates.

Le'an Liukeng Dong main hall's chamber upper floor has "敕书阁" (Imperial Edict Pavilion) storing imperial documents.The Dong clan produced 30 jinshi and one zhuangyuan in Song—imperial edicts certainly numerous.

Smaller halls (ordinary branch/sub-branch) mostly skip the chamber, building shrines in the second-bay worship hall.If insufficient, expand to side rooms.Smallest halls are just one hall room.

Very few halls build a wide corridor hall along the central axis between worship hall and chamber, connecting them in an I-shape (工字形).E.g., Jiande Xinye Village's Chongren Hall and some Yongkang halls.

Several kilometers from Xinye, Tongshan Houjin Village has two Jin branch halls with extremely special typology: worship hall and chamber connected into one longitudinal hall, with beam frames perpendicular to the central axis—completely contrary to Chinese architecture's traditional transverse interior space.

Even the village 《金氏宗谱》 notes it with incomprehension.Main halls usually have a spacious kitchen beside the worship hall or chamber for cooking sacrifices during spring/autumn grand rituals.Proximity keeps sacrificial food clean.

In southern provinces, ancestral halls are the highlight of village architectural art.Regarding the front facade: simplest is three-bay exposed-pillar gatehouse—steady and deep.

Under the ridge purlin: tang board; central bay has door; door sill stones have a pair of drum-shaped stones (抱鼓石).

Front eave corridor simple and bright, flat ridge, exposed pillars; some have lattice doors and railings between front eave pillars—e.g., Wuyuan Hong Village's Hong main hall.

Another type: brick archway (砖牌楼)—single-bay or three-bay three-story.Water-polished bricks applied to the gate's front brick wall, mostly imitating wood structure—e.g.

, Lanxi Zhuge Village's Yongmu Hall and "乡会两魁" Hall.Not only complete beams and brackets, but also node details like hemp-leaf heads (麻叶头) and sparrow brackets (雀替).

Pillar tops, beams, backing boards covered in low-relief carving, patterns basically imitating painted decoration (浮雕化彩画).

Under eaves: delicate brick-carved bracket sets or multi-layer openwork line moldings; simpler ones do ice-disk lines; some use 45-degree斜出 bricks forming "wolf-tooth" (狼牙) moldings.

Fuzhou area: wolf-tooth moldings can stack 3–4 layers; some gates transform "wolf teeth" into full curved lotus-petal shapes, very plump.

Le'an Huping and Liukeng villages: some brick archways use wooden bracket sets—simpler and more reasonable工艺.

Complex purely decorative bracket sets mostly cross like nets; villagers say this brick-imitating-wood archway gate marks a clan with highly successful exam candidates—hence central "恩荣" (imperial grace) vertical plaque, between upper/lower beams text like "荷宠凝庥".

But most actually lacked such "imperial favor" glory—faking for vanity, anyway no one investigates.More ornate: wooden archway gate (木牌楼)—usually three-bay three-story or five-story, sometimes more complex.

Formally independent, actually integrated with the gatehouse.Complex example: Wuyuan Wangkou Yu clan hall's archway gate—three roof tiers, upper two xieshan (歇山) style, lowest hard-gable (硬山) style.

Net-style bracket sets project five tiers diagonally.Timber frame covered in relief and painting, mostly themes of filial piety, loyalty, righteousness from novels or drama.

Eave pillars also have lattice railings.Wuyuan Huang Village's Jingyi Hall: gate pillars stone, above all wood—very elegant proportions.

Yixian Nanping Village's Ye clan hall has a three-bay three-story wooden archway gate.Gate sides have drum stones; doors painted with full-body standing warrior door gods.

Lanxi Zhuge Village's Zhuge Liang专祠 "Dagong Hall" gatehouse: central bay two pillars support a xieshan roof and two wing corners, eaves high and vivid—very lively.

More solemn and ancient: Yongjia Huatan Village's Zhu clan Yongmu Hall ("乌府") gate—three-bay five-story wooden frame, bracket sets very robust, true ang (真昂) and true arch (真拱), construction similar to Song 《营造法式》.

Small halls, e.g., some in Dongguan Nanshe Village, have only gatehouse and main hall.

Three-bay gatehouse front eaves mostly use stone exposed pillars and beams, but central bay has no following beam.

Some small halls' gates are wall-attached doors (随墙门) with a slight brick lintel above—but carving extremely ornate, especially on the main ridge.Inside the wall door: a wooden-frame awning.This reflects local climate.

Each time a clan produces a juren or jinshi, a pair of wooden poles is erected before the main hall gate—called "桅" (mast).

Masts carry "斗" (dou): juren one per pole, jinshi two per pole.

Some halls with long screen walls in a narrow front courtyard have masts leaning against the screen wall's inner side—e.g.

, Wuyuan Hong Village's Hong main hall Guangyu Hall has seven mast pairs: six against the screen wall, one before the front courtyard's west gate.

However, their mast-holding stones mostly刻 empty titles like "奉政大夫", "朝议大夫" obtained through donation; only one pair is from a special-exam jinshi, status not high.

Some main halls have brilliant front layouts.E.g.

, Le'an Liukeng Dong main hall: before the double-eave xieshan three-bay gatehouse is a rectangular pond (ink pond); opposite the pond, a three-bay three-story brick screen wall (archway).

Pond's left/right banks each have a three-bay three-story wooden archway.Outside those, each has a three-story brick archway.

The gatehouse plus these five archways form a square before the main hall, lined with nearly 100 mast pairs—over 30 for jinshi alone.Scholars truly "glorify ancestors.

" Inside the gatehouse: a pair of bell/drum towers.This gate complex has many layers, rich silhouette, brilliant colors, large yet harmonious formal variation—rare in rural areas.

Qingtian Nantian Town's Liu Bowen (Ming founding minister)专祠 "Wencheng Temple": temple gate faces a long screen wall, forming a long, slightly enclosed small square; left/right entrances each have a three-bay three-story wooden archway—east with 《帝师》 (Imperial Tutor) plaque, west with 《王佐》 (Royal Assistant) plaque.

Archways tall, deep eaves, style solemn and dignified—showing Liu Bowen's status.

文教建筑

Educational Buildings
6
节
5.1 文教建筑与科举
Section 1

一、文教建筑与科举 中国人热爱读书。无分南北，也无分城乡，稍稍整齐一点的人家，大门门扇上最常见的一副对联是"忠孝传家久，诗书继世长"，堂屋里最常见的两副对联则是"数百年旧家无非积德，第一等好事还是读书"和"一等人忠臣孝子，两件事耕田读书"。

条案中央供着一块朱漆描金的神牌，上面写的是"天地君亲师"，香火四季不断。天地撇开不论，现实世界上，"师"仅居"君、亲"之后，地位很高了。其实，激发中国人读书热情的，主要是科举制度，就是隋唐以后"学而优则仕"这一条大家都可以走一走的道路；其次是商业的发展。主要不是由于要积德济世，也不是要格物致知。

乡土社会中，村里的文教建筑大多和科举有关。一类是教学用的，如社学、义塾、家塾、书馆之类，主要用于基础教育。又有文馆，是上了年纪的读书人淡出功名，以文会友，切磋学问的场所，也是他们定期考核本村子弟为功名而学习的情况的场所。

另一类是旌表科考成就用的，明代以往，考中了进士可以立牌坊、竖"桅"、造"进士第"。后来举人也有竖桅甚至立牌坊的了。

又一类是崇祀用的，如文昌阁（魁星楼）、文峰塔、文笔、焚帛炉，用来祈求宗族和个人的文运。此外，稍大一点的庙宇多有几间房子、一所别院给读书人住下来安心准备考试。

少数村子还有文庙，文庙和宗祠就可能有房子给少年人读书。一些村落有藏书楼、书斋之类，往往是科名有成，当了几年官，晚年致仕退食的人们造来读书作画待客用的。有些没有功名的商人，老来也会造一所小院幽斋做书屋，以颐养天年。

宋元时期，个别地区，如江西，有书院供学者聚徒讲学，探究义理，但对乡土社会影响不大。文教建筑多的地方，大多就是科举成绩比较突出的地方，所谓文风鼎盛之乡，领头的是苏南、浙江，后面有江西、福建、皖南、广东、两湖。

这些地区，一来是商业经济发达，经济既是科举成就的背后支柱，也是文教建筑得以普及的依靠；二来是宗族的结构和管理制度稳固有力，子弟读书已经成了传统。

科举主要是朝廷的取士制度，所以民间启蒙诗里有句："天子重英豪，文章教儿曹"，它始于隋代，明代以后，措施已经十分完备，但科举同时也是平民百姓进仕的制度，为了扶掖和激励本族子弟读书以登上青云之路，宗族用公产兴学、助读、贴补赴考的费用，高低中了个功名，就给以很高的荣誉和实际的奖励。是宗族接续和完成了朝廷的科举制度，助它普及，产生巨大的影响。

乡土社会中的文教建筑，绝大部分是宗族兴建的。凡宗族结构破坏的地方，科举成就便很差，文教建筑也必寥寥。然而，经济发达和宗族关系稳定的地方未必就一定有比较高的科举成绩，如晋中和皖南，从明代起，到清代出了一大批长袖善舞、经营四方的商人，但那里的科举成绩并不很好。

到了清末，每况愈下，以致清·刘大鹏《退想斋日记》说山西太谷风气，"视读书甚轻，视商业为甚重，才华秀美之子弟，率皆出门为商，而读书者寥寥无几，甚且有既游庠序竟弃儒就商者，亦谓读书之士，多受饥寒，曷若为商之多得银钱，俾家道之丰裕也。

"浙江省兰溪市诸葛村的《高隆诸葛氏宗谱》里给一个商人立传，这位商人有话说："与其读万卷之书，孰若积千金之产。"千余年的价值观被颠倒过来了。经商有了钱还可以不经十年寒窗而花钱买个虚衔爵位，清代朝廷为了敛钱，"大夫"、"司马"之类的衔头，都有明码标价。科举就是通过定期考试，从读书人中选拔各级文职官员的制度。

隋代之前，两汉和魏晋南北朝时期，官员的选任完全由强宗豪门把持，弊端丛生；世袭的豪强更有势力威胁最高统治者的地位，有碍真正人才的发现和提拔，形成社会阶级分野的僵化以致容易发生动乱。为了克服这些弊端，隋代开始试行由地方官员荐举人才经中央考试之后从中选拔官员的办法。以后历代都有改进，形成了影响重大的科举制度。

科举制度的特点，也便是它的优点，就是把进仕的途径向全社会开放，公平竞争，避免了强势阶层对官职的垄断，而给弱势阶层以平等的机会。除了极少数"贱民"（如浙江的堕民，广东的疍民）、操"贱业"的人（如娼、优、皂隶、乐户）、犯了罪的人、居父母丧的人、罢闲官吏等之外，只要户籍有据，学历合格，原则上人人可以应试，而且考试的方法和管理很严密，防范了不公平的事情发生。

进仕途径向全社会开放，对专制统治者来说，第一个好处是虽然不能做到"野无遗贤"，朝廷毕竟得以网罗一些杰出人才担任各级官员，加强政府效能。隋唐以后，历代名臣贤相都自科举出身，所以唐代贞观初年（627—632），太宗李世民在进士放榜之日于皇宫的端门上观望，见新科进士陆续出来，对侍臣们说："天下英雄入吾彀中矣！"非常高兴。

向庶民开放的科举制度大大促进了全中国文化教育的普及。读书成为一种社会风尚。"为父兄者以其子与弟不文为咎，为母妻者以其子与夫不学为辱"，甚至有人提出了"读书人人有份"的主张。科举制度大盛之时，正逢中国雕版印刷普及。雕版印刷从唐末成熟，宋代达于完美，有了这一项技术，书籍得来比较容易，比较廉价，更为科举制度推波助澜。

科举考试吸引了大批社会精英，使他们埋头于官方设定的知识范围中"皓首穷经"，"两耳不闻窗外事，一心只读圣贤书，"以致整个社会都专注于科考，社会"科举化"了。北宋真宗皇帝写了一首著名的《劝学诗》，影响久远。诗道： 富家不用买良田，书中自有千钟粟。安房不用架高梁，书中自有黄金屋。

娶妻莫恨无良媒，书中有女颜如玉。出门莫恨无人随，书中车马多如簇。男儿欲遂平生志，六经勤向窗前读。汉武帝时候董仲舒建议的"罢黜百家，独尊儒术"，经过一千年左右，直到科举时代才在"粟"、"屋"、"玉"、"车"的引诱下真正落实到全社会。孙承泽说："夫科目之设，天下之士群趋而奔向之。上意所向，风俗随之，人才之高下，士风之醇漓，率由是出。"通过科考，"上意"引领了风俗，影响了士子们的知识范围和眼界。

科举成功首先是个人可以获得许多好处。明末清初的学者计六奇在《明季北略》中写道："常见青衿子，朝不谋夕，一叨乡荐便无穷举人，及登甲科，遂钟鸣鼎食，肥马轻裘，非数百万则数十万，……彼且身无赋，产无徭，田无粮，物无税，且庇护奸民之赋、徭、粮、税，其入之正未艾也。

" 明、清时期，举人就是正途出身，已经有资格做官了，一般做个县里的官学教习之类，也有机会被"大挑"为知县。一旦中了进士，就脱离了"百姓"阶层，享有许多政治经济特权，例如全家可免赋税、徭役。

进士有可能任高官，明清时期，进士大多先被选入翰林院，翰林院是高官的储备处，凡任中枢机构高官的，必出自翰林。

清代，大学士都从翰林中选任，另一部分翰林到各部当主事，小部分下放地方任知县，不须候补，并有比较多的机会升迁。明、清两代，科第高中者还更有一种长远意义的荣耀，这就是可以在家乡建牌坊、立桅杆，祠堂里挂匾。

明初洪武二十一年（1388年），任亨泰中了状元，太祖朱元璋下令用官帑在任亨泰家乡湖北襄阳起造一座牌坊以旌表他的成就。

这大约是第一座科名牌坊，从此以后，科名牌坊和桅杆就渐渐在各地流行起来，并且下及于举人。明中叶成化、弘治朝，甚至还给以前没有建牌坊的进士补建。

后来，进士们的父亲和祖父可以在获得皇帝诰封和驰封之后也造相同式样的牌坊。这些牌坊大多造在州县城里，以致到了明代晚期万历朝（1573—1620）时候，许多州县城里已经是科第牌坊林立了。

由于造牌坊的费用很大，从清代嘉庆朝（1796—1820）起不再用公帑建造，但科名牌坊数量并不见少，因为宗族情愿出钱建造。沈德符在《万历野获编》里说：万历初年申时入阁，吴县地方官府给他竖立"状元宰辅"大旗，高高悬在他家门上。

此后迅速传了开来，连"诸生出贡，皆高竿大旗，飘摇云汉，每入城市，弥望不绝"，而"鼎甲及得选庶常（入选翰林）者，复另植黄竿，另张大旗，比乡、会更加数倍。" 一个"田舍郎"，经过刻苦攻读，取得考试的成功，便能登上"天子堂"，达到如此辉煌的境地，这是对每一个有读书可能性的人的极大诱惑，激发了平头白丁奔向举业。宗族为了全族的共同利益，支持有志的青少年读书，纷纷创办学塾，造成文化在农村的大普及。

以致很穷困的小山村也有些有学塾，如浙江永嘉一个很小的村子叫林坑，村的西南角山坡上有一个小小的"学堂"，它的楼板之下是牛棚。山西省吕梁市山区有一个非常偏僻的窑洞村叫陈家塄，很小，但是一进村门，就有一幢挂着乾隆时期老匾的三合院，曾是书塾。散布在黄土峭壁之上的另一个窑洞村彩家庄，竟有两间小小的平房，它们是村子的学塾。那是在一次地震引起黄土峭壁崩塌的全村大灾难之后，重建村落时选了最安全的地点造起来的，时间大约在清代中叶。

科举制度也对少数民族开放，促进了他们文化的普及。例如，湖南省西南角上汉、侗、苗多民族杂居的会同县高椅村《杨氏族谱·八景诗》中有两首诗是写学馆的，其一是："一村几个读书堂，起凤腾蛟各有光，附近教人眠不得，五更犹听诵文章。"诗写得很真切。科举制度大大提高了普遍的文化水平，意义就不仅仅限于个人或者宗族的成败了。

一个人中了举人进士，能给整个宗族带来很大的利益，所以，在科举时代，宗族总是鼓励和支持子弟们读书的。宗族鼓励和支持子弟读书应试，是接续和完成了朝廷创设的科举制度，是科举制度得以成功的重要条件，它几乎是这个制度的组成部分。

南宋淳佑十年（1250年），浙江省温州昆阳凤凰山的《宜都陈氏家乘序》一开头就写道： 温之昆阳，大族为多，而门第之赫奕，子姓之繁昌，则未有加于陈氏者也。盖门第之赫奕实由于子姓之繁昌。藉使徒繁昌而无贤哲之士，其欲门第之赫奕者，宁可得乎？陈氏自李唐迁居昆阳，其子姓登文科、武科、特科及补入太学、请漕试，与夫勉解、进纳、边赏、荫叙者不啻百有余人，此门第所以赫奕而非他族所能加也。这个陈氏宗族之所以"赫奕"，重要原因之一是有子姓登科。

所以，清代光绪十六年（1890年）安徽《寿州龙氏宗谱·家规》里有一项《务读书》： 士农与工商，读书为第一。勿偷闲，勿贪嬉，愤发以前在勉力。俸禄享千钟，黄金收万镒，皆从读书苦中来，一寸光阴宜自惜。凡我族人，期于克振家声，宜从诗书上苦心著力。天下惟读书人不可限量！云梯千里，凤翮九霄，上为父祖增光，下为子孙创业，岂独一身荣显已哉！

切莫浮慕无实，图侥幸以获功名，庶为有志之士。这一项不但讲了许多读书人可能获得的好处，还从宗族的整体利益上着眼来衡量子弟读书的好处，许许多多的宗谱都有类似的教训和规定。安徽黟县关麓村汪氏支祠有一副楹联，写的是："一水护田，常看秋敛春耕，俾小子先知稼穑；五经堆案，更喜夏萤冬雪，助后人永守诗书。

"这便是耕读社会中宗族对子弟的期望。除了一般的鼓励，宗族采取了许多具体实在的措施，以支持子弟读书并参加科考。这些措施中最普遍的有：设村塾和义塾，聘明师，资助贫寒而有志的子弟学习，建文馆，定期举办文会，提供学子参加科举考试的费用，给科考成功的子弟以物质的和荣誉的奖励，等等。

一切费用都由族中公有的膏火田（即学田）的收入来支出。这是民间对科举制度的呼应、补充和完成。清代同治十一年（1872年），浙江省镇海县方氏族内一些比较富裕而"家有余赀"的人，"慨然有志于赡族之举"，他们采取的赡族办法是创办一所义塾。

创办之初，订立了一篇《义塾规则》，写得非常具体详尽，比较重要的有： 本堂设立义塾，为族内无力延师者陶教子弟。其师由本堂聘请，修金即由本堂送奉。凡来就学者，概无须出赀。塾中有才质迈众，学可造就而其家或无力卒业者，本堂自当另行筹酌助给书资。无力之家或并笔墨书纸等不能自具，先行告明登册，本堂备给。义塾是宗族为贫寒子弟开设的，少数由富裕人家捐田创办。

有钱人家自办"专馆"，就是一家人家延师设馆，专教家里的子弟。这些"专馆"的师资会好一点，多是在乡里有名气的老塾师。还有一种"散馆"，由几家人合资聘师教习子弟。还有"家塾"和"私塾"，或叫"座馆"，是老师在自己家里设馆，各家送子弟来学习，老师酌情收取学资。有些村子，出公积建造很好的学堂，如山西省临县孙家沟村，位置很偏僻，地势很局促，农田不多，却在村口最美的高地上建了一座很漂亮的学塾。村民在极窘迫的情况下，把摆脱穷困的希望都寄托在孩子的读书成绩上了。

凡参加科考的，宗族继续予以鼓励支持。例如同治十三年（1874年）本《东粤宝安南头黄氏族谱·族规》里有详细规定： 童生有县名应府试者，每名给花银二两。童生有府名应院试者，每名给花银三元。生员有志科考等第，每名给花银二元。

文武生员及贡、监考遗才者，每名给花银二元。以上是资助科考费用的。赴考乡试、会试的，往往在府县的"宾兴馆"（聚贤馆）会合之后集体出发，由府县出资补助。但大多数宗族仍旧自行出资补助，数额也写在《族规》里。考试成功的，宗族有奖励。

例如，这个《东粤宝安南头黄氏族谱·族规》接着写： 游泮（即中了秀才）谒祖，每一名花红银伍拾元，真银花一对，重伍钱，马花红绸一匹。至是日，祠中酒席费用众出，花银四十大元，依每房一人同办。廪贡谒祖，每一名花红银捌拾两；真银花一对，重五钱；马花红绸一匹。凡所有买桅、竖桅及酒席费用，俱是祠出。

（桅即旗杆） 文武举人谒祖，每一名花红银二百两，真银花一对，重七钱；马花红绸一匹。买桅、竖桅及酒席费用俱祠出。京费花银一百两。文武进士谒祖，每一名花红银三百两，真银花一对，重一两。写花红绸一匹。买桅、竖桅及酒席费用俱祠办。

翰林、部属、侍卫谒祖，加花红银三百两，余与进士同。鼎甲谒祖，加花红银五百两，余与进士同。买桅、竖桅就是立一对大木杆，杆上有"斗"。每杆之上，举人一只斗，进士两只斗。

这个族规是清代同治年间的，所以没有提建进士牌坊的事。顺治十五年（1658年），还曾"赐进士彩花、牌坊银三十两，一甲三名各再加五十两。

"嘉庆朝（1796—1820）起，朝廷不出钱建进士牌坊了，虽然宗族中还有建造的，但已不便于写进宗谱族规。有些旺族便建"世科坊"，便是造一座石坊，把本族历届的进士甚至举人，陆续刻上去。有奖便也有罚。

明代初年，浙江省浦江郑氏义门立《郑氏规范》，有一条是："子弟未冠者，学业未成，不听食肉。古有是法，非惟有资于勤苦，抑欲其识齑盐之味。"康熙三十五年（1696年）毗陵《长沟朱氏宗谱·族范·祠规》里有一条："立义学。族中贫不能延师者，俱送子入祠读书。如幼童品质颖秀，其父甘于废弃，不送读书，罚银一两。有从旁谤议阻挠，不肯成人之美，定责二十板。"受罚的是为父者和谤议者。

只要中一个秀才，虽然没有官职，在乡土社会中就是头面人物。村里的公共事务，都要他们出头露面，俨然缙绅。宗祠大祭的时候，秀才可以不顾"在朝以爵，在乡以齿"的常例，大摇大摆位于前辈尊长之上，受到各种礼遇。

清代道光五年（1825年）《京江柳氏宗谱·宗祠条例》里规定，每逢宗祠大祭： 祭毕，管年者分胙，议定进士、举人猪胙三斤、羊胙二斤，生员、贡、监猪胙三斤、羊胙一斤，无职者猪羊各一斤。妇人及未成丁者不分，惟孀妇虽子未成丁，亦送猪羊胙各一斤，重节也。

事实上，进士一般都外出当官，举人也大多出任公职而不再在乡，村子里就只有秀才（生员、贡、监）或致仕的官员是"博学能文"之士了。多分胙肉更重要的是一种身份，一种荣誉，也便是一种鼓励。

明代进士可以在州县建牌坊，后来举人也有建的，清代嘉庆朝取消了这种"恩荣"，但仍有人在村里建造。至于"进士第"则几乎是必建的。

进士和举人的"桅"，初时只建于宗祠门前，后来连住宅门前也建了起来。总之，唐人牛希济在《贡士论》里写的登科的荣耀，"秋风八月，鞍马九衢，神气扬扬，行者避路。取富贵若咳唾，视州县如奴仆。"这份神气，在乡土社会中都会一一落到实处，不论是唐朝还是清朝。

从兴学、资助到给予荣耀，这便是宗族对科举制度的回应、支持和最后完成。因为朝廷眼里的取士制度在宗族看来是一个"进仕制度"，出于自身的利益考虑，它有巨大的热情去实现这个制度。正是宗族组织，成就了科举制度一千多年的作为。科举制度本来是帝王择优取士的制度，也是乡社可以利用来培养人才改善宗族地位和生活的制度。但这制度又毫无疑问有利于普遍提高民众的文化水平和行为教养。

中国早期商品经济的发展，起初大多在科举成绩比较好的地区。后来，如山西中、南部和安徽南部，商品经济又夺走了人才，以致当地科举成绩下降。不过，这仅仅是社会文化重点的转移而不是它的退步。科举取仕不能杜绝官员们的贪墨，"三年清知府，十万雪花银"不是极少数的现象，但是，"两袖清风"毕竟成了官吏们的道德标准，并非毫无影响。

浙江省浦江郑氏义门立《郑氏规范》里写道："子孙出仕，有以赃墨闻者，生则于谱图上削去其名，死则不许入祠堂。"也就是读书当官而贪污就得开除出家门了，族谱里也会除名。可见古人已经懂得对当了官的人更应该严加管束。"读圣贤书，所学何事？"这是民族英雄文天祥的"天问"，他以最忠诚的操守和战斗，回答了这个问题。几百年后的史可法和张苍水，在经历了极其艰苦的又一场斗争后也忠诚地献出了生命。张苍水在战斗时期到过杭州，写下了一首诗： 国亡家破复何之？西子湖头有我师。

日月双悬于氏墓，乾坤半壁岳家祠。不少家训、族规之类，谆谆教戒子弟读书首先为了做人，而不是为了做官。又如《训俗遗规》引《昆山朱氏家训》里朱用纯写的一篇《劝言》说："圣贤之书，不为后人中举人进士而设，是教千万世做好人。

"《训俗遗规》里又收了王士晋写的一篇《宗规》，里面说：教育子弟"将正经书史严加训迪，务使变化气质，陶熔德性。他日若做秀才、做官，固为良士、为廉吏，就是为农为工为商，亦不失为醇谨君子"。这些思想，都已经跳出了科举求仕狭隘的功利性束缚，提高了读书的意义。因此一些清廉为民，守土卫国的历史人物便得到了人民的尊重，永远纪念。乡土环境中就有了一种纪念这些人物的建筑，有祠庙，有牌楼，有故居。

这是些很有历史价值和教育意义的建筑物，例如，浙江省永康市方岩村的方岩山上，便有一座规模不小，香火很旺的胡公庙，纪念宋代的胡则，他曾经在灾荒之年为遭难百姓申请了免税。永康的邻县东阳，在北宋时出过一位朝廷重臣李纲，他在金兵南下入侵的时候力主抵抗，高呼"渡河"，吐血而亡，百姓为他建造了专祠。

赣东、浙东、皖南农村里还有大量的汪公庙，是祭祀越国公汪华的，他是隋、唐间义军领袖，曾占有宣、杭、睦、婺、饶五州，在天下大乱的形势下保护了五州人民，所以深得百姓感恩。这些庙虽然在当时的大环境中也不免染了些迷信色彩，但受祭祀的确实是真正的历史人物，做过利国利民的好事。这些人做好事，老百姓礼拜这些人，多少也受到社会文化程度提高的影响。

所以提倡读圣贤书也并非只着眼于升官发财，而有重大的社会历史意义。

1.Cultural-Educational Architecture and Imperial Examinations Chinese people love reading.

North or south, city or village, reasonably well-off households most commonly display on their main gate the couplet: "Loyalty and filial piety pass down the family long; poetry and books continue generations.

" In the main hall, the two most common couplets are: "A centuries-old family is nothing but accumulated virtue; the first and best good deed is still reading" and "First-class people: loyal ministers and filial sons; two occupations: farming and reading.

" At the center of the long altar table stands a red-lacquered, gold-painted spirit tablet inscribed "Heaven-Earth-Sovereign-Parent-Teacher" (天地君亲师), with incense burning year-round.

Setting aside Heaven and Earth, in the real world "Teacher" ranks only after "Sovereign" and "Parent"—very high status indeed.

Actually, what primarily激发 Chinese reading enthusiasm was the imperial examination system (科举)—the Sui-Tang path of "those who excel in study become officials" (学而优则仕), a road anyone could try; second was commercial development.

It was not primarily about accumulating virtue to help the world, nor about investigating things to attain knowledge (格物致知).In rural society, village cultural-educational buildings mostly relate to the examinations.

One category is for teaching: community schools (社学), charitable schools (义塾), family schools (家塾), study halls (书馆)—mainly basic education.

Then there are literary halls (文馆): older scholars who have stepped back from official ambition, gathering friends through literature, discussing learning, and periodically assessing village children's exam-preparation progress.

Another category commemorates exam success: from Ming onward, jinshi graduates could erect memorial archways (牌坊), flagpoles (桅), and build "jinshi mansions" (进士第).

Later, juren graduates also erected flagpoles and even archways.

Another category is for worship: Wenchang pavilions (文昌阁/魁星楼), Wenfeng pagodas (文峰塔), writing brushes (文笔), paper-burning furnaces (焚帛炉)—praying for clan and individual literary fortune.

Additionally, larger temples often have rooms or a separate courtyard for scholars to live and prepare for exams.

A few villages have Confucian temples (文庙), which along with ancestral halls may house young students.

Some villages have library towers and studios—often built by successful exam candidates who served as officials, then retired in old age to read, paint, and receive guests.

Some merchants without official titles, in old age, also build small quiet courtyards as study retreats.

In Song-Yuan, a few regions like Jiangxi had academies (书院) where scholars taught disciples and explored philosophical principles, but these had little impact on rural society.

Places with many cultural-educational buildings are mostly places with strong exam performance—so-called "lands of flourishing literary culture," led by southern Jiangsu and Zhejiang, followed by Jiangxi, Fujian, southern Anhui, Guangdong, and the two Hubei/Hunan regions.

These areas: first, had developed commercial economies—economy was both the backer of exam success and the basis for widespread educational buildings; second, had stable, powerful clan structures and management systems, where children's reading had become tradition.

The examination system was primarily the state's official-selection system—hence folk启蒙 verse: "The Son of Heaven values heroes; articles teach children." It began in Sui, became fully developed after Ming.

But it was also a system for commoners to enter officialdom.

To support and激励 clan children to study and climb the "blue cloud path," clans used public property to found schools, assist reading, subsidize exam travel, and upon obtaining any degree, grant high honor and tangible rewards.

Clans接续 and completed the state's examination system, helping it spread and产生巨大影响.Rural cultural-educational buildings were overwhelmingly built by clans.Where clan structures were destroyed, exam performance was poor and educational buildings few.

However, economically developed and clan-stable regions did not necessarily have high exam performance.

Central Shanxi and southern Anhui, from Ming through Qing, produced many skilled merchants operating across the country, but their exam performance was not strong.By late Qing, it declined further.

Liu Dapeng's 《退想斋日记》 describes Taigu (Shanxi)风气: "Reading is viewed lightly, commerce heavily; talented children all go into trade, few study; some even abandon Confucian study for commerce after entering school—saying scholars suffer hunger, while merchants gain silver and family prosperity.

" Lanxi Zhuge Village's 《高隆诸葛氏宗谱》 includes a merchant biography with his words: "Rather than reading ten thousand books,不如 accumulating a thousand gold in property." A thousand-year value system was inverted.

With money from commerce, one could buy empty titles without ten years of hard study—Qing court, to raise revenue, had fixed prices for titles like "大夫" and "司马".

The examination system selected civil officials through periodic exams from among the educated.Before Sui, in Han, Wei-Jin, and Northern-Southern Dynasties, official selection was entirely controlled by powerful clans—rampant abuse.

Hereditary strongmen threatened the supreme ruler, hindered true talent discovery, and caused rigid class stratification leading to instability.

To overcome these abuses, Sui began trial-recommending talent by local officials, then selecting through central exams.Subsequent dynasties refined this into the hugely influential examination system.

The system's feature—and advantage—was opening official careers to all society, fair competition, avoiding powerful class monopoly and giving weaker classes equal opportunity.Except for极少数 "base people" (e.g.

, Zhejiang's duomin 堕民, Guangdong's danmin 疍民), those in "base occupations" (prostitutes, actors, yamen runners, musician households), criminals, those in parental mourning, and dismissed officials—anyone with registered household and qualified education could, in principle, take the exams.

Exam methods and administration were rigorous, preventing unfairness.

For autocratic rulers, opening official careers to all society's first benefit: though not achieving "no talent left in the wild," the court could网罗 outstanding talent for official positions, strengthening governance.

After Sui-Tang, all famous ministers and chancellors came from the exams.

Hence in early Zhenguan (627–632), Emperor Taizong, watching new jinshi graduates emerge on announcement day at the palace gate, told attendants: "All heroes under heaven have entered my trap!

" (天下英雄入吾彀中矣)—very pleased.The exam system, open to commoners, greatly promoted cultural-educational普及 across China.Reading became a social custom.

"Fathers and older brothers blame sons/younger brothers for not being literary; mothers and wives are ashamed if sons/husbands do not study." Some even proposed "everyone has a share in reading.

" The exam system's peak coincided with woodblock printing普及.Woodblock printing matured in late Tang, perfected in Song—making books easier and cheaper, further fueling the exam system.

Exams attracted大批 social elites, burying them in officially set knowledge—"white-haired from studying classics" (皓首穷经), "ears deaf to outside matters, heart only on sage books"—so that whole society focused on exams; society became "examination-ized.

" Northern Song Emperor Zhenzong wrote a famous 《劝学诗》 (Poem Encouraging Study), long influential: The rich need not buy good fields—books hold a thousand bushels of grain.

Building a house need not raise high beams—books hold a house of gold.Marrying need not lament no good matchmaker—books hold a beauty like jade.Going out need not lament no retinue—books hold crowds of carriages and horses.

If a man would fulfill his life's ambition, diligently study the Six Classics before the window.

Dong Zhongshu's Han-dynasty proposal "reject all schools, honor only Confucianism" (罢黜百家，独尊儒术), after about a thousand years, only truly reached all society in the exam era—lured by "grain, house, jade, carriage.

" Sun Chengze said: "Once the exam system was established, scholars everywhere flocked to it.What the upper intent favors, custom follows; the quality of talent and the purity of scholar ethos all derive from this.

" Through exams, "upper intent" led custom, shaping scholars' knowledge scope and horizons.Exam success first brought个人 many benefits.

Late Ming-early Qing scholar Ji Liuqi wrote in 《明季北略》: "I often see blue-gowned youths (students) unable to plan from morning to evening; once they pass the provincial exam, they become endless juren; once they pass the palace exam, they dine to bells and eat from tripods, ride fat horses in light furs—worth not millions but hundreds of thousands.

..they pay no personal tax, no labor service, no grain tax, no commodity tax, and even shelter wicked people from taxes and labor—their income is just beginning.

" In Ming-Qing, juren were "proper-path" graduates, already qualified for office—usually county school instructors, with chance of being "great selection" (大挑) as county magistrate.

Once jinshi, one left the "commoner" class, enjoying many political-economic privileges—e.g., whole family exempt from taxes and labor.

Jinshi could hold high office; in Ming-Qing, most jinshi first entered the Hanlin Academy (翰林院)—the reserve for high officials; all central-government high officials came from Hanlin.

In Qing, grand secretaries (大学士) were selected from Hanlin; other Hanlin became department directors, a few became county magistrates without waiting, with more promotion opportunities.

In Ming-Qing, high exam graduates also had a longer-term glory: building archways and flagpoles in hometown, hanging plaques in ancestral halls.

In early Ming Hongwu 21 (1388), Ren Hengtai became zhuangyuan (first-place jinshi); Emperor Taizu ordered official funds to build an archway in his hometown Xiangyang (Hubei) to honor him.

This was likely the first exam-success archway.Thereafter, exam archways and flagpoles gradually spread everywhere, extending to juren.

Mid-Ming Chenghua-Hongzhi era, even earlier jinshi without archways got them built retroactively.Later, jinshi fathers and grandfathers, after receiving imperial titles, could build same-style archways.

These archways were mostly built in county seats—so by late Ming Wanli (1573–1620), many county seats were dense with exam archways.

Due to high cost, from Qing Jiaqing (1796–1820) the state stopped funding them, but numbers did not decrease—clans willingly paid.

Shen Defu wrote in 《万历野获编》: In early Wanli, when Shen Shixing entered the grand secretariat, Wuxian local officials erected a "Zhuangyuan Grand Secretary" great flag high at his gate.

This quickly spread—even "students becoming tribute students all raise high poles and great flags, fluttering in the clouds; entering cities, they fill the view.

" And "top-three graduates and those selected as Hanlin scholars raise yellow poles and great flags separately, several times more than provincial and metropolitan exam graduates.

" A "farm boy" (田舍郎), through diligent study and exam success, could ascend to the "Son of Heaven's hall" (天子堂)—such brilliance was a tremendous temptation to anyone capable of reading,激发 commoners to pursue the exams.

Clans, for collective benefit, supported ambitious youth to study, founding schools everywhere—causing widespread literacy in rural areas.Even very poor mountain villages had schools: e.g.

, a tiny Yongjia village called Linkeng had a small "school" on its southwest hillside, with a cattle shed below its floor.

In Shanxi's Lüliang mountains, a very remote cave village called Chenjialeng—small, but upon entering the village gate, a three-courtyard house with a Qianlong-era old plaque, once a school.

Another cave village, Caijiazhuang, scattered on loess cliffs, had two small single-story houses serving as the village school—built after an earthquake caused loess cliff collapse and village disaster, rebuilt at the safest location in mid-Qing.

The exam system was also open to ethnic minorities, promoting their cultural普及.E.g.

, in Hunan's southwest corner, multi-ethnic Gaoyi Village (Han, Dong, Miao) 《杨氏族谱·八景诗》 has two poems about study halls; one: "A village has several reading halls, each shining with rising phoenixes and leaping dragons; nearby people cannot sleep—at the fifth watch still hear reciting articles.

" Very vivid.The exam system greatly raised general cultural level—meaning beyond individual or clan success/failure.

One person becoming juren or jinshi brought great benefit to the whole clan—hence in the exam era, clans always encouraged and supported children's study.

Clan encouragement and support of children's exam study接续 and completed the state-founded exam system, a key condition for its success—almost part of the system itself.

In Southern Song Chunyou 10 (1250), Wenzhou Kunyang Fenghuang Mountain's 《宜都陈氏家乘序》 opens: In Kunyang of Wenzhou, there are many great clans, but none surpass the Chen in illustrious status and prosperous descendants.

Illustrious status truly results from prosperous descendants.If merely prosperous without wise men, how could status be illustrious?

Since Tang, the Chen's descendants passed civil, military, special exams, entered the Imperial Academy, took provincial exams, and received office through recommendation, border merit, or hereditary privilege—over a hundred people.

This is why the Chen's status is unsurpassed.This Chen clan's "illustriousness" importantly came from descendants passing exams.

Hence Qing Guangxu 16 (1890) Anhui 《寿州龙氏宗谱·家规》 has a "Must Study" section: Scholars, farmers, artisans, merchants—reading is first.Do not idle, do not play, strive diligently.

Salary of a thousand bushels, gold of ten thousand taels—all come from the bitterness of study; cherish every inch of time.All our clansmen, aiming to revive family reputation, should devote heart to books.

Only scholars have unlimited potential!Climbing a thousand-li ladder, soaring to the nine heavens—above bringing glory to fathers and ancestors, below establishing enterprise for descendants—not merely personal honor!

Do not crave empty fame, seek success by luck; be a person of ambition.This not only lists benefits of reading but measures children's study from the clan's overall interest.Many genealogies have similar teachings and rules.

Shexian Guanlu Village's Wang branch hall has a couplet: "One stream protects fields, watching autumn harvest and spring plowing, so children first know farming; Five Classics piled on desks, delighting in summer fireflies and winter snow, helping descendants forever keep books.

" This is the clan's expectation for children in a farming-reading society.Beyond general encouragement, clans took many concrete measures to support children's study and exams.

Most common: establish village and charitable schools, hire good teachers, subsidize poor but ambitious children, build literary halls, hold regular literary gatherings, provide exam travel expenses, give material and honor rewards to successful candidates—all expenses from clan-owned "study-field" (膏火田/学田) income.

This was the民间 response, supplement, and completion of the exam system.In Qing Tongzhi 11 (1872), wealthy members of Zhenhai Fang clan (Zhejiang), "generously aspiring to clan-support," founded a charitable school.

At founding, they established detailed 《义塾规则》; key points: This hall establishes a charitable school to educate children of clan members unable to hire teachers.

Teachers are hired by the hall, salaries paid by the hall.All students pay nothing.For students of outstanding talent whose families cannot support completion, the hall will separately provide book funds.

For families unable to provide even brush, ink, paper, books—register in advance, the hall provides them.Charitable schools were founded by clans for poor children; a few by wealthy families donating land.

Rich families ran "private exclusive schools" (专馆)—one family hiring a teacher exclusively for its children, with better teachers (respected village old teachers).There were "joint schools" (散馆)—several families jointly hiring a teacher.

And "family schools" (家塾) / "private schools" (私塾) / "seat schools" (座馆)—teachers running schools in their own homes, families sending children, teachers charging modest fees.Some villages built excellent schools from public funds: e.g.

, Linxian Sunjiagou Village (Shanxi)—remote, cramped, little farmland, yet built a beautiful school on the most beautiful high ground at the village entrance.

Villagers, in dire poverty, pinned their escape-from-poverty hope on children's exam success.For those taking exams, clans continued support.E.g.

, Tongzhi 13 (1874) 《东粤宝安南头黄氏族谱·族规》 detailed: Students with county qualification for prefectural exam: 2 taels silver each.Students with prefectural qualification for academy exam: 3 yuan silver each.

Students aspiring to exam ranking: 2 yuan silver each.Military/civil students and tribute/imperial exam candidates: 2 yuan silver each.These subsidized exam expenses.

Those taking provincial and metropolitan exams often gathered at the prefecture/county's "Binxing Hall" (宾兴馆) for collective departure, subsidized by prefecture/county.

But most clans still subsidized independently, amounts written in clan rules.Successful candidates received clan rewards.

The same Huang clan rules continue: Youcai (passing xiucai) visiting ancestors: 50 yuan silver each, pair of real silver flowers (5 qian), one bolt of red silk.

That day, hall banquet expenses shared by all, 40 yuan silver, one person per branch.Lin-gong (tribute student) visiting ancestors: 80 taels silver; pair of real silver flowers (5 qian); one bolt red silk.

All flagpole purchase/erection and banquet expenses paid by hall.Military/civil juren visiting ancestors: 200 taels silver; pair real silver flowers (7 qian); one bolt red silk.Flagpole and banquet expenses paid by hall.

Capital exam expense: 100 taels.Military/civil jinshi visiting ancestors: 300 taels silver; pair real silver flowers (1 tael); one bolt red silk.Flagpole and banquet expenses paid by hall.

Hanlin, department officials, imperial guards visiting ancestors: additional 300 taels, rest same as jinshi.Top-three graduates: additional 500 taels, rest same as jinshi.

Buying/erecting flagpoles means raising a pair of large wooden poles with "dou" (斗) on top.Juren: one dou per pole; jinshi: two dou.This clan rule is Tongzhi-era, so does not mention jinshi archways.

In Shunzhi 15 (1658), the court "awarded jinshi colored flowers and 30 taels archway silver, top three an additional 50 taels each.

" From Jiaqing (1796–1820), the court stopped funding jinshi archways—though clans still built them, it was no longer convenient to write into clan rules.

Some prosperous clans built "generation-exam archways" (世科坊)—a stone archway刻上 successive clan jinshi and even juren names.Rewards had corresponding punishments.

Early Ming, Pujiang Zheng clan's 《郑氏规范》: "Uncapped children with unfinished studies may not eat meat.This is ancient law—not only aiding diligence, but让 them know the taste of hardship.

" Kangxi 35 (1696) Piling 《长沟朱氏宗谱·族范·祠规》: "Establish charitable school.Poor clan members unable to hire teachers must send children to study in the hall.If a talented child's father willingly wastes him, not sending to study—fine 1 tael.

Those who gossip and obstruct, refusing to help others—20 strokes." Punished are fathers and gossipers.

Even passing xiucai (student), though no official position, made one a prominent figure in rural society.Village public affairs required their presence—like gentry.

At grand ancestral sacrifices, xiucai could ignore the rule "at court by rank, in village by age" (在朝以爵，在乡以齿), boldly positioning above elders, receiving various courtesies.

Qing Daoguang 5 (1825) 《京江柳氏宗谱·宗祠条例》 stipulates at grand sacrifices: After sacrifice, the manager distributes sacrificial meat: jinshi/juren get 3 jin pork, 2 jin mutton; students/tribute/imperial students get 3 jin pork, 1 jin mutton; those without office get 1 jin each of pork and mutton.

Women and minors get none; but widows, even if sons are minors, get 1 jin each of pork and mutton—valuing chastity.

In fact, jinshi generally served as officials away from home, juren also mostly took public office and left—only xiucai (students, tribute, imperial students) or retired officials remained as "learned" men in the village.

More sacrificial meat importantly meant status, honor, and encouragement.Ming jinshi could build archways in counties; later juren too.Qing Jiaqing取消 this "imperial grace," but some still built in villages.

As for "jinshi mansions" (进士第), they were almost always built.Jinshi and juren "flagpoles" initially only before ancestral halls, later also before residences.

In sum, Tang Niu Xiji wrote in 《贡士论》 of exam glory: "Autumn wind, eighth month, saddle and horse on nine avenues, spirit soaring, passersby making way.Gaining wealth like spitting, viewing counties like servants.

" This swagger, in rural society, all became real—whether Tang or Qing.From founding schools, subsidizing, to granting honor—this was the clan's response, support, and final completion of the exam system.

Because the state's official-selection system, in clans' view, was an "official-entry system"—out of self-interest, they had tremendous enthusiasm to implement it.It was clan organization that achieved the exam system's thousand-year success.

The exam system was originally the emperor's system for selecting talent, and also a system rural communities could use to培养 talent and improve clan status and life.But it undoubtedly helped raise general cultural level and behavioral cultivation.

China's early commercial economy initially developed mostly in regions with strong exam performance.Later, in central/southern Shanxi and southern Anhui, commercial economy drew away talent, causing local exam performance to decline.

But this was merely a shift in social-cultural focus, not its decline.

The exam system could not eliminate official corruption—"three years as an honest prefect, ten thousand snowflake silver" was not rare—but "two sleeves full of breeze" (两袖清风, honest) became officials' moral standard, not without influence.

Pujiang Zheng clan's 《郑氏规范》: "Descendants serving as officials, if known for corruption—while alive, strike their name from the genealogy; when dead, forbid entry to the ancestral hall.

" That is: studying to become an official but corrupting means expulsion from the family and genealogy.Shows ancients understood officials needed stricter discipline."What does reading sage books teach?

" This was national hero Wen Tianxiang's "heavenly question"—he answered with the most loyal conduct and battle.Centuries later, Shi Kefa and Zhang Cangshui, after extremely hard struggle, also loyally gave their lives.

Zhang Cangshang, visiting Hangzhou during battle, wrote: Nation fallen, family broken—where to go?By West Lake's shore I have my teachers.Sun and moon hang together at Yu's tomb; heaven and earth half-supported at Yue's shrine.

Many family instructions and clan rules earnestly taught children to read first to become good people, not to become officials.E.g.

, 《训俗遗规》 quotes 《昆山朱氏家训》 Zhu Yongchun's 《劝言》: "Sage books were not written for later people to become juren/jinshi—they teach countless generations to be good people.

" 《训俗遗规》 also includes Wang Shijin's 《宗规》: educating children "strictly teach proper classics and histories, transforming their temperament and cultivating virtue.

If they later become students or officials, they will be good scholars and honest officials; even if farmers, artisans, or merchants, they will still be prudent gentlemen.

" These thoughts transcended the narrow utilitarian束缚 of exam-seeking officialdom, elevating reading's meaning.Hence honest, people-serving, territory-defending historical figures gained people's respect and eternal commemoration.

Rural environments had buildings commemorating them: temples, archways, former residences.These are historically valuable and educational buildings.E.g.

, Yongkang Fangyan Village's Fangyan Mountain has a sizable, incense-rich Hu Gong Temple commemorating Song dynasty Hu Ze, who secured tax exemption for disaster-stricken people.

Yongkang's neighboring Dongyang produced Northern Song important official Li Gang, who advocated resistance when Jin troops invaded south, shouting "Cross the river!" (渡河), vomiting blood and dying—people built a dedicated temple.

In eastern Jiangxi, eastern Zhejiang, southern Anhui rural areas, many Wang Gong Temples worship Duke of Yue Wang Hua—a Sui-Tang rebel leader who controlled Xuan, Hang, Mu, Wu, Rao prefectures, protecting five prefectures' people in chaos—hence deeply grateful.

These temples, though inevitably tinged with superstition in their era, worshiped real historical figures who did beneficial deeds for nation and people.

These people did good; commoners worshiped them—influenced in part by raised social-cultural level.Hence advocating reading sage books was not merely about official promotion and wealth, but had major social-historical significance.
