5.2 耕读生活一例——楠溪江诸村
Section 2

二、耕读生活一例——楠溪江诸村 用科举取士制度代替门阀世袭制度，对乡土社会来说，至少促进了文化教育的大普及、大提高，并进而提高了乡土社会的整体建设。

一方面是平民百姓都有了比较公平的进仕机会，激发了青少年为争取进入社会上层而努力读书习文；另一方面是当官没有终身制，到了年限，便要卸职致仕，其中不少人要回归田园，从而把知识和阅历带回农村，对农村建设和文化教育甚至经济发展作出贡献。中国农耕时代乡土社会里的文化教育状态，可以用浙江省永嘉县楠溪江中游的村落群作为实例来考察。这是一个普普通通的山区，向来默默无闻，但在我国广大的农村里，很有典型意义。

楠溪江主流长145公里，流域面积2429平方公里，村落260余座。村民从事的主要是稻作农业，由于自然条件很好，衣食无虑，但只靠日出而作，日入而息，经济难以发达。一直到20世纪90年代初，绝大多数村子里还没有小店，买点针头线脑、火柴蜡烛，都靠偶或一来的货郎担。

然而在"五日一风、十日一雨，帝力于我何有哉"的悠然生活之中，却不忘读书明理，也撇不开"朝为田舍郎，暮登天子堂"的科名追求。永嘉开发很晚，西晋末年，中原大乱，南渡的中原士族用先进的文化改造了瓯越文化，楠溪江中游开始了新的历史。东晋时设永嘉郡，楠溪江流域是它的辖区。

由于一时人文荟萃江右，初建的永嘉郡，六朝时竟有幸得中国文化史上几颗灿烂夺目的星辰来任郡守，先后有东晋大文学家、大书法家王羲之，注《三国志》的刘宋史学家裴松之，玄言诗人、赋家孙绰，诗人、骈文家、文论家颜延之，中国第一位山水诗人谢灵运，萧梁文学家、骈文高手丘迟。这些当时中国文化的精英，以"助人伦，成教化"为从政的最高理想。乾隆《永嘉县志》转引《旧志》说："晋立郡城，生齿日繁，王右军导之以文教，谢康乐继之，乃知向方，自是家务为学，至宋遂为小邹鲁。

"又说"王羲之治尚慈惠，谢灵运招士进学，由是人知向学，民风一变。"王谢风流，培养出楠溪江浓郁的人文气息。明末清初诗人梅调元有永嘉《王谢祠》诗，写的是： 前守推王谢，荒祠倚郡城， 千秋传墨妙，六代擅诗名。沼古鹅还浴，塘春草自生， 风流今古事，俯仰一含情。

楠溪江最灿烂的文化高峰在南宋，中原衣冠又一次大规模南渡，像东晋一样，偏安之地人文荟萃，来任温州"一把手"的如张九成、王十朋、楼钥和杨简，都是一时俊彦。张九成在《咨目》里写道："永嘉道德之乡，贤哲相踵，前辈虽往，风流犹存。"他们也都以礼乐教化为从政的第一要务。这对于提高永嘉的文化水平，起了很大作用。乾隆《永嘉县志·学校》说："永嘉于宋，名贤辈出，登洛闽之堂者，后先相望，郁郁彬彬，至称为小邹鲁，何其盛哉！"永嘉在北宋有程门弟子十三人，在南宋有朱门弟子十六人。

在国学里，先后有永嘉籍的元丰九先生和淳熙六君子，"俱以道德性命传程朱之学"。（见乾隆《永嘉县志·风俗》）南宋时形成的理学中的"永嘉学派"，以薛季宣、陈傅良、郑伯熊和叶适为代表，其中郑、叶为楠溪江人。郑伯熊原籍塘湾村，叶适童年时代在岩头村由金姓抚养并读书（见《岩头金氏宗谱》）。溪口村戴氏家族，北宋时有戴述[元符三年（1100年）进士]、戴迅两兄弟从二程学。

到南宋，有戴述子戴栩（嘉定进士），是叶适的学生，著作《五经说》、《诸子辩论》、《东都要略》等。戴迅子戴溪[淳熙五年（1178年）进士]，据嘉靖《温州府志·人物》说他"由礼部郎中凡六转为太子詹事，兼秘书监。景献太子命类《易》、《诗》、《书》、《春秋》、《语》、《孟》、《资治通鉴》各为说以进。

权工部尚书，除文华阁学士，卒赠端明殿学士，谥文端。太子亲书"明经"匾其堂，有《岷隐集》。宁宗称他为"诸儒之宗"。叶适评戴溪说，"少望天下奇才，于今世不过数人"。戴溪的亲侄子戴蒙[绍熙庚戌（1190年）进士]曾从学朱熹于武夷，著作有《易、书、四书家说》，《六书故》等；戴蒙长子戴仔，不乐仕进，著有《诸经补义》、《通鉴补纪》、《说林文集》等。

蒙次子侗[淳佑辛丑（1241年）进士]，著有《六书设》和一些杂著文集。这戴氏一门，学术成就不同寻常，溪口戴氏大宗祠里有一副楹联写道： 入程朱门迭奏埙篪理学渊源双接绪； 历南北宋并称邹鲁春官第甲六登墀。塘湾村郑伯熊三兄弟都是南宋进士。郑伯熊"德行夙成，尤邃经学，登绍兴第，历官国子司业，宗正少卿。

乞外，以龙图阁知宁国府。卒谥文肃，绍兴末，伊洛之学稍息，复于伯熊得之。弟伯英、（从弟）伯海皆知名，由是永嘉之学宗郑氏。有《郑景望集》"。（嘉靖《温州府志·人物》）伯英是隆兴癸未年（1163年）进士，著有《归愚集》。从弟伯海是绍兴辛未年（1151年）进士，设帐授徒，生徒常达五百人。

全祖望《宋元学案》说："乾淳之间，永嘉学者联袂成帷，然无不以先生兄弟为渠率。"伯熊弟子枫林人木待问为隆兴状元。此外，岙底上湾村有陈揆，登绍兴癸丑陈亮榜进士，与叶适相善，有诗集二十余卷、文集五卷传世。芙蓉村陈宝之，绍兴进士，从吕祖谦学，与陈亮为诗友，宗谱存"送陈同父"和"挽吕东莱"诗各一首。

同村又有陈虞之，咸淳元年（1265年）进士，响应文天祥号召，起兵勤王，率全村义士八百多人据守芙蓉峰抗元，全部殉难。乾隆《永嘉县志》记载，朱熹任两浙路常平盐茶公事的时候，曾到楠溪江来访问当地的理学家，先到岩头村访问门人"以理学鸣于世"的刘愈，说："过楠溪不识刘进之，如过洞庭不识桔。

"不巧没有见到，又去谢岙访问门人谢复经，再访溪口戴蒙、戴侗及蓬溪村李时靖，并在蓬溪留下了墨迹。楠溪江地区所处荒僻，却与当时的主流文化保持着这样密切的关系，达到这样的水平。学术带动了科举和仕进。从唐代到清代，历代进士中可以确认为楠溪江村子中人的总计至少有五十多位。

溪口村戴氏，豫章村胡氏，塘湾村郑氏，花坦村朱氏，苍坡村李氏，芙蓉村陈氏，都是"簪缨鹊起，甲第蝉联"的名门望族。

田父野老引以为乡土光荣的，是宋代豫章村一门三代五进士，溪口村戴氏一门四代六进士，花坦村朱氏和塘湾村郑氏的兄弟进士，枫林村有南宋隆兴元年（1163年）状元木待问。科甲盛，当官的自然多。

光绪《永嘉县志·人物》统计：永嘉县"自宋以来，位宰执者六人，侍从台谏五十余人，监司郡守百十余人，可谓盛矣。"其中芙蓉村在南宋就有过"十八金带"，便是有十八个人在临安当过朝中高官。宋代楠溪江科甲之盛，虽然和当时朝廷扩大科举录取名额有关，但晋、宋两次中原大乱，衣冠望族大量来到楠溪江流域安居更有不少的关系。

宋元、元明和明清三次易代都在楠溪江发生过战争，破坏严重，明代嘉靖之后，又遭倭寇侵扰。不过，元、明、清三朝，楠溪江文风依然尚有可观。元明之间，鹤垟村出了个谢德瑀，他"博通经史，为时名儒"，著有《狂斐集》、《家礼会通》等。同时的花坦村朱谧，著有《四书述义》、《四书补注》、《太极图说》、《西铭集》等，从祀郡庠。

豫章胡氏、鹤垟谢氏、岩头金氏、花坦朱氏、溪口戴氏这些望族，在明清两代还有过一些科举功名的成就。明代，胡氏出过一位中书舍人，戴氏出过一位御史，谢氏则出过一位锦衣卫指挥佥事。清代，豫章村《胡氏宗谱》康熙三十四年（1695年）的"旧序"说："至清鼎革，变起沧桑，兵燹之余，世家右族不无徙迁，集泽哀鸣，未能常聚。

"在这种情况下，学术和科名成绩大大落后了。整个清代将近三百年，值得一书的学术著述几乎没有。道光三十年（1850年）的《重修鹤垟谢氏宗谱序》夸耀谢氏在普遍衰落的情况下又出了两名进士道："至今犹想见谢家之门第，即为溪山之生色者，历久弗衰矣！" 楠溪江中游的岩头村有一条大约三百米长的遮雨廊，沿河而建，叫丽水街。

中段有一副楹联："萍风碧漾观鱼栏，柳浪翠泠闻莺廊"，很美。耕读生活培养出来的乡村知识分子，科场得意走上仕途的是少数，成为理学家的更是寥寥。他们大多留在村子里生活，自然成为上层文化的代表，与郡县官吏如明代的郡守何文渊和文林、清代的县令汤成烈一起，在乡里担起了"化民成俗"的责任。

文林制定了《族范》，作为各姓宗谱里必有的家法族规的范本。汤成烈在咸丰《县志》稿里写道："永嘉在宋有邹鲁之风，维时士大夫先达者多从二程朱子游，居乡恒以讲学为业，故能诱掖后进，式化乡闾，薰为善良，浸成风俗。户有弦诵，邑无巫觋，人怀忠信，女行贞洁，冠昏丧祭，厚薄适中，奢俭当礼。疾病不祷祈，婚配不听星命。岁时娱乐，弛张合宜，其于养生送死之制，盖秩如也。

自元而明，去古渐远，风尚亦漓，轨物废而邪说行，儒术衰而异端起，奁资盛而女溺，宴食腆而讼繁。疾病薄骨肉之亲，报赛侈鬼神之会。婚丧之仪非复曩制。至于上元灯火，端午竞渡，争奇炫彩，靡财奢费，略不顾惜。士女游观，靓妆华服，阗城溢郭，有司莫之能禁。"（见光绪《永嘉县志·风土》）他把过去风俗之好，归功于读书人向理学家学习，回家之后居乡讲学；把当时风俗之漓，归咎于"轨物废而儒术衰"。他寄希望于"士大夫"，也便是盼在乡知识分子来挽世风于既颓。

这时候，楠溪江中游古来文化比较领先的村落，已经有人从商，有些人"权子母，量出入，铢积寸累，握算持筹"。但是，许多乡贤士绅，还是保持了引领读书风气的传统。例如《棠川郑氏宗谱》记载，乡绅郑公谔"旷达多才，好稽古，善词赋，筑美室，置图书，列古画玩物以供清赏。读诵之暇，惟以弹琴栽花为乐。遇风日晴和，则汲泉煮茗，拂席开樽，与二三知己，啸傲于烟霞泉石间，不复知有人世荣辱事。且课子有程，义方之外，更以诗书陶镕其气质。

"明代嘉靖朝（1796—1820）岩头村的金九峰，"性闲静，每日闲坐一室，凡经史以及诸子百家书无不娴，而尤究心于星学，陶情音律。至于制艺歌词，皆其余事耳。……设绛帐以诲生徒，春风四座，化雨一庭，询是师儒领袖。"（《岩头金氏宗谱·九峰先生五旬寿序》）明代花坦村的朱伯清，"丰神秀逸，嗜学有文，不乐仕进，志存林壑……家事付之诸子，惟以文墨自娱。凡石、树、虫、鱼、水泉、花药之会心寓目者，咸属吟咏。

其间，遇风和日暖，角巾鹿裘，从以弟子，徘徊乎水光山色，拂云坐石，手挥丝桐，目送飞鸿，逍遥自乐。"（《珍川朱氏宗谱·伯清公珍川十咏序》）同村的朱谧，"读书好古，淳朴自持，利欲不能移其心，荣禄不足夺其志，孝以事亲，友以处弟"。

（《珍川朱氏宗谱·明义堂处士墓志铭》）以致《珍川朱氏宗谱》夸赞花坦村"秀士成群，多含英咀华之彦；古怀如晤，有庄襟老带之风，可谓文质彬彬，野处多秀者已。" 各村各姓的宗谱里所推崇的贤士们虽然都不求仕进而嗜学乐道，但这都是儒者"退则独善其身"的生活，而他们并没有忘记"达则既济天下"的抱负。

他们都关怀族中年轻人的仕途，不但自己设帐授徒，而且运用他们的影响力，促进宗族大兴办学之风。楠溪江大小血缘村落的族谱，都在《家训》或《族规》里规定子弟务必要读书。《岩头金氏宗谱·家规》写道："每岁延敦厚博学之士以教子弟，须重以学俸，隆以礼文，无失故家轨度。

子弟有质士堪上进而无力从学者，众当资以祠租曲成之。"在当时，读书的目的首先科考直取功名。《茗川胡氏大宗谱·田川胡氏义塾规》说："是以愿人文蔚起，高拔五桂之芳；门第常新，足兆三槐之瑞。……愿沼芹叠采，云路同登。"和各地一样，宗祠对子弟读书，赴考，中式之后各方打点等都由义田所出予以资助。

凡科举有成绩的，都能得到表彰。读书主要为了进仕，但不专为进仕。《珍川朱氏合族副谱》里有一篇《如在堂记》写道："使我拥书万卷，何减积粟千钟，然则后之子若孙，苟不忘此意，必将奋志诗书，骧首云逵，上以绳其祖武，下以贻厥孙谋，无忝先世科甲之荣，不振前朝理学之绪，则不惟有光于近祖，亦且善述乎大宗矣！"既要有科甲之荣，又要振理学之绪，目标比较宽阔。除了科甲和理学，读书还有更大的目的。

又是这个花坦村朱氏，在《珍川朱氏宗谱·族范盟辞》里写得明白："不学则夷乎物，学则可以立，故学不亦大乎。学者尽人事所以助乎天也。天设其伦，非学莫能敦；人有恒纪，非学莫能叙。贤者由学以明，不贤者废学以昏。大匠成室，材木盈前，程度去取而不乱者，由绳墨之素定。君子临事而不骇，制度而不扰者，非学安能定其心哉。是故学者君子之绳墨也。"乾隆《永嘉县志·学校》说到教育："此吏治所首重，民风所视以转移也。

"对文化教育的这种既深又宽的理解和热烈追求，给楠溪江的村子笼罩了一层浓浓的高远的生活理念。所以，楠溪江各村落对教育事业和子弟的要求很高。《鹤垟谢氏宗谱·义学条规》说："义学之设，原为国家树人至计，非以为后生习浮艳、取青紫而已也。凡系生徒，务须以《白鹿洞规》身体力行……凡肄业弟子，必须一举足疾徐，一语言进止，事事雍容审详，安雅冲和。

"义学是专为贫寒子弟办的公费学校，仍然强调取青紫之外还要讲究操守品行。要求身体力行的《白鹿洞规》，是南宋理学家朱熹于淳熙六年（1179年）为白鹿洞书院订下的学行规范。淳佑元年（1241年），宋理宗亲笔书写赐给太学生作为教规，于是通行天下，直至穷乡僻壤的农村义塾。它的纲领性内容是： 父子有亲，君臣有义，夫妇有别，长幼有序，朋友有信（右五教之目）。

博学之，审问之，慎思之，明辨之，笃行之（右为学之序）。言忠信，行笃敬，惩忿窒欲，迁善改过（右修身之要）。正其义不谋其利，明其道不计其功（右处事之要）。己所不欲，勿施于人，行有不得，反求诸己（右接物之要）。这个规范完全是关于修身养性的。和这个《白鹿洞书院规》相似而更详细且严格的，是明太祖给国子监建的"卧碑"，后来顺治九年（1653年）又补充了一部分，在全国官学推行。

所补充的有一条是："军民一切利病，不许生员上书陈言，如有一言建白，以违制论，黜革治罪。"贤才是不许论政的，只要议论过一句，便是有罪，要开除学籍。所以，农村的初级书塾具有两重性，一方面为求得科考成就，一方面为铸造未来知识分子的思想品格。这种教育的影响及于普通农民，乾隆《永嘉县志》记载，县丞何森为了平定民风强悍的楠溪江地区的动乱，措施之一是在枫林村办了一所"楠溪义学"。

宗族在《族规》里立的育人目标，和朝廷是完全一致的。乾隆《永嘉县志·学校》说，永嘉"乡闾社学，本古党庠术序，亦较他州为多"。楠溪江村落的学校，最基础的是社学和义塾，几乎村村都有，有些村且不止一处。社学、义塾以学习识字、计数为主，读些初级启蒙教材准备升学。

有些学行高卓的人，如明代岩头村的金九峰和花坦村的朱伯清，他们办的可能是私塾，既然以弟子从游于山光水色，并且"春风四座、化雨一庭，询是师儒领袖，"显然所教的已经不是蒙童。家塾、私塾所在往往是住宅的一部分，通常为一个别院，如芙蓉村西端的司马第，家塾在大宅前北侧独立的小花园里。比较高级的教育则由书院来承担。

楠溪江最早的书院之一，溪口村的东山书院，是南宋进士、曾任太子讲读的著名理学家戴蒙辞官之后办的，由于成绩斐然，皇上赐额"明文"。明代主持朱垟村白岩书院的朱广文和主持花坦村凤南书院的朱墨臞，都是当地著名的学者，颇有著述。

墨臞的学生王瓒于弘治九年（1496年）中进士一甲二名，曾任两京国子祭酒、礼部侍郎，也有著作问世。明孝宗因此亲书"溪山第一"匾赐给朱墨臞。豫章村明代的石马书院也得退休还乡的中书公胡宗韫来论学题诗。此外，花坦村还有西园书院，芙蓉村中心有芙蓉书院，等等。

书院都有自己专用的独立的建筑。这些书院的水平，大都以主持的山长而变，一旦任山长的学者不再能教学，后继乏人，便会沦落为普通的学塾。在康熙《温州府志》里，竟已将溪口村的明文书院称为菰田塾，"所以启童蒙也"。楠溪江中游芙蓉村的中心芙蓉池，它边上的芙蓉书院，面向东。

它的大门开在北侧墙的前端，靠村子的主街如意街。进门小院里左手有"半亩方塘"，右手有一道棂星门式的仪门，门前有桅杆一对。进仪门，隔院子是明伦堂，堂前有杏坛，仿孔子讲学处，坛宽3.2米，长6.4米，略高于周边地面。明伦堂的后院有一座讲堂。明伦堂和讲堂都是三开间的。

这一路通长52米，宽12.8米，布局很规矩。讲堂前檐廊右（南）端开腰门通花园，山长的三间住宅在花园里，面东。花园很大，有水渠、有土丘、有石假山，树木和翠竹长得郁郁葱葱。由宗族公建而规模比较大或者层次比较高的书院，一般都选址在风景最佳的地方。豫章村的石马书院，位于"渠口寨山之麓，后枕高岳石壁，下临溪流深渊"。

塘湾村的栳甡甡书院造在屏风岩侧，"岩后百武许有小瀑布，……下有重磨岩。"因此，各地的"十景"、"八景"，大多有一景甚至两景和书院有关系。书塾的建设和管理一般由宗族负责，乡绅们常常是主持人。

《茗川胡氏大宗谱·东山书塾记》生动地记述了这种情况："茗屿胡氏旧有读书楼，在居之东，极其幽静……尝延师以诲子弟，由是族属衣冠济济，咸知以礼律身……（后读书楼废，文运遂衰）嘉靖癸丑仲至冬日，源泉、乔西二公谋于众曰：……今宜续建精舍，以陶后进，庶几书香不泯，愿克肖者听。皆曰善。于是改卜地于东山之屏……期年而舍成……望之岿然，名之曰东山书塾。

量出田租若干石，以为累岁延师教育之费。" 楠溪江村落另三类比较重要的文教建筑是文昌阁、文峰塔和牌楼。它们虽然和科举制度有关，但已经远远超脱了科举之上了。

文昌阁祭祀文昌帝君，文昌帝君主管人间功名，因此受到普遍祭祀。在楠溪江的廊下、花坦、岩头、水云各村，都曾有过文昌阁。

它们通常和书塾、书院相呼应或内有堂庑作为书塾、书院的讲堂。因为关系到科举成就，也就是关系到宗族的兴衰，所以宗族都以兴建文昌阁为大事，也成为乡绅们的善举之一。《珍川朱氏合谱·慎轩公传》记载朱光润捐赀在花坦村"创建文阁……经营结构，鸟革翚飞。

"主体是一幢两层楼阁，两庑用作书院讲堂，"珍川之胜，于此称第一焉"。文昌阁大多造于村外的"水口"，即村子所在的小盆地内地表水聚合后流出盆地的隘口。

由于风水师简单地认为中国的地势是西北高而东南低，"此天地之大势也"，所以村子的选址多在隘口的西北，以致水口大多在村子的东南方，即巽方。水口往往山丘夹岸，树木茂盛，风景美好。

如岩头村的文昌阁，创建于乾隆庚申年（1740年），位于全楠溪江流域最大的乡土园林的南端、汤山的北麓，在园林主体建筑塔湖庙（孝祐庙）的西侧，前临智水湖，左傍一条水量丰沛的小溪。阁背后较高处有一座文峰塔。

由于环境优美，所以楠溪江两岸村子的"十景"、"八景"里常有一景是文昌阁或书院，为文人们吟咏的对象。鹤垟村的书院叫"环翠楼"，"八景"里有"环翠书声"："幽阁崚嶒碧树荣，琅琅中有读书声，半空掷地金钱解，五岳朝天玉佩鸣。

"花坦村的《十景诗》里有《文昌登眺》二首，其一："杰阁凌云起，溪山入眼奇……游身图画里，俯仰展须眉。"其二："……竹疏风弄影，花暗鸟鸣阴，古树浮波静，空潭落月深……" 文峰塔起源于风水迷信，认为科甲不利的村子，在甲、巽、丙、丁的方位上造一座塔或立一支文笔，便可以振兴文运。

一般以造在巽位上的为多，因为水口建筑群也大多在村外的巽位上，文峰塔和水口建筑群相表里，更为生色。楠溪江流域层峦起伏，都是火山流纹岩，经过亿万年的侵蚀，有不少圆锥形的山峰。

风水术数上可以认它们为"文笔"，所以这里人造的文峰塔不多，仅岩头村和塘湾村各有一座。岩头村的文峰塔是明代桂林公（金氏）于嘉靖年间（1522—1566）建造的，和水亭书院、森秀轩同时。

它位于村子东南端文昌阁后面的山坡上，全用灰白色大理石筑成，从残石看，塔可能为七层楼阁式，高仅四米左右。村子里的文人们常在风景佳丽之地造幽斋读书。岩头村的金氏桂林公便把塔湖庙的斋堂改建成了书斋森秀轩，背对右军池，面向镇南湖。桂林公诗《题森秀轩·其二》中有两联： 门植垂堤陶公柳，院开洗砚右军池； 谈棋石磴风频至，烹茗松轩月上时。斋里的文化生活品味很高。

水亭书院、森秀轩、文峰塔、文昌阁、戏台和右军池等一起形成了岩头村的文化建筑群落。

塘湾村的《十景诗》之一咏"巽吉山"云："耸然特立一高峰，恰位东南秀气钟；巽吉更加崇宝塔，文风焕发笔游龙。"这座文峰塔是造在山上的，山便在村子的巽方，即东南方。有些文士乡绅则在住宅里营造书香气。

明代初年洪武、永乐间（1368—1424），鹤垟村有一位谢德玹，家里有一间书斋，濒临澄江。他自制《临水书斋》诗： 碧流湛湛涵长天，小斋横枕清堪怜， 牙签插架三万轴，灯火照窗二十年。长日尘埃飞不到，常时风月闲无边， 已知圣道犹如此，乐处寻来即自然。同村同宗谢廷循，宣德年间（1426—1435）曾供职于锦衣卫，晚年在故乡旧宅里造了一幢静乐轩，宗谱写道："士大夫与之游者，皆为赋静乐之诗"。

连宣宗皇帝也写了一首《静乐诗》赠他："暮色动前轩，重城欲闭门。残霞收赤气，新月破黄昏。已觉乾坤静，都无市井喧。阴阳有恒理，斯与达人论。" 谢廷循的朋友，豫章村的胡宗韫，明代宣德时任中书舍人，归田时同僚赠诗送行，有句："诛茆今日野，把钓旧时溪。晒药晴檐短，安书夜榻低。"（陈斌）以及"烟霞三亩宅，霜露百年心，黄菊陶潜兴，清风梁父吟。"（陈中）胡宗韫回乡后在故宅"中翰第"造了一座紫微楼作为颐养之所。

《豫章胡氏宗谱》写他："植竹种花，终日坐卧其间，时临墨迹，随兴吟诗，优游自乐，或与密友笑谈、围棋、饮酒，如是二十余年"。这些乡间知识分子所标榜、所追求的生活方式，"超脱于物，求之在心"的态度，对乡土文化生活不可能不产生引领的作用。楠溪江流域的文教建筑里，还有一种比较重要的，是牌楼。光绪《永嘉县志·古迹》里写到坊表，说："古人志厥宅里，树之风声，可法可传，政教攸系。

"楠溪江人对牌楼的教化作用是很重视的，一般造得很讲究，位置在宗祠或村门近旁，成为村落礼制中心的一部分。花坦村的牌楼最多也最壮美。明代英宗正统年间（1436—1449），在大宗祠敦睦堂正门前左右侧为兵科给事中朱良暹各建了一座牌楼，相对而立，东边一座额"乌府"，西边一座额"黄门"。

面对着敦睦堂，又有一座牌楼，题额"奕世簪缨"，为明代嘉靖（1522—1566）进士朱腆立。它和"乌府"、"黄门"两座牌楼形成品字，在敦睦堂前围出一个小小空场，给大宗祠增添了气色。这种品字形的布局多流行于城乡之文风较盛者。

"黄门"牌楼西侧，沿大路又有"乡贤"牌楼，明代正德朝（1506—1521）温州知府何文渊为学政朱思宁立。再西侧为"钟秀"牌楼，是明代嘉靖朝朱腆中举人时所立。

再西为嘉靖丙寅（1566年）冬永嘉知县程文著为朱双溪立，题额"公直谆良"。再西为"翕和"牌楼，是乡绅西华王公为朱莲溪立，大约也在明代晚期。大路上最后一座牌楼是"溪山第一"牌楼，为乡进士知凤阳县令朱义川立，朱腆书匾。

这座牌楼就是花坦村的西门。另外还有一座"宪台"牌楼，在村中央宪台祠堂大门前正中，是明代弘治乙丑年（1505年）温州知府李端、永嘉知县刘经为工部给事中朱良以立的。在西园书院里又有"鸢飞鱼跃"牌楼，是中书舍人周令为朱幽独建的。

以上这些牌楼，都是为表彰一些读书中了科甲又当了官的人，目的在于荣耀宗族，激励后人。另有邑令伍公为朱小山立的"为公宣力"牌楼（朱小山的身份、事绩不见记载）和明末崇祯已巳（1629年）巡按使徐吉公为节妇邵孺人立的"松柏寒贞"牌楼，只见于宗谱，已在"文化大革命"中拆毁，不知位置何在。

岩头村有一座牌楼，是明世宗赐给大理寺左寺右寺副、后来迁任瑞州知府金昭的。这座牌楼和花坦村的宪台牌楼风格近似，都是四柱四楼式，斗拱雄大，制度近于宋式，实在很难得。

楠溪江流域两千多平方公里的范围，文教如此发达，却又长期不闻于世，它提供了一个很典型的江南纯农业地区乡土社会文教状态的实例，也很典型地叙说了乡土社会文教建筑兴建的背景、动力、追求、环境和风貌。

2.

Farming-Reading Life: Nanxi River Villages Replacing the hereditary aristocratic system with the imperial examination system, for rural society, at least promoted the widespread普及 and great improvement of cultural education, and further enhanced overall rural construction.

On one hand, common people gained relatively fair opportunities to enter officialdom,激发 youth to study diligently to enter the upper social stratum; on the other hand, official positions were not lifelong—after their term, officials had to retire, and many returned to the countryside, bringing knowledge and experience back to rural areas, contributing to rural construction, cultural education, and even economic development.

The cultural-educational state of rural society in China's agrarian era can be examined through the village cluster in the middle reaches of Nanxi River, Yongjia County, Zhejiang Province.

This is an ordinary mountainous region, long unknown to the world, but highly typical of China's vast countryside.The Nanxi River main stream is 145 km long, with a drainage area of 2,429 sq km and over 260 villages.

Villagers mainly practice rice agriculture; due to favorable natural conditions, they have no worries about food and clothing, but relying solely on "rising at sunrise, resting at sunset," the economy could not develop.

Until the early 1990s, most villages had no shops—buying needles, thread, matches, candles depended on occasional peddlers.Yet in this leisurely life of "wind every five days, rain every ten, what has the emperor's power to do with me?

" they never forgot reading to understand principle, nor could they let go of the exam ambition of "morning a farm boy, evening ascending the Son of Heaven's hall." Yongjia was developed late.

In late Western Jin, central China was in chaos; migrating central plains aristocrats transformed Ou-Yue culture with advanced culture, and the middle Nanxi River began a new history.

In Eastern Jin, Yongjia Commandery was established, with the Nanxi River basin under its jurisdiction.

Due to the concentration of cultural figures on the right bank of the Yangtze, the newly established Yongjia Commandery, during the Six Dynasties, was fortunate to have several brilliant stars of Chinese cultural history serve as commandery governors: Eastern Jin great writer and calligrapher Wang Xizhi; Liu-Song historian Pei Songzhi (annotator of Records of the Three Kingdoms); metaphysical poet and rhapsodist Sun Chuo; poet, parallel prose writer, and literary theorist Yan Yanzhi; China's first landscape poet Xie Lingyun; and Xiao-Liang writer and parallel prose master Qiu Chi.

These cultural elites of the time took "assisting human relations, completing moral transformation" (助人伦，成教化) as the highest ideal of governance.

Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer quotes the Old Gazetteer: "When Jin established the commandery city, population grew; Wang Youjun (Wang Xizhi) guided with culture and education, Xie Kangle (Xie Lingyun) continued—people then knew the right direction; from then on every family pursued learning, and by Song it became a 'little Zou-Lu' (hometown of Confucius and Mencius).

" It also says: "Wang Xizhi governed with kindness and benevolence; Xie Lingyun recruited scholars to advance learning—hence people knew to study, and local customs changed.

" Wang-Xie elegance cultivated Nanxi River's rich humanistic atmosphere.

Late Ming-early Qing poet Mei Diaoyuan wrote a poem "Wang-Xie Shrine" in Yongjia: Former governors Wang and Xie, their desolate shrine leans by the commandery city; Through a thousand years their calligraphy's wonder passed, six dynasties excelled in poetic fame.

The ancient pond still has geese bathing, spring grass grows by the pond; Elegance is an ancient and modern matter, looking up and down one feels emotion.Nanxi River's most brilliant cultural peak was in Southern Song.

Central plains aristocrats again migrated south on a large scale; like Eastern Jin, the refuge region became culturally rich.

Those serving as Wenzhou's "top officials"—Zhang Jiucheng, Wang Shipeng, Lou Yue, Yang Jian—were all outstanding talents of the time.

Zhang Jiucheng wrote in his "Memorandum": "Yongjia is a land of morality, sages follow one after another; though predecessors have passed, their elegance remains.

" They all took ritual-music education as the first priority of governance, greatly raising Yongjia's cultural level.

Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer · Schools says: "Yongjia in Song produced famous worthies one after another; those entering the halls of Luo (Cheng Hao/Cheng Yi) and Min (Zhu Xi) followed one after another, lush and refined—called 'little Zou-Lu,' how prosperous!

" Yongjia had 13 Cheng-school disciples in Northern Song, 16 Zhu-school disciples in Southern Song.

In the Imperial Academy, Yongjia natives successively included the "Nine Yuanfeng Gentlemen" and "Six Chunxi Gentlemen," "all transmitting Cheng-Zhu learning through moral nature.

" (See Qianlong Yongjia County Gazetteer · Customs) The "Yongjia School" of Neo-Confucianism formed in Southern Song, represented by Xue Jixuan, Chen Fuliang, Zheng Boxiong, and Ye Shi—Zheng and Ye were Nanxi River natives.

Zheng Boxiong was originally from Tangwan Village; Ye Shi was raised and studied by the Jin clan in Yantou Village in childhood (see Yantou Jin Clan Genealogy).

Xikou Village's Dai clan: in Northern Song, Dai Shu [jinshi of Yuanfu 3 (1100)] and Dai Xun brothers studied under the Two Chengs.

In Southern Song, Dai Shu's son Dai Xu (Jiading jinshi), a student of Ye Shi, authored Five Classics Commentary, Disputations of Masters, Essentials of the Eastern Capital, etc.

Dai Xun's son Dai Xi [jinshi of Chunxi 5 (1178)], according to Jiajing Wenzhou Prefecture Gazetteer · Figures, "from Ministry of Rites director, through six promotions became Crown Prince's Supervisor, concurrently Imperial Library Director.

The Crown Prince Jingxian ordered him to compile commentaries on Changes, Poetry, Documents, Spring and Autumn, Analects, Mencius, Comprehensive Mirror for Governance.

Acting Minister of Works, appointed Wenge Academician; posthumously granted Duanming Palace Academician, posthumous name Wenduan.

The Crown Prince personally wrote 'Understanding Classics' plaque for his hall; he has Muyin Collection.Emperor Ningzong called him 'the patriarch of all Confucians.

'" Ye Shi evaluated Dai Xi: "A rare talent under heaven from youth, in this age no more than a few.

" Dai Xi's nephew Dai Meng [jinshi of Shaoxing Gengxu (1190)] studied under Zhu Xi at Wuyi, authored Family Commentaries on Changes, Documents, Four Books, and Six Books Explained, etc.

Dai Meng's eldest son Dai Zai, not seeking office, authored Supplements to Classics, Supplements to Comprehensive Mirror, Saying Forest Collection, etc.

Meng's second son Dai Tong [jinshi of Chunyou Xinchou (1241)] authored Six Books and various miscellaneous collections.

This Dai clan's scholarly achievements were extraordinary; Xikou Dai's main ancestral hall has a couplet: Entering Cheng-Zhu's gate, playing xun and chi in succession, Neo-Confucian origins doubly connected; Through Northern and Southern Song, called Zou-Lu together, six times topped the spring official examination.

Tangwan Village's Zheng Boxiong three brothers were all Southern Song jinshi.

Zheng Boxiong "virtue formed early, especially deep in classical learning; passed Shaoxing exam, served as Imperial Academy Director, Imperial Clan Court Vice Minister.

Requested external post, served as Ningguo Prefect with Longtuge rank.Posthumous name Wensu.In late Shaoxing, Yi-Luo learning had somewhat declined, revived through Boxiong.

Brother Boying and (cousin) Bohai were both famous—hence Yongjia learning followed the Zheng clan.Has Zheng Jingwang Collection.

" (Jiajing Wenzhou Prefecture Gazetteer · Figures) Boying was jinshi of Longxing Guiwei (1163), authored Guiyu Collection.

Cousin Bohai was jinshi of Shaoxing Xinwei (1151), taught disciples, often reaching 500 students.

Quan Zuwang's Song-Yuan Learning Cases says: "During Qianchun period, Yongjia scholars lined up like curtains, yet all followed these brothers as leaders.

" Boxiong's disciple, Fenglin native Mu Daiwen, became Longxing zhuangyuan (first-place jinshi).

Additionally, Aodi Shangwan Village had Chen Kui, jinshi of Shaoxing Guichou (Chen Liang's list), friendly with Ye Shi, with over 20 volumes of poetry and 5 volumes of prose surviving.

Furong Village's Chen Baozhi, Shaoxing jinshi, studied under Lü Zuqian, was a poetry friend of Chen Liang; genealogy preserves poems "Sending Chen Tongfu" and "Mourning Lü Donglai.

" Same village had Chen Yuzhi, jinshi of Xianchun 1 (1265), responding to Wen Tianxiang's call, raised troops to aid the throne, led over 800 village righteous men to defend Furong Peak against Yuan, all died martyrs.

Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer records that when Zhu Xi served as Liangzhe Circuit salt-tea commissioner, he visited Nanxi River to consult local Neo-Confucians: first to Yantou Village to visit disciple Liu Yu, "renowned for Neo-Confucian learning," saying: "Passing Nanxi without knowing Liu Jinzhi is like passing Dongting without knowing oranges.

" Unfortunately not meeting him, he went to Xie'ao to visit disciple Xie Fujing, then visited Xikou's Dai Meng, Dai Tong, and Pengxi Village's Li Shijing, leaving calligraphy in Pengxi.

Nanxi River region, though remote, maintained such close relations with mainstream culture and reached such a level.Scholarship drove examinations and official careers.

From Tang to Qing, at least 50+ jinshi can be confirmed as Nanxi River village natives.

Xikou Dai, Yuzhang Hu, Tangwan Zheng, Huatan Zhu, Cangpo Li, Furong Chen—all were "official hats rising like magpies, top degrees following one after another" prominent clans.

What farmers and elders took as local glory: Song-era Yuzhang Village had three generations of five jinshi in one clan; Xikou Dai had four generations of six jinshi; Huatan Zhu and Tangwan Zheng had brother jinshi; Fenglin Village had Southern Song Longxing 1 (1163) zhuangyuan Mu Daiwen.

With prosperous exams, many became officials.Guangxu's Yongjia County Gazetteer · Figures statistics: Yongjia County "since Song, six served as grand councilors, over 50 as attendants/censors, over 100 as circuit supervisors/prefects—how prosperous!

" Among them, Furong Village in Southern Song had "Eighteen Gold Belts"—eighteen people served as high court officials in Lin'an.

Song-era Nanxi River's exam prosperity, though related to the court expanding exam quotas, was more related to the two great central plains chaos (Jin and Song) bringing aristocratic clans to settle in the Nanxi River basin.

Three dynastic changes (Song-Yuan, Yuan-Ming, Ming-Qing) all brought war to Nanxi River, causing severe destruction; after Ming Jiajing, it also suffered wokou raids.

Nevertheless, in Yuan, Ming, Qing, Nanxi River's literary culture remained notable.

Between Yuan and Ming, Heyang Village produced Xie Deyu, "broadly versed in classics and history, a famous Confucian of the time," authoring Kuangfei Collection, Family Rituals Compendium, etc.

Contemporary Huatan Village's Zhu Mi authored Four Books Expounded, Four Books Supplements, Taiji Diagram Commentary, Western Inscription Collection, etc., enshrined in the prefectural school.

Yuzhang Hu, Heyang Xie, Yantou Jin, Huatan Zhu, Xikou Dai—these prominent clans still had some exam success in Ming-Qing.

In Ming, Hu produced a Zhongshu Sheren (palace secretary), Dai produced a censor, Xie produced a Brocade Guard commander.

In Qing, Yuzhang Village's Hu Clan Genealogy (Kangxi 34, 1695) "old preface" says: "To the Qing dynastic change, chaos arose; after war's destruction, prominent clans migrated, gathered in sorrow, unable to always gather.

" Under these conditions, scholarly and exam achievement greatly declined.In nearly 300 years of Qing, almost no scholarly works worth recording.

Daoguang 30 (1850) "Preface to Rebuilding Heyang Xie Clan Genealogy" boasted that Xie, amid general decline, produced two more jinshi: "To this day one can still imagine the Xie clan's status, bringing color to the streams and mountains, enduring without decline!

" Yantou Village in middle Nanxi River has a ~300m rain corridor along the river, called Lishui Street.

Its middle section has a couplet: "Duckweed wind green ripples viewing fish railings; willow waves green cold hearing orioles corridor"—very beautiful.

Rural intellectuals cultivated by farming-reading life: few succeeded in exams and entered official careers, even fewer became Neo-Confucians.

Most stayed in villages, naturally becoming representatives of upper culture, and together with county officials—like Ming prefects He Wenyuan and Wen Lin, Qing magistrate Tang Chenglie—shouldered the responsibility of "transforming people and forming customs" (化民成俗) in the countryside.

Wen Lin established Clan Norms as a model for family rules in all clan genealogies.

Tang Chenglie wrote in Xianfeng's Gazetteer draft: "Yongjia in Song had Zou-Lu ethos; then scholar-official pioneers mostly studied with Two Chengs and Zhu Xi, living in villages always engaged in teaching—hence they could guide later generations, transform villages, cultivate goodness, form customs.

Every household had stringed recitation, no shamans in the county; people cherished loyalty and trust, women practiced chastity; capping, marriage, funeral, sacrifice—moderate in thickness, appropriate in luxury and frugality.

Illness not prayed for, marriage not guided by astrology.Seasonal entertainment, relaxation and tension appropriate; systems for nurturing the living and sending off the dead were orderly.

From Yuan to Ming, farther from antiquity, customs also declined; norms abandoned and heterodoxies spread, Confucianism declined and异端 arose; dowry wealth increased and female infanticide, banquets lavish and lawsuits numerous.

Illness estranged flesh-and-blood, sacrifices extravagantly honored spirits.Marriage and funeral rituals no longer followed old systems.

As for Lantern Festival lights, Dragon Boat boat races—competing in splendor, wasting wealth, no regard.Men and women sightseeing, in makeup and fine clothes, filling cities—officials could not prohibit.

" (See Guangxu Yongjia County Gazetteer · Local Conditions) He attributed past good customs to scholars studying Neo-Confucianism and returning to teach in villages; attributed current decline to "norms abandoned and Confucianism declined.

" He placed hope in "scholar-officials"—expecting village intellectuals to reverse declining customs.

At this time, villages in middle Nanxi River with historically leading culture already had some people going into commerce, some "weighing principal and interest, measuring income and expenditure, accumulating penny by penny, holding abacus and tallies.

" But many local worthies and gentry still maintained the tradition of leading reading culture.E.g.

, Tangchuan Zheng Clan Genealogy records local gentleman Zheng Gong'e: "Broad and talented, fond of antiquity, skilled in rhapsody; built a fine house, placed books, displayed ancient paintings and curios for refined appreciation.

Between reading, only took joy in playing qin and planting flowers.

On fine days, drew spring water to brew tea, opened mats and wine cups, with two or three close friends, proudly roaming among mist, clouds, springs and rocks, no longer knowing worldly honor or shame.

And teaching sons with schedule, beyond proper guidance, further refined their temperament with poetry and books.

" Ming Jiajing era (1796–1820) Yantou Village's Jin Jiufeng: "By nature quiet and still, daily sitting alone in a room; all classics, histories, and masters' hundred schools books none not familiar, especially devoted to astrology, finding joy in music.

As for examination essays and lyrics—all mere side matters...Set up a red curtain to teach students, spring breeze filling four seats, transforming rain filling one courtyard—truly a leader among teacher-Confucians.

" (Yantou Jin Clan Genealogy · Preface to Mr.Jiufeng's Fiftieth Birthday) Ming Huatan Village's Zhu Boqing: "Handsome and elegant, fond of learning with literary talent, not seeking official advancement, ambition in forests and ravines...

family affairs entrusted to sons, only amusing himself with writing and ink.All rocks, trees, insects, fish, springs, flowers that caught heart and eye—all became subjects of chanting.

Among these, on warm sunny days, in square scarf and deerskin robe, with disciples following, wandering among water-light and mountain-color, brushing clouds, sitting on rocks, waving silk tong, watching flying geese—carefree and self-content.

" (Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Genealogy · Preface to Boqing's Ten Chants of Zhenchuan) Same village's Zhu Mi: "Reading and loving antiquity, simple and self-sustaining, profit and desire could not move his heart, glory and salary could not seize his will; filial to parents, friendly to brothers.

" (Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Genealogy · Epitaph of Mingyi Hall Gentleman) Hence Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Genealogy praises Huatan Village: "Talented scholars in groups, many with refined beauty; ancient spirit as if meeting, with dignified bearing and old-style grace—truly cultured and refined, the countryside abounds in worthy men.

" Worthies praised in various clan genealogies, though not seeking official advancement but loving learning and the Way, all lived the Confucian "in retirement, cultivate oneself" (退则独善其身) life—but they never forgot the ambition of "in success, benefit all under heaven" (达则济天下).

They all cared for young clansmen's official careers: not only teaching disciples themselves, but using their influence to promote clans' vigorous school-founding.

All Nanxi River blood-relation village genealogies stipulate in Family Instructions or Clan Rules that children must study.

Yantou Jin Clan Genealogy · Clan Rules writes: "Each year hire honest and learned scholars to teach children; must pay generous salaries, honor with ritual and culture, not losing old family standards.

Children of talent capable of advancement but lacking means to study—all should support with ancestral hall rents to help them succeed." At the time, reading's primary purpose was exam success and official rank.

Mingchuan Hu Main Clan Genealogy · Tianchuan Hu Charitable School Rules says: "Hence we wish for literary talent to rise, highly plucking the fragrance of five cassias; family gates ever new, foretelling the auspiciousness of three locusts...

May the marsh celery be repeatedly gathered, cloud paths ascended together.

" Like everywhere, ancestral halls funded children's study, exam travel, and post-success expenses from charitable fields; all with exam success received commendation.

Reading mainly for official advancement, but not exclusively for it.Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Combined Genealogy has "Record of Ruzai Hall": "If I hold ten thousand books, how is that less than storing a thousand bushels of grain?

Then later descendants, if not forgetting this intent, will surely strive in poetry and books, gallop to cloud paths—above continuing ancestors' footsteps, below leaving plans for grandchildren; not disgracing ancestors' exam glory, reviving former dynasty's Neo-Confucian legacy—then not only bringing glory to recent ancestors, but also well continuing the great clan!

" Both exam glory and Neo-Confucian revival—broader goals.Beyond exams and Neo-Confucianism, reading had an even greater purpose.

Again this Huatan Zhu clan, in Zhenchuan Zhu Clan Genealogy · Clan Norms Oath, writes clearly: "Without learning, one is like a thing; with learning, one can stand—so is learning not great?The learner exhausts human affairs to assist heaven.

Heaven established human relations—without learning none can be earnest; people have constant order—without learning none can arrange.The wise become clear through learning; the unwise become dull through abandoning learning.

A great master building a house, timber filling the front, measuring and selecting without confusion—because the ink-line was set beforehand.

The gentleman facing affairs without alarm, managing systems without disturbance—without learning how could his heart be settled?Hence learning is the gentleman's ink-line.

" Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer · Schools says of education: "This is the first priority of governance, what local customs look to for transformation.

" This deep and broad understanding and passionate pursuit of cultural education enveloped Nanxi River villages in a lofty life philosophy.Hence Nanxi River villages had high demands for education and children.

Heyang Xie Clan Genealogy · Charitable School Regulations says: "Charitable schools were established for the nation's utmost plan of nurturing people—not merely for youth to learn flowery style and gain official rank.

All students must practice the White Deer Grotto Rules personally...All studying disciples must have measured steps, measured speech and conduct—everything dignified and careful, peaceful and refined.

" Charitable schools were public schools for poor children, yet still emphasized character beyond official rank.

The White Deer Grotto Rules, required personal practice, were established by Southern Song Neo-Confucian Zhu Xi in Chunxi 6 (1179) for White Deer Grotto Academy.

In Chunyou 1 (1241), Emperor Lizong personally wrote them and granted to Imperial Academy students as teaching regulations—hence they spread nationwide, even to remote rural charitable schools.

Their纲领 content: Father and son have affection; sovereign and minister have righteousness; husband and wife have distinction; elder and younger have order; friends have trust (right: five teachings' aims).

Learn broadly, inquire carefully, think cautiously, distinguish clearly, practice earnestly (right: learning's sequence).

Speak with loyalty and trust, act with earnestness and respect; restrain anger and curb desire; move toward good and correct faults (right: self-cultivation's essentials).

Uphold righteousness without seeking profit; clarify the Way without counting merit (right: handling affairs' essentials).

Do not do to others what you do not wish for yourself; when actions fail, seek within yourself (right: interacting with things' essentials).This regulation is entirely about self-cultivation.

Similar but more detailed and strict than White Deer Grotto Academy Rules was the "Lying Stele" (卧碑) established by Ming Taizu for the Imperial Academy; later Shunzhi 9 (1653) supplemented part,推行 nationwide in official schools.

One supplemented clause: "All military and civilian advantages and harms—students are forbidden to submit written opinions; if one word of proposal is made, treated as violating regulations, expelled and punished.

" Talents were forbidden from discussing politics—even one word of discussion was a crime, expulsion from school.

Hence rural elementary schools had a dual nature: on one hand for exam achievement, on one hand for shaping future intellectuals' ideological character.This education's influence reached ordinary farmers.

Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer records that county assistant He Sen, to pacify unrest in the tough-customed Nanxi River region, one measure was founding a "Nanxi Charitable School" in Fenglin Village.

Clans' educational goals in Clan Rules were完全 consistent with the court.Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer · Schools says Yongjia "village community schools, following ancient village and district schools, are also more than other prefectures.

" Nanxi River village schools: most basic are community schools and charitable schools, almost every village has them, some villages more than one.

Community and charitable schools mainly teach literacy and counting, reading elementary primers to prepare for advancement.

Some people of high learning and conduct, like Ming Yantou Village's Jin Jiufeng and Huatan Village's Zhu Boqing, may have run private schools—since disciples wandered with them amid mountain and water scenery, and "spring breeze filling four seats, transforming rain filling one courtyard, truly teacher-Confucian leaders"—clearly they taught beyond young children.

Family and private schools were often part of a residence, usually a separate courtyard—e.g., Furong Village's western Sima Mansion, family school in an independent small garden north of the main house.

Higher-level education was undertaken by academies.

One of Nanxi River's earliest academies, Xikou Village's Dongshan Academy, was founded after Southern Song jinshi and famous Neo-Confucian Dai Meng (former Crown Prince lecturer) resigned from office; due to outstanding results, the emperor granted the plaque "Mingwen" (Clear Literature).

Ming-era Zhu Guangwen, heading Zhuyang Village's Baiyan Academy, and Zhu Moqu, heading Huatan Village's Fengnan Academy, were both famous local scholars with writings.

Moqu's student Wang Zan became jinshi first-rank second place in Hongzhi 9 (1496), served as both capitals' Imperial Academy director and Ministry of Rites vice minister, also with writings.

Emperor Xiaozong hence personally wrote "Xishan First" (溪山第一) plaque for Zhu Moqu.Yuzhang Village's Ming-era Shima Academy also had retired Zhongshu Sheren Hu Zongyun come to discuss learning and compose poetry.

Additionally, Huatan Village had Xiyuan Academy, Furong Village center had Furong Academy, etc.Academies all had their own dedicated independent buildings.

These academies' levels mostly varied with their presiding shanzhang (academy head); once the presiding scholar could no longer teach, with no successor, they declined to ordinary schools.

In Kangxi's Wenzhou Prefecture Gazetteer, Xikou Village's Mingwen Academy was already called Gutian School, "for enlightening young children.

" Furong Academy, beside Furong Pool at the center of Furong Village in middle Nanxi River, faces east.Its main gate opens at the front of the north wall, by the village's main street Ruyi Street.

Entering the small courtyard: left has "Half-Mu Square Pond" (半亩方塘), right has a Lingxing Gate-style ceremonial gate, with a pair of flagpoles before it.

Entering the ceremonial gate, across the courtyard is Minglun Hall (明伦堂); before it is an Apricot Altar (杏坛), imitating Confucius's teaching place—altar 3.2m wide, 6.4m long, slightly higher than surrounding ground.

Minglun Hall's rear courtyard has a lecture hall.Both Minglun Hall and lecture hall are three-bay.This entire axis is 52m long, 12.8m wide, layout very regular.

The lecture hall's front eave corridor right (south) end opens a side door to the garden; the shanzhang's three-bay residence is in the garden, facing east.

The garden is large, with water channels, earthen mounds, rockery, trees and bamboo growing lushly.Academies publicly built by clans, of larger scale or higher level, were generally sited in the most scenic locations.

Yuzhang Village's Shima Academy is located "at the foot of Qukou Zhai Mountain, backed by high cliff, overlooking deep stream abyss.

" Tangwan Village's Laoshengshen Academy was built beside Pingfeng Rock: "behind the rock about a hundred paces there is a small waterfall...below there is Chongmo Rock.

" Hence various places' "Ten Scenes," "Eight Scenes" mostly have one or even two scenes related to academies.School construction and management were generally the clan's responsibility, with local gentry often as directors.

Mingchuan Hu Main Clan Genealogy · Record of Dongshan School vividly records this: "Mingyu Hu clan formerly had a Reading Tower, east of the residences, extremely quiet...

once hired teachers to teach children, hence clan members dressed as officials, all knowing to discipline themselves with ritual...

(later Reading Tower fell into disuse, literary fortune declined) Jiajing Guichou mid-winter day, Yuanquan and Qiaoxi two gentlemen proposed to all: ...

now we should continue building a refined lodge to cultivate later generations, so that book fragrance does not die out—those willing to follow may listen.All said good.Hence chose land at Dongshan's screen...after a year the lodge was completed...

looking majestic, named Dongshan School.Set aside several shi of field rent as annual teacher-hiring and education expenses.

" Three other important types of cultural-educational buildings in Nanxi River villages are Wenchang Pavilions (文昌阁), Wenfeng Pagodas (文峰塔), and memorial archways (牌楼).

Though related to the exam system, they have far transcended it.Wenchang Pavilions worship Wenchang Emperor (文昌帝君), who governs human worldly fame and success—hence widely worshipped.

In Nanxi River's Langxia, Huatan, Yantou, Shuiyun villages, all once had Wenchang Pavilions.They usually echoed schools/academies or had halls serving as school/academy lecture rooms.

Because related to exam success—i.e., clan prosperity—clans regarded building Wenchang Pavilions as a major event, also one of local gentry's good deeds.

Zhenchuan Zhu Combined Genealogy · Biography of Shenxuan Gentleman records Zhu Guangrun donating funds in Huatan Village to "build a literary pavilion...structure and construction, birds soaring and wings flying.

" The main body is a two-story pavilion, with two side wings serving as academy lecture rooms—"Zhenchuan's scenery, here ranks first.

" Wenchang Pavilions were mostly built at the village's "water mouth" (水口)—the narrow outlet where surface water from the village's small basin gathers and flows out.

Since fengshui masters simply believed China's terrain is northwest high and southeast low, "this is the great tendency of heaven and earth," villages were mostly sited northwest of the outlet, so water mouths were mostly southeast of the village—the xun (巽) direction.

Water mouths often have hills on both banks, lush trees, beautiful scenery.E.g.

, Yantou Village's Wenchang Pavilion, founded in Qianlong Gengshen (1740), is located at the southern end of the entire Nanxi River basin's largest rural garden, at the northern foot of Tang Mountain, west of the garden's main building Tahu Temple (Xiaoyou Temple), facing Zhishui Lake in front, beside a stream with abundant water on the left.

Behind the pavilion, at a higher point, stands a Wenfeng Pagoda.

Due to beautiful surroundings, Nanxi River两岸 villages' "Ten Scenes," "Eight Scenes" often include a scene of Wenchang Pavilion or academy, as objects for scholars' chanting.

Heyang Village's academy is called "Huancui Tower" (环翠楼); its "Eight Scenes" includes "Huancui Reading Sound": "Secluded pavilion steep among green trees, inside resounds reading sound; mid-air throwing to earth gold coins解, five mountains facing heaven jade pendants鸣.

" Huatan Village's Ten Scenes Poems includes two poems "Wenchang Ascent and Gaze": first: "Outstanding pavilion rises to the clouds, streams and mountains enter the eye wondrously...

body wandering in painting, looking up and down spreading beard and brows." Second: "...bamboo sparse wind playing shadows, flowers dark birds singing shade, ancient trees floating waves still, empty pool setting moon deep...

" Wenchang Pagodas originated from fengshui superstition: believing villages with poor exam luck could build a pagoda or erect a writing brush in the jia, xun, bing, ding directions to revive literary fortune.

Most were built in the xun direction, since water-mouth building complexes were also mostly outside the village in xun direction—Wenchang Pagoda and water-mouth complex complement each other, more vivid.

Nanxi River basin has rolling mountains, all volcanic rhyolite, after hundreds of millions of years of erosion, with many conical peaks.

In fengshui numerology these could be recognized as "writing brushes"—hence few man-made Wenfeng Pagodas here, only one each in Yantou and Tangwan villages.

Yantou Village's Wenfeng Pagoda was built by Ming Guilin Gentleman (Jin clan) in Jiajing era (1522–1566), contemporaneous with Shuiting Academy and Senxiu Studio.

It is located on the hillside behind the Wenchang Pavilion at the village's southeast end, entirely built of gray-white marble; from remnants, the pagoda was likely seven-story pavilion style, only about 4m high.

Village scholars often built quiet studios in scenic spots for reading.Yantou Village's Jin Guilin Gentleman converted Tahu Temple's vegetarian hall into study Senxiu Studio, backed by Youjun Pond, facing Zhennan Lake.

Guilin Gentleman's poem "Inscription on Senxiu Studio · Second" has two couplets: Door planted with embankment Tao Gong willows; courtyard opened with ink-washing Youjun pond; Playing chess on stone steps wind frequently arrives; brewing tea in pine studio moon rises at the time.

The studio's cultural life taste was very high.Shuiting Academy, Senxiu Studio, Wenfeng Pagoda, Wenchang Pavilion, stage, and Youjun Pond together formed Yantou Village's cultural building complex.

Tangwan Village's Ten Scenes Poems, one chanting "Xunji Mountain": "Solemnly standing alone a high peak, precisely positioned southeast gathering elegant air; xun auspicious further adding a precious pagoda, literary style flourishing brush roaming dragons.

" This Wenfeng Pagoda was built on the mountain—the mountain is in the village's xun direction, i.e., southeast.Some scholar-gentry created bookish atmosphere within their residences.

Early Ming Hongwu-Yongle era (1368–1424), Heyang Village had Xie Dexuan, with a study overlooking the clear river.

He composed his own "Waterside Study" poem: Green currents vast contain long sky; small study横枕 clear and pitiable; Toothpicks holding thirty thousand scrolls; lamp light illuminating windows twenty years.

Long days dust cannot fly in; constant wind and moon leisure boundless; Already knowing the sage Way is like this; joy found comes naturally.

Same village same clan Xie Tingxun, Xuande era (1426–1435) served in Brocade Guard, in old age built a "Jingle Xuan" (静乐轩) in his hometown old residence; genealogy writes: "Scholar-officials who visited him all composed Jingle poems.

" Even Emperor Xuanzong wrote a "Jingle Poem" to gift him: "Twilight moves the front pavilion, heavy city about to close gates.Remaining sunset gathers red air, new moon breaks dusk.

Already feel heaven and earth still, no market noise.Yin and yang have constant principle, this discussed with the free man.

" Xie Tingxun's friend, Yuzhang Village's Hu Zongyun, Ming Xuande era Zhongshu Sheren, when returning to farm had colleagues present farewell poems: lines: "Cutting thatch today in the wild, fishing old stream as before.

Drying medicine sunny eaves short, arranging books night bed low." (Chen Bin) and "Mist and clouds three- mu residence, frost and dew hundred-year heart; yellow chrysanthemum Tao Qian's delight, clear wind Liangfu's chant.

" (Chen Zhong) After returning, Hu Zongyun built a Ziwei Tower in his old residence "Zhonghan Di" as a retirement place.

Yuzhang Hu Clan Genealogy writes of him: "Planting bamboo and flowers, daily sitting and lying among them, at times touching ink, composing poems as inspired, carefree and self-content, or laughing and talking with close friends, playing go, drinking wine—like this for over twenty years.

" These rural intellectuals' advocated and pursued lifestyle, the attitude of "transcending things, seeking within the heart," inevitably had a leading influence on rural cultural life.

Among Nanxi River basin's cultural-educational buildings, another important type is memorial archways (牌楼).

Guangxu's Yongjia County Gazetteer · Ancient Sites writes about archway tablets: "Ancients marked their residences and villages, establishing their reputation—worthy of emulation and transmission, related to governance and education.

" Nanxi River people valued archways' educational role highly, generally building them exquisitely, positioned near ancestral halls or village gates, becoming part of the village's ritual center.

Huatan Village has the most and most magnificent archways.

Ming Yingzong Zhengtong era (1436–1449), at the left and right of the main ancestral hall Dunmutang's front gate, for War Section Secretariat Zhu Liangxian, two archways were built facing each other: east one inscribed "Wu Fu" (Black Office, censorate), west one inscribed "Huang Men" (Yellow Gate, palace secretariat).

Facing Dunmutang, another archway inscribed "Yishi Zanying" (Generations of Official Hats), erected for Ming Jiajing (1522–1566) jinshi Zhu Tian.

It and "Wu Fu," "Huang Men" archways form a pin (品) character shape, enclosing a small open space before Dunmutang, adding spirit to the main ancestral hall.

This pin-character layout was popular in culturally prosperous urban and rural areas.

West of "Huang Men" archway, along the main road, is "Xiangxian" (Local Worthy) archway, Ming Zhengde era (1506–1521) Wenzhou Prefect He Wenyuan erected for education official Zhu Sining.

Further west is "Zhongxiu" (Gathered Excellence) archway, erected when Zhu Tian passed juren in Ming Jiajing.

Further west, Jiajing Bingyin (1566) winter Yongjia Magistrate Cheng Wenzhu erected for Zhu Shuangxi, inscribed "Gongzhi Chunliang" (Public, Upright, Sincere, Good).

Further west is "Xihe" (Harmony) archway, local gentleman Xihua Wang erected for Zhu Lianxi, roughly late Ming.

The last archway on the main road is "Xishan First" archway, erected for local jinshi and Fengyang Magistrate Zhu Yichuan, plaque written by Zhu Tian.This archway is Huatan Village's west gate.

Additionally, "Xiantai" (Censorate) archway, at the center before Xiantai Ancestral Hall's main gate, Ming Hongzhi Yichou (1505) Wenzhou Prefect Li Duan and Yongjia Magistrate Liu Jing erected for Works Section Secretariat Zhu Liangyi.

In Xiyuan Academy, there is "Yuanfei Yuyue" (Kites Flying, Fish Leaping) archway, Zhongshu Sheren Zhou Ling built for Zhu Youdu.

All these archways honored people who studied, passed exams, and became officials—purpose: glorify the clan,激励 later generations.

Additionally, county magistrate Wu Gong erected "Wei Gong Xuanli" (Serving the Public with Strength) archway for Zhu Xiaoshan (Zhu Xiaoshan's identity and deeds unrecorded), and late Ming Chongzhen Jisi (1629) Surveillance Commissioner Xu Jigong erected "Songbai Hanzhen" (Pine and Cypress Cold Chastity) archway for chaste widow Shao—only recorded in genealogy, demolished during the Cultural Revolution, location unknown.

Yantou Village has an archway, granted by Ming Shizong to Jin Zhao, left/right assistant of the Court of Judicial Review, later promoted to Ruizhou Prefect.

This archway and Huatan Village's Xiantai archway are similar in style—both four-pillar four-story, with grand bracket sets, system close to Song style—truly rare.

The Nanxi River basin, over 2,000 sq km, with such developed culture and education yet long unknown to the world, provides a very typical example of rural society's cultural-educational state in a purely agricultural region of Jiangnan, and also typically narrates the background, motivation, pursuit, environment, and style of rural cultural-educational building construction.

5.3 学塾、书院
Section 3

三、学塾、书院 在乡土社会里，书院和学塾两种称谓的区别并不很确定。层次较低的学塾有称为书院的，而层次较高的书院却没有称为学塾的。

有的私人书院自称为"精舍"、"山房"、"斋"之类，求其雅而脱俗，元代的理学家吴澄便命名自己的书院为"草庐"。书院和学塾的建筑型制变化很大，没有一定的规例。不过一般都有课读的书房和山长或塾师的住房而已。

浙江省兰溪市的诸葛村、武义市的俞源村、江西省乐安县的流坑村，村里的学塾内部模仿科考场所的布局。老夫子坐馆授徒的私塾，大都很小，通常在住宅的"别厅"即小跨院里。江南诸省，有些小康人家的家塾，也设在别厅里。

别厅面向正院的侧墙，堂屋居中，供朱子像，一个次间为课室，容量不大；另一次间为塾师卧室兼书房。有个小小的吸壁天井，贴正房侧墙建水池，池取朱熹"半亩方塘一鉴开，天光云影共徘徊，问渠那得清如许，为有源头活水来"的诗意。池边陈列几盆幽兰、茉莉之类。

书声伴花香，小小别厅也很清雅。这样的别厅书塾，在浙江、江西、安徽、福建等地很普遍。在经济发达，文风丕盛的地区，学塾和初级书院很多。江西省乐安县流坑村，据明代万历年间（1573—1620）董氏宗谱，有学堂二十六座，清代道光年宗谱记录有二十八座。

福建省连城县培田村，以竹木生意而繁荣，有乡谚说它："十户一祠堂，五户一书院，三户一店铺"，看似夸张，其实并不夸张。

旧皖南徽州六邑，村村有很多私家独门独户的"学堂屋"，其中黟县关麓村，只有四十三座住宅，却有十七座精致典雅的独立的学堂屋，既可作为退休商人高朋雅集、过琴棋书画休闲生活的场所，也可用作子弟课读的家塾，聘来的塾师也住在里面。

学堂屋尺度比住宅小一点，布局比较自由，空间有变化，讲究情趣，装修和装饰很精致典雅，处处显得玲珑，大多带一个小园。关麓村还有多座书屋，多为独院式小楼，三间两层，有花园式的前院、环廊，点缀些仿形门，如蕉叶形、画卷形等。门额和两侧的白粉墙上镶匾和联，所题的字多为清水砖刻，或髹石绿、石青色。室内天花上满布鱼藻之类的彩画，色泽和谐清雅。

婺源县（今属江西省）理坑村也有一些学堂屋，与住宅完全分离，独立于村前小河的对岸，参差比肩而建，形成一个小区，它们各自有前后两幢屋，三开间，中为小院。前后屋的明间有曲廊连接。廊一侧从河里引水进院成小池，凭槛可数池鱼，另一侧植花木。

前进两次间可为学童读书处，后进一个次间为塾师书斋，明间及另一个次间合而为敞厅，布置很潇洒。这类学堂屋大都留意于园林趣味，福建省永安县吉山的萃园和稍小一点的西洋福庄的问渠书屋，远离村舍，建筑和家具都十分精致。萃园规模很大，正屋三开间，前后厅。左右都有跨院，花木扶疏，园前有个宽阔的大水池。

它名为书院，实际功能已远远超出。又如，江西省婺源县李坑村的智仁书屋，面南，三间两层，前檐通面阔为玲珑桶扇花窗。西边另贴一间卧室。不宽的前院，满铺卵石，图案极为精致。书屋前墙外是一条水量丰沛的五米左右宽的小溪，溪对岸的小山上竹木荫翳茂盛。书屋之北为一所大花园，宽十二米多，长约二十三米。

东侧又是一座花园，宽十五米多，长约十米，中央挖一个直径略小于十五米的半圆形水池，叫月池。书屋西侧小院是主人的读书厅，叫新轩，轩前一所花园，中央凿七米见方的莲池，一面贴新轩南墙，三面围以石栏，池中锦鳞出没于莲叶之下。再西侧，围墙外，又有一个约五米见方的水池，叫日池。广东省河源市南园村有一座柳溪书院，规模不大，布局很紧凑，又很复杂。

它面南有正方形两圈建筑，内圈正厅一大间，是低班学子的课堂，它明间门前有一座亭子式的方形敞轩，叫"杏坛"，仿孔子讲学的场所。宽与正厅相等的一圈方形围墙围住杏坛。围墙左右开洞门。墙的外侧，三面有狭窄的天井，东面为大门，南、西两面隔天井有房子，南面的房子是两层的，底层分为小间，给高班学子读书。楼上住塾师，西端一间是他的书房，塾师坐在书房里，可以俯视正厅和杏坛里的情况。

书院的内院常植玉兰花和金桂花各一株，寄意"兰桂齐芳"。宗祠举办的义塾经费由公共财产的义田中划出若干"学田"来提供，建筑质量稍平常一点。这种义塾的型制虽然还是没有定规，但有为科考而建的功利性特点。

比较简单的，如浙江省武义县俞源村的义塾培英书屋，是一个横长的院落，大门在西端，北边一排大房间，给低班学童用，南边一排四个很小的房间，是给高班学童用的。东端地势高，上七步台阶之后有几间居住用房，是塾师的卧室和书斋。南边小房间有一扇窗花上刻着四个字，是"读圣贤书"，所以村人把这书屋叫"家训阁"。

浙江省兰溪市诸葛村有一所义塾，叫笔耘轩，也是横长的院子，大门在南房正中，门两侧各有四间，划分为很小的房间。门厅正对北房正中的香火堂，它左右各为两大间教室。浙江省建德市新叶村的义塾、福建省南靖县石桥村步云斋书屋，也都类似这样。

这种横排小间的布局是仿科考的场屋，让高班的学童习惯它们。北房正中文昌帝君的香火堂也祭朱子（即朱熹）。义塾也有少数是富裕的"善人"捐出田亩来创办的。浙江省永嘉县芙蓉村的近邻岩头村，有一座桂林公专祠，叫水亭祠，面朝北。它本来是金氏桂林公在明代晚期建造的水亭书院。

《岩头金氏宗谱·宗祠》说，嘉靖年间（1522—1566）桂林公"原创水亭为子孙课业计，自兹文学振兴，叨膺科第，至今胶序蝉联，绳绳不绝"。

进三楼式砖砌大门之后，先见一方大水池（24.5米×21.4米），绕过这池水，中轴线上是仪门，进门，眼前又是一方大水池（25.0米×21.4米），池正中一道平平的石板桥，可达池中央的方亭（4米×4米）。

穿亭而过，再经桥引向后面的讲堂。讲堂面阔7开间，左右侧还有廊子。这座书院的布局构思奇特，极为少见。桂林公对岩头村的建设作出过全面的贡献，殁后族人把书院改为他的专祠。

较大的私塾也有住宅型的，如徽州六邑之一婺源县延村西南角的一座私塾，是两个两层的三合院并肩而成的，其中一座因地形所限平面不很规则。学生是住读的，有七小间宿舍，教师也有两间卧室。另有食堂和厨房，突出在它东南角。楼上有外廊，正对着院子里的金桂、银桂各一株。桂树是学业有成，科考得捷的象征，考中了就叫"折桂"。婺源县的甲路村也有一座楼房，楼上三间通开为学塾，前后檐均辟大窗，内部空间敞朗。

楼梯十分宽阔平缓，以免拥挤。后檐大窗外的底层屋面上还有疏散措施，保障学童的安全。这学塾的功能推敲很周到。婺源县汪口镇上深巷里有一座小小的院落，院门额上篆"掩翠"二字，正屋完全与住宅相同，三间两层。院前有短墙，左前方小门上方嵌"养源书院"额。

前院里，四季香溢的月月桂下，侧墙上镶着一方青石碑，刊刻的是光绪十年（1884年）婺源县正堂吴的告示，公布了"汪口封职俞光銮"的一则呈文，并明确予以批准和支持。呈文的主要内容是："职少孤贫，成童后贸易江西，辛勤积累，随置田亩。因思承先裕后，励学为先。而励学则储田为要，除存祀田慰先灵、微派田亩为六子分析外，仍余之田另立户册完课，存为后人膏火之资。

……唯恐日后弊生，或有不肖之子孙举此田而私废之，则励学将堕于半途，而砚田莫贞于悠远，为此，吁叩恩赏给示，以禁私废而杜私受。"这座养源书院是一所真正意义上的义塾，用俞光銮捐出的田亩收益创办并维持。和浙江省楠溪江流域的村子相同，各地都有些村落在风景佳丽之地建造书院，甚至形成一个"景点"。

福建省连城县培田村有好几个书院，其中"南山书院"创建于清代乾隆三十年（1765年）。它位于卧虎山北麓，创始人吴锦江取陶渊明"采菊东篱下，悠然见南山"诗意，命名为"南山书院"。

"南山书院"是培田新八景之一，吴受仁有诗： 步上南山境僻幽，琅玕诵读韵悠悠， 蕉窗雨冷偏逢夜，竹院风凉又报秋。金石一声天地震，简编万卷古今搜， 朝晴早起人倾听，鸟语书声乐唱酬。南山书院由三座院落相聚组成。

东院大门居中，为牌坊式，清人曾瑞春《南山书院记》说："书'德造庐'于门之外，'培兰植桂'于门之内，'朱子读书乐诗'于东西壁"。现在所见略有不同，大门内侧门额以上书"南山书院"四字，门外两侧门柱上是裴应章尚书题的对联"距汀城郭虽百里，入孔门墙第一家"。

门内墙上书朱子语录："观古者圣贤所以教人为学之要，莫不使之讲明义理，以修其身，然后推己及后。"正房五开间，两层，底层当心间正厅供孔子牌位，其余各间为学生教室。西院比东院低七步台阶，是一所两层楼的四合院，西、南两面有前檐廊和美人靠，是当年塾师居住、读书的地方。东、西两院之间夹着一个狭长的小院，有小门向南通院外。

书院前有一个半月形水塘，作为泮池，又叫"砚池"，与书院的朝山文笔峰相映成"文笔蘸墨"的风水。浙江省兰溪市诸葛村，村北有南阳书舍，为"高隆八景"之首。

明代正德年间（1506—1521），陆凤仪写《南阳书舍》诗： 花竹绕庭除，图书万卷余， 云藏扬子宅，人识卧龙居。景物随游惬，江山入望舒， 悠然栖息者，谁羡武陵墟。这座书院不但藏书丰富，而且环境优美，江山景物望之舒而游之惬。在这样的场合读书，"坛杏飞红铺砌畔，泮芹分翠入轩中。春风绛帐频施教，夜雨青灯好课功"（清人王以璋诗二、三联），真是人生快事。

距诸葛村不远，今建德市铜山后金村是元代最大的学者金履祥（字仁山）的故里，村口外，有一座仁山书院，格局完全与中等宗祠相同，疑为后人所筑。浙江省宁海县跃麟庵为方孝孺读书处，前童村有方孝孺讲学的鹿山书院。方孝孺少年时曾在宁海南谷草堂读书，中年时作《草堂歌》纪事： 草堂坐对陵南谷，勤把诗书向窗读。学门长掩寂无人，惟有白云相伴宿。昨日溪头罢钓归，花笑莺啼芳草绿。

猿鹤嘹嘹哀怨啼，萧瑟自理山家曲。当年这书院环境风光也是十分秀丽的。除了学塾、书院之外，江南较大的村子里又常有一座"文馆"，北方也有但少见。文馆是"文会"的活动场所，文会的成员主要是村子里的文化人、读书人，包括致仕退食的官员和困顿场屋但也曾熟读经书的人，等等。他们形成村子的舆论集体，有威信、有影响，宗族的大事常要请他们参议，族人有犯过失甚至涉罪的，先由他们问审，决定是否送官。

不过他们日常的活动是到文馆里交谊，谈诗论文，拨弦吹竹，品茶斗棋。村里的童生、秀才，每月两度到文馆，或携卷呈交，或受题当场作文，由文会中前辈评审、指点。同治安徽《黟县三志·艺文》有康熙庚寅（1710年）知县李登龙写的《聚奎文会序》，其中说："黟县各都之设有文会，一以敦气谊，一以广观摩，诚美举也……余所望会中诸子，正其谊不谋其利，明其道不计其功。

日有课，月有会……经旨有未晰者折衷而商订之，文义有未善者讲论而开导之……有过必折，有善必规。"浙江省兰溪市诸葛村，在乾隆年间（1736—1795）由族人殷实者捐田、捐银，建立了一个"登瀛文会"，诸葛氏宗谱里的《重整登瀛文会记》说："月数聚士子课制艺，优者给以膏火之费，乡会试赠以宾兴之资，从无间断。"说的就是文会提携后生搏科举的事。文馆的建筑都很精致。

江西省乐安县流坑村董氏大宗祠的右侧，广东省始兴县东湖坪村的曾氏大宗祠左侧，都有文馆。它们的型制几乎和宗祠相同，三进两院，宏堂高轩，常用的功能空间都在两厢里。

有些文馆的建筑则别有深意，如江西省广昌县驿前村的文馆，紧贴抚江左岸，厅堂馆屋不作纵深排列而是横向沿江展开，并依江岸而微曲，只有大厅三间是以轴线向江的。从江上望去，长长一带粉墙上悬出几间敞廊，跌宕有致，典雅而洒脱。它的前院有一座小屋，从内部来看，形式完全仿船舱，拱顶，内部墙面都处理成船篷编织形状。安徽省黟县关麓村有一座双桂书屋，村人就叫它"船屋"，它的一个突出墙外的厅，平面呈弧形三角形，有尖，宛如船的前端。

另有一座住宅里的暖阁就叫"船厅"，厅左右均有敞廊，廊外侧为水池。江西省乐安县流坑村有两座船形住宅，一座是明经巷的"董步汀仙舫"，一座是上巷的"董演四仙舫"，都建于光绪年间（1875—1908），悬"仙舫"匾额。村人叫它们为"船屋"。舫体"前舱"为甲板，"中舱"为客厅，"后舱"为卧室，屋后有"泮池"。

江西省、安徽省和福建省，还有些村里的大宅，正房前檐的平面呈弧形，酷似船舷。关于这种特殊形状的文馆和书屋，如今有多种解说，但大约以象征"学海无涯苦作舟"的俚语或者"为学如逆水行舟，不进则退"这类的教导为近似。

3.Schools and Academies In rural society, the distinction between the terms "academy" (书院) and "school" (学塾) was not firmly fixed.

Lower-level schools were sometimes called academies, while higher-level academies were never called schools.

Some private academies called themselves "refined lodges" (精舍), "mountain chambers" (山房), "studies" (斋), and the like—seeking elegance and refinement.Yuan dynasty Neo-Confucian Wu Cheng named his own academy "Thatched Hut" (草庐).

The architectural forms of academies and schools varied greatly, with no fixed rules.

Generally, however, they had reading rooms for classes and residences for the academy head (shanzhang) or schoolmaster.

In Zhuge Village (Lanxi, Zhejiang), Yuyuan Village (Wuyi, Zhejiang), and Liukeng Village (Le'an, Jiangxi), village schools internally imitated the layout of examination halls.

Private schools where old masters taught were mostly small, usually located in a residence's "separate hall" (别厅), i.e., a small side courtyard.

In Jiangnan provinces, some moderately well-off families' family schools were also in separate halls.

The separate hall faces the main courtyard's side wall; the central hall houses a Zhu Xi statue; one secondary room is a classroom of modest capacity; the other secondary room is the schoolmaster's bedroom cum study.

There is a small attached light well (吸壁天井), with a water pool built against the main house's side wall—the pool evoking Zhu Xi's poem: "Half-mu square pond opens like a mirror; sky light and cloud shadows wander together.

Ask how the canal stays so clear?Because flowing water comes from the source." By the pool stand several pots of orchids, jasmine, and the like.Reading sound accompanied by flower fragrance—the small separate hall is quite elegant.

Such separate-hall schools were common in Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Anhui, Fujian, and elsewhere.In economically developed, culturally flourishing regions, schools and elementary academies were numerous.

Liukeng Village (Le'an, Jiangxi), according to Ming Wanli-era (1573–1620) Dong clan genealogy, had 26 school buildings; Qing Daoguang-era genealogy records 28.

Peitian Village (Liancheng, Fujian), prosperous from bamboo and timber trade, has a local saying: "One ancestral hall per ten households, one academy per five households, one shop per three households"—seemingly exaggerated, actually not.

In old Huizhou's six counties, every village had many private, independent "school houses" (学堂屋); among them, Guanlu Village (Yixian) had only 43 residences but 17 exquisitely elegant independent school houses—serving both as venues for retired merchants' elegant gatherings (qin, chess, calligraphy, painting leisure) and as family schools for children's study, with hired schoolmasters living inside.

School houses were slightly smaller than residences, with freer layout, varied spaces, attention to charm, refined decoration, everywhere delicate—most with a small garden.

Guanlu Village also had multiple study houses, mostly independent-courtyard small buildings, three-bay two-story, with garden-style front courtyards, surrounding corridors, and decorative shaped doors (banana-leaf form, painting-scroll form, etc.

).Door lintels and side white-plaster walls bore plaques and couplets, mostly in clear-water brick carving or painted stone-green/stone-blue.

Interior ceilings were covered with colorful paintings of fish and water plants, harmonious and elegant in color.

Likeng Village (Wuyuan, now Jiangxi) also had school houses, completely separated from residences, independently built across the small river in front of the village, arranged unevenly side by side forming a small district.

Each had front and rear buildings, three-bay, with a small courtyard between.The central bays of front and rear buildings were connected by a winding corridor.

On one side of the corridor, water was channeled from the river into a small pool—leaning on the railing one could count the fish; on the other side, flowers and trees were planted.

The front building's two secondary rooms could serve as children's reading spaces; the rear building's one secondary room was the schoolmaster's study; the central bay and another secondary room combined into an open hall—layout very free and easy.

Such school houses mostly paid attention to garden charm.Cuiyuan (萃园) at Jishan (Yong'an, Fujian) and the slightly smaller Wenqu Study House (问渠书屋) at Xiyang Fuzhuang, far from village houses, had both buildings and furniture very refined.

Cuiyuan was large-scale: main house three-bay, front and rear halls.Both sides had side courtyards with lush flowers and trees; before the garden was a broad large pool.

Called an academy, its actual functions far exceeded that.

Another example: Zhiren Study House (智仁书屋) at Likeng Village (Wuyuan), facing south, three-bay two-story, front eave full width of exquisite lattice flower windows.West side attached a bedroom.

The modest front courtyard was fully paved with pebbles in extremely refined patterns.Outside the study house's front wall was a stream about 5m wide with abundant water; on the opposite bank's small hill, bamboo and trees were lush.

North of the study house was a large garden, over 12m wide, ~23m long.East side was another garden, over 15m wide, ~10m long, with a semicircular pool slightly under 15m diameter in the center, called Moon Pool (月池).

The study house's west side small courtyard was the owner's reading hall, called Xin Xuan (新轩); before it was a garden with a 7m-square lotus pool in the center, one side against Xin Xuan's south wall, three sides fenced with stone railings—carp appeared and disappeared among lotus leaves.

Further west, outside the wall, another ~5m-square pool, called Sun Pool (日池).Liuxi Academy (柳溪书院) at Nanyuan Village (Heyuan, Guangdong) was modest in scale, compact yet complex in layout.

Facing south, it had two square rings of buildings: the inner ring's main hall was one large room, the classroom for lower-level students; before its central bay was a pavilion-style square open veranda called "Apricot Altar" (杏坛), imitating Confucius's teaching place.

A square enclosing wall equal in width to the main hall surrounded the Apricot Altar.The wall had arched doors on left and right.

Outside the wall, three sides had narrow light wells; east side was the main gate; south and west sides had buildings across light wells—the south building was two-story, ground floor divided into small rooms for higher-level students.

Upstairs lived the schoolmaster; the west-end room was his study—sitting in his study, the schoolmaster could overlook the main hall and Apricot Altar.

The academy's inner courtyard often planted one magnolia and one osmanthus, symbolizing "orchid and osmanthus together fragrant" (兰桂齐芳).

Charitable schools (义塾) run by ancestral halls were funded by setting aside "study fields" (学田) from public charitable fields; building quality was somewhat ordinary.

Though their form had no fixed rule, they had the utilitarian characteristic of being built for examinations.

Simpler examples: Peiying Study House (培英书屋), the charitable school at Yuyuan Village (Wuyi, Zhejiang), was a horizontally long courtyard—main gate at west end; north side a row of large rooms for lower-level students; south side a row of four very small rooms for higher-level students.

East end was higher; after seven steps up were several residential rooms—the schoolmaster's bedroom and study.

One south small room's window lattice was carved with four characters "Read Sage Books" (读圣贤书), hence villagers called it "Family Instruction Pavilion" (家训阁).

Zhuge Village (Lanxi) had a charitable school called Biyun Xuan (笔耘轩), also a horizontally long courtyard—main gate in the center of the south building, four rooms on each side divided into very small rooms.

The entrance hall faced the central incense hall of the north building; its left and right were each two large classrooms.

The charitable school at Xinye Village (Jiande, Zhejiang) and Buyun Zhai Study House (步云斋) at Shiqiao Village (Nanjing, Fujian) were similar.

This horizontal-row small-room layout imitated examination halls, letting higher-level students get used to them.The north building's central Wenchang Emperor incense hall also worshipped Zhu Xi.

A few charitable schools were founded by wealthy "good people" donating fields.Near Furong Village (Yongjia, Zhejiang), Yantou Village had a Guilin Gong dedicated shrine called Shuiting Shrine (水亭祠), facing north.

It was originally the Shuiting Academy (水亭书院) built by Jin clan's Guilin Gong in late Ming.

Yantou Jin Clan Genealogy · Ancestral Halls says that in Jiajing era (1522–1566), Guilin Gong "originally created Shuiting for descendants' study; from then literature flourished, received examination degrees, to this day schools continue unbroken.

" Entering the three-story brick main gate, first one saw a large pool (24.5m × 21.4m);绕过 the pool, on the central axis was the ceremonial gate; entering, before one was another large pool (25.0m × 21.

4m); in the pool's center a flat stone bridge led to a square pavilion (4m × 4m).Passing through the pavilion, another bridge led to the rear lecture hall.

The lecture hall was 7-bay wide, with corridors on both sides.This academy's layout was ingenious and extremely rare.

Guilin Gong made comprehensive contributions to Yantou Village's construction; after his death, clansmen converted the academy into his dedicated shrine.

Larger private schools could also be residence-type.E.g.

, a private school at the southwest corner of Yancun Village (Wuyuan, one of Huizhou's six counties) was two two-story three-courtyard compounds side by side—one had an irregular plan due to terrain.

Students boarded: seven small dormitory rooms; teachers had two bedrooms.Additionally a dining hall and kitchen protruded at the southeast corner.Upstairs had an outer corridor facing one golden osmanthus and one silver osmanthus in the courtyard.

Osmanthus was a symbol of academic success and examination victory—passing was called "plucking osmanthus" (折桂).

Jialu Village (Wuyuan) also had a building: upstairs three bays opened through as a school, front and rear eaves both had large windows, interior space open and bright.The staircase was very wide and gentle to avoid crowding.

Outside the rear-eave large window, on the ground-floor roof, there were evacuation measures ensuring children's safety.This school's functional design was very thorough.

In a deep alley of Wangkou Town (Wuyuan), a small courtyard had a gate lintel with seal-script "Concealed Green" (掩翠); the main house was exactly like a residence, three-bay two-story.

Before the courtyard was a low wall; above the small gate at left front was embedded "Yangyuan Academy" (养源书院) plaque.

In the front courtyard, under the fragrant monthly osmanthus, the side wall bore a blue stone stele engraved with a Guangxu 10 (1884) Wuyuan County Magistrate Wu's proclamation—publicizing a petition by "Wangkou titled official Yu Guangluan" and explicitly granting approval and support.

The petition's main content: "I was orphaned and poor in youth; after coming of age I traded in Jiangxi, diligently accumulating, purchasing fields.Thinking of honoring ancestors and benefiting descendants, encouraging learning is first.

And encouraging learning requires storing fields as essential—besides keeping sacrificial fields to comfort ancestral spirits and allocating small fields for six sons' division, the remaining fields I register under a separate household to pay taxes, kept as later generations' study-fund resources.

...

Fearing future abuses, or unworthy descendants privately abolishing these fields, then learning encouragement would fall halfway, and the 'inkstone field' would not endure long—hence I humbly request your honor's proclamation to forbid private abolition and prevent private misappropriation.

" This Yangyuan Academy was a true charitable school, founded and maintained by Yu Guangluan's donated field income.

Like villages in Zhejiang's Nanxi River basin, various places had villages building academies in scenic spots, even forming a "scenic spot.

" Peitian Village (Liancheng, Fujian) had several academies; among them "Nanshan Academy" (南山书院) was founded in Qing Qianlong 30 (1765).

Located at the northern foot of Wohu Mountain, founder Wu Jinjiang took Tao Yuanming's poem "Picking chrysanthemums by the eastern fence, calmly seeing the southern mountain" to name it "Nanshan Academy.

" It was one of Peitian's New Eight Scenes; Wu Shouren wrote a poem: Stepping up Nanshan, realm secluded and quiet, bamboo reading rhymes lingering; Banana-window rain cold偏偏 meets night, bamboo-courtyard wind cool again reports autumn.

Metal-stone one sound heaven and earth shake, bamboo-slips ten thousand volumes ancient and modern search; Morning clear early rise people listen, bird songs and reading sound joyfully respond.

Nanshan Academy consisted of three courtyards clustered together.

The east courtyard's main gate was centered, archway-style; Qing person Zeng Ruichun's Record of Nanshan Academy says: "Inscribed 'Virtue-Built Lodge' outside the gate, 'Cultivating Orchid and Osmanthus' inside the gate, 'Zhu Xi's Reading Joy Poem' on east and west walls.

" What remains differs slightly: inside the gate, above the lintel, "Nanshan Academy" four characters; outside the gate, on both side pillars, a couplet by Minister Pei Yingzhang: "Though a hundred li from Ting city wall, the first family entering Confucius's gate.

" Inside the gate wall was Zhu Xi's quotation: "Observe how ancient sages taught the essentials of learning—none did not make them clarify moral principle, cultivate themselves, then extend to others.

" The main house was five-bay, two-story; ground floor central bay main hall enshrined Confucius's tablet; remaining bays were student classrooms.

The west courtyard was seven steps lower than the east, a two-story quadrangle with front-eave corridors and "beauty rests" (美人靠) on west and south sides—where schoolmasters lived and studied.

Between east and west courtyards was a narrow small courtyard with a small gate leading south outside.

Before the academy was a crescent-shaped pond serving as the Pan Pool (泮池), also called "Inkstone Pool" (砚池), echoing the academy's facing mountain Writing-Brush Peak in the fengshui of "writing brush dipping ink.

" Zhuge Village (Lanxi, Zhejiang), north of the village, had Nanyang Study House (南阳书舍), first of "Gaolong Eight Scenes.

" Ming Zhengde era (1506–1521), Lu Fengyi wrote a poem Nanyang Study House: Flowers and bamboo surround the courtyard, books and pictures over ten thousand scrolls; Clouds hide Yangzi's residence, people recognize Wolong's dwelling.

Scenery follows wandering content, rivers and mountains enter gaze comfortably; Carefree dweller here, who would envy Wuling's paradise?

This academy not only had rich book collections but beautiful environment—rivers and mountains comfortable to gaze and wander.

Reading in such a setting: "Altar apricot blossoms red paving the courtyard edge, Pan celery green entering the veranda.

Spring breeze red curtain frequently teaches, night rain green lamp good for lessons" (Qing poet Wang Yizhang's poem, second and third couplets)—truly a joy of life.

Not far from Zhuge Village, today's Tongshan Houjin Village (Jiande) was the hometown of Yuan dynasty's greatest scholar Jin Lüxiang (courtesy name Renshan); outside the village entrance was Renshan Academy (仁山书院), its layout exactly like a medium ancestral hall—suspected to be built by later generations.

Yuelin Nunnery (跃麟庵) at Ninghai (Zhejiang) was Fang Xiaoru's reading place; Qiantong Village had Lushan Academy where Fang Xiaoru lectured.

Fang Xiaoru studied at Nangu Thatched Cottage (南谷草堂) in youth; in middle age he wrote Thatched Cottage Song to record: Thatched cottage facing Lingnan Valley, diligently reading poetry and books by the window; School gate long closed silent no one, only white clouds accompanying lodging.

Yesterday returned from fishing at the stream head, flowers smiling orioles singing fragrant grass green; Apes and cranes sadly calling, bleakly playing the mountain family tune.

That academy's environment and scenery were also very beautiful back then.Beyond schools and academies, larger Jiangnan villages often had a "Literary Hall" (文馆), rare in the north.

The Literary Hall was the activity venue for "Literary Societies" (文会)—members mainly village cultural figures and readers, including retired officials and those who struggled in examinations but had thoroughly studied the classics.

They formed the village's opinion collective, with prestige and influence; clan major affairs often required their consultation; clansmen committing faults or even crimes were first interrogated by them, deciding whether to send to officials.

But their daily activities were gathering at the Literary Hall for friendship, discussing poetry and prose, playing string and wind instruments, tasting tea and playing chess.

Village students and xiucai (秀才) came twice monthly to the Literary Hall—either submitting essays or composing on assigned topics on the spot, reviewed and guided by senior society members.

Tongzhi-era Anhui Yixian Three Gazetteers · Literature has a Preface to Jukui Literary Society (聚奎文会序) by Kangxi Gengyin (1710) County Magistrate Li Denglong: "Yixian's each district has literary societies—one to cultivate friendship, one to broaden observation and emulation, truly a fine endeavor.

..What I hope of society members: uphold righteousness without seeking profit, clarify the Way without counting merit.Daily lessons, monthly gatherings...

classical meanings not yet clear—compromise and discuss; literary meanings not yet good—lecture and guide...faults must be corrected, goodness must be encouraged.

" Zhuge Village (Lanxi), in Qianlong era (1736–1795), had clansmen of means donate fields and silver to establish "Dengying Literary Society" (登瀛文会); Zhuge clan genealogy's Record of Reorganizing Dengying Literary Society says: "Monthly gather scholars several times to test examination essays; excellent ones given study-fund expenses; provincial and metropolitan exams given travel funds—never interrupted.

" This describes literary societies guiding later generations in examination pursuit.Literary Hall buildings were all refined.

Right of Dong clan's main ancestral hall at Liukeng Village (Le'an, Jiangxi), and left of Zeng clan's main ancestral hall at Donghuping Village (Shixing, Guangdong), both had Literary Halls.

Their form was almost identical to ancestral halls—three entries, two courtyards, grand halls and high pavilions, with functional spaces in the two side wings.Some Literary Hall buildings had deeper meaning: e.g.

, the Literary Hall at Yiqian Village (Guangchang, Jiangxi), tightly against the left bank of the Fu River—halls and rooms not arranged in depth but horizontally along the river, slightly curving with the bank; only the three-bay main hall had its axis toward the river.

Viewed from the river, a long stretch of white plaster wall with several open verandas cantilevered out—rhythmic, elegant and free.

Its front courtyard had a small building that, internally, was entirely shaped like a ship's cabin—vaulted ceiling, interior walls treated as woven ship-canopy form.

Guanlu Village (Yixian, Anhui) had Shuanggui Study House, villagers called it "Ship House" (船屋)—one hall protruding beyond the wall had an arc-triangular plan with a point, like a ship's bow.

Another residence's warm pavilion was called "Ship Hall" (船厅), with open corridors on both sides and a pool outside the corridors.

Liukeng Village had two ship-shaped residences: one "Dong Buting Immortal Boat" (董步汀仙舫) in Mingjing Alley, one "Dong Yansi Immortal Boat" (董演四仙舫) in Shang Alley—both built in Guangxu era (1875–1908), with "Immortal Boat" plaques.

Villagers called them "Ship Houses." The boat body's "front cabin" was a deck, "middle cabin" a living room, "rear cabin" a bedroom; behind the house was a "Pan Pool.

" In Jiangxi, Anhui, and Fujian, some village large residences had curved front-eave plans, exactly like a ship's side.

About these specially shaped Literary Halls and study houses, there are various interpretations today—but most likely they symbolize the saying "the sea of learning is boundless, diligence is the boat" (学海无涯苦作舟) or teachings like "learning is like rowing upstream—not advancing means retreating" (为学如逆水行舟，不进则退).
