5.4 孔庙、科名牌坊、桅
Section 4

四、孔庙、科名牌坊、桅 孔庙又称文庙，按例，只有县以上建置方可建文庙，但极少数村子经曲阜衍圣公府批准也建了文庙。山西省阳城县郭峪村和不远的沁水县西文兴村各有一座，浙江省永嘉县的芙蓉村也有。

文庙的地位高过于文昌阁，按规定，它的"典籍官"也要由衍圣公府正式任命。郭峪村的文庙位于村内西城墙根。明代成化六年（1470年），在这里的古代公用建筑废墟上复建了一座"里馆"，"选老人以掌乡之政令教化"，大约相当于一个村政府。万历初，因张居正掌朝政改制被毁。

遗址于"崇祯时始赎归里，焕宇王君（即王重新）议诸绅士而据馆废墟建庙焉"，这便是孔子庙，后来叫文庙。到清代乾隆十二年（1747年）重修时，将庙址扩大，等级提高，成为当地最壮观的建筑物之一。文庙后期有庙产地十余亩，都是乡人捐献。郭峪村所在的"里"，从唐代到清初，出了一百多位"乡贤"，本村在清代初年又出了文渊阁大学士、《康熙字典》总裁官之一陈廷敬。

清代所建郭峪村文庙坐北面南，四合院，占地面积大约四千平方米。地势北高南低，大门前要上十几级台阶。大门五开间，中央三间为明柱厦廊，正殿为大成殿，面阔五开间，正中供孔子坐像，两侧按昭穆分列颜回、曾子等孔门七十二贤人的牌位。

大成殿结构用斗拱，前檐有格扇门窗，殿前有月台，便是"杏坛"。大殿左右各有耳房两间，供储存祭仪用品，管理人员也住在这里。东西配殿各八间，为乡贤祠，殿内供郭峪及附近各村（属郭峪里）的乡贤牌位一百多个，并有名贤碑七座，其中两座刻着自唐代至清代一千多年郭峪里考取功名的人的姓名，有八十八位之多。乡谚说，"金谷十里长，才子出郭峪"。金谷是郭峪村所在的山谷的名称。

郭峪文庙内另有各种纪事石碑一百余块，并有文昌阁一座。文庙大门的厦廊是科考张榜的地方，平日里孩子不得在这里玩耍，闲杂人等不得在这里喧哗，颇有严肃之气。每年春秋二季有隆重的祭祀，生员以上的文化人才有资格参加。

参加祭祀的人必须长袍马褂、衣冠整齐、形象端庄，并且事先要洗脸剃头。参祭的人按品级年龄先在大门外排队，然后徐徐鱼贯进入庙内，在杏坛上举行隆重的典礼。杏坛上布陈祭品，人们焚香跪拜，行三献礼，燃放鞭炮。祭毕孔子，再祭拜乡贤。

"大社"（乡间的行政组织，高于"社"一级）出资做嫩豆腐，祭礼完毕，分给社中儿童吃掉，相信可以补脑，读书聪明，将来登科进仕。山西省沁水县西文兴村的文庙也是附近西乡各村共祀。

民国十年（1921年）的西文兴村《重修文昌阁、文庙碑记》写道："春秋祀期，往之邑侯下临，或遣学官为代表，率西乡士子习礼讲学于其中，渐摩以诗、书、礼、乐之化，故当时科举联翩，民俗亦为之敦厚。

……自前清道光年间殿宇倾圮，呈请移此圣木主于县城文庙，嗣后父老子弟不复睹衣冠文物之盛，习礼讲学之风遂以中辍，文风亦因之不振，迄今百有余年。" 这座文庙在村子正门之内，正门之上为奎星阁。文庙北邻为圣庙，内祀历代帝王圣贤的牌位。

圣庙之北为文昌阁，文昌阁恰位于村内正街东口，街内有进士牌楼两座。文庙的西侧有敬惜字纸的焚帛炉两座。这一组文教建筑占了全村不小的面积。福建省连城县培田村有"文武庙"，建成于清代乾隆己亥年（1779年）。

两层楼阁，上层祀孔子，下层祀关羽。文圣、武圣共处一楼。《吴氏宗谱》里写道："每修皆大发，诚敬必高升。" 中了科举功名，不但仕途通畅，而且光宗耀祖，自己更可以得到一份永久的纪念。明初洪武二十一年（1388年），太祖朱元璋下诏用公帑给新科状元任亨泰建造一座牌坊。

从此进士牌坊便流行起来，到了明代中叶成化、弘治朝，还给以前没有建牌坊的进士补建，不久，州府和一些乡村都可以看到壮观的进士牌坊了。清代虽然自嘉庆朝起停止用官帑给进士造牌坊，但听宗族自建。

"自建"引发有些举人也造起了牌坊，不过数量不多。清初的雍正皇帝说过，"四民以士为长，农次之，工商其下"，光绪年间（1875—1908）编就的《大清会典》说："崇本抑末，载诸会典，若为常经，由来已久。"这些仕进牌坊，把"士"的首要地位形象地告示于天下。对牛角挂书的田舍郎，这又是一个有力的激励。

因为纪念性建筑求耐久，早在元末明初，仕进牌坊就有用石材的或木、石并用的了，多雨潮湿的南方诸省以石柱的为多，也有大量整体都为石材的。但石质构件的式样和做法等仍仿木构。北方诸省因干燥而仍多全身木质的。

牌坊式样有两大类，一类由古代"衡门"发展而来，大约在宋代开始用作纪念性的牌坊；另一类由古代"乌头门"（或称"棂星门"）发展而来，用冲天柱。乌头门式的牌坊大约出现于明代弘治、正德年间（1488—1521），明末盛行，到清代成为主要的型制。

这两类牌坊都可以跨街巷而建，作为地标，引人注意。（但贞节牌坊不许人在下面穿过，所以多贴墙而建，并在柱间密列栏杆，处理得很严肃。） 牌坊的规格有双柱单楼或三楼、四柱三间三楼或五楼几种。"楼"，指的是一段狭窄的双坡的小屋顶。

双柱单楼式牌坊是最简单的一种，它可以用山西省沁水县西文兴村的一对全石质乡进士牌坊为代表作。

它们是为炫耀明代成化十六年（1480年）乡进士柳騄和明代嘉靖二十五年（1546年）乡进士柳遇春的科举成就而立的，分别造于1544年和1550年。

二者式样和尺寸一模一样，结构和比例完全模仿木结构，左右对称地竖立在村子居住区主门永庆门前的横向主街上。柳騄的牌坊刻"丹桂传芳"四字，柳遇春的刻"青云接武"。它们相距大约二十五米，和永庆门一起组成了全村建筑的核心。

三间五楼式牌坊是仕进（进士）牌坊中最华丽有气派的，只有衡门式而不可能有冲天柱式，因为三间而有五楼，便是在中央一对柱顶正上方支一小段双坡式顶子。例子之一是安徽省绩溪县冯村的冯瑢进士牌坊。

冯瑢于明代成化十四年（1478年）考中进士，屡任福州推官，北京兵部车驾司主事，弘治二年（1489年）致仕。这座牌坊建于成化十五年（1479年），即中进士的次年。

它四根柱子都是石质的，前后都有抱鼓形的"靠背石"，增加牌楼的稳定性和厚重感。明间和次间之上的木质歇山式楼顶各有两攒斗拱，夹在中间的两个楼顶只各有一攒斗拱。斗拱出三跳，并有斜出的拱，很轻巧华丽。脊上的吻和宝瓶的尺度都很夸张，以致轮廓跳动而有喜庆的气息。

明间的下枋上雕一对狮子滚绣球，这是民间抒写欢快而热烈心情常用的题材。次间的下枋上雕的是鹿，谐音"禄"，读书考进士为的是当官，也便是求禄。明间上下枋之间的"字牌"上镌刻"进士第"三字，它上方，有竖向匾额刻"恩荣"二字。

恩荣二字表示牌坊的建造是由皇上恩准了的。也有些牌坊在这块匾额上刻"圣旨"或"敕建"等字，是同样的意思。

类似的四柱三间五楼式进士牌坊还有浙江省遂昌县独山村的进士牌坊和福建省连城县培田村武进士吴拔祯的牌坊。

吴拔祯护卫慈禧太后西狩有功，所以牌坊上刊刻对联： 世有凤毛迭荷宸慈颁紫綍； 身随豹尾曾陪仙仗列黄麾。

浙江省永嘉县楠溪江中游岩头村幸存的进士牌坊，是明世宗嘉靖年间（1522—1566）为进士金昭造的，四柱三间三楼，但中央明间两根柱子是石质的，断面为方形。每根柱子也都是前后有抱鼓石式的靠背石夹住。

这座牌坊的特点是结构近似宋式，斗拱雄大而且用真昂，最上面两层昂的后尾合力托住脊檩，它们下面一层昂的后尾又在中段托住它们。整个牌坊的造型非常刚健有力。它通面宽8.46米，柱高4.40米，总高7.63米，前后各出檐1.65米，很飘洒。瓦脊的曲线十分柔和轻巧。

虽然斗拱复杂但整体很简洁，没有装饰，然而比例和谐。永嘉县花坦村的宪台牌楼和朱氏大宗祠（敦睦祠）的大门以及苍坡村的大门，结构和风格都与这座进士牌楼相似。三开间进士牌坊也有全部用石料建造的，不过数量少。

实例之一是浙江省兰溪市长乐村的进士牌坊。它三开间，正贴村门，几乎成了村门的主体。可惜在文化大革命时遭到了严重的破坏。

除了为个别的进士建造牌坊之外，宗族或大家族还出资造一种"世科牌坊"，就是造一座牌坊，它的明间的上部横着石板或木板，把本宗族或家族历届举人以上的科名陆陆续续都刻在上面，集体荣耀。

例如山西省阳城县黄城村和郭峪村都有几座这种家族性的"世科牌坊"，其中有陈氏家族相同的一对分别在黄城村村口和郭峪村陈昌言老宅门口先后建造，它们都是清初《康熙字典》总裁官之一陈廷敬家族的。因为黄城村和郭峪村都属同一个陈氏家族。陈昌言是陈廷敬的伯父，也有功名。郭峪村还有张好古一门三进士、张鹏云"祖孙兄弟科甲"等的世科牌坊。与郭峪村相邻的上庄、中庄和下庄也都有。

江西省乐安县流坑村则有"五桂坊"，纪念董氏三代五人于宋仁宗明道二年（1033年）同榜中了进士。又有一种和科举有很大关系的牌坊，就是揄扬一个家族的仕途成就的，如"四世一品"、"同胞翰林"、"父子尚书"等等。

这些牌坊的形式和进士牌坊没有差别，而且常常造在一起，形成牌坊群。

另有一种"集体性"的进士牌坊，如山西省阳城县城里的"九凤朝阳"和"十凤齐鸣"坊，两坊都是纪念同一位老师的十名弟子于清代顺治丙戌年（1646年）同榜高中进士。这种牌坊数量当然很少。

这两座牌坊的重复是因为中榜的进士里有一位的喜报迟到了些日子。这教后人看到弟子们中进士之后老师和乡亲们急切地炫耀的心情。进士牌坊和牌坊群在村子里并没有一定的位置。

常见的为：第一，在大宗祠门前附近，如浙江省永嘉县岩头村的进士金昭牌坊；第二，在村子的主街上，如山西省沁水县西文兴村的"丹桂传芳"和"青云接武"两座牌坊，于明代嘉靖年间（1522—1566）分别为柳騄、柳遇春两位乡进士建立的。

牌坊因为形式特殊，又有炫耀公众的意义，所以对村子的景观起很大的作用。当若干个牌坊组合在一起的时候，很能形成一幅壮丽的图景。例如，安徽省歙县棠樾村村口大路上一溜七座石牌坊，浙江省永嘉县花坦村大宗祠前大道上的八座牌坊。可惜后者经"文化大革命"的摧残，已经只剩下三座了。

总之，牌坊的建造目的在于表彰个人、荣耀宗族、教化大众，所以总要选择在容易被乡人们见到的位置，以充分发挥它们的作用。有一些地方，不少牌坊和宗祠的正立面相结合，就是牌坊贴到宗祠正面，而以当心间框住宗祠正门的门洞。

例如浙江省兰溪市诸葛村的房派宗祠行原堂的正面，以"乡会两魁"为主题做三间贴墙牌坊。单间的有雍睦堂。

还有一种牌坊和纪念性建筑物结合的方式，便是用牌坊作为主建物正门前小广场的门，例如浙江省青田县南田镇的明代开国元勋刘基（伯温）庙前，小广场左侧牌坊门书"帝师"，右侧牌坊门书"王佐"，正前方为一道矮墙。它们既形成了庄严华丽的庙前空间，又写出了庙主的历史地位。

类似于牌坊的旌表科名成就的建筑，还有独立的楼、门等等，如江西省乐安县流坑村的西主门"状元楼"，追纪南宋绍兴十八年（1148年）董德元得中状元。楼的下部为一座砖石高台，中央有门洞穿过，很像一段城门。高台上为木构的方形两层楼式建筑。

同村还有东主门"翰林门"，是为被荐为翰林院编修参与编纂《永乐大典》的举人董琰造的，门洞两侧有大学士杨士奇题的联： 国史总裁，望重一时锁闼； 英才乐育，名高天下崇师。

除了牌坊，浙江、江西、福建诸省，凡得了举人以上功名的还可以立"桅"。桅是一根长长的笔直的木杆或石杆，高高竖立在祠堂大门前，或门前广场周边。它下端有大石座或者一对夹杆石把它稳住。

它上段，近杆顶处，装着木板做的"斗"，凡进士的，上下两只斗，举人的，仅有一只斗。它们向外村人炫耀着一个家族的成就和光荣，对本家族的后裔则是强有力的鞭策和推动。它们的高度，大约在十米左右，通常是超过宗祠门楼的檐口。这些垂直竖立的桅，和华丽的祠堂正门相辉映，使整个画面十分活泼。

也有些宗祠把这些桅集中立在门前小广场上或者广场周边。功名成绩较好的宗姓，它们形成了一大片桅的丛簇，例如，江西省新建县程氏"汪山土库"之前，三十余座桅杆密拥如林。

福建省西部不少村落，功名桅杆全身用整块巨石雕凿而成，秀气又挺拔，如永安县西洋福庄邢氏宗祠前空场三面立着六根石桅杆，为环境增加不少活气。

桅和牌坊除了基本的旌表作用外，对装饰和活跃村落的景观起了很大的作用。

4.

Confucian Temples, Examination Archways, and Flagpoles Confucian temples (孔庙), also called Culture Temples (文庙), by regulation could only be built at county level or above—but a very few villages, with approval from the Duke of Yansheng's office in Qufu, also built them.

Guoyu Village (Yangcheng, Shanxi) and nearby Xiwenxing Village (Qinshui, Shanxi) each have one; Furong Village (Yongjia, Zhejiang) also has one.

Culture Temples ranked higher than Wenchang Pavilions; by regulation, their "Classics Officer" (典籍官) had to be formally appointed by the Duke of Yansheng's office.

Guoyu Village's Culture Temple stands at the base of the west city wall inside the village.

In Ming Chenghua 6 (1470), on the ruins of an ancient public building here, a "Village Hall" (里馆) was rebuilt—"selecting elders to manage village governance and moral transformation," roughly equivalent to a village government.

In early Wanli, due to Zhang Juzheng's political reforms, it was destroyed.The site was "redeemed by the village in Chongzhen era; Wang Huanyu (i.e.

, Wang Chongxin) discussed with gentlemen and built a temple on the hall's ruins"—this was the Confucius Temple, later called Culture Temple.

In Qing Qianlong 12 (1747), during reconstruction, the temple site was expanded and its rank raised, becoming one of the area's most spectacular buildings.

The temple later had over ten mu of temple land, all donated by villagers.

The "village district" (里) where Guoyu Village is located produced over a hundred "local worthies" (乡贤) from Tang to early Qing; the village itself, in early Qing, produced Chen Tingjing—Wenyuan Pavilion Grand Secretary and one of the chief editors of the Kangxi Dictionary.

The Qing-built Guoyu Culture Temple faces south, a quadrangle covering ~4,000 sq m.Terrain is high north, low south—over ten steps up before the main gate.

Main gate is five-bay, central three bays with exposed-pillar eave corridors.

The main hall is Dacheng Hall (大成殿), five-bay wide; center enshrines a seated Confucius statue; both sides, by zhaomu order, display tablets of Yan Hui, Zengzi, and the other seventy-two disciples.

Dacheng Hall uses bracket sets (斗拱), front eave has lattice doors and windows; before the hall is a moon terrace (月台), which is the "Apricot Altar" (杏坛).

On both sides of the main hall are two side rooms each, storing ritual supplies; management staff also live there.

East and west side halls are eight bays each, serving as Local Worthy Shrines (乡贤祠)—inside enshrine over 100 local worthy tablets from Guoyu and nearby villages (belonging to Guoyu district), with seven famous-worthy stelae, two of which刻 names of those who obtained examination degrees in Guoyu district over a thousand years from Tang to Qing—88 people.

A local saying: "Jingu Valley ten li long, talents come from Guoyu." Jingu is the name of the valley where Guoyu Village lies.

Guoyu Culture Temple also has over 100 various commemorative stone stelae, and one Wenchang Pavilion.The Culture Temple main gate's eave corridor was where examination results were posted.

On ordinary days, children were forbidden to play there, idlers forbidden to make noise—quite a solemn atmosphere.Each year, in spring and autumn, there were grand sacrifices.

Only educated people at student (生员) level or above qualified to participate.Participants had to wear long gowns and mandarin jackets, dress neatly and dignified, and wash their faces and shave beforehand.

Participants, by rank and age, first lined up outside the main gate, then slowly entered in single file, holding grand ceremony at the Apricot Altar.

On the altar, sacrificial offerings were laid out; people burned incense, knelt, performed the three-offering ritual (三献礼), and set off firecrackers.

After sacrificing to Confucius, they worshipped local worthies.

The "Great Society" (大社—rural administrative organization, one level above "society") funded tender tofu; after the ritual, it was distributed to village children to eat—believed to nourish the brain, make them read smartly, and pass examinations in the future.

Xiwenxing Village's (Qinshui, Shanxi) Culture Temple was also jointly worshipped by nearby West Township villages.

The 1921 Xiwenxing Village "Record of Rebuilding Wenchang Pavilion and Culture Temple" writes: "At spring and autumn sacrifice periods, the county magistrate would come in person, or send a school official as representative, leading West Township scholars to practice ritual and lecture there—gradually transformed by poetry, books, ritual, and music; hence at that time examinations were continuously successful, and local customs became honest and generous.

...

Since late Qing Daoguang era, halls collapsed; petitioned to move the sacred tablet to the county city Culture Temple; thereafter fathers, sons, and elders no longer saw the splendor of dress and artifacts; the custom of ritual practice and lecturing ceased, and literary style declined—now over a hundred years.

" This Culture Temple is inside the village's main gate; above the main gate is Kuixing Pavilion (奎星阁).North of the Culture Temple is Sage Temple (圣庙), enshrining tablets of successive emperors and sages.

North of Sage Temple is Wenchang Pavilion, precisely at the east end of the village's main street; inside the street are two jinshi archways.

West of the Culture Temple are two paper-burning furnaces (焚帛炉) for respectfully disposing of written paper.This group of cultural-educational buildings occupies a significant area of the village.

Peitian Village (Liancheng, Fujian) has a "Civil-Military Temple" (文武庙), built in Qing Qianlong Jihai (1779).Two-story pavilion: upper floor enshrines Confucius, lower floor enshrines Guan Yu.

Civil sage and military sage share one building.The Wu Clan Genealogy writes: "Every restoration brings great fortune; sincere reverence must bring promotion.

" Obtaining examination degrees not only smoothed official careers and brought glory to ancestors and clan, but also gave oneself a permanent memorial.

In early Ming Hongwu 21 (1388), Emperor Taizu Zhu Yuanzhang decreed using public funds to build an archway for new zhuangyuan Ren Hengtai.

From then on jinshi archways became popular; by mid-Ming Chenghua-Hongzhi era, archways were even retroactively built for earlier jinshi; soon, prefectures, counties, and some villages could see spectacular jinshi archways.

In Qing, though from Jiaqing era public funds for jinshi archways stopped, clans were allowed to build them themselves.

"Self-building" led some juren to also build archways, though in smaller numbers.Early Qing Yongzheng Emperor said: "Among the four peoples, scholars rank first, farmers second, artisans and merchants below.

" The Guangxu-era (1875–1908) Collected Regulations of the Great Qing says: "Honoring the root and suppressing the branches, recorded in the Collected Regulations, as constant principle, from long ago.

" These official-advancement archways visually proclaimed the scholar's primary status to all under heaven.For farm boys with books hanging from ox horns, this was another powerful激励.

Because commemorative buildings sought durability, as early as late Yuan-early Ming, official-advancement archways used stone or wood-stone combinations.In rainy, humid southern provinces, stone-pillar archways were common, with many entirely stone.

But stone components' forms and methods still imitated wooden construction.Northern provinces, due to dryness, still had many entirely wooden archways.

Archway styles fall into two major categories: one developed from ancient "Heng Gate" (衡门), beginning to be used as commemorative archways around Song dynasty; the other developed from ancient "Black-Head Gate" (乌头门, also called Lattice-Star Gate 棂星门), using soaring pillars.

Black-Head Gate style archways appeared around Ming Hongzhi-Zhengde era (1488–1521), flourished in late Ming, and became the dominant form in Qing.

Both types could be built across streets as landmarks, drawing attention.

(But chastity archways forbade people passing underneath—hence mostly built against walls, with dense railings between pillars, treated very solemnly.

) Archway specifications include: two-pillar single-roof or three-roof; four-pillar three-bay three-roof or five-roof."Roof" (楼) refers to a narrow gabled small roof section.

The two-pillar single-roof archway is the simplest type, represented by a pair of entirely stone local-jinshi archways at Xiwenxing Village (Qinshui, Shanxi).

They were built to炫耀 the examination achievements of local jinshi Liu Lu (Ming Chenghua 16, 1480) and Liu Yuchun (Ming Jiajing 25, 1546), built in 1544 and 1550 respectively.

Both are identical in style and dimensions, structure and proportion entirely imitating wooden construction, symmetrically erected on the horizontal main street before the village residential area's main gate Yongqing Gate.

Liu Lu's archway is刻 "Cassia Fragrance Passed On" (丹桂传芳); Liu Yuchun's is刻 "Blue Clouds Following Martial Steps" (青云接武).They stand ~25m apart, and together with Yongqing Gate form the core of the village's architecture.

The three-bay five-roof archway is the most ornate and imposing of official-advancement (jinshi) archways—only Heng-Gate style, never soaring-pillar style, because three bays with five roofs means a small gabled roof section directly above the central pair of pillar tops.

One example is the Feng Rong jinshi archway at Feng Village (Jixi, Anhui).

Feng Rong passed jinshi in Ming Chenghua 14 (1478), served successively as Fuzhou judicial official, Beijing Ministry of War carriage-office director, and retired in Hongzhi 2 (1489).

This archway was built in Chenghua 15 (1479), the year after passing jinshi.Its four pillars are all stone, with drum-shaped "back-rest stones" (靠背石) front and back, increasing stability and massiveness.

Above the central and side bays, wooden hip-and-gable roofs each have two cluster bracket sets; the two middle roofs each have one cluster.

Bracket sets project three tiers, with diagonal brackets—light and ornate.Ridge ornaments and treasure vases are exaggerated in scale, making the silhouette lively and festive.

The central bay's lower lintel is carved with a pair of lions playing with embroidered balls—a common folk motif for joyful, warm feeling.

The side bays' lower lintels are carved with deer, homophone for "salary" (禄)—reading to pass jinshi was to become an official, i.e., seek salary.

Between the central bay's upper and lower lintels, the "name plaque" (字牌) is engraved "Jinshi Mansion" (进士第); above it, a vertical plaque is刻 "Imperial Grace" (恩荣).

"Enrong" indicates the archway's construction was approved by the emperor.Some archways刻 "Imperial Edict" (圣旨) or "Imperially Built" (敕建) on this plaque—same meaning.

Similar four-pillar three-bay five-roof jinshi archways include the Dushan Village (Suichang, Zhejiang) jinshi archway and the military-jinshi Wu Bazhen archway at Peitian Village (Liancheng, Fujian).

Wu Bazhen meritoriously escorted Empress Dowager Cixi's western flight, hence the archway bears a couplet: The world has phoenix feathers, repeatedly receiving imperial grace issuing purple edicts; Body followed leopard tails, once accompanied immortal retinue in yellow banners.

The surviving jinshi archway at Yantou Village (middle Nanxi River, Yongjia, Zhejiang), built for jinshi Jin Zhao in Ming Jiajing era (1522–1566), is four-pillar three-bay three-roof—but the central bay's two pillars are stone, square in section.

Each pillar is also clamped front and back by drum-stone back-rest stones.

This archway's特点 is structure approximating Song style: bracket sets grand and using true ang (真昂); the rearmost tails of the top two ang tiers jointly support the ridge purlin, and the ang tier below them supports them at mid-section.

The entire archway's form is very robust and powerful.It is 8.46m wide overall, pillars 4.40m high, total height 7.63m, eaves projecting 1.65m front and back—very graceful.Tile ridge curves are soft and light.

Though bracket sets are complex, the whole is simple, without decoration, yet proportions harmonious.

Huatan Village's Xiantai Archway, the Zhu Clan Main Ancestral Hall (Dunmu Hall) gate, and Cangpo Village's gate—all similar in structure and style to this jinshi archway.

Three-bay jinshi archways also exist entirely built of stone, though fewer.One example is the Changle Village (Lanxi, Zhejiang) jinshi archway.

It is three-bay, directly attached to the village gate, almost becoming the village gate's main body.Unfortunately severely damaged during the Cultural Revolution.

Beyond building archways for individual jinshi, clans or large families also funded "Generation-Examination Archways" (世科牌坊)—one archway whose central bay's upper part has a horizontal stone or wooden plank, on which successive juren-and-above examination names of the clan or family are刻 one after another—collective glory.

E.g.

, Huangcheng Village and Guoyu Village (Yangcheng, Shanxi) each have several such family "generation-examination archways"; among them, an identical pair of the Chen family was built successively at Huangcheng Village entrance and at Guoyu Village's Chen Changyan old residence gate—both belonging to early Qing Kangxi Dictionary chief editor Chen Tingjing's family.

Because Huangcheng and Guoyu both belong to the same Chen family.Chen Changyan was Chen Tingjing's uncle, also with examination degrees.

Guoyu Village also has generation-examination archways for Zhang Haogu's "one family three jinshi" and Zhang Pengyun's "grandfather-grandson-brother examination degrees.

" Neighboring Shangzhuang, Zhongzhuang, Xiazhuang also have them.

Liukeng Village (Le'an, Jiangxi) has "Five Cassia Archway" (五桂坊), commemorating five Dong family members across three generations who passed jinshi on the same list in Song Renzong Mingdao 2 (1033).

Another type of archway closely related to examinations praises a family's official-career achievements—e.g.

, "Four Generations First Rank" (四世一品), "Brother Hanlin Scholars" (同胞翰林), "Father-Son Ministers" (父子尚书), etc.

These archways' form is no different from jinshi archways, and they are often built together, forming archway groups.

Another "collective" jinshi archway: in Yangcheng city (Shanxi), "Nine Phoenixes Facing the Sun" (九凤朝阳) and "Ten Phoenixes Singing Together" (十凤齐鸣) archways—both commemorate ten disciples of the same teacher who passed jinshi on the same list in Qing Shunzhi Bingxu (1646).

Such archways are naturally very few.The duplication of these two archways occurred because one of the passing jinshi's good news arrived a few days late.

This teaches later generations of the eager炫耀 mood of teachers and villagers after disciples passed jinshi.Jinshi archways and archway groups have no fixed position in villages.

Common positions: first, near the main ancestral hall's front gate—e.g., Yantou Village's jinshi Jin Zhao archway; second, on the village's main street—e.g.

, Xiwenxing Village's "Cassia Fragrance Passed On" and "Blue Clouds Following Martial Steps" archways, built in Ming Jiajing era (1522–1566) for local jinshi Liu Lu and Liu Yuchun respectively.

Because archways have special form and public炫耀 significance, they greatly affect the village's landscape.When several archways combine, they can form a magnificent scene.E.g.

, seven stone archways in a row along the entrance road at Tangyue Village (Shexian, Anhui); eight archways along the avenue before Huatan Village's main ancestral hall (Yongjia, Zhejiang)—unfortunately the latter, after Cultural Revolution destruction, only three remain.

In short, archways' purpose is to commend individuals, glorify clans, and educate the public—hence always positioned where villagers can easily see them, to fully发挥 their role.

In some places, many archways combine with the ancestral hall's front facade—the archway is贴 to the ancestral hall's front, with the central bay framing the ancestral hall's main gate opening.

E.g., the branch ancestral hall Xingyuan Hall at Zhuge Village (Lanxi, Zhejiang) has, on its front, a three-bay wall-attached archway themed "Two Champions in Township and Provincial Examinations" (乡会两魁).

Single-bay examples include Yongmu Hall.Another way archways combine with commemorative buildings: using archways as gates of the small square before a main building's front entrance.E.g.

, before the temple of Ming founding merit official Liu Ji (Bowen) at Nantian Town (Qingtian, Zhejiang), the small square's left archway gate is inscribed "Imperial Teacher" (帝师), right archway gate "Royal Assistant" (王佐), with a low wall straight ahead.

They both form a solemn, ornate temple-front space and express the temple patron's historical status.Buildings similar to archways in commemorating examination achievements include independent towers and gates.E.g.

, Liukeng Village's west main gate "Zhuangyuan Tower" (状元楼), commemorating Southern Song Shaoxing 18 (1148) Dong Deyuan becoming zhuangyuan.

The tower's lower part is a brick-stone high platform with a gate opening through the center, much like a section of city gate.On the platform is a wooden square two-story tower building.

The same village has east main gate "Hanlin Gate" (翰林门), built for juren Dong Yan, who was recommended as Hanlin Academy compiler and participated in compiling the Yongle Encyclopedia; on both sides of the gate opening is a couplet by Grand Secretary Yang Shiqi: National history chief editor, prestige heavy in one era's palace gates; Outstanding talents happily nurtured, name high under heaven revering teachers.

Beyond archways, in Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian provinces, those obtaining juren-and-above degrees could also erect "flagpoles" (桅).

A flagpole is a long, straight wooden or stone pole, erected high before an ancestral hall's main gate or around the front square.Its lower end is stabilized by a large stone base or a pair of pole-clamping stones.

Its upper section, near the top, has wooden "dou" (斗, bracket-like blocks): jinshi graduates have two dou (upper and lower), juren only one.

They炫耀 to outsiders a family's achievements and glory, and to the family's descendants are a powerful鞭策 and推动.Their height is about 10m, usually exceeding the ancestral hall gate tower's eave line.

These vertically erected flagpoles, echoing the ornate ancestral hall main gate, make the whole scene very lively.Some ancestral halls集中 erect these flagpoles on the front small square or around it.

Clans with better examination records form a large cluster of flagpoles—e.g., before the Cheng clan's "Wangshan Earth Warehouse" (汪山土库) at Xinjian County (Jiangxi), over 30 flagpoles stand dense as a forest.

In many villages of western Fujian, merit flagpoles are entirely carved from single massive stone blocks—elegant and upright.E.g.

, before the Xing clan ancestral hall at Xiyang Fuzhuang (Yong'an, Fujian), six stone flagpoles stand on three sides of the open square, adding much vitality to the environment.

Flagpoles and archways, beyond their basic commemorative role, greatly contribute to decorating and enlivening the village landscape.

5.5 文峰塔、文昌阁、奎星楼
Section 5

五、文峰塔、文昌阁、奎星楼 书院、学塾、文馆之外，最重要的文教建筑就数文昌阁、文峰塔、功名牌坊、惜字亭等等了。

村办的学堂，有些就和村口的文昌阁和文峰塔一起。文峰塔是风水术的一种道具，以迷信的方式改变村落原来的自然环境，使它"有利于"大发科甲。风水典籍《相宅经纂》说： "凡都、省、州、县、乡村，文人不利，不发科甲者，可于甲、巽、丙、丁四字方位择其吉地，立一文笔尖峰，只要高过别山，即发科甲。

或于山上立文笔，或于平地建高塔，皆为文笔峰。" "文笔"是一个垂直的实心的圆柱或四方抹角的石柱，顶上尖尖如笔端，很简单，一般也不高，五米上下而已。"高塔"指的就是文峰塔，多层，木构、砖构或二者合构均有，以纯砖构的为多，纯木构的较少。内为砖砌多边形筒构，外围木构架檐廊的也有而少见。造型以楼阁式为多。大的可以登临，小的多为实心的。通常有七层，二三十米高。

《相宅经纂》虽说文笔可建在四个方位，但实建的大多在巽位，即村子的东南方。这是因为村子一着手选址的时候，就要把村子和水口的关系定下来。水口就是村子所在地一定范围之内的地表水汇合后流出这个范围去的口子。风水术上把水比作财，所以不希望水流直泻而去，而希望"去水有情"，于是，就一来要求溪河在水口处曲折。

二来要求水口两侧有一对小山丘，一个峻峭一点，为"狮"；一个平缓一点，为"象"，二者对峙，叫做"狮象把门"。三来最好再有一些亭阁之类的建筑物点缀一下，加强对水口的闭锁，文峰塔就是很合适的闭锁水口的建筑。

中国的大地势，照风水术的说法，是西北高而东南低，宋代王洙等撰的风水典籍《地理新书》说道："西北高，东南低，水流出巽，为天地之势也。

"于是，村子的选址就常使水口处在村子的巽位上，并常在水口造些风雨桥、亭阁、庙宇之类形体自由而很美的建筑。水口既是众水的出口，地势当然就低，那就更希望在那里造一座塔"高过别山"了。

但这"高"其实是象征性的，大多数的塔并不真的能够"高过别山"，风水术士诡称，这类风水塔高度的计算法是一寸等于一丈。或者造在村边山峰上，那就另编一套风水说法。因为造价很高，文峰塔并非村村都有，只有富而大且重文教的村子才造。

浙江省建德市新叶村在东南方（巽方）水口上有一座抟云塔，通高约三十余米，砖砌楼阁式，正六边形，七层，每层有叠涩砖檐，并有券窗三个，错层而开。塔内有楼板，以木梯上下。建于明代隆庆、万历年间（1567年始建，1574年落成）。

《玉华叶氏宗谱》里有主持建塔的白崖山人写的《抟云塔记》，记下了当年一位风水师的建议："凡通都大邑，巨聚伟集，于山川赳缺之处，每每借此（按：指塔）以充填挽之助。虽假人之力以俾天之功，而萃然巍然，凌霄耸兀，实壮厥观"。于是，"友松翁暨弟侄辈拟于所居之东，叠级而层垣焉，使天柱之高标与玉华、道峰相鼎峙，以补巽方之不足也"。这其实就是《相宅经纂》里的话。

但塔的体量当然远远比不上玉华山和道峰山，所谓均衡，不过是风水术上的一种象征性的安慰而已。《抟云塔记》又说：初建的塔"凡高一百四十尺有奇，围得高之三一，外辟通明之户者三，内为升梯者六，下作周廊，视其周倍之"。"是役也，虽曰仿浮屠之制万一，堪舆之左券可执，则将来之题名纪捷者当籍籍乎其蝉联而骥附也。如是则古所称雁塔者岂得专其美于前耶？

故兹之名抟云者亦曰于方为巽，取象则风，当夫秋飙迅发、彼鹍鹏起者负乘天之云抟扶摇而上九万里，将拭目俟之矣！"可惜，乐观的预言没有实现，新叶村的后人渐渐转向商业，文运反不如前。不过，文峰塔确实给村落风光增色不少。原徽州六邑之一的婺源县碧山村的文峰塔就在大学者俞正燮居停过的碧山书院一侧。

山西介休焦家堡村的奎星塔，楼阁式，砖砌实心，六边七层，高二十三米，底层壶门塑奎星像，第七层有"文光射斗"匾，塔顶为葫芦宝瓶式琉璃塔刹。它立在河岸边，确实为大环境生色不少。州县的文峰塔在南方诸省多见，以"官办"代替"民办"来祈一方的文运，也算是为官者的"德政"。

因为州县辖区大，塔址不见得都限于巽位，这种州县的文峰塔的选址便甲、巽、丙、丁四方都有，多在小山巅上，如婺源县城的就造在丁峰上，而塔形仍旧与村中的相类，是"仿浮屠之制"。

山西省介休县的文峰塔，建于城东南（巽方）二十公里外的天峻山顶端，是一个石砌实心的平顶圆柱形建筑，有收分，形式很别致，高二十三点五米，始建于明代万历年间，由知县史某主持建造。广州市小水口的赤岗塔也是一座文峰塔。

广州位于东南海滨，堪舆家素来把中华全国地形简化为西北高而东南低的"天地之大势"，所以，清代屈大均在所著《广东新语》里记录："形家者以为中原气力至岭南而薄，岭南地最卑下"，而广州"其东水口空虚，灵气不属，法宜以人力补之。补之莫如塔，于是以赤岗为巽而塔其上，觚棱峻起，凡九级，特立江干，以为人文之英锷"。

这座塔不但是为了振兴广州的文运而建，且是关锁水口的重要建筑物之一。用塔来促文运，这风俗也普及到西南各地的兄弟民族中去。贵州省都匀市剑江岸边的文峰塔，"为明代万历年间一位姓桂的总兵率领乡人所建。原为五层木塔，后因年久失修而倒塌。

道光十九年（1839年），都匀籍（布依族）的甘肃按察使陶廷杰致书乡里，并捐银一千两，资助重建此塔。"这座塔重建后为石质，六边形，七层楼阁式，高三十一米。多民族杂居的湖南会同县高椅村，村前有巫水流过，通航，陆上有驿道，水陆交会，于是造了一座文峰塔。嘉庆二十年（1815年）《杨氏族谱》有诗赞曰："斜阳翘首塔流光，照耀全村景运昌，况是巽峰偏得玄，子孙代代姓名香。

"有些村落财力弱，而又盼望文风大兴，便借用略近笔尖形的天然山峰而称文笔峰。又因为州县的辖区大，自然环境的选择范围宽，所以州县的文峰塔多能造在风景很优美的地方，点缀风景的作用很大。有一部分文峰塔占据地势，远迎水陆交通线，成了州县的地标，给人以此地居民奋发有为的印象。

例如浙江省江山县于宋代在城边山上造了百祐和凝秀两座塔，前者七级六面，高二十四米，后者九级六面，高三十米，均为楼阁式砖塔。从江上放舟而下，遥望双塔，小城充满了生气。以塔象征文风、文运的起因，可能是唐代新科进士都要到长安大雁塔上留名的缘故。科举时代另一种标志性文教建筑是文昌阁。

文昌阁祭祀文昌帝君。《史记·天官书》里说："北斗之上有六星，合称为文昌宫，掌人间文运。

" 文昌帝君主文运，就是主科举应考者的成败，而科考的成败又不仅关系到每一个读书人本身，甚至关系到一个宗族的命运，因此，文昌阁的兴建就和村落的兴衰息息相关。《道园学古录》作者宋元间人虞集所撰《四川顺庆路蓬州相如县大文昌万寿宫记》里说："宋亡蜀残，民无孑遗，鬼神之祀消歇。

自科举废而文昌之灵异亦寂然者四十年余，延祐初，元天子特出睿断，明诏天下以科举取士，而蜀人稍复治文昌之祠焉。"相如县清泉乡慕蔺里抢先造了一座文昌宫。虞集叹道："于戏，圣天子赫然兴科举，未及期月，万里之外，岩绝之邑，已有闻风而兴起者，信乎其神矣。" 到了明代，朝廷诏"天下学宫皆立文昌祠"，而且从学宫又普及到几乎所有村落。

清代嘉庆六年（1801年）仁宗颁上谕："文昌帝君君着海内崇奉与关圣大帝相同，宜列入祀典，同光文治。"每年农历二月三日文昌帝君圣诞，都要派官员祭拜。文昌阁的型制，大体是一所合院，前后两堂，左右有厢房或无厢房而有厢廊，甚至连厢廊都没有。前堂之上有楼阁，供文昌帝君像。

后堂常用为学塾的讲堂。由于楼阁居前堂之上，又多用翼角翻飞的歇山顶，所以文昌阁的外形高耸而轮廓参差，正脊两端吻饰则塑为变形的鲤鱼，以首向下。因为民间以"鲤跃龙门而化龙"比喻平民在科考中一举成功而改变身份，所以鱼尾变形为细细的龙身形状，轻快而灵活，几经大弯大曲向上冲腾，动感极强。这是象征"青云直上"，也是科场成功的常用比喻。

浙江省建德市新叶村和相邻的上吴方村的文昌阁吻饰为这种型制的典型。浙江省江山市廿八都村是仙霞关戍兵退役以后留居而成的大杂姓村落，有一百四十多个姓氏，几十种乡音，所以没有宗祠，却有两座文昌阁。

都是三进两院，楼阁在第二进，三层楼阁，三开间，歇山顶，有腰檐，气势很盛。这两座文昌阁成了全村最宏丽的公共建筑。它们两侧安静整洁的跨院为讲堂和山长住所。小型的文昌阁则是一个独立的两层阁子。

前徽州六邑之一的婺源县西武乡黄村造在水口上的文昌阁只有方方的一大间加一圈廊步，两层，四坡顶，像一座玲珑轻巧的亭子。古人深知，为学不可有市井气，所以文昌阁常和比较高层次的书院等组合在一起形成一个建筑群。可作为代表的是安徽歙县雄村的竹山书院，由曹氏宗族初创于清代乾隆年间（1736—1795）。

书院主体厅堂有前后两进，上堂三间，太师壁左右悬蓝底金字板联一副： 竹解心虚，学然后知不足； 山由篑进，为则必要其成。右厢房一侧有门通向内院。院内布局活泼，药畦花圃之间，有学生上课的教室和山长的书斋、住房。一条游廊引向一座花园，内有"清旷轩"，悬书法家郑莱小篆"所得乃清旷"匾。厅内有屏风，上书乾隆时诗人曹学诗的"清旷赋"。

曹氏宗族立下了一条规矩，凡科举得了功名的子弟，可以在园里种一棵桂花树，以应读书人"蟾宫折桂"的故事，这个清旷轩因此俗名"桂花厅"。桂花厅东北方有文昌阁，筑于高台上，呈八角形，俗称"八角亭"。

这座竹山书院和文昌阁很清新脱俗，给求学的和教书的一个高雅的环境。文昌阁与书院一样，园林化是一个极普遍的现象。

外借天然山色水光，内则种花栽草，如浙江省兰溪市诸葛村的文昌阁，据1947年《高隆诸葛氏宗谱·重建文昌阁碑记》里描写："为堂三楹，架以杰阁，而奉帝座于其巅。……启窗则岩峦之秀出者咸若蜿蜒盘曲而环拱于其前，俯槛则桃李竹桂之属缤纷掩映于其下。"可惜"文化大革命"时阁被拆毁，竹木也被伐尽。

为了远避市井气，乡村士绅知识分子很重视文昌阁的选址。浙江省永嘉县珍溪《朱氏合族副谱·改建文昌阁记》里记载，清初雍正年间（1723—1735），廊下村乡绅们集资建了一座文昌阁。"然其地卑下，树木蔽障"，邑庠生朱闻轩觉得不满意，遂邀朋友们登上桂松岭，到了"广可亩余"的一处山阿，"见潭水漈洄而涵影，秀峰耸拔以连云；文笔插其右，斗山踞其左；山川环绕，若绣若绮。

因喜不胜曰：此真文昌阁基地，可以安神灵而聚风气矣！"于是在乾隆二年（1737年）将原来的文昌阁拆迁到这块新址重建。新阁"门临水曲，地耸云端，拱群峰之突屹，面万木之郁葱，珍川之胜，于此称第一焉。登斯阁者，晨夕之赏心各异，四时之兴趣不穷，文思秀发，颖悟宏开。

"（《珍川朱氏合谱·慎轩公传》）它"右文笔、左斗山"，借堪舆风水之术以求科考兴盛，未能脱俗。一般情况下，水口也都是村子近处风景最好的地方，流水在这里弯曲，两岸山丘对峙，林木葱茏，数百年不伐。

而且水口又是文峰塔、庙宇、水碓、亭桥等等的聚集之所。这些建筑形体活泼而变化丰富，没有住宅之类的干扰，所以很容易形成优美的建筑群，于是，文昌阁也常常会侧身其间。

文昌阁不但按风水术的要求参与了"关锁去水"，并且以它耸拔活泼的轮廓、华丽的装饰，大大使水口建筑群生色。所以水口建筑群常常成为村子的"八景"或"十景"之一。

福建省连城县培田村水口的文昌阁为"新八景"之首，有《杰阁吟风》诗： 一望云霄势欲冲，巍巍高阁插空中，披襟快我开怀抱，琢句惊人夺化工。檐际抑扬鸣铁马，天边往复送霜鸿。凭栏益壮凌云志，直拟扶摇万里风。

浙江省建德市新叶村的水口，文昌阁和名为抟云塔的文峰塔、观音堂以及五谷祠（即土地庙）一起组成的建筑群在柏树林的衬托下非常生动。文昌阁、文峰塔、观音堂和五谷祠的组合，是中国千年"耕读文化"的绝妙诠释。

文昌阁是村子里的公共建筑，营造费用一般是宗祠的公款，但也有私人乐捐的。前徽州六邑之一婺源县的延村（今在江西）有一方关于建造文昌阁的碑记，全文是："本村水口关帝庙左首，金霁坪自愿输租八秤，与众换田，独建文昌阁，为合里肇开文运，颇当大观。

楼上恭奉神像四座，楼下恭奉神位二尊，计用费二千金。子孙笃志诗书，世守勿替也。嘉庆八年秋月霁坪金盖亮记"。个人有了钱，给全村造一座文昌阁作为公益事业，祈求文运肇开，不论文昌帝君是否灵验，也确是善举。类似的记载在婺源各村还有不少。和文昌阁相似的是奎星楼或魁星楼。

奎星和魁星都是天上星宿，都被认为"主文运"，因奎与魁二字同音，民间把它们混同了，以致奎（魁）星楼和文昌阁也有混同现象，反正是科举时代祈求考试得意的地方罢了。山西省沁水县西文兴村既有文昌阁也有魁星阁。文昌阁在村里街口，街上有两座进士牌坊。

魁星阁就造在村子正门门洞之上，它的右侧是关帝庙，进了洞门，里面便是文庙。关帝是武圣人，文武二圣在一起，也是常见的组合。清代嘉庆辛未年（1811年）西文兴村建魁星阁，《魁星阁新建记》碑里说道："文庙功成而魁星阁未建，建章公曰：村之东南（按即巽方）地势渐下，将欲修一阁以补之，祀魁星神。

"它的选址完全符合风水术的要求，如《相宅经纂》所说，只消在聚落的甲、巽、丙、丁四个方位之一上造个高耸的建筑物便可以变"不发科甲"的地形为"即发科甲"。这座魁星阁造在巽位的村门之上，显然就是为了增加高度。阁两层，三开间，上层为歇山顶，下层有腰檐。它加强了村门的表现力，使进入村子所在的小盆地的人抬眼便见它耸立于一个台地的边缘，魁星阁成了村子的标志。

5.

Wenfeng Pagodas, Wenchang Pavilions, and Kuixing Towers Beyond academies, schools, and literary halls, the most important cultural-educational buildings include Wenchang Pavilions (文昌阁), Wenfeng Pagodas (文峰塔), merit archways, and character-respecting pavilions (惜字亭).

Village-run schools were sometimes located together with the village entrance's Wenchang Pavilion and Wenfeng Pagoda.

Wenfeng Pagodas are a tool of fengshui, using superstitious means to alter a village's original natural environment to make it "favorable" for abundant examination success.

The fengshui classic Xiangzhai Jingzuan (相宅经纂) says: "All capitals, provinces, prefectures, counties, and villages where scholars are disadvantaged and examinations do not flourish—one may choose an auspicious site in the jia, xun, bing, or ding directions, erect a writing-brush pointed peak; as long as it rises higher than other mountains, examinations will flourish.

Or erect a writing brush on a mountain, or build a tall tower on flat ground—both are writing-brush peaks.

" A "writing brush" (文笔) is a vertical solid cylindrical or square-chamfered stone pillar, pointed at the top like a brush tip—very simple, generally not tall, around 5m.

A "tall tower" refers to Wenfeng Pagoda: multi-story, wooden, brick, or composite construction—mostly pure brick, rarely pure wood.Interior is brick polygonal cylinder; exterior wooden-frame eave corridors exist but are rare.

Form is mostly pavilion-style (楼阁式).Large ones can be climbed; small ones are mostly solid.Usually seven stories, 20–30m high.

Though Xiangzhai Jingzuan says writing brushes may be built in four directions, actual construction was mostly in the xun direction—the village's southeast.

This is because when village site selection began, the relationship between village and water mouth (水口) had to be determined.

The water mouth is the outlet where surface water within the village's defined area gathers and flows out.

In fengshui, water is compared to wealth—hence one does not wish water to flow straight away, but hopes "outgoing water has feeling" (去水有情).Thus: first, require streams to bend at the water mouth.

Second, require a pair of small hills on both sides of the water mouth—one steep, called "lion" (狮); one gentle, called "elephant" (象)—facing each other, called "lion and elephant guarding the gate" (狮象把门).

Third, ideally some pavilions and towers decorate the spot, strengthening the water mouth's closure—Wenfeng Pagodas are very suitable buildings for closing water mouths.

China's great terrain, per fengshui, is northwest high and southeast low; Song dynasty Wang Zhu's fengshui classic Dili Xinshu (地理新书) says: "Northwest high, southeast low, water flows out through xun—this is the tendency of heaven and earth.

" Hence village sites often place the water mouth in the village's xun direction, and often build wind-rain bridges, pavilions, temples—free-form, beautiful buildings—at the water mouth.

Since the water mouth is the outlet of all waters, terrain is naturally low—hence one more hopes to build a tower there "higher than other mountains.

" But this "height" is actually symbolic; most towers cannot truly be "higher than other mountains." Fengshui masters诡称 that for such fengshui towers, the height calculation is one cun (inch) equals one zhang (ten feet).

Or built on a village-edge mountain peak—then another set of fengshui explanations is invented.Because construction cost was high, Wenfeng Pagodas were not in every village—only wealthy, large, culture-valuing villages built them.

Xinye Village (Jiande, Zhejiang) has Tuanyun Pagoda (抟云塔) at its southeast (xun) water mouth, ~30m+ total height, brick pavilion-style, regular hexagon, seven stories, each story with corbelled brick eaves and three arched windows opening on alternate stories.

Inside has floors, with wooden ladders.Built in Ming Longqing-Wanli era (founded 1567, completed 1574).

The Yuhua Ye Clan Genealogy contains "Record of Tuanyun Pagoda" by Baiya Shanren, who presided over construction, recording a fengshui master's suggestion: "All great cities and large gatherings, where mountains and streams are deficient, often use this [pagoda] to fill and supplement.

Though using human power to assist heaven's work, yet gathered and majestic, soaring to the clouds, truly strengthening the scene.

" Hence "Yousong Weng and brothers/nephews planned, east of their residences, to build tiered walls, making the pillar of heaven's height stand tripod-like with Yuhua and Daofeng mountains, to supplement the xun direction's deficiency.

" This is essentially what Xiangzhai Jingzuan says.But the pagoda's mass is of course far less than Yuhua and Daofeng mountains—so-called balance is merely a symbolic comfort in fengshui.

The Record further says: the initially built pagoda "over 140 chi high, circumference one-third of height, outside three bright windows, inside six ladders, below a surrounding corridor twice the circumference.

" "This work, though imitating one ten-thousandth of stupa form, the fengshui guarantee can be held—then future names recorded in success will abundantly follow in succession.

Thus the ancient so-called Wild Goose Pagoda could not monopolize beauty before?

Hence this name Tuanyun also means: in direction it is xun, in image it is wind; when autumn winds swiftly rise, that great bird rises, carrying heaven's clouds, whirling upward ninety thousand li—we will watch and wait!

" Unfortunately, the optimistic prophecy did not come true; Xinye Village's descendants gradually turned to commerce, and literary fortune declined.

Nevertheless, Wenfeng Pagoda truly added much to the village's scenery.

The Wenfeng Pagoda at Bishan Village (Wuyuan, one of old Huizhou's six counties) stands beside Bishan Academy where great scholar Yu Zhengxie once stayed.

The Kuixing Pagoda at Jiaojiabao Village (Jiexiu, Shanxi) is pavilion-style, solid brick, hexagonal seven-story, 23m high; ground floor arched door has a Kuixing statue; seventh floor has "Literary Light Shoots the Dipper" (文光射斗) plaque; top is gourd-vase-style glazed tile finial.

Standing by the river, it truly adds much to the larger environment.

Prefecture/county Wenfeng Pagodas are common in southern provinces—using "official construction" instead of "private construction" to pray for a region's literary fortune,也算 an official's "virtuous governance.

" Because prefectures/counties have large jurisdictions, pagoda sites are not limited to xun direction—these pagodas' sites can be in jia, xun, bing, ding all four directions, mostly on small mountain peaks.E.g.

, Wuyuan county town's is built on Ding Peak; pagoda form still resembles village ones, "imitating stupa form.

" Jiexiu County's (Shanxi) Wenfeng Pagoda, built at the top of Tianjun Mountain 20km southeast (xun) of the city, is a solid stone flat-top cylindrical building with entasis, distinctive form, 23.

5m high, founded in Ming Wanli era, presided over by Magistrate Shi.Guangzhou's Chigang Pagoda at the small water mouth is also a Wenfeng Pagoda.

Guangzhou lies on the southeast coast; fengshui masters have long simplified China's terrain as "northwest high, southeast low—the great tendency of heaven and earth.

" Hence Qing Qu Dajun's Guangdong Xinyu (广东新语) records: "Shape-masters believe central plains' energy thins at Lingnan, Lingnan land is lowest"; and Guangzhou "its east water mouth is empty, spiritual energy does not belong—by principle should supplement with human power.

Nothing supplements like a pagoda—hence using Chigang as xun and building a pagoda on it, angular and soaring, nine levels, standing alone by the river, as the cutting edge of human culture.

" This pagoda was built not only to revive Guangzhou's literary fortune, but also as one of the important buildings closing the water mouth.

The custom of using pagodas to promote literary fortune also spread to fraternal ethnic groups in the southwest.

The Wenfeng Pagoda by the Jian River in Duyun (Guizhou) "was built by a General Gui leading villagers in Ming Wanli era.Originally a five-story wooden pagoda, later collapsed from long neglect.

In Daoguang 19 (1839), Duyun-native (Buyei) Gansu Surveillance Commissioner Tao Tingjie wrote to his hometown and donated 1,000 taels to fund reconstruction." Rebuilt as stone, hexagonal, seven-story pavilion-style, 31m high.

Gaoyi Village (Huitong, Hunan), multi-ethnic mixed, has Wu River flowing before the village (navigable), land post road, water-land junction—hence built a Wenfeng Pagoda.

Jiaqing 20 (1815) Yang Clan Genealogy has a praising poem: "Setting sun raises head, pagoda flows light, illuminating whole village's prosperous fortune; moreover xun peak especially obtains mystery, descendants' names fragrant generation after generation.

" Some villages with weak finances, yet hoping for literary flourishing, borrow natural mountain peaks slightly brush-tip-shaped and call them writing-brush peaks.

Because prefectures/counties have large jurisdictions and wide natural-environment choice, their Wenfeng Pagodas can mostly be built in very scenic places, with great landscape-decoration role.

Some Wenfeng Pagodas occupy terrain, facing water-land transportation lines from afar, becoming prefecture/county landmarks—giving the impression that local residents are ambitious and accomplished.E.g.

, Jiangshan County (Zhejiang) in Song built two pagodas, Baiyou and Ningxiu, on mountains by the city: former seven-level six-sided 24m high, latter nine-level six-sided 30m high, both pavilion-style brick pagodas.

Boating down the river, viewing the twin pagodas from afar, the small city is full of vitality.

The origin of using pagodas to symbolize literary style and fortune may be that Tang new jinshi graduates all went to Chang'an's Great Wild Goose Pagoda to inscribe their names.

Another landmark cultural-educational building of the exam era is the Wenchang Pavilion.Wenchang Pavilions worship Wenchang Emperor (文昌帝君).

Records of the Grand Historian · Heavenly Officials says: "Above the Northern Dipper are six stars, collectively called Wenchang Palace, governing human literary fortune.

" Wenchang Emperor governs literary fortune—i.e.

, governs the success or failure of exam candidates; exam success or failure relates not only to each reader himself, but even to a clan's destiny—hence Wenchang Pavilion construction is closely tied to village prosperity.

Song-Yuan scholar Yu Ji, author of Daoyuan Xuegu Lu, wrote in "Record of the Great Wenchang Longevity Palace at Xiangru County, Pengzhou, Shunqing Circuit, Sichuan": "Song fell, Shu was devastated, people had no survivors, spirit worship ceased.

Since exams were abolished, Wenchang's spiritual efficacy was also silent for over forty years; in early Yanyou, the Yuan emperor with exceptional judgment clearly decreed the empire to select officials through exams, and Shu people gradually resumed Wenchang temple worship.

" Xiangru County's Qingquan Township Mulin Village rushed to build a Wenchang Palace.

Yu Ji sighed: "Alas, the sage emperor vigorously revived exams; before a month passed, beyond ten thousand li, in remote cliff counties, there were already those who rose upon hearing the wind—truly its spirit is efficacious!

" In Ming, the court decreed "all empire's schools establish Wenchang shrines"—and from schools this spread to almost all villages.

Qing Jiaqing 6 (1801), Emperor Renzong issued an edict: "Wenchang Emperor is worshipped throughout the empire same as Guan Yu the Great; should be列入 sacrificial canon, equally illuminating civil governance.

" Each year on lunar 2/3, Wenchang Emperor's birthday, officials were sent to worship.

Wenchang Pavilion form: generally a courtyard compound, front and rear halls, left and right with side rooms or no side rooms but side corridors, sometimes even no side corridors.

Above the front hall is a pavilion housing the Wenchang Emperor statue.The rear hall often serves as a school's lecture hall.

Because the pavilion sits above the front hall and often uses hip-and-gable roofs with flying wing corners, Wenchang Pavilion's exterior is tall with varied silhouette; the main ridge's end ornaments are molded as transformed carp, heads downward.

Because folk use "carp leaping the dragon gate to become dragon" to metaphor commoners' one-shot exam success and identity change, the carp tail transforms into a thin dragon-body shape—light and flexible, after several great bends surging upward, very dynamic.

This symbolizes "soaring straight to the blue clouds" (青云直上), also a common metaphor for exam success.Xinye Village and neighboring Shangwufang Village's Wenchang Pavilion ridge ornaments are typical of this form.

Nianbadu Village (Jiangshan, Zhejiang), a large mixed-surname village formed by retired Xianxia Pass garrison soldiers, has over 140 surnames and dozens of dialects—hence no ancestral hall, but two Wenchang Pavilions.

Both are three-entry two-courtyard, pavilion at second entry, three-story pavilion, three-bay, hip-and-gable roof with waist eaves—very imposing.

These two Wenchang Pavilions became the village's most magnificent public buildings.Their两侧 quiet, tidy side courtyards serve as lecture halls and shanzhang residences.

Small Wenchang Pavilions are independent two-story pavilions.

The one at Huang Village, Xiwu Township (Wuyuan, old Huizhou), built at the water mouth, is only one large square room plus a surrounding corridor, two-story, four-slope roof—like an exquisite, light pavilion.

Ancients well understood that learning must not have marketplace atmosphere—hence Wenchang Pavilions often combine with higher-level academies to form building complexes.

A representative is Zhushan Academy (竹山书院) at Xiongcun Village (Shexian, Anhui), founded by Cao clan in Qing Qianlong era (1736–1795).

The academy's main halls have front and rear entries; upper hall three-bay, with a blue-background gold-character board couplet on both sides of the master's wall: Bamboo understands hollow heart, learning then knows insufficiency; Mountain advances by basketfuls, acting then requires completion.

The right side room has a door to the inner courtyard.Inner courtyard layout is lively: among herb beds and flower gardens are student classrooms and shanzhang's study/residence.

A covered corridor leads to a garden containing "Qingkuang Xuan" (清旷轩), with calligrapher Zheng Lai's seal-script plaque "What is obtained is clear and broad.

" Inside the hall is a screen with Qianlong-era poet Cao Xueshi's "Qingkuang Rhapsody.

" The Cao clan established a rule: any clan member obtaining exam degrees may plant an osmanthus tree in the garden, corresponding to the scholar's story "plucking osmanthus in the toad palace" (蟾宫折桂)—hence Qingkuang Xuan is commonly called "Osmanthus Hall.

" Northeast of Osmanthus Hall is a Wenchang Pavilion, built on a high platform, octagonal, commonly called "Octagonal Pavilion.

" This Zhushan Academy and Wenchang Pavilion are fresh and refined, giving learners and teachers an elegant environment.Like academies, Wenchang Pavilions' gardenization is extremely common.

Borrowing natural mountain/water scenery outside, planting flowers and grass inside—e.g.

, Zhuge Village's (Lanxi, Zhejiang) Wenchang Pavilion, per 1947 Gaolong Zhuge Clan Genealogy · Record of Rebuilding Wenchang Pavilion: "Three-bay hall, topped by a great pavilion, enshrining the emperor's seat at its peak.

...Opening windows, the graceful peaks all seem to wind and curve, surrounding before it; leaning on rails, peaches, plums, bamboo, osmanthus all colorfully shade below it.

" Unfortunately during the Cultural Revolution the pavilion was demolished, trees and bamboo also cut down.

To avoid marketplace atmosphere, rural gentry intellectuals valued Wenchang Pavilion site selection highly.

Yongjia Zhenxi Zhu Clan Combined Genealogy · Record of Rebuilding Wenchang Pavilion records: in early Qing Yongzheng era (1723–1735), Langxia Village gentry pooled funds to build a Wenchang Pavilion.

"But its site was low, trees blocked it"—county student Zhu Wenxuan was dissatisfied, so invited friends up Guisong Ridge to a mountain hollow "over one mu wide," where they "saw pool water swirling and reflecting images, graceful peaks soaring to clouds; writing brush pierces its right, Dipper Mountain sits its left; mountains and streams surround, like embroidery and brocade.

Delighted, they said: This is truly Wenchang Pavilion site, can settle spirits and gather atmosphere!" Hence in Qianlong 2 (1737), the original Wenchang Pavilion was dismantled and rebuilt at this new site.

The new pavilion "gate by winding water, ground soaring to clouds, arching sudden peaks, facing lush ten-thousand trees—Zhenchuan's scenery, here ranks first.

Those ascending this pavilion find morning/evening delights different, four seasons' interests endless, literary thoughts luxuriant, understanding broad.

" It has "right writing brush, left Dipper Mountain"—using fengshui to seek exam prosperity, not escaping convention.

Generally, the water mouth is also the best scenery near the village: water bends here, hills on both banks face each other, trees lush, uncut for centuries.

And the water mouth is also the gathering place of Wenfeng Pagodas, temples, water-powered trip hammers, pavilion bridges, etc.

These buildings have lively, varied forms, without residence interference—hence easily form beautiful building complexes, and Wenchang Pavilions often join them.

Wenchang Pavilions not only participate in "closing outgoing water" per fengshui requirements, but with their tall lively silhouettes and ornate decoration greatly enhance the water-mouth building complex.

Hence water-mouth building complexes often become one of the village's "Eight Scenes" or "Ten Scenes.

" Peitian Village's water-mouth Wenchang Pavilion ranks first of "New Eight Scenes," with a poem "Outstanding Pavilion Chanting Wind": One look at clouds, momentum about to soar; towering high pavilion pierces the sky; Opening robes, I joyfully open my embrace; crafting verses, astonishingly surpassing nature's craft.

At eaves, iron horses rise and fall; at horizon, frost geese come and go.Leaning on rails, strengthens soaring-to-clouds ambition; straightly planning to whirl ten thousand li in wind.

Xinye Village's water mouth—Wenchang Pavilion, Tuanyun Pagoda (Wenfeng Pagoda), Guanyin Hall, and Wugu Shrine (i.e.

, Earth God Temple)—together form a building complex, very vivid against cypress forest.

The combination of Wenchang Pavilion, Wenfeng Pagoda, Guanyin Hall, and Wugu Shrine is a wonderful interpretation of China's thousand-year "farming-reading culture.

" Wenchang Pavilion is a village public building; construction cost generally from ancestral hall public funds, but also private donations.

Yancun Village (Wuyuan, old Huizhou, now Jiangxi) has a stele about building a Wenchang Pavilion, full text: "At the left of Guandi Temple at this village's water mouth, Jin Jiping voluntarily donated eight cheng of rent, exchanged land with others, solely built Wenchang Pavilion, to inaugurate literary fortune for the whole community, quite a grand sight.

Upstairs respectfully enshrine four deity statues; downstairs respectfully enshrine two deity seats; total cost 2,000 gold.Descendants devoted to poetry and books, generations preserve without replacement.

Jiaqing 8 autumn, Jiping Jin Gailiang inscribed.

" An individual with money building a Wenchang Pavilion for the whole village as public welfare, praying for literary fortune—whether Wenchang Emperor is efficacious or not, it is truly a good deed.

Similar records exist in many Wuyuan villages.Similar to Wenchang Pavilions are Kuixing Towers (奎星楼) or Kuixing Towers (魁星楼).

Kuixing and Kuixing are both celestial constellations, both believed to "govern literary fortune"; because "kui" and "kui" are homophones, folk confused them—hence Kui (Kui) Star Towers and Wenchang Pavilions also show confusion phenomena—anyway they are places praying for exam success in the exam era.

Xiwenxing Village (Qinshui, Shanxi) has both Wenchang Pavilion and Kuixing Pavilion.

Wenchang Pavilion is at the village street intersection; the street has two jinshi archways.

Kuixing Pavilion is built above the village main gate's gate opening; its right side is Guandi Temple; entering the gate opening, inside is the Culture Temple.Guandi is the military sage—civil and military sages together, also a common combination.

In Qing Jiaqing Xinwei (1811), Xiwenxing Village built Kuixing Pavilion; the "Record of Newly Building Kuixing Pavilion" stele says: "Culture Temple completed but Kuixing Pavilion not built; Jianzhang Gong said: village's southeast (i.

e., xun direction) terrain gradually lowers, wish to build a pavilion to supplement it, worship Kuixing deity.

" Its site完全符合 fengshui requirements—as Xiangzhai Jingzuan says, merely building a tall building in one of the settlement's jia, xun, bing, ding four directions can transform "no exam success" terrain into "immediate exam success.

" This Kuixing Pavilion built above the xun-direction village gate is clearly to increase height.Pavilion two-story, three-bay, upper floor hip-and-gable roof, lower floor with waist eaves.

It strengthens the village gate's expressiveness, making anyone entering the village's small basin look up and see it standing on a terrace edge—Kuixing Pavilion became the village's landmark.

5.6 惜字亭
Section 6

六、惜字亭 乡土社会中还有一种重要的文教建筑，便是"惜字亭"，或者叫"焚帛炉"、"苍颉亭"，是用来焚烧有字迹的废纸的。文字是人类最伟大的创造。人类的智慧来自信息的积累和传递，而积累和传递信息的最有效的工具是文字。

四川省民间流行的传单《敬惜字纸文》说："千里之遥，付数言可以相通；万古产业，皆赖字迹为据。"说的便是文字信息的传递可以突破空间和时间的限制。百姓把社会强势群体叫"识文断字"的人，说弱势群体"西瓜大的字识不了一箩筐"。是不是识字，识多少字，能决定一个人在社会中的地位。文字既然有这样大的威力，人们采取的上策是努力学会识字，摆脱"睁眼瞎"，同时，又不禁油然而生对文字的敬畏之忱，甚至带一点神秘色彩。

几乎普及于全中国的一种巫咒说：凡脚踩了有字迹的纸张，必会瞎眼，更不用说拿来做污秽的用途了。四川省同治《合江县志》有清代乾隆年间（1736—1795）当地解元罗文思写的《惜字引》，说："赤文绿字，无非天地精灵；鸟迹龙章，尽是圣贤心血。"于是有诗道： 世间字纸藏经同，见者须当付火中， 灰送长流埋净土，后世子孙必昌荣。把敬重成文的字，扩大到敬重零星的字迹，为了避免亵渎文字，就得把有字的废纸烧掉，把灰送进河流中去或者掩埋于土中，以免被糟踏。

民间广泛成立"惜字会"或"惜字社"，起名为"崇文"、"广善"、"德文"、"拾遗"等等。会员自己身体力行，或出资雇人，背个篓子到处捡拾有字迹的纸；同时，向住户、商店、学校等处散发传单，呼吁敬惜字纸以积阴德。他们把收集到的字纸集中焚烧，为此募款建造专门的焚烧炉。

焚烧炉通常叫"惜字亭"，也有叫"焚帛亭"的，因为古人在纸张发明之前在帛上写字；也有些地方叫"苍颉亭"，因为传说苍颉是中国文字的发明人，是"字祖"。四川县合江县《同治旧志》有一篇罗允猷写的《惜字炉碑文》说："苍颉作书，功侔造化，启文明而有象，衍圣教于无穷，字之功用大矣！

"有些惜字亭就造在文昌宫边上，把苍颉和文昌帝君并列。书塾大门两侧墙上经常有焚字纸的壁炉。台湾《噶玛兰志略·卷十一》记载："兰中字纸，虽村氓童妇皆知敬惜。士人于文昌宫左筑有敬字亭，立为惜字会，雇丁搜觅，洗净焚化。

每年以二月三日文昌帝君诞辰，通属士庶齐集宫中，演剧设筵，结彩张灯，推年长者为主祭，配以仓颉神位。三献礼毕，即奉仓颉牌于彩亭，将一年所焚字灰，装以巨匣。凡启蒙诸童子皆具衣冠，与衿耆护送至北门外渡船头，然后装入小船。用彩旗鼓吹，沉之大海而回。"这段资料很生动地记载了捡字纸、洗净、焚化、积灰，并以隆重的仪式将字纸灰最后送入大海的过程。

惜字亭遍及全国城乡，一个村子往往不止有一座惜字亭，立在人们常到的地方。惜字亭的形状，是建筑式的，多是小小一座歇山顶或者攒尖顶的砖砌小方亭子，只有一米来高，下面再垫着一米来高的座子。

另一种是瓶式的，圆腹，四面开圆孔，上面或者是攒尖式的建筑屋顶，或者叠几个连珠、莲花，总高也不过两米左右。这两种都做得很精致。四川省合江县许多村里都有一座石砌的惜字亭，为五层至七层楼阁式的塔，六边形，高度在六米至八米之间，有一些在塔身上安两个小龛用来祭仓颉和文昌帝君的像。它们或者起着文峰塔的作用。建造年代从明至清，以清代为多。

有些塔身上刻一篇《序》或《记》，有些只刻"增福禄"或"天开文运"之类的吉祥话。合江县福宝场的惜字塔，在字纸入口处有额书"字库"二字，左右一副对联： 双笔归杜库， 一画入曹仓。塔身上还刻着清代中叶嘉庆年间重庆府训导邑人赵予际撰的一篇序文，是研究福宝场历史的重要文献。

台湾桃园县龙潭乡凌云村竹窗子段的圣迹亭，是一座惜字亭，初建于光绪元年（1875年），经光绪十八年（1892年）和民国十四年（1925年）的两度扩建，成了一个规模不小的建筑群，占地南北长46.7米，东西宽21.7米。

它坐北面南，圣迹亭居于北端，它从下而上有正方形台基、八边形亭座、正方形炉身、六边形的上段和壶芦攒尖顶几部分，总高6.92米。

圣迹亭的核心是炉身，它正面的炉门口，有两副对联，外侧比较大的一副刻的是"鸟喙笔峰光射斗，龙潭墨浪锦成文"，内侧一副小的是"文章到十分火候，笔墨走百丈银澜"。横批分别为"文运宏开"和"过化存神"。亭前面向南伸出中轴上的石板路，两侧铺草地。

中轴路的北端，圣迹亭的台基前，有供台，南端有祭台。祭台之外是中门，门两侧有弧形云墙一段。云墙尽端各立一根石质的"文笔"。再往南为头门，是比较简单的一对砖质方柱体。

头门之外是1979年扩展的外院，它的轴线为东西向，东侧建四柱三间三楼式高大的砖质仿木构牌楼门，面向东，体量远大于圣迹亭本身，西侧则建三开间冲天式石质牌楼一座，它的又西侧建一座大照壁，上面书写圣迹亭建造的经过。

这一个圣迹亭建筑群的规模之大是全国少见的。惜字亭日常管理和祭祀仪典由村里的民间组织"文会"负责。书院、学塾一般都有自己焚字纸的炉子，常见到的是嵌在墙上，像个壁龛，多为葫芦形，都很精致。龛口镶一圈砖浮雕花边，上方再加一些如意云头或者昆卢帽式的装饰。

福建省连城县培田村南山书院的化纸炉有联："赐火曾传汉；遗灰尚憾秦"，气概很大。对字纸的珍惜甚至敬畏，其实是对文化的珍惜和敬畏，更现实的考虑则是惜字纸者会有好报应，而最好的报应便是后人中科名。四川省合江县人罗文思在《惜字引》里说： 杨全善埋字而世掇巍科，实为盛事； 王沂公捡废而子登鼎甲，最是美谈。对文化的珍惜和敬畏，其实也是很功利的。

6.

Character-Respecting Pavilions (Xizi Ting) Another important cultural-educational building in rural society is the "character-respecting pavilion" (惜字亭), also called "silk-burning furnace" (焚帛炉) or "Cangjie pavilion" (苍颉亭)—used to burn waste paper bearing writing.

Writing is humanity's greatest creation.Human wisdom comes from accumulation and transmission of information, and the most effective tool for accumulating and transmitting information is writing.

A popular Sichuan flyer "Text Respecting Written Paper" says: "A thousand li away, a few words can communicate; ten-thousand-generation property all relies on written records as evidence.

" This means written information transmission can break through spatial and temporal limits.

Common people called the socially powerful "those who know writing and judge characters" (识文断字), and called the weak "can't recognize a watermelon-sized character in a whole basket.

" Whether one can read, how many characters one knows, determines one's social position.

Since writing has such great power, people's best strategy was to strive to learn to read, escape "blind eyes" (睁眼瞎)—while at the same time spontaneously feeling reverence for writing, even with a touch of mystery.

A curse spread almost throughout all China: anyone stepping on paper bearing writing will surely go blind, let alone using it for filthy purposes.

Sichuan Tongzhi "Hejiang County Gazetteer" contains a "Preface to Character Respecting" by local juren Luo Wensi from Qing Qianlong era (1736–1795), saying: "Red writing and green characters are nothing but heaven and earth's spirits; bird-trace and dragon-seal are all sages' heart's blood.

" Hence a poem says: Worldly written paper is same as sutras, those who see must put into fire, Ash sent to flowing river buried in pure earth, later descendants will surely prosper.

Extending respect for finished writing to respect for scattered traces—to avoid blaspheming writing, one must burn waste paper with writing, send the ash into rivers or bury it in soil, to prevent it from being trampled.

Folk widely established "character-respecting societies" (惜字会) or "character-respecting associations" (惜字社), named "Revering Culture" (崇文), "Broad Goodness" (广善), "Virtuous Culture" (德文), "Gathering the Lost" (拾遗), etc.

Members practiced themselves, or funded hired workers carrying baskets to collect paper with writing everywhere; simultaneously distributed flyers to households, shops, schools, calling for respecting written paper to accumulate hidden virtue.

They centrally burned collected paper, and for this raised funds to build dedicated furnaces.

Burning furnaces are usually called "character-respecting pavilions," also called "silk-burning pavilions"—because ancients wrote on silk before paper was invented; some places call them "Cangjie pavilions," because legend says Cangjie invented Chinese writing, the "character ancestor.

" Sichuan Hejiang County "Tongzhi Old Gazetteer" contains a "Character-Respecting Furnace Stele Inscription" by Luo Yunyou: "Cangjie made writing, merit equal to creation, inaugurating civilization with images, extending sage teaching infinitely—writing's function is great!

" Some character-respecting pavilions were built beside Wenchang Palaces, placing Cangjie and Wenchang Emperor side by side.School gate's two side walls often had wall furnaces for burning written paper.

Taiwan "Kavalan Gazetteer Brief · Volume 11" records: "In Lan, written paper, even village women and children know to respect.

Scholars built a character-respecting pavilion left of Wenchang Palace, established a character-respecting society, hired workers to search, wash clean and burn.

Each year on 2/3 Wenchang Emperor's birthday, all scholars and commoners gather in the palace, perform drama and banquets, hang colored lanterns, elect eldest as chief officiant, paired with Cangjie deity seat.

After three-offering ceremony, carry Cangjie tablet in colored pavilion, put one year's burned character ash in large box.

All newly enlightened children wear official clothes, with elders escort to north gate ferry head, then load into small boat.With colored flags and music, sink into the great sea and return.

" This material vividly records the process of collecting paper, washing, burning, accumulating ash, and with solemn ceremony finally sending character ash into the sea.

Character-respecting pavilions spread throughout urban and rural China; a village often had more than one, placed where people frequently go.

Their shape is architectural: mostly a small brick square pavilion with hip-and-gable or pyramidal roof, only about 1m high, below padded with a ~1m high base.

Another type is bottle-shaped: round belly, round holes on four sides, top either pyramidal architectural roof or stacked several pearls/lotus—total height no more than ~2m.Both types are exquisitely made.

Many villages in Hejiang County (Sichuan) have a stone character-respecting pavilion: a five-to-seven-story pavilion-style pagoda, hexagonal, 6–8m high; some have two small niches on the pagoda body for Cangjie and Wenchang Emperor statues.

They may also serve as Wenfeng Pagodas.Construction dates from Ming to Qing, mostly Qing.

Some pagoda bodies carve a "Preface" or "Record"; some only carve auspicious phrases like "Increase Fortune and Blessing" or "Heaven Opens Literary Fortune.

" Hejiang County Fubao Market's character-respecting pagoda has a horizontal plaque "Character Treasury" (字库) at the paper entrance, with a couplet on both sides: Twin brushes return to Du's treasury, One stroke enters Cao's granary.

The pagoda body also carves a preface by Zhao Yuji, Chongqing Prefecture instructor and local, from mid-Qing Jiaqing era—important document for studying Fubao Market history.

Shengji Pavilion (圣迹亭) at Zhuchuangzi Section, Lingyun Village, Longtan Township, Taoyuan County (Taiwan) is a character-respecting pavilion, first built in Guangxu 1 (1875), expanded twice in Guangxu 18 (1892) and Republic 14 (1925), becoming a sizable building complex: site 46.

7m north-south, 21.7m east-west.

It faces south, Shengji Pavilion at north end; from bottom up: square platform base, octagonal pavilion seat, square furnace body, hexagonal upper section, and gourd pyramidal roof—total height 6.

92m.

The core of Shengji Pavilion is the furnace body; its front furnace mouth has two couplets: the larger outer one carves "Bird-beak brush peak light shoots the dipper, Longtan ink waves brocade into writing"; the smaller inner one is "Writing reaches ten-tenths火候, brush and ink walk hundred-zhang silver waves.

" Horizontal inscriptions are "Literary Fortune Grandly Opens" and "Transforming and Preserving Spirit." South of the pavilion extends a central-axis stone path, with grass on both sides.

At north end of central path, before Shengji Pavilion's platform, is an offering table; south end is a sacrifice altar.

Beyond sacrifice altar is middle gate, with curved cloud walls on both sides.At cloud wall ends each stands a stone "writing brush." Further south is head gate—a simpler pair of brick square pillars.

Beyond head gate is the 1979-expanded outer courtyard, axis east-west: east side builds a tall four-column three-bay three-story brick imitation-wood archway gate facing east, mass far larger than Shengji Pavilion itself; west side builds a three-bay soaring stone archway; further west builds a large screen wall writing the history of Shengji Pavilion's construction.

This Shengji Pavilion building complex's scale is rare nationwide.Daily management and sacrificial rituals of character-respecting pavilions are handled by the village folk organization "Literary Society" (文会).

Academies and schools generally had their own paper-burning furnaces—commonly embedded in walls, like a wall niche, mostly gourd-shaped, all exquisite.

Niche mouth镶 a circle of brick relief border, above adding ruyi cloud-heads or Kunlu-cap-style decoration.

Peitian Village's (Liancheng, Fujian) Nanshan Academy's paper-transforming furnace has a couplet: "Bestowing fire once transmitted Han; remaining ash still regrets Qin"—very grand spirit.

Cherishing and even revering written paper is actually cherishing and revering culture; a more realistic consideration is that character-respecters will have good retribution, and the best retribution is descendants obtaining exam degrees.

Hejiang County native Luo Wensi says in "Preface to Character Respecting": Yang Quanshan buried characters and generations obtained high degrees, truly a grand event; Wang Yigong gathered waste and son attained top graduate, most a fine tale.

Cherishing and revering culture is actually also quite utilitarian.
