7.3 神的居所
Section 3

三、神的居所 有神就得有神待的地方，便于善男信女叩头烧香。极少数的神灵，只和日常生活发生关系，多待在百姓家里，如灶神、门神、厕神、井神、圈神、马王爷、狐仙、仓官爷等等。简单一点的，只在红纸上写个神号，或买一张印在红纸上的木刻神像，贴到他们各自职司所在的位置上。稍稍郑重一点的，在这些位置上做一个小小的龛，大多是砖的，也有些雕刻得很精致。少数用木材做。龛里则大多只贴一幅木刻印刷的神像，有些人家会放一尊瓷的或泥的塑像在里面，常常不明身份，只是有形有相，作为此处有神灵的表示而已。

神像前设香炉、烛台，都很简陋。广东，尤其是它的南部，常用琉璃烧出彩色的神龛，里面有神像，重重叠叠砌在房屋的正脊上和它的两侧。它们把正脊打扮成了十分华丽的装饰带，错落缤纷，热闹得很。

有些地方，如山西省的东南部和四川省的一些镇子，从事商业和手工业的人家比较多，则多在自家堂屋里墙上挂一个木龛祭祀本家从事的行业的保护神，如鲁班爷、杜康、清音童子、梅葛仙翁等等。有的还外加一个财神。

福建、安徽和江西，住宅堂屋中央太师壁两侧腋门上方设雕镂极精的神橱，一侧供高、曾、祖、祢四代祖先，一侧供几位神仙、菩萨。少数人家，在太师壁正中设一个大大的神橱，里面供祖先也供神仙菩萨。

太师壁、尤其是腋门上方，十分幽暗，敬神的烛光摇曳，神橱上的贴金闪烁出光芒，很有神圣的气象。左右腋门后长年各有一个香案，分祀鲁班爷和杨筠松。

鲁班爷到这里受香火，不是因为他的技艺，而是因为他掌握一座房子的"小风水"，如大门的朝向和尺寸、堂屋和门屋的宽度、屋檐的高度，等等。杨筠松则主管房屋的大风水，即它和大范围里地貌、地物的关系。

兴建宅屋之初，这两位大小风水大师各以一根木桩为代表，被竖立在房基地中轴线两端，作为房屋布局的座标点。房屋建成之后便搬迁到正厅左右腋门后面，永久奉祀。经常在百姓家里供奉着的还有财神、寿星、观音菩萨和姜太公。前面三位大多有个瓷像或木雕像，所在位置不定。观音像的礼拜者大多是妇女，观音菩萨是她们最贴心的神灵，她们多把像放在卧室里，早晚点一炷香，拱手作几个揖。

有些妇女还定期吃"观音斋"。她们把这位本来无性的菩萨硬是塑成女相，因为女性更富有同情心，更细致，更能理解她们的苦恼和希望。而且妇女把女性的神像放在卧室里，随时诉说心曲，在那个时代也可以少一点疑忌。姜太公为人谦和、爱护百姓，成了神还是这样，受到人民永远的敬重。山西人在住宅院落中央用砖或石垒一个像方凳大小的墩子，就叫它为"中宫爷"，这便是姜太公的象征。朔望点香进馔。不许在中宫爷上坐，也不许踩踏，更不许向它倾泼脏物秽水。

中宫爷名称的由来，是因为乡间住宅四合式的布局正合乎"九宫格"的样式，院落便是中宫。福建闽东，有些住宅在正房屋脊中央用砖搭一个很小的亭子形的神龛，叫"太公亭"，那便是姜太公的岗位。亭子是空的，里面没有塑像，只是个象征而已。

山西民宅还有两处常设神龛，一处是大门内影壁中央，一处是大门门屋侧壁。影壁中央大多供赐福的天官，门屋侧壁的神比较杂乱，有的供门神、有的供土地。

在江西、福建和广东，住宅正房堂屋的太师壁前香案下中央有土地公婆的神位，正规的称号是"福德正神之位"。左右有对联，如"福与土并厚；德配地无疆"，隐括了"福德"和"土地"两个称号。在土地神之前一步，便是这座宅子的风水穴眼。

这套配置鲜明地反映出农耕文明时代乡民和土地的亲密关系。绝大多数的神灵都奉祀在庙里。庙有大有小，最小的庙供与人们的生活福祉最有密切关系的神，那就是土地庙和三官庙。土地庙和三官庙最多，分布也随意。湖南、四川、浙江等省，村里村外，街头田间，都可能有土地庙，小的高不过两尺。

湖南省会同县高椅村，竟有这种小土地庙四十七座之多，几乎每座小庙都有一副相同的对联，写的是真心的祈求："念百姓疾苦，系一方平安。"大的土地庙也不过是局促的单间，通常兼作路亭。

除了专门的庙宇之外，村子的各种庙宇里，神台上大多会有土地公婆的一角位置。但也有更"高级"的待遇，如浙江省武义县俞源村的洞主庙里为奉祀土地公婆有一个专设的偏院，很宽阔，正殿有三开间。山西省临县西头村西云寺的前院一边也有个独立的土地庙。土地神的最大特点是一方土地有一位，本地出身，只管小小一方土地上的事。

坐在小土地庙里或者大庙神台一角的，都是明清以后，由对本村本地有功的"好人"充当的土地神，职位很低，管辖的范围很小，只过问些琐碎的生活杂事，所以说"当方土地当方灵"。在皖南和浙西的杂姓村里，偶有三间正房带前院或不带前院的社庙，远大于一般的土地庙。

《公羊传》注："社者，土地之主"。这种"社庙"，远承殷周时期以广阔的大地为神的自然崇拜的传统，那地位就远远高于后来的"土地庙"了，但它们的性质还是土地庙。

有些地方，如浙江省的江山县，江西省的丰城县，山西省的临县，凡杂姓的村落，都以"社"为基本的社会单位。一个村分几个"社"，每社大约二十五户左右，由推选的社首主管。

每个社都有社庙、水井和学塾。社神是地方神，"庇护"一方地面。

社庙还要定期举行节庆活动和祭祀活动，一般为春社（春分后戊日）和秋大社（秋分后戊日）两次。

唐末诗人王驾有一首著名的《社日》诗，写道：鹅湖山下稻粱肥，豚栅鸡栖半掩扉，桑柘影斜春社散，家家扶得醉人归。诗把社庙和人们生活的关系写得很亲切。

浙江省江山县三卿口是以烧瓷为生的碗窑村，在水口黄氏大宗祠对面有一座社庙，三开间，做工很精致。每逢龙窑里装满了碗坯，点火之前，窑主和窑工都要来祭拜，供猪头、鱼、鸡，点香烛，烧纸，并放鞭炮。

安徽省歙县的棠樾村，村口有一座三开间的社庙，它的绰号叫"花子亭"，因为它向流浪的乞丐开放，晚上收容他们住宿。村人说这是祖先留下来的规矩。

土地庙也有三间而带前院的，那就常常同时供着五谷神，例如浙江省建德市新叶村的土地庙，也叫土谷祠，和文昌阁并肩相倚。庙宇多而不大，遍布村内村外的，还有三官庙，就是奉祀赐福的天官、赦罪的地官和解厄的水官三位神祇的庙。

这三位神祇的功力和职能涵盖了农业社会中乡民生活的一切需要和理想。或许正因为如此生活化，乡民们感到他们亲切而毫无神秘崇高的凛凛威风，并不用庄严巍峨的宏大庙宇来祭拜他们，只让他们小小的庙宇位置在村里、田头或者妇女们经常浣洗的水圳旁边，亲切地融入人们日常生活之中。

浙江省永嘉县，在田间给农人们遮阳、避雨、歇气的两千多座路边小亭子，绝大多数都供着三官大帝的塑像，就叫三官庙。或者也可以说，凡三官庙必有敞屋、长椅，供人躲雨、休息、交谊。虽然散处田野之中，山路之旁，而且规模很小，但有一些也颇为精致，神龛和藻井都是很高水平的杰作，如花坦村东门口的三官庙。

山路边的小凉亭和三官庙里还备有锅灶、柴禾、炊具甚至崭新的草鞋，从立夏到秋分甚至还有大缸的凉茶，再加上些避暑的草药。它们都供过客免费取用，由村里宗祠的公费开支，也有的由稍稍富裕一点的人家作为给父母祈福的善事来承担开支，就叫"孝子亭"。这些措施体现出乡村人们相互间似乎平淡如水而切实有用的关怀。

正宗一点的庙宇的选址常由风水术士决定。多数的庙座落在村落聚居区之外，照风水术数的说法，庙宇阴气太重，不宜和居民混杂。伪托朱熹著的风水典籍之一《雪心赋》里说："所戒者，神前佛后"，也就是说，不论阴宅阳宅，都不要靠近庙宇。

注释说："其地既为神灵之所栖，则幽栖相触，钟鼓相惊，恐居之不安。"村聚不可能为建庙而搬迁，所以只好把庙建造在村外。

其实，把庙放在聚居处之外，应该是有很现实的理由的：一是庙中常有香火，容易引起火灾，如庙在居住区，很不安全；二是有了庙，就会有外村人来烧香，招引他们在村里进出，也不很安全；三是大型的庙宇每有庙会，或逢神诞日，香客拥挤杂沓，如庙在村中，则对村民的生活干扰太大。

较大的庙还有戏台，每有演出，四邻八乡的人都来看戏，村中因此难免扰攘不宁；四是把庙造在村外，还可以利用它们来起风水术数上增补或禳解的作用；第五，最重要的是，也可以给下田的、赶路的作为休息、避雨的场所。中国建筑绝大多数是木构的，中国农村绝大多数是聚居的，木构建筑聚而成村，最怕的是火灾。既怕火灾，就得造出个神来防火制火。

阴阳家在"四象说"里把玄武定为北方之神，又据阴阳家"四德"的说法，北方为水德，玄武便成了水神，民间遂请玄武大帝来防火制火，玄武庙因而遍布全国，一般都造在村落的北面。

河北省蔚县，二百多座村落，村村围以长方形的土墙，一条街贯穿正中，南端为村门，北端起高台，台上造玄武庙一座。这便是企图依仗风水巫术来防火救火。村子必有"水口"，就是溪河从村落所在的小盆地流出之处，必在村子的下游。

水口最好左右有山夹峙，叫"狮象把门"或"龟蛇把门"，以致水道较狭且有弯曲，"紧如葫芦喉"，这样就可以使"去水曲折有情"。风水术上把水比为财，去水有情就寓意能保住财富和气运不致流失。

为了加强水口的关锁，又据风水经典《雪心赋》说："坛庙必居水口"，注释道："大约神坛佛庙，宜居水口，镇塞地户，以关锁内气为妙也"。

因为中国全境是西北高而东南低，风水术士把这个整体地形叫做"天地之大势"，村落选址就喜欢选在西北高而东南低的地方，居于村子下游的水口因而也多选在村子的东南方，也便是巽方，于是，宜于在巽位的文昌阁正好就常常是关锁水口的庙宇之一，经常和文笔、水碓、长明灯、风雨桥（即廊桥）合称为"五生"，例如旧徽州六邑之一婺源县理坑村的水口和黟县西武乡黄村的水口。

浙江省武义县郭洞村，因为水口不在巽位，便以观音庙和关帝庙双双造在水口，合称"海麟院"，用加倍的力度以补不足。

水口必须植林加强闭锁，坛庙和常建在水口的文峰塔又是体形比较自由的建筑，所以水口建筑群大多是村落最美的建筑群，是建筑艺术和自然风光结合的杰作，如浙江省武义县的樊岭脚村，水口便有关帝庙、文昌阁、土地庙和廊桥，还有几棵合抱的大树。

自然环境中比较容易出险情的地方，如河流急弯处位于"弓背"可能受"反弓水"冲刷而崩塌的段落，或者暴雨时节可能滑坡的陡崖下，常建关帝庙来"镇住"。例如浙江省永嘉县蓬溪村村口正对"反弓水"，于是就在河岸上造了一座不小的五开间两进的关帝庙。相传关公既急公好义，又战无不胜，一切妖魔鬼怪都会在他面前逃窜，所以就借他的神威制服反弓水。如此这般地"禳解凶煞"，也是风水术的招数。

庙宇也可以用来改善村落风水呈式的不足或缺陷。在一个比较匀称的"形局"中，如左侧的"青龙砂"稍稍弱于右侧的"白虎砂"，为避免"白虎压青龙"的"凶相"，就在青龙砂的低处或缺处造一座庙或塔来加强它。

村子的"天门"（上水口）来水不宜很曲折，以免象征"财"的水来得不很顺当，但如果水道过于无遮无拦直冲村子而来，也要造一个庙来"缓冲"一下，例如江西省乐安县流坑村天门岸边的三官庙。

同样道理，如果有山路陡峭地直冲村子而下，也要有一座庙或者一座有神像的路亭挡一挡，风水上也说是防"冲"，如安徽省黟县关麓村背后山脊上的山神庙。因为在没有水路的地方，山路就代替水路而成为风水要素。这类野庙往往是村子的边界，能造成村子的领域感。

多少代外出谋生或赴试的人们别妻离子，家人们又送往盼归，它们便沉积了浓重的亲情乡愁。相传由唐代形势派风水宗师杨筠松选定而由他的亲授弟子曾文辿和六传弟子廖瑀的后人居住的江西省兴国县三僚村（原名山寮村，近年方改为三僚村），被认为是中国的"风水祖地"。

它四面环山，东有木形山峰，叫"木星降世"，南有火形山峰，叫"火星落槽"，西有金形山峰，叫"金星盖门"，而北面的"水星相依"山峰为水形。到明代晚期，曾、廖两姓的人通力合作，分别在它们的峰顶上造了东华庵、南箕庵、西竺庵和北斗庵四座庙宇，为的是强化风水的作用。

后来三僚村的风水业大为发展，仅同治《兴国县志》里留名的风水师就有二十一位之多。乡人们把这个行业的兴旺归功于这四座庵。虽是迷信，却鼓励了一种巫术的传承。有一种风水作用则是来自视觉形象的象征性。

例如，如果山口左右的山坡舒缓而略近对称，而且坡形饱满，则山口往往被附会成女阴，这种情况下，就会在山口造一座庙，庙里的众神之间有一位是送子娘娘，例如安徽黟县关麓村后西屏山和武亭山之间西武岭上的西闲庵；或者再在近处山上对着山口造一座塔，象征男根，以祈村子里人丁兴旺。例如，浙江省建德市新叶村道峰山和玉华山之间山口上的玉泉寺和遥相对应的文峰塔。

风水术士在给长期"不发"的血缘村落做改善环境的建议时，可能提出在村边某个地点造一座庙宇、佛塔。塔的风水意义远远超出它的宗教意义。例如山西省阳城海会寺（龙泉寺）的双塔，它使丘陵环境里一块低地中的小村子（大桥村）成了耀眼的地标，活跃了很大一片地方。

又有山西省介休县龙凤村附近的凌空塔，它在村外龙凤河的急转弯处，高三十八米，九层，造于1732年。塔下有一座小小的石鼻庵，是塔的附属建筑，庵名来自河的急弯，这里有山岩凸出。这座凌空塔便是一座风水塔，是"镇水"用的。海会寺塔和石鼻庵塔虽然未必改变了村落的命运，但它们确实大大美化了村落和田野！

在浙江、福建和广东等省，由于庙宇大多要造在村子聚居区之外，又要有风水的讲究，所以常不免有扎堆的现象。如浙江省永嘉县岩头村的上水口"双浚头"，很小一片平地就有三圣庙、太阴庙和卢氏娘娘庙三座庙。庙的院子里又附有几个小庙。

三圣庙里主祀从西域带回多子的石榴的张骞（张仙）；太阴庙主祀月神；卢氏娘娘庙即孝祐夫人庙。据乾隆《永嘉县志》载："唐，卢氏居卢岙，尝与母出樵，遇虎将噬其母，女急投虎喙，以代其母死。后人见女跨虎而行，遂祠祀之，宋理宗谥号孝祐夫人。"永嘉有很多孝祐夫人庙，这是表彰孝女，社会伦理性的，与宗教本来没有关系。

山西和河北有一些村子周边围以土墙而成堡寨状，庙宇就在堡门外或跨堡墙扎堆。最典型的例子是山西省介休县的张壁村和河北省蔚县的西古堡。两村的布局模式都很整齐。张壁村北门有大小庙十座，南门有十一座。南门东侧在堡墙之上跨堡墙内外而建的庙是"可罕庙"；城门头上有"西方胜境庙"，应是佛教净土宗的寺庙；南门外的主庙是关帝庙，传说关帝曾在明代末年"显圣"帮村民在南门口吓走了一帮武装的贼寇。

在这三座庙的里外旁侧，有观音庙、地藏堂、龙神庙等等。张壁村北门门口城墙之上有三座庙，正中是真武庙（即玄武庙），真武是坐镇北方的主水之神。

它东侧是空王庙，《创建空王行祠碑记》说：古佛系陕西凤翔府人，俗姓田氏，寄居在太原府榆次县原涡村，长任里长，因褊护穷人而受官府谴责，遂辞亲出家为僧，居介休洪济寺，曾命徒施雨救旱灾，后隐于张壁村南的绵山。乡民以他为司雨水之神，香火极旺。真武庙西侧为三大士殿，即观音、文殊和普贤三位菩萨，是佛教寺庙。它正殿居中面南，两侧有配房，形成一个院子。北门外有瓮城，向东开门，门头上有吕祖阁。

北门外正中轴线上有规模很大的二郎庙，祭祀的是李冰的次子，帮李冰治水（一说为杨二郎。但神像脚下无哮天犬，额上无天眼），因为张壁村南高北低，落差很大，南边山洪下来，穿过村子中心的"龙街"直冲北门而去，风水术士说，这样会冲走全村的财气，所以北面要有一位治水的神来协助真武大帝抑制水势，这神就是李二郎。

于是就造了一幢坐北向南三开间的二郎庙。面对二郎庙，背靠北门瓮城，造了全村唯一的大戏台，所以二郎庙向北后退，留出一大片"观众席"。在这些庙宇之间有很小的痘母宫等小庙。北门内侧十八米，街西有兴隆寺，正殿祀如来佛。

真正的佛寺在农村中很少见，它也并不单纯，在正殿两侧还有姑嫂殿和阎王殿，这对姑嫂不知出于何典，至今村中已经没有人知道，不过香火依然不断，这叫做"神佛不嫌磕头人"。

蔚县西古堡的情况大致也这样，南北堡门外各有正方形的瓮城，庙宇都在瓮城里，南瓮城有地藏庙、观音庙和一座戏台，北瓮城有真武庙、娘娘庙和一座已毁而失名的庙。两个瓮城内各自还有几座小庙。

蔚县有二百几十座堡式村落，各个布局方正，正中一条道路直穿南北，北端高圪台上端立着北方之神玄武的庙，即真武庙。庙不大，但前面有高高的大台阶，台阶上有牌楼，构成很庄严神圣的景象。有些位置在水道航路关节点上的大村或镇店，往往在高地上造庙作为它们的地标。

江西省乐安县流坑村的乌江东岸梅岭山上曾有东华寺，山西省临县黄河边的碛口镇则有卧虎山上的黑龙庙，都从很远便教艄公看见，知道村镇已到，应该准备靠岸了。船上的旅客，也会站起来，远望码头，仔细寻觅人群中的妻儿了。南方各地的丘陵区，有山、有水、有木、有竹，风景绝佳，所以许多村子都有"十景"、"八景"，而这些"景"里，总有一个甚至几个和庙宇有关。

例如浙江省兰溪市的诸葛村，它的"八景"之一叫"翠岫晓钟"，它的主建筑是翠峰禅院。明代正德年间（1506—1522）有人写"八景诗"，说它：半山梵宇住烟霏，隐隐钟鸣出翠微；响逗残云来远岫，声传清曙到扃扉……它给村落增多了可爱的生气。庙宇常选址在山、水、林木的最美处，成为景区的主角。

以它们玲珑的楼阁，粉墙黛瓦、飞檐游脊，更丰富了自然的美。例如浙江省永嘉县林坑村村口小小的白鹤大帝庙、武义县俞源村的洞主庙都给青山小溪点染了无限秀色。各地的庙宇中，有多少古老和厚重，极富于历史的沧桑感和辽阔感。如山西省高平县的法源寺和晋城的青莲寺则增添了山峦的壮美。还有陕西省佳县的香炉寺和湖北省石宝寨的玉印山寺则分别烘托了滚滚黄河和万里长江奔流的宏阔雄伟。

乾隆皇帝有一句话，说："天下名山僧占多"，寺庙给天下风景反哺了多少秀色、豪气。中等规模以上的庙宇，大多数有戏台，是村落的艺术中心和文化中心。它们不但建筑高大华丽，飞檐走脊，而且大多包含着木雕、砖雕、石雕、灰塑等装饰，十分精美。

山西省和广东省有些庙宇，屋脊上的琉璃制品，包括"三山聚顶"、鸱吻、正脊等都是杰出的艺术品。戏台的藻井、照面枋和殿宇的牛腿，也大都是小木作和木雕的精品。

寺庙里往往有许多石碑，它们是村落历史的重要资料。四川省合江县的尧坝镇，四周有九条山路进镇，这个风水"形局"叫"九龙抢珠"。每条路在进镇之前都有一道桥，每道桥头有一座高不过三米的单间小屋，供着观音菩萨，叫"桥头观音"。

观音在人们心里是很亲切的，"有求必应"，这些观音路亭就给了来尧坝赶场的乡人们一种亲切之感。

3.Dwellings of the Gods Where there is a god, there must be a place for the god to stay, convenient for devout men and women to kowtow and burn incense.

A very few deities, only related to daily life, mostly stay in common people's homes—such as Stove God, Door God, Toilet God, Well God, Pen God, Horse King, Fox Immortal, Granary Official Lord, etc.

Simpler ones: just write the god's title on red paper, or buy a woodblock-printed god image on red paper, and paste it at the position of their respective functions.

Slightly more solemn ones: make a small niche at these positions—mostly brick, some exquisitely carved.A few made of wood.

Inside the niche mostly only paste a woodblock-printed god image; some families place a porcelain or clay statue inside, often of unclear identity—just having form and shape, as an indication that there is a deity here.

Before the god statue set incense burner and candle holder, all very simple.

In Guangdong, especially its south, colored shrines are often fired from colored glaze, with god statues inside, stacked layer upon layer on the main ridge of the house and its two sides.

They dress up the main ridge into a very ornate decorative band, scattered and colorful, very lively.

In some places, such as southeastern Shanxi and some towns in Sichuan, where there are relatively many families engaged in commerce and handicrafts, they mostly hang a wooden niche on the wall of their own main hall to worship the protector god of the family's industry—such as Luban Lord, Dukang, Qingyin Tongzi, Mei-Ge Immortal, etc.

Some additionally add a God of Wealth.

In Fujian, Anhui, and Jiangxi, above the side doors on both sides of the master's wall in the center of the residence's main hall, exquisitely carved god cabinets are set—one side enshrines four generations of ancestors (great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, father), the other side enshrines several immortals and bodhisattvas.

A few families set a large god cabinet in the center of the master's wall, inside enshrining both ancestors and immortals and bodhisattvas.

The master's wall, especially above the side doors, is very dim; the god-worshipping candlelight flickers, the gold leaf on the god cabinet glitters—very sacred atmosphere.

Behind the left and right side doors, year-round each has an incense table, separately worshipping Luban Lord and Yang Yunsong.

Luban Lord receives incense here not because of his skill, but because he masters a house's "small feng-shui"—such as the main gate's orientation and dimensions, the width of the main hall and gate house, the height of the eaves, etc.

Yang Yunsong manages the house's "large feng-shui"—i.e., its relationship with the landforms and features in the larger area.

At the beginning of building a house, these two large and small feng-shui masters, each represented by a wooden stake, are erected at both ends of the house foundation's central axis, as reference points for the house layout.

After the house is completed, they are moved behind the left and right side doors of the main hall, permanently worshipped.Also often worshipped in common people's homes are the God of Wealth, Longevity Star, Guanyin Bodhisattva, and Jiang Taigong.

The first three mostly have porcelain or wooden statues, with unfixed positions.

Guanyin statue's worshippers are mostly women—Guanyin Bodhisattva is their most intimate deity; they mostly place the statue in the bedroom, burning one stick of incense morning and evening, folding hands and making a few bows.

Some women also regularly observe "Guanyin fasts." They force this originally genderless bodhisattva into female form—because women are more compassionate, more delicate, better able to understand their distress and hopes.

Moreover, women placing female god statues in the bedroom,随时 confiding their hearts—in that era could also reduce a bit of suspicion.Jiang Taigong was modest and loved the people—after becoming a god still so, receiving people's eternal respect.

Shanxi people, in the center of the residential courtyard, use brick or stone to pile a stool-sized block, calling it "Central Palace Lord" (中宫爷)—this is the symbol of Jiang Taigong.

On the first and fifteenth of each month, burn incense and offer food.Not allowed to sit on Central Palace Lord, nor step on it, nor pour dirty things or filthy water on it.

The name Central Palace Lord comes because the courtyard-style layout of rural residences conforms to the "Nine Palaces Grid" pattern—the courtyard is the central palace.

In eastern Fujian, some residences use brick to build a very small pavilion-shaped shrine in the center of the main house ridge, called "Taigong Pavilion"—that is Jiang Taigong's post.

The pavilion is empty, no statue inside, just a symbol.

Shanxi residences also have two permanent shrine locations: one is the center of the screen wall inside the main gate, the other is the side wall of the gate house.

The center of the screen wall mostly enshrines the fortune-bestowing Heavenly Official; the god on the gate house side wall is more mixed—some enshrine Door God, some enshrine Earth God.

In Jiangxi, Fujian, and Guangdong, under the incense table before the master's wall in the residence's main hall, in the center, there is the Earth God and Goddess's deity position—the formal title is "Position of the God of Blessing and Uprightness" (福德正神之位).

Left and right have couplets, such as "Fortune as thick as earth; virtue matching boundless land"—implicitly including both "blessing" and "earth" titles.

One step before the Earth God is this house's feng-shui acupoint eye.This configuration vividly reflects the intimate relationship between rural people and land in the agrarian civilization era.

The vast majority of deities are enshrined in temples.Temples are large and small.

The smallest temples enshrine the deities most closely related to people's life and well-being—that is, Earth God temples and Three-Official temples.

Earth God temples and Three-Official temples are the most numerous, distributed casually.

In Hunan, Sichuan, Zhejiang and other provinces, inside and outside villages, on streets and in fields, there may be Earth God temples—the small ones no more than two chi high.

In Gaoyi Village, Huitong County, Hunan, there are as many as forty-seven such small Earth God temples—almost every small temple has the same couplet, writing a sincere prayer: "Mind the people's sufferings, protect one place's peace.

" Large Earth God temples are no more than cramped single rooms, usually also serving as roadside pavilions.

Besides dedicated temples, in various village temples, the god platform mostly has a corner position for the Earth God and Goddess.

But there are also more "高级" treatments—such as in the Dongzhu Temple at Yuyuan Village, Wuyi County, Zhejiang, there is a dedicated side courtyard for enshrining the Earth God and Goddess, very spacious, with a three-bay main hall.

On one side of the front courtyard of Xiyun Temple at Xitou Village, Linxian County, Shanxi, there is also an independent Earth God temple.

The biggest characteristic of the Earth God is: one piece of land has one, local origin, only manages affairs on a small piece of land.

Those sitting in small Earth God temples or in a corner of large temple god platforms are all, after Ming and Qing, Earth Gods played by "good people" who had merit for the local village—low position, small jurisdiction, only handling trivial daily matters—hence the saying "the local earth god is locally efficacious.

" In multi-surname villages of southern Anhui and western Zhejiang, occasionally there are three-bay main-hall Village God temples (社庙) with or without a front courtyard—far larger than ordinary Earth God temples.

Commentary to the Gongyang Commentary: "The village god is the master of the land.

" This kind of "Village God temple" remotely inherits the nature-worship tradition of the Yin-Zhou period, which worshipped the vast earth as a god—its status far higher than later "Earth God temples," but their nature is still Earth God temples.

In some places, such as Jiangshan County in Zhejiang, Fengcheng County in Jiangxi, and Linxian County in Shanxi, all multi-surname villages take "village god society" (社) as the basic social unit.

A village is divided into several "societies," each about twenty-five households, managed by an elected society head.Each society has a Village God temple, a well, and a school.The Village God is a local god, "protecting" one area.

Village God temples also regularly hold festival and sacrificial activities—generally two times: Spring Society (the wu day after Spring Equinox) and Autumn Great Society (the wu day after Autumn Equinox).

Late Tang poet Wang Jia has a famous poem "Society Day": "At the foot of Ehu Mountain rice and sorghum are fat, pig pens and chicken roosts half-close doors; mulberry and zhe shadows slant as spring society disperses, every family helps the drunken home.

" The poem writes the relationship between Village God temples and people's lives very intimately.Sanqingkou in Jiangshan County, Zhejiang, is a porcelain-kiln village making a living from firing porcelain.

Opposite the Huang Family Great Ancestral Hall at the water mouth, there is a Village God temple—three bays, very exquisite workmanship.

Whenever the dragon kiln is filled with bowl blanks, before lighting the fire, the kiln owner and kiln workers all come to worship—offering pig head, fish, chicken, lighting incense and candles, burning paper, and setting off firecrackers.

At Tangyue Village in Shexian County, Anhui, at the village entrance there is a three-bay Village God temple—its nickname is "Beggar Pavilion"—because it is open to wandering beggars, housing them at night.

Villagers say this is a rule left by ancestors.

Earth God temples also have three bays with a front courtyard—then they often simultaneously enshrine the Five-Grain God, such as the Earth God temple at Xinye Village, Jiande City, Zhejiang—also called Earth-Grain Shrine, standing side by side with the Wenchang Pavilion.

Also numerous but not large, spread inside and outside villages, are Three-Official temples—temples enshrining the three deities: fortune-bestowing Heavenly Official, sin-pardoning Earthly Official, and misfortune-relieving Water Official.

The power and functions of these three deities cover all needs and ideals of rural people's lives in agrarian society.

Perhaps precisely because so生活化, rural people feel them亲切 and without mysterious and sublime awe—they do not use solemn and towering grand temples to worship them, only letting their small temples be located in the village, at the field edge, or beside the water channels where women often wash clothes—intimately融入 people's daily lives.

In Yongjia County, Zhejiang, among the more than two thousand roadside small pavilions that shade farmers from sun, shelter from rain, and let them rest in the fields, the vast majority enshrine statues of the Three-Official Great Emperor—called Three-Official temples.

Or one could say: every Three-Official temple must have open rooms and long benches, for people to shelter from rain, rest, and socialize.

Although scattered in fields and beside mountain paths, and very small in scale, some are quite exquisite—the shrines and caisson ceilings are high-level masterpieces, such as the Three-Official temple at the east entrance of Huatan Village.

Roadside small pavilions and Three-Official temples also备有 stoves, firewood, cooking utensils, and even brand-new straw sandals—from Start of Summer to Autumn Equinox there are even large vats of herbal tea, plus some heat-relieving herbs.

They are all for passersby to use free of charge—expenses paid by the village ancestral hall's public funds, or by slightly wealthier families as a good deed to pray for their parents' blessings—called "Filial Son Pavilions.

" These measures reflect the seemingly plain but practically useful care among rural people.The site selection of more orthodox temples is often decided by feng-shui masters.

Most temples are located outside the village's residential area—according to feng-shui numerology, temples have too much yin energy, unsuitable to mix with residents.

In one of the feng-shui classics falsely attributed to Zhu Xi, "Snow Heart Essay" (雪心赋), it says: "What is warned against: before gods, behind Buddhas"—that is, whether yin or yang residences, do not approach temples.

The commentary says: "Since this place is where deities dwell, then the secluded dwellings touch each other, bells and drums alarm each other—fear that living there is not peaceful.

" Villages cannot relocate to build temples, so they have to build temples outside the village.

In fact, placing temples outside residential areas should have very practical reasons: first, temples often have incense, easily causing fires—if a temple is in the residential area, very unsafe; second, with a temple, there will be outsiders coming to burn incense, attracting them in and out of the village—also not very safe; third, large temples have temple fairs, or on deity birthdays, pilgrims crowd and jostle—if the temple is in the village, too much interference with villagers' lives.

Larger temples also have opera stages—whenever there are performances, people from all around come to watch, the village inevitably becomes noisy and restless; fourth, building temples outside the village can also use them for feng-shui numerology supplementation or resolution; fifth, most importantly, they can also serve as rest and rain-shelter places for those going to fields or traveling.

The vast majority of Chinese architecture is wooden; the vast majority of Chinese rural villages are clustered—wooden buildings clustered into villages—most afraid of fire.

Since afraid of fire, one must create a god to prevent and control fire.

Yin-Yang scholars in the "Four Symbols theory" designated Xuanwu as the god of the north; and according to Yin-Yang scholars' "Four Virtues" theory, the north is of water virtue—so Xuanwu became a water god.

Folk people then invited Xuanwu Great Emperor to prevent and control fire—hence Xuanwu temples spread nationwide, generally built north of villages.

In Yu County, Hebei, among more than two hundred villages, every village is surrounded by rectangular earthen walls, one street runs through the center, south end is the village gate, north end raises a high platform, on which a Xuanwu temple is built.

This is an attempt to rely on feng-shui witchcraft to prevent and fight fires.

A village must have a "water mouth" (水口)—that is, where the stream flows out of the small basin where the village is located, necessarily downstream of the village.

The water mouth is best with mountains flanking left and right, called "lion-elephant guarding the gate" or "turtle-snake guarding the gate"—so that the water channel is narrower and curved, "tight as a gourd throat"—thus making "outgoing water winding and affectionate.

" In feng-shui, water is compared to wealth—outgoing water being affectionate symbolizes keeping wealth and fortune from流失.

To strengthen the water mouth's locking, according to feng-shui classic "Snow Heart Essay": "Altar temples must reside at the water mouth"—the commentary says: "Generally god altars and Buddhist temples should reside at the water mouth, suppressing and blocking the earth gate, to lock internal qi as the best.

" Because all of China is high in the northwest and low in the southeast, feng-shui masters call this overall terrain "the great trend of heaven and earth"—village site selection prefers places high in northwest and low in southeast; the water mouth downstream of the village thus mostly selects the village's southeast, i.

e., the xun position.

Hence the Wenchang Pavilion, suitable for the xun position,正好 often is one of the temples locking the water mouth—often together with writing brush, water-powered trip hammer, eternal lamp, and wind-rain bridge (i.

e.

, covered bridge) collectively called "Five Lives" (五生)—for example, the water mouth of Likeng Village in Wuyuan County (one of the old Huizhou six counties) and the water mouth of Huang Village in Xiwu Township, Yixian County.

In Guodong Village, Wuyi County, Zhejiang, because the water mouth is not in the xun position, both a Guanyin temple and a Guandi temple are built at the water mouth, collectively called "Hailin Courtyard"—using doubled strength to make up for the deficiency.

The water mouth must plant forests to strengthen locking; altar temples and the Wenfeng Pagoda often built at the water mouth are buildings with relatively free forms—so water mouth building complexes are mostly the most beautiful building complexes of a village, masterpieces combining architectural art and natural scenery.

For example, at Fanlingjiao Village, Wuyi County, Zhejiang, the water mouth has a Guandi temple, Wenchang Pavilion, Earth God temple, and covered bridge, plus several trees with arm-span-thick trunks.

In natural environments where danger is more likely—such as river sharp bends at the "bow back" possibly受 "reverse-bow water" erosion and collapse, or under steep cliffs that may landslide during rainstorms—Guandi temples are often built to "suppress.

" For example, at the village entrance of Pengxi Village, Yongjia County, Zhejiang, directly facing "reverse-bow water," a not-small five-bay two-courtyard Guandi temple was built on the riverbank.

Legend says Lord Guan was both public-spirited and righteous, and invincible in battle—all demons and ghosts flee before him—so they borrow his divine power to subdue the reverse-bow water.Such "resolving evil sha" is also a feng-shui trick.

Temples can also be used to improve deficiencies or defects in a village's feng-shui form.

In a relatively symmetrical "form configuration," if the left "Azure Dragon sand" is slightly weaker than the right "White Tiger sand," to avoid the "inauspicious form" of "White Tiger pressing Azure Dragon," a temple or pagoda is built at the low or missing point of the Azure Dragon sand to strengthen it.

The village's "Heaven Gate" (upper water mouth) incoming water should not be too winding, lest it symbolize that "wealth" water comes not smoothly—but if the water channel is too unobstructed and rushes straight toward the village, a temple is also built to "buffer" it—for example, the Three-Official Temple at the Heaven Gate bank of Liukeng Village, Le'an County, Jiangxi.

Similarly, if a mountain path rushes steeply straight down toward the village, there should also be a temple or a roadside pavilion with a god statue to block it—feng-shui also calls this preventing "rush"—such as the Mountain God Temple on the ridge behind Guanlu Village, Yi County, Anhui.

Because in places without water routes, mountain paths replace water routes as feng-shui elements.Such wild temples are often village boundaries, creating a sense of village domain.

For generations, people going out to make a living or take exams left wives and children; family members saw them off and longed for their return—these temples accumulated deep familial affection and nostalgia.

Sanliao Village (originally Shanliao Village, recently renamed Sanliao) in Xingguo County, Jiangxi—legend says its site was selected by Tang dynasty topographical feng-shui master Yang Yunsong, and inhabited by descendants of his direct disciple Wen Wenchan and sixth-generation disciple Liao Yu—is considered China's "feng-shui ancestral land.

" It is surrounded by mountains on all sides: east has a wood-shaped peak called "Wood Star Descending to World"; south has a fire-shaped peak called "Fire Star Falling into Trough"; west has a metal-shaped peak called "Metal Star Covering Gate"; and the north "Water Star Interdependent" peak is water-shaped.

By late Ming, the Zeng and Liao surname families worked together, respectively building four temples—Donghua Nunnery, Nanji Nunnery, Xizhu Nunnery, and Beidou Nunnery—on their peaks, to strengthen feng-shui effects.

Later Sanliao Village's feng-shui industry greatly developed—only in Tongzhi's Xingguo County Gazetteer there are as many as twenty-one named feng-shui masters.

Villagers attributed the industry's prosperity to these four nunneries.Though superstition, it encouraged a kind of witchcraft传承.One kind of feng-shui effect comes from the symbolism of visual images.

For example, if the mountain pass's left and right slopes are gentle, nearly symmetrical, and full in shape, the pass is often interpreted as female genitalia—in this case, a temple is built at the pass, and among the temple's gods there is a Child-Giving Lady—such as Xixian Nunnery on Xiwu Ridge between Xiping Mountain and Wuting Mountain behind Guanlu Village, Yi County, Anhui; or additionally, on a nearby mountain facing the pass, a pagoda is built, symbolizing male genitalia, to pray for the village's population prosperity.

For example, the Yuquan Temple at the pass between Daofeng Mountain and Yuhua Mountain in Xinye Village, Jiande City, Zhejiang, and the corresponding Wenfeng Pagoda.

When feng-shui masters give environmental improvement suggestions to blood-relation villages that have long been "not prosperous," they may propose building a temple or Buddhist pagoda at a certain location near the village.

The pagoda's feng-shui meaning far exceeds its religious meaning.

For example, the twin pagodas of Haihui Temple (Longquan Temple) in Yangcheng, Shanxi—they made the small village (Daqiao Village) in a lowland among hills a dazzling landmark, enlivening a large area.

Another is the Lingkong Pagoda near Longfeng Village, Jiexiu County, Shanxi—at the sharp bend of the Longfeng River outside the village, 38 meters high, nine stories, built in 1732.

Below the pagoda is a small Shibi Nunnery, an附属 building of the pagoda—the nunnery name comes from the river's sharp bend, where rock protrudes.This Lingkong Pagoda is a feng-shui pagoda, used for "suppressing water.

" Though Haihui Temple pagoda and Shibi Nunnery pagoda may not have changed the village's fate, they certainly greatly beautified the village and fields!

In Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangdong and other provinces, because temples mostly must be built outside the village's residential area and also have feng-shui considerations, there is often a clustering phenomenon.

For example, at the upper water mouth "Shuangjuntou" of Yantou Village, Yongjia County, Zhejiang, on a very small flat land there are three temples: Sansheng Temple, Taiyin Temple, and Lu Shi Niangniang Temple.

The temple courtyards also have several small temples attached.

Sansheng Temple primarily enshrines Zhang Qian (Zhang Xian), who brought back the multi-seeded pomegranate from the Western Regions; Taiyin Temple primarily enshrines the Moon God; Lu Shi Niangniang Temple is the Xiaoyou Furen Temple.

According to Qianlong's Yongjia County Gazetteer: "Tang dynasty, Lu family lived in Lu'ao, once went out to gather firewood with mother, encountered tiger about to bite mother, daughter urgently threw herself into tiger's beak to die in mother's place.

Later people saw daughter riding tiger, thus built temple to worship; Song Lizong bestowed posthumous title Xiaoyou Furen.

" Yongjia has many Xiaoyou Furen temples—this is commendation of filial daughters, social-ethical, originally unrelated to religion.

In Shanxi and Hebei, some villages are surrounded by earthen walls in fortress form, with temples clustered outside the fortress gates or straddling the fortress walls.

The most typical examples are Zhangbi Village in Jiexiu County, Shanxi, and Xigubao in Yu County, Hebei.Both villages' layout patterns are very orderly.

Zhangbi Village's north gate has ten temples large and small; south gate has eleven.

East of the south gate, built on the fortress wall straddling inside and outside, is the "Khan Temple" (可罕庙); on the gate tower is the "Western Pure Land Temple," should be a Buddhist Pure Land temple; the main temple outside the south gate is Guandi Temple—legend says Lord Guan once "manifested holiness" in late Ming to help villagers scare away an armed band of thieves at the south gate.

Beside and around these three temples, there are Guanyin Temple, Dizang Hall, Dragon God Temple, etc.Above the city wall at Zhangbi Village's north gate there are three temples: center is Zhenwu Temple (i.e.

, Xuanwu Temple)—Zhenwu is the water god presiding over the north.

East of it is the Empty King Temple; "Stele Record of Establishing Empty King Traveling Shrine" says: the ancient Buddha was from Fengxiang Prefecture, Shaanxi, secular surname Tian, lived in Yuanwo Village, Yuci County, Taiyuan Prefecture, served as village head, because he protected poor people and was condemned by authorities, thus left family to become monk, lived in Hongji Temple in Jiexiu, once ordered disciples to perform rain to relieve drought, later hid in Mian Mountain south of Zhangbi Village.

Villagers took him as the god in charge of rain, with very strong incense.West of Zhenwu Temple is the Three Great Masters Hall—i.e., Guanyin, Manjushri, and Samantabhadra bodhisattvas—a Buddhist temple.

Its main hall is centered facing south, with side rooms on both sides, forming a courtyard.Outside the north gate there is an outer fortress (瓮城), opening east, with a Lüzu Pavilion on the gate tower.

On the central axis outside the north gate there is a large-scale Erlang Temple, sacrificing the second son of Li Bing, who helped Li Bing control water (some say Yang Erlang.

But the god statue has no Howling Celestial Dog at feet, no Celestial Eye on forehead)—because Zhangbi Village is high in south and low in north, with large elevation difference; southern mountain floods come down, pass through the village center's "Dragon Street" and rush straight out the north gate.

Feng-shui masters said this would wash away the whole village's wealth energy, so the north needed a water-controlling god to assist Zhenwu Great Emperor in suppressing water force—this god is Li Erlang.

Thus a three-bay Erlang Temple facing south was built.

Facing the Erlang Temple, with its back against the north gate outer fortress, the village's only grand opera stage was built—so the Erlang Temple receded northward, leaving a large "audience seating" area.

Between these temples there are very small temples such as Doumu Palace.Eighteen meters inside the north gate, west of the street there is Xinglong Temple, main hall enshrining Tathagata Buddha.

True Buddhist temples are rare in rural areas; it is also not pure—on both sides of the main hall there are also Sister-in-Law Hall and King Yama Hall.

This pair of sisters-in-law is unknown from any canon; no one in the village knows today, but incense still continues—this is called "gods and Buddhas don't mind those who kowtow.

" Xigubao in Yu County is roughly similar: north and south fortress gates each have square outer fortresses, temples all inside the outer fortresses; south outer fortress has Dizang Temple, Guanyin Temple, and an opera stage; north outer fortress has Zhenwu Temple, Niangniang Temple, and a destroyed unnamed temple.

Each outer fortress also has several small temples.

Yu County has over two hundred fortress-style villages, each with square layout, a central road running straight north-south; at the north end on a high platform stands the temple of the north god Xuanwu, i.

e., Zhenwu Temple.The temple is not large, but in front there are high grand steps, with a memorial archway on the steps—forming a very solemn and sacred scene.

Some large villages or towns located at key points of water routes or navigation often build temples on high ground as their landmarks.

On Meiling Mountain east of the Wu River at Liukeng Village, Le'an County, Jiangxi, there was once Donghua Temple; at Qikou Town on the Yellow River in Linxian County, Shanxi, there is the Black Dragon Temple on Wolong Mountain—both can be seen by boatmen from far away, knowing the village or town has arrived, should prepare to dock.

Passengers on the boat would also stand up, look far at the dock, carefully searching for their wives and children among the crowd.

In hilly areas of the south, with mountains, water, trees, bamboo—the scenery is excellent—so many villages have "Ten Scenes" or "Eight Scenes," and among these "scenes" there is always one or even several related to temples.

For example, Zhuge Village in Lanxi City, Zhejiang—one of its "Eight Scenes" is called "Green Peak Morning Bell," its main building is Cuifeng Chan Temple.

During Ming Zhengde era (1506–1522), someone wrote "Eight Scenes Poetry," saying: Half-mountain Buddhist dwelling in mist, faint bell sounds out from green peaks; sound stirs remnant clouds from distant peaks, voice carries clear dawn to door leaves……It added lovely vitality to the village.

Temples are often sited at the most beautiful places of mountains, water, and forests, becoming the protagonists of scenic areas.

With their exquisite pavilions, white walls and black tiles, flying eaves and wandering ridges—they further enrich natural beauty.

For example, the small White Crane Great Emperor Temple at the entrance of Linkeng Village, Yongjia County, Zhejiang, and the Dongzhu Temple at Yuyuan Village, Wuyi County—both add infinite beauty to green mountains and small streams.

Among temples everywhere, how many are ancient and厚重, extremely rich in historical vicissitudes and vastness.For example, Fayuan Temple in Gaoping County, Shanxi, and Qinglian Temple in Jincheng—add to the magnificence of mountains.

Also, Xianglu Temple in Jiaxian County, Shaanxi, and Yuyinshan Temple at Shibaozhai, Hubei—respectively set off the grand and majestic flow of the rolling Yellow River and the ten-thousand-li Yangtze River.

Emperor Qianlong had a saying: "Under heaven, famous mountains are mostly occupied by monks"—temples give back how much beauty and heroism to the world's scenery.

Temples of medium scale and above, most have opera stages, serving as the village's art center and cultural center.

They not only have tall and ornate architecture with flying eaves and wandering ridges, but also mostly include wood carving, brick carving, stone carving, gray sculpture and other decorations—very exquisite.

Some temples in Shanxi and Guangdong have glazed products on the ridge, including "Three Mountains Gathering at Top," chiwen, main ridge—all outstanding artworks.

The opera stage's caisson ceiling, face beam, and the hall's corbel brackets (牛腿)—also mostly fine small-woodwork and wood-carving masterpieces.

Temples often have many stone steles, which are important materials for village history.

Yaoba Town in Hejiang County, Sichuan, has nine mountain roads entering the town from all around—this feng-shui "form configuration" is called "Nine Dragons Snatching the Pearl.

" Before each road enters the town there is a bridge; at each bridgehead there is a single-bay small house no more than three meters high, enshrining Guanyin Bodhisattva—called "Bridgehead Guanyin.

" Guanyin is very亲切 in people's hearts, "responsive to every request"—these Guanyin roadside pavilions give villagers coming to Yaoba for market a sense of intimacy.

7.4 庙宇的型制
Section 4

四、庙宇的型制 庙宇的型制虽然也有一定模式，但变化比宗祠多。这是因为：第一，环境变化多，有一些庙处在优美的山水之间，地形比较复杂。

还有许多侧身在村镇之中，环境局促；第二，它们的组成也比较复杂，除了极少数有佛、道两教正神之外，大多是各种地方神祇的小庙小殿的集合体；第三，稍大一点的寺观，都有庙祝或僧道们的生活区、香客们的寄宿区，甚至有专供读书人借住攻读的房舍；第四，常有碑廊、塔院、藏经楼，等等。最简单的庙宇是一间或三间正殿，有的加一圈围墙，前面开一个随墙门。

青山绿水之间，小庙也有很美的，如浙江省永嘉县楠溪江流域林坑村的白鹤大帝庙，西岸村的关帝庙（后改为送子娘娘庙）和篁南村的陈五侯王庙，都为环境生色不少。规模中等的庙，则多正殿三间，左右耳殿，两厢为配殿，前面倒座做杂用房。有些庙有个侧院，供庙祝或僧人住宿，香积厨和斋堂便在院内。

香积厨为制备祭品并供斋饭而设，斋饭是给香客们吃的，吃一份就得交一份香火钱，当然比市值要高，这在庙宇是一笔收入，在香客是一份功德。

《全宋文》里有一篇《修玉局院记》，作者为彭乘，写到扩建后道家的玉局观："东西长七十七步，南北长七十五步，中建三清殿七间，东厢三官堂、钟楼暨玉局祠屋，西厢九曜堂、太宗皇帝御书楼并斋厅、厨、库、门屋、周回廊宇，共一百三十五间。"这虽是道观，却也是常规的庙宇格局，从宋代一直沿用到近代。

大一点的庙，靠山门向后造个戏台，山门两侧建钟鼓楼。

戏台极少完全在山门门屋里，一般后背连接门屋而面向庙内凸出，也有处在这两式之间的。戏台面向正殿。这时，两厢往往建两层楼，楼上为士绅家男女看戏的席位，就叫"看楼"，左厢为男看楼，右厢为女看楼，男女分开。楼下及院落为乡民看戏的席位，男女不分。

有些位于缓坡上的庙，利用地形落差，看楼造在两厢的前段，两厢的后段地面高出，仍为配殿。院落也分相同的前后段，配殿和正殿在高台上，如山西省临县碛口镇的黑龙庙、阳城县郭峪村的汤帝庙。再大一点的庙，就有前后院，甚至几进院落。例如山西省临县西头村的栖云寺，浙江省永嘉县卢岙村的圣湖庙和四川省合江县尧坝街的天后宫属这一类。栖云寺坐北面南，大门有三个窑洞。正殿是木结构的，三间，歇山顶。两厢各五间箍窑，平顶。

正殿后又是个大院子，后殿三间，两层，底层是箍窑，上层是木结构，硬山顶，左右厢也是木结构，瓦顶起脊。庙门前街上左右有一对双券洞的过街牌楼，偏南的券洞上左右分立钟鼓楼，都是十字脊歇山顶。

两座过街牌楼之间，街南有一道墙，墙里大院子南端是朝北的戏台，看戏的人都在大院里。栖云寺是一座典型的杂合庙，它正殿为单层，供关公大帝，周仓和关平侍立左右，两侧山墙根还有些兵士的塑像。后殿为两层，楼下是道家的三清殿，供元始天尊、灵宝天尊和道德天尊。东耳殿（东厢）叫"十和殿"，供佛家的十殿阎王，里面布置成十八层地狱。西耳殿（西厢）供真武大帝。

后殿楼上三开间，中央是玉皇大帝的宝座，左右各有一位女神。两侧山墙前列着二十八宿的拟人像。浙江省永嘉县卢岙村圣湖庙稍有不同，它的戏台照一般模式造在庙门内，贴前墙。中央是大殿，供卢氏孝祐娘娘。后殿上了陡坡，也是两层楼房，底层中央供孝祐娘娘的母亲，专管助人生育。神像前的台座上放满了小巧而精美的绣鞋，求子息的人来进香并相信"偷"一双鞋回去，便能生育。生了，就做一双或几双绣鞋送来还愿，供给别人偷。

楼上两端向前凸出一对方形敞轩，面对宽阔的河湾。闲倚美人靠，看蚱蜢舟轻盈地往还，在水面上划出一道道亮线，风光秀丽如画。山西省蔚县的重泰寺，整体型制比较规范。第一进为山门，第二进为天王殿，第三进为千佛殿（面向前）和观音殿（面向后），第四进为地藏殿，第五进为大雄宝殿。但第六进比较特殊，是合并供奉释、道、儒的"三教楼"，释迦牟尼居中，老子居左，孔夫子居右。楼台很高而阶梯陡峻，有十九级，高六米，很有气势。

楼后一溜是禅房。四川省合江县尧坝街的东岳庙，第一进为山门连戏台，面对广阔的前院和第二进前的大台阶，第二进为灵官殿，第三进为东皇殿（供东岳大帝，今称天王殿），第四进为观音殿，最后为地方神的川主庙。庙随山坡层层升高，前后高差达十五米。东皇殿前大台阶大约有六米高，在前面宽阔大院的衬托下，十分庄严。

稍大一点的庙宇，供奉的会有释、道、儒三教再加上大量的地方杂神。例如甘肃省宁县城的宇村庙，大致在清代乾隆年间（1736—1795）建成，自西向东，进深一百米左右。它有正殿、献殿各三间，左右分别为圣母宫和药王祠。前有戏楼，后有菩萨殿和钟、鼓楼。前门外崖下还有几孔窑洞，叫三教洞。它后殿供文殊菩萨、真武祖师和雷祖。

显圣王庙供子孙娘娘，孙真人祠供药王、"三清"、释迦牟尼、孔子，还有"天、地、君、亲、师"神位。它非常清晰地表现出中国人功利主义的杂神崇拜。大型的寺观，有许多是长时期里陆续建成的，殿堂常常不能都串在一条轴线上，就依几条轴线、几所院落安排。

例如陕西省葭芦堡（今佳县）的白云观，从正东的山门进去，沿东西向轴线经石牌坊、木牌楼，进入五龙宫大院，出院再经头天门、二天门，来到长长的"点墨廊"院落。廊之北有两条南北向轴线。东侧的依次排列着七圣楼、真人洞、三圣楼、娘娘庙和东岳庙，每个院子都有厢房陪伴着。

西侧的排列着影壁、三天门、四天门、乐楼（即戏台）、真武大殿、三官殿、藏经阁、超然阁。每个院子也都有厢房。超然阁后面偏西又有南北向的短轴线，东侧的前后为玉皇楼、五老庙和圣母庙，西侧是一所大四合院，正殿为三清殿，院门向南正对着养真楼。

在这些殿堂之外，零散着的有水神庙、财神庙、关帝庙、佛殿、文昌阁、元辰殿、玉皇庙和魁星楼，一共五十多座殿堂楼阁。这座白云观始建于宋代，扩建于明代万历年间（1573—1620）。它前临黄河、背倚白云山，经七百多级石阶，把建筑一直牵引上山巅。自然景观和建筑景观都十分丰富、雄伟。

不过它已经不是纯粹乡土性的道观，虽然孤独地造在野山上，却是陕西的道教中心了。充分发挥了自然景观的美，而且把建筑融合进去的，还有浙江省武义县俞源村的洞主庙、陕西省葭芦城的香炉寺和山西省晋城市的青莲寺，等等。俞源村洞主庙背靠在浓荫蔽天的山坡前，一反常规，横向展开。中央院落供奉着一位来历不明的孩童神——可能是沉香。右边小院供土地，左边小院供观音，按常规又有许多神佛陪祀。观音院前是庙祝的房间，再向外延伸是斋堂。

土地院前是圆梦楼，因为洞主庙的求梦是重要特色。由于地形关系，圆梦楼下还有一层，是六间客房、供求梦人住宿。最有特色的是庙门前的高高台阶，它不在轴线上，而是从右向左贴墙而上。庙墙是白色的，自由活泼的体形在林木衬托下非常活泼。葭芦城的香炉寺不大，造在从黄河边缘笔直挺起两百米左右高的天然悬岩顶上，俯视黄河奔流，惊心动魄。

左前方一座十余米长的小桥，跨过裂隙，通向一块独立的柱子形状的石崖，在悬岩之外独自挺立，约二十来米高，顶上立一座小小的观音堂。从寺、堂向四面望去，起伏的黄土高原，无边无际；滔滔黄河，奔泻万里。真是惊心动魄。庙宇和宗祠相似，都是村镇里的公共活动场所。

所以，一般情况，凡宗祠多而强的村、镇，庙宇就比较少而且小，位置也不重要；宗祠少的村、镇，庙宇就比较多，所以位置也比较重要。也就是说，比较稳定的血缘村落里庙宇就可能少而且小，相反，杂姓村落里庙宇就可能大而且多。

浙江、江西、福建、安徽等省，大体说来，宗族关系比较完整和稳定，宗祠的力量就比庙宇大，而且规模也大，庙宇一般建在村外，甚至没有，如福建省福安安贞堡。

山西、河北、陕西等省，战乱多而烈，宗族关系就比较弱，村子里庙宇的重要性和力量便会大大胜过宗祠，有不少村子甚至没有宗祠。例如山西省阳城市的郭峪村。四川省合江县的两个村子，福宝场和尧坝场，都是张献忠屠川后同时由"湖广填四川"的新移民建设成的，因此都是杂姓村。它们各在一条从合江进贵州的要道上，一个在县城东南、一个在西南，相去不远，都是跑运输的马帮住宿的一站。

然而，这两个聚落的结构和风格却大不相同，在庙宇的布局等方面有很强的表现。老福宝场穿村主街大约六百米长，沿街有十一座小庙之多，相距大体均匀，规模都不大。其中两座稍大一些的有戏台。这些庙，其实都是外来移民的同乡会所，各自招呼老乡们生活中的各种事宜。如江西人的万寿宫、福建人的天后宫和湖北人的禹王宫等等。

日常管事的叫"庙祝"。它们规模不大，房舍简朴，外形大致和住宅差不多，只有两家有磨砖门脸和两家门口有石刻门联。每逢场日，各村来的摊贩们都到关系固定的"庙"里去设摊。尧坝场的长度比老福宝场的稍长一些，为八百多米，但它只有中心部位有一座东岳庙，规模很大，占地达六千平方米左右。

庙门内有大戏台和看戏的大广场，后面，依山势层层向上，依次有观音殿、东皇帝和川主殿三座大殿和两侧的一些小殿。有僧人，据说由绅耆和商贾出资以及信徒们捐"无妄费"维持，当然其实是大有利可图。尧坝还有九条短短的出村的侧巷，每条巷子的外端都有一个单间的观音庙，其实就是赶路人避雨的场所，是由一位富商捐建的。

从尧坝场和福宝场看来，村子的建设并没有一定的格式，而且各场之间可能相差很远。不墨守成规的还有采用了地方性的空间结构方法的一些庙宇。例如浙江省永嘉县岩头村的普安寺，它不用几座独立房屋合成院落的布局，而是用钩连搭式屋顶和方格形柱网结构覆盖一大片空间，只留几个方格作为采光天井。在这空间里灵活分隔出各种活动区和功能区。这样的建筑在整个江南地区都是少见的。由于历史条件不同，乡土性庙宇的规模和质量在各地也颇为悬殊。

一般说来，江南各地的血缘村落，宗族势力强大，乡村庙宇的规模和质量普遍在宗祠之下，甚至还不及一些住宅。如江西省乐安县流坑村和福建连城县培田村。不过它们的"级别"仍可能比较显赫，以致小小的庙宇会有斗拱、歇山式屋顶之类。

在北方和四川，由于长年战乱，宗法制遭到严重破坏，以杂姓村落为多，村子里没有宗祠，或者只有很简陋的宗祠，庙宇的地位就高于一切其他建筑了。如四川省合江县福宝场、山西省阳城县郭峪村。前者老街大约六百米长，街上有九座有模有样的庙，大多数其实是"湖广填四川"时候移民的同乡会所。

其中北端的张爷庙和中央的万寿宫有戏台。后者在村子西部有汤帝庙和文庙，东门外苍龙岭上有白云观、文昌阁和文峰塔，规模既大，质量更好。

文庙经曲阜衍圣公府立案批准，汤帝庙的"规格级别"也很高，正殿达九开间，有戏台和钟鼓楼。在极特殊情况下，也有把庙宇和宗祠建在一起的，如山西省临县李家山村。

这是一个很偏僻的窑洞小村，村边上有一座关帝庙，庙里有一块清代的石碑，刻《重修庙宇碑记》如下："盖闻铺钟铸于郊庙，古帝之功冠千秋；寺观立于中朝，先圣之芳流百代，是知尊神敬祗典至钜也。

余李家山村，栖神虽有庙宇，献戏实无亭台，因而庙侧坡前，有余李氏宗亲之地一处，情愿施舍公社，为后修乐楼计也。迨至咸丰五年，村人共议，筮日动工。先修正面石窑三眼，又修下面石窑亦三眼。及同治五年，两廊竖石窑三眼，向北盖乐楼一座。重建关帝、观音之堂，补葺喜、贵、财神之宇，则神安人庆，永享其福矣。

又东面向南，修石窑一眼，及李氏独施钱六拾千文，以祀先祖，不与公社相干，是家庙也。原与陈、崔二姓公议，实为李氏一家私为，而且功程浩荡，殊非独力所能，即今告厥成功之日，谨将施钱信士之名勒石坚珉，以垂百世不朽云。大清同治五年九月二十八日立"。庙很小，碑文也不长，但文中所含的信息量却不少。关帝、观音和财神同堂受拜，再加出钱的李家祖先。

李家出了钱，它就成了李家的家庙，再外加戏台一座，向受崇祀的神、人献戏，这便是北方农村庙宇的典型状态，也便是一种文化的状态。不过它现在叫天官庙。乡间庙宇的兴建有几种常见的方式。

数量极少的正宗佛寺大多由一两个出家人立志募化费用（叫"无妄费"），由善男信女、商号富户为祈福或还愿捐建，还有些行业神庙则由各行业从业人员出资；又一种由村中地缘性的"社"或宗族里的长老士绅出面组成专门的"会"发动建庙。

"会"又分两种，一种是负责组织募化和管理，另一种是一些人见到建庙有利可图，实行认股集资，股份可以转让和继承。也可以当女儿的嫁妆。几乎所有的庙宇都有几块大碑，详细记录本庙为初建、扩建、修缮历次募化时出资人的芳名录，连捐十文钱或一勺粮的农妇的名字都不遗漏。

碑末还有木匠、瓦匠、染匠、妆銮匠等的名字，当然也有负责全部工作的各种职司人员和纠首的名字。极少数的寺观庙宇由公帑修建，如道光四川《安岳县志》载：宋嘉定十二年（1219年）县中重修天庆观，"自殿宇以及于肃客之所，悉更新之。竹木筒瓦石工廪费悉从官给，一毫弗以累民"。

其实，为造庙捐钱是一种功德，人们相信可以捐钱纳福，所以很踊跃。山西省泽州县冶底村东岳庙正殿的几棵石柱上有捐资人的名字，如："五岳殿王琮施石柱一条"和"五岳殿石匠段高施石柱一条"等，时间分别为元丰二年（1079年）和三年（1080年）。门楣石上也有同类刻字。

更常见的是庙内殿堂廊下立碑，刊刻捐款人姓名及额度。农村的杂庙，规模不很大的，没有僧道等出家人，通常由在俗的一位庙祝（或香师）管理。小庙则连庙祝都没有，由社或会出资雇人定时上香、打扫。

寺庙的流水收入来自善男信女的香火功德和有事人家做法会道场、点长明灯、吃斋饭、求签、圆梦、占卜吉凶等等的布施。至于经常的收入，多数寺庙都靠"香火田"。

香火田在建庙时便有信士捐献，以后陆续由捐献而增加，一般都租佃出去，庙祝收租谷并保答备用。也有些寺庙拥有捐献来的房产和店面，收入便更富裕。庙务的管理由村里专设的"社"或"会"来担当。山西省临县碛口镇的黑龙庙由"九社一镇"管理。

社有两大类，一类是常设性纯地缘的行政管理组织，一类是专题募化组织起来的机构。"一镇"是街上的商会。这些"社"要出善款养活庙祝、维修房屋、重妆神像、组织庙会等等，如逢灾年还要用积存的香火钱办好赈济。庙里演戏另外有专设的"社"负责。

股份制的"会"则靠办各种迷信活动而获利，成员按股取息。为了寺庙能在经营中获得丰厚收入，各庙都会编造一些关于自己庙中神灵如何"有求必应"、"应验如响"等等的神话传说。浙江省武义县俞源村的洞主庙，传说是应一个七岁神童（可能是救母的目莲，即沉香）托梦给牧牛人而建造的，这个庙便以求梦之灵验闻名一方，因此庙旁还造了一座两层的圆梦楼，专供求梦人租住。

每逢旧历六月二十六神诞之前一日，不但圆梦楼客满，连两三里长的村路边都睡满了人。求梦人先要上香燃烛祈祷，得梦之后还要请庙祝解梦，这些"手续"都须付钱，庙里收入相当可观。所以洞主庙的股份不但可以作为遗产传承，有一部分还曾经作为女儿嫁妆，由俞姓富户手中到了李姓手中。

4.Forms of Temples Although temple forms also have certain patterns, they vary more than ancestral halls.

This is because: first, environments vary greatly—some temples are among beautiful mountains and waters, with relatively complex terrain.

Many others are tucked within villages and towns, with cramped environments; second, their composition is also relatively complex—besides very few with orthodox Buddhist and Daoist deities, most are aggregates of small temples and halls of various local deities; third, slightly larger temples and monasteries all have living areas for temple keepers or monks and Daoists, lodging areas for pilgrims, and even rooms specifically for scholars to borrow and study in; fourth, there are often stele corridors, pagoda courtyards, scripture libraries, etc.

The simplest temples are one or three-bay main halls, some with a surrounding wall, with a gate opened in the wall at the front.

Among green mountains and clear waters, small temples can also be very beautiful—such as the White Crane Great Emperor Temple at Linkeng Village in the Nanxi River basin, Yongjia County, Zhejiang; the Guandi Temple at Xi'an Village (later changed to Child-Giving Goddess Temple); and the Chen Wuhou King Temple at Huangnan Village—all add much to the environment.

Medium-scale temples mostly have a three-bay main hall, left and right ear halls, two side wings as side halls, and the front reverse-side building as utility rooms.

Some temples have a side courtyard for temple keepers or monks to live in; the incense kitchen and vegetarian hall are in the courtyard.

The incense kitchen is for preparing sacrificial offerings and providing vegetarian meals—vegetarian meals are for pilgrims to eat; eating one portion requires paying one portion of incense money, of course higher than market value—this is income for the temple, and merit for the pilgrim.

In Complete Song Prose there is a "Record of Repairing Yuju Courtyard" by Peng Cheng, describing the expanded Daoist Yuju Temple: "East-west length seventy-seven bu, north-south length seventy-five bu; center builds Seven Purities Hall seven bays; east wing Three-Official Hall, bell tower and Yuju shrine rooms; west wing Nine-Luminaries Hall, Emperor Taizong's Imperial Calligraphy Building, together with vegetarian hall, kitchen, storehouse, gate house, surrounding corridor buildings—total one hundred thirty-five bays.

" Although this is a Daoist temple, it is also a conventional temple layout, used from Song dynasty一直 to modern times.

Larger temples, behind the mountain gate, build an opera stage; on both sides of the mountain gate build bell and drum towers.

Opera stages are very rarely completely within the mountain gate house—generally their back connects to the gate house and they protrude toward the temple interior; there are also forms between these two.

The opera stage faces the main hall.

At this time, the two wings often build two-story buildings—upstairs are seats for gentry families' men and women to watch opera, called "Viewing Buildings"—left wing is men's viewing building, right wing is women's viewing building, men and women separated.

Downstairs and the courtyard are seats for villagers to watch opera, men and women not separated.

Some temples on gentle slopes use terrain elevation difference—viewing buildings built in the front section of the two wings; the rear section of the two wings is higher ground, still serving as side halls.

The courtyard is also divided into similar front and rear sections; side halls and main hall are on high platforms—such as the Black Dragon Temple at Qikou Town, Linxian County, Shanxi, and the Tang Emperor Temple at Guoyu Village, Yangcheng County.

Even larger temples have front and rear courtyards, even several courtyards.

For example, Qiyun Temple at Xitou Village, Linxian County, Shanxi; Shenghu Temple at Lu'ao Village, Yongjia County, Zhejiang; and Tianhou Palace at Yaoba Street, Hejiang County, Sichuan—belong to this category.

Qiyun Temple faces south, with three cave dwellings at the gate.The main hall is wooden structure, three bays, hip-and-gable roof.

Two wings each have five cave dwellings (箍窑), flat roofs.

Behind the main hall is another large courtyard; the rear hall is three bays, two stories—ground floor is cave dwellings, upper floor is wooden structure, gable roof; left and right wings are also wooden structure, tile roofs with ridges.

On the street in front of the temple gate, left and right there is a pair of double-arched street-crossing memorial archways; on the southern archway, left and right stand bell and drum towers, both cross-ridge hip-and-gable roofs.

Between the two street-crossing archways, south of the street there is a wall; inside the wall, at the south end of the large courtyard, is a north-facing opera stage—people watching opera are all in the large courtyard.

Qiyun Temple is a typical mixed temple—its main hall is single-story, enshrining Great Emperor Guan, with Zhou Cang and Guan Ping attending left and right; at the roots of both side gable walls there are also some soldier statues.

The rear hall is two stories—downstairs is the Daoist Three Purities Hall, enshrining Primordial Heavenly Venerable, Numinous Treasure Heavenly Venerable, and Moral Heavenly Venerable.

East ear hall (east wing) is called "Ten Harmony Hall," enshrining the Buddhist Ten Kings of Hell, with interior arranged as eighteen layers of hell.West ear hall (west wing) enshrines Zhenwu Great Emperor.

The rear hall upstairs is three bays—center is the Jade Emperor's throne, left and right each have a goddess.In front of both side gable walls are lined personified statues of the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions.

Shenghu Temple at Lu'ao Village, Yongjia County, Zhejiang, is slightly different—its opera stage, following the conventional pattern, is built inside the temple gate, against the front wall.

The center is the main hall, enshrining Lu Shi Xiaoyou Lady.The rear hall, up a steep slope, is also a two-story building—ground floor center enshrines Xiaoyou Lady's mother, specifically in charge of helping childbirth.

On the platform before the god statues are placed many small and exquisite embroidered shoes—people seeking children come to burn incense and believe that "stealing" a pair of shoes home will enable childbirth.

After giving birth, they make one or several pairs of embroidered shoes to return as vow fulfillment, for others to steal.

Upstairs, both ends protrude forward with a pair of square open pavilions, facing the broad river bend.

Leaning leisurely on beauty-rests, watching grasshopper boats lightly come and go, drawing bright lines on the water surface—the scenery is beautiful as a painting.Chongtai Temple in Yu County, Shanxi, has a relatively standardized overall form.

First courtyard is mountain gate; second is Heavenly Kings Hall; third is Thousand-Buddha Hall (facing front) and Guanyin Hall (facing rear); fourth is Ksitigarbha Hall; fifth is Mahavira Hall.

But the sixth courtyard is special—it is a "Three-Religions Building" jointly enshrining Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism—Sakyamuni in center, Laozi on left, Confucius on right.

The building is very tall with steep stairs—nineteen steps, six meters high—very imposing.Behind the building is a row of meditation rooms.

Dongyue Temple at Yaoba Street, Hejiang County, Sichuan—first courtyard is mountain gate connected to opera stage, facing the broad front courtyard and the grand steps before the second courtyard; second is Lingguan Hall; third is Donghuang Hall (enshrining Dongyue Great Emperor, now called Heavenly Kings Hall); fourth is Guanyin Hall; finally is the local god's Chuanzhu Temple.

The temple rises layer by layer along the hillside, with front-rear elevation difference reaching fifteen meters.

The grand steps before Donghuang Hall are about six meters high—set off by the broad front courtyard, very solemn.

Slightly larger temples enshrine Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism, plus a large number of local miscellaneous gods.

For example, Yucun Temple at Ning County City, Gansu—roughly built in Qing Qianlong era (1736–1795), from west to east, depth about one hundred meters.

It has main hall and offering hall each three bays; left and right respectively are Holy Mother Palace and Medicine King Shrine.

Front has opera tower; rear has Bodhisattva Hall and bell and drum towers.

Below the cliff outside the front gate there are also several cave dwellings, called Three-Religions Cave.Its rear hall enshrines Manjushri Bodhisattva, Zhenwu Patriarch, and Thunder Ancestor.

Holy Sage King Temple enshrines Child-Bearing Lady; Sun Zhenren Shrine enshrines Medicine King, "Three Purities," Sakyamuni, Confucius, and also "Heaven, Earth, Monarch, Parent, Teacher" deity position.

It very clearly expresses Chinese people's utilitarian miscellaneous-god worship.

Large temples and monasteries—many were built successively over long periods, halls often cannot all be strung on one axis—so they are arranged along several axes and several courtyards.

For example, Baiyun Temple at Jialu Fort (now Jiaxian County), Shaanxi—entering from the east mountain gate, along the east-west axis through stone archway, wooden archway, entering the Five-Dragon Palace large courtyard; exiting the courtyard through First Heaven Gate, Second Heaven Gate, arriving at the long "Ink-Dot Corridor" courtyard.

North of the corridor there are two north-south axes.The east side sequentially arranges Seven-Sages Tower, Zhenren Cave, Three-Sages Tower, Niangniang Temple, and Dongyue Temple—each courtyard accompanied by side rooms.

The west side arranges screen wall, Third Heaven Gate, Fourth Heaven Gate, Music Tower (i.e., opera stage), Zhenwu Great Hall, Three-Official Hall, Scripture Library, and Chaoran Pavilion.

Each courtyard also has side rooms.

Behind Chaoran Pavilion, slightly west, there is another north-south short axis—east side front and rear are Jade Emperor Tower, Five-Elders Temple, and Holy Mother Temple; west side is a large quadrangle, main hall is Three Purities Hall, courtyard gate facing south directly opposite Yangzhen Building.

Besides these halls, scattered are Water God Temple, Wealth God Temple, Guandi Temple, Buddha Hall, Wenchang Pavilion, Yuanchen Hall, Jade Emperor Temple, and Kuixing Tower—altogether over fifty halls, towers, and pavilions.

This Baiyun Temple was founded in Song dynasty, expanded in Ming Wanli era (1573–1620).

It faces the Yellow River in front, backs against Baiyun Mountain—through over seven hundred stone steps, the buildings are drawn all the way up to the mountain peak.

Both natural landscape and architectural landscape are very rich and majestic.However it is no longer a purely rural Daoist temple—although solitary built on a wild mountain, it is the Daoist center of Shaanxi.

Also fully exploiting the beauty of natural landscape and integrating architecture into it are the Dongzhu Temple at Yuyuan Village, Wuyi County, Zhejiang; Xianglu Temple at Jialu City, Shaanxi; and Qinglian Temple at Jincheng City, Shanxi, etc.

Dongzhu Temple at Yuyuan Village backs against a thickly shaded hillside, contrary to convention, spreading horizontally.The central courtyard enshrines a child god of unknown origin—possibly Chenxiang.

Right small courtyard enshrines Earth God; left small courtyard enshrines Guanyin—following convention, many gods and Buddhas accompany in worship.

Before the Guanyin courtyard are the temple keeper's rooms, further extending outward is the vegetarian hall.

Before the Earth God courtyard is the Dream-Fulfilling Tower—because dream-seeking at Dongzhu Temple is an important feature.Due to terrain, below the Dream-Fulfilling Tower there is another layer, six guest rooms for dream-seekers to lodge.

The most distinctive is the high steps before the temple gate—not on the axis, but rising from right to left against the wall.

The temple walls are white; the free and lively form, set off by trees, is very lively.

Xianglu Temple at Jialu City is not large—built on top of a natural cliff rising straight up about two hundred meters from the Yellow River edge, overlooking the rushing Yellow River, breathtaking.

Left front, a small bridge over ten meters long crosses a crack, leading to an independent pillar-shaped stone cliff—standing alone outside the main cliff, about twenty meters high—on top stands a small Guanyin Hall.

Looking in all directions from the temple and hall: undulating Loess Plateau, boundless; surging Yellow River, rushing ten thousand li.Truly breathtaking.

Temples, like ancestral halls, are public activity venues in villages and towns.

Therefore, generally, in villages and towns where ancestral halls are many and strong, temples are relatively few and small, with unimportant locations; in villages and towns where ancestral halls are few, temples are relatively many, so their locations are also relatively important.

That is to say, in relatively stable blood-relation villages, temples may be few and small; conversely, in mixed-surname villages, temples may be large and many.

In Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian, Anhui and other provinces, generally speaking, clan relations are relatively complete and stable—the power of ancestral halls is greater than temples, and their scale is also larger; temples are generally built outside the village, or even absent—such as Anzhen Fort in Fu'an, Fujian.

In Shanxi, Hebei, Shaanxi and other provinces, with frequent and fierce wars, clan relations are relatively weak—the importance and power of temples in villages greatly surpass ancestral halls, and many villages even have no ancestral hall.

For example, Guoyu Village in Yangcheng City, Shanxi.

Two villages in Hejiang County, Sichuan—Fubao Town and Yaoba Town—were both built by new immigrants from "Huguang filling Sichuan" after Zhang Xianzhong's massacre of Sichuan, so both are mixed-surname villages.

They are each on a main road from Hejiang into Guizhou—one southeast of the county seat, one southwest—not far apart, both are stops for transport horse caravans to lodge.

However, the structure and style of these two settlements are quite different, strongly expressed in temple layout and other aspects.

Old Fubao Town's main street through the village is about six hundred meters long, with as many as eleven small temples along the street, roughly evenly spaced, all not large in scale.

Two of the slightly larger ones have opera stages.

These temples are actually hometown association halls for immigrants, each handling various matters in fellow villagers' lives—such as Jiangxi people's Wanshou Palace, Fujian people's Tianhou Palace, and Hubei people's Yuwang Palace, etc.

The daily manager is called "temple keeper.

" They are not large in scale, with simple buildings,外形 roughly similar to residences—only two have polished brick gate facades and two have stone-carved gate couplets.

On market days, vendors from various villages set up stalls in the "temples" with fixed relationships.

Yaoba Town is slightly longer than Old Fubao Town, at over eight hundred meters, but it only has one Dongyue Temple in the central area—very large in scale, occupying about six thousand square meters.

Inside the temple gate there is a grand opera stage and a large square for watching opera; behind, rising layer by layer along the mountain slope, are依次 Guanyin Hall, Donghuang Emperor Hall, and Chuanzhu Hall—three main halls and some small halls on both sides.

There are monks, said to be maintained by gentry and merchants' funding plus believers' "unexpected expense" donations—of course actually very profitable.

Yaoba also has nine short side alleys leading out of the village; at the outer end of each alley there is a single-bay Guanyin Temple—actually just a shelter for travelers to avoid rain, donated by a wealthy merchant.

From Yaoba Town and Fubao Town, it appears village construction has no fixed format, and towns can differ greatly from each other.Also not following conventions are some temples adopting local spatial structure methods.

For example, Pu'an Temple at Yantou Village, Yongjia County, Zhejiang—it does not use the layout of several independent buildings forming a courtyard, but uses interlocking roofs and a grid-shaped column network to cover a large space, leaving only a few grid cells as light wells.

Within this space, various activity areas and functional areas are flexibly separated.Such architecture is rare throughout the Jiangnan region.

Due to different historical conditions, the scale and quality of rural temples vary considerably across regions.

Generally speaking, in blood-relation villages of Jiangnan, with strong clan power, the scale and quality of rural temples are generally below ancestral halls, even inferior to some residences—such as Liukeng Village in Le'an County, Jiangxi, and Peitian Village in Liancheng County, Fujian.

However, their "rank" may still be relatively prominent—so much so that small temples may have bracket sets (斗拱), hip-and-gable roofs, etc.

In the north and Sichuan, due to long-term warfare, the patriarchal clan system was severely damaged—mostly mixed-surname villages, with no ancestral hall in the village, or only very crude ones—the status of temples is higher than all other buildings.

Such as Fubao Town in Hejiang County, Sichuan, and Guoyu Village in Yangcheng County, Shanxi.

The former's old street is about six hundred meters long, with nine decent temples on the street—most are actually hometown association halls for immigrants from "Huguang filling Sichuan.

" Among them, the Zhangye Temple at the north end and the Wanshou Palace in the center have opera stages.

The latter has Tang Emperor Temple and Confucian Temple in the west of the village; outside the east gate on Canglong Ridge there are Baiyun Temple, Wenchang Pavilion, and Wenfeng Pagoda—both large in scale and better in quality.

The Confucian Temple was approved by filing with the Duke of Yansheng's office in Qufu; the Tang Emperor Temple's "specification level" is also very high—main hall reaches nine bays, with opera stage and bell and drum towers.

In extremely special circumstances, temples and ancestral halls are built together—such as Lijiashan Village in Linxian County, Shanxi.

This is a very remote cave-dwelling small village; at the village edge there is a Guandi Temple, with a Qing dynasty stone stele engraved with "Record of Rebuilding the Temple": "It is said that bells were cast in suburban temples, ancient emperors' merits crown a thousand years; temples and monasteries established in the central court, former sages' fragrance flows through a hundred generations—thus knowing that honoring gods and respecting spirits is a most grand ceremony.

Our Lijiashan Village, though having temples for dwelling gods, has no pavilion for offering opera—therefore, before the slope beside the temple, there is a piece of land belonging to our Li clan relatives, willingly donated to the public association, for later building an opera tower.

By Xianfeng fifth year, villagers collectively discussed, choosing an auspicious day to start work.First repaired three front stone caves, then repaired three lower stone caves.

By Tongzhi fifth year, erected three stone caves in both corridors, built one opera tower facing north.

Rebuilt Guandi and Guanyin halls, repaired Joy, Wealth, and God of Wealth shrines—then gods at peace and people celebrating, forever enjoying blessings.

Also facing south on the east, repaired one stone cave, and the Li family alone donated sixty thousand cash to worship ancestors—not related to the public association, this is a family temple.

Originally discussed publicly with Chen and Cui surnames, actually done privately by the Li family alone—and the project was vast, certainly not achievable by single strength; now on the day of completion, respectfully engrave the names of donating believers on durable stone, to last a hundred generations without decay.

Established on the 28th day of the 9th month, Qing Tongzhi fifth year." The temple is very small, the inscription not long, but the信息量 contained is considerable.

Guandi, Guanyin, and God of Wealth worshiped together in the same hall, plus the donating Li family ancestors.

The Li family paid money, so it became the Li family's family temple—plus one opera stage, offering opera to worshiped gods and people—this is the typical state of rural temples in northern China, and also a state of culture.

However it is now called Tianguan Temple.There are several common ways rural temples are built.

Very few orthodox Buddhist temples are mostly funded by one or two monastics vowing to solicit donations (called "unexpected expense"), built by donations from devout men and women, merchant households for blessing or vow fulfillment; some industry god temples are funded by practitioners of each industry; another way is by village geopolitical "associations" or clan elders and gentry forming specialized "societies" to initiate temple building.

"Societies" are divided into two types—one responsible for organizing solicitation and management, another where some people see temple building as profitable, implementing share-based fundraising—shares can be transferred and inherited.

Can also be used as daughter's dowry.

Almost all temples have several large steles, detailed recording the honor roll of donors for initial construction, expansion, and repairs—even the names of peasant women donating ten cash or a spoonful of grain are not omitted.

At the end of steles are also names of carpenters, bricklayers, dyers, statue decorators, etc.—of course also names of various staff responsible for all work and chief organizers.

Very few temples and monasteries are built with public funds—such as recorded in Daoguang Sichuan "Anyue County Gazetteer": Song Jiading twelfth year (1219), county rebuilt Tianqing Temple, "from halls to guest reception places, all renewed.

Bamboo, wood, tiles, stone work, grain expenses all from official funds, not burdening people at all.

" Actually, donating money for temple building is a kind of merit—people believe donating money can bring blessings, so very enthusiastic.

On several stone pillars of the main hall of Dongyue Temple at Yedi Village, Zezhou County, Shanxi, there are donors' names—such as "Five-Peaks Hall Wang Cong donates one stone pillar" and "Five-Peaks Hall mason Duan Gao donates one stone pillar," dated Yuanfeng second year (1079) and third year (1080).

Similar inscriptions are also on door lintel stones.More common is erecting steles in temple halls and corridors, engraving donors' names and amounts.

Rural miscellaneous temples, not large in scale, without monks or Daoists, are usually managed by a lay temple keeper (or incense master).

Small temples don't even have a keeper—the association or society hires someone to regularly burn incense and clean.

Temples' ongoing income comes from incense merits of devout men and women, and donations from families with matters holding Dharma ceremonies, lighting eternal lamps, eating vegetarian meals, drawing lots, dream interpretation, divining fortune, etc.

As for regular income, most temples rely on "incense fields.

" Incense fields are donated by believers at temple construction, later increased by successive donations—generally rented out, the temple keeper collects rent grain and keeps it for use.

Some temples also have donated houses and shopfronts, income even more abundant.Temple affairs management is undertaken by village-specific "associations" or "societies.

" The Black Dragon Temple at Qikou Town, Linxian County, Shanxi, is managed by "nine associations and one town.

" Associations have two categories—one is permanent pure-geopolitical administrative organization, one is institution organized for specific fundraising."One town" is the street chamber of commerce.

These "associations" must donate funds to support temple keepers, repair buildings, redecorate god statues, organize temple fairs, etc.

—in disaster years, they must use accumulated incense money to provide relief.Opera performances in temples are additionally handled by specialized "associations.

" Share-based "societies" profit from organizing various superstitious activities, members receive interest by shares.

For temples to obtain丰厚 income in operation, each temple fabricates mythological legends about how its gods are "responsive to every request," "answering like an echo," etc.

Dongzhu Temple at Yuyuan Village, Wuyi County, Zhejiang—legend says it was built in response to a seven-year-old child prodigy (possibly Mulian saving his mother, i.e.

, Chenxiang) appearing in a dream to a cowherd—this temple became famous in the region for the efficacy of dream-seeking, so beside the temple a two-story Dream-Fulfilling Tower was built, specifically for dream-seekers to rent.

Every year on the day before the god's birthday on the 26th of the 6th lunar month—not only is the Dream-Fulfilling Tower fully occupied, even the two-three-li village roadside is full of sleeping people.

Dream-seekers must first burn incense and candles to pray; after getting a dream, they must ask the temple keeper to interpret it—these "procedures" all require payment, temple income相当可观.

Therefore Dongzhu Temple's shares can not only be inherited as heritage, but some were once used as daughter's dowry, passing from wealthy Yu family to Li family.
