7.5 庙宇的公共功能
Section 5

五、庙宇的公共功能 庙宇的用途其实是多方面的，不仅仅用于崇祀或巫术迷信活动。正因为它们有许多公共性的功能，所以它们常常是很世俗化、很现实化的。农村中庙宇多的原因，第一中国向来没有真正意义的宗教，有的是功利性的实用主义的自然神和人格神崇拜。

凡农业社会中生产、生活的各种需要和愿望，都有相应的"有求必应"的神灵主管。这种泛神论的神谱很广，而且是开放性的，随意可以增添。因此，只要有闲钱可用，"淫祀"就越来越多，庙宇也就多了。

山西省介休县的张壁村，不大，大约有一百三十户住宅，但从商者多，竟有大小庙宇二十二座。第二，农村中，庙宇一般都有公共建筑的功能，介休更有这种风俗。嘉庆《介休县志》卷十二有一篇雍正七年（1729年）任（王从）撰写的《新东村观音堂记》，记中说道："维斯堂在百室之中，农人得憩夏畦，行旅获舒劳足。而且月朗风清，野老常于此话桑麻、论今昔。

即有讼端，可以解纷；或有发召，可以集议。正不独夕梵涤我尘心，晨钟发人深省也。"《介休县志》中又有一篇马绶写的《新田堡净明寺记》更有意思，他说："抑今贫者日困，富者日悭，一闻福田利益之说，则不必劝而施，不必夺而予。而鳏寡孤独或得祝发以寄食其中，不饿殍以死，斯亦何背于先王之政乎？……余思梵刹之设，虽以供养菩提，而吾徒每假之为鼓歌弦诵之地，忆里中先哲，曾于此中讲学论文而登甲第，不佞亦踵相接焉……而圣贤之道之传，亦藉是维系不坠。

脱若后有昌黎诸贤，相与倡明圣教，则此选佛之场，即为鹿洞鹅湖，亦何不可哉"。寺庙被当做了一种世俗的公共文化建筑看待，所以建庙是一种公益活动，庙宇建筑大多有一种公共建筑的性格，造在村门口内外，大一点的还有戏台。浙江省永嘉县有将近两千座"三官庙"，建在田野间、河埠头、山路边。

它们实际上是供下田人避雨、歇晌用的亭子，路人也可以在庙里煮饭、饮水、换草鞋、喝避暑的药茶。在村边上的，更是老人和孩子的乐园。有些庙有闲院净室供人居停。县衙里长官下乡公干，常住在这些场所，它们就会成为临时的公廨，折狱、放粮都可以在这里办理。过路客商、官眷、赴考学子也常常住在庙里。元代王实甫《崔莺莺待月西厢记杂剧》第一本"楔子"里老夫人说："先夫弃世之后，老身与女孩儿扶柩至博陵安葬，因路途有阻，不能得去，来到河中府，将这灵柩寄在普救寺内。

这寺是先夫相国修造的，是则天娘娘香火院，况兼法本长老又是俺相公剃度的和尚，因此俺就在这西厢下一座宅子安下。"第二折，张生迷恋莺莺，想搬进普救寺居住，对长老说："因恶旅邸冗杂，早晚难以温习经史，欲假一室，晨昏听讲，房金按月，任意多少。"长老回答："塔院侧边西厢一间房，甚是潇洒，正可先生安下。……老僧准备下斋，先生事毕便来。"这段故事把普救寺的兴建、性质和经营管理的一个侧面写得很生动了。

所以历代官僚的"毁淫祠"都是对乡土社会毫无了解而采取的野蛮暴行。除了以上所说的各种用处之外，寺庙还常被用作同乡会馆，如全国各地，都有天后宫（祀妈祖）作为福建同乡会馆，万寿宫（祀许旌阳真人）作为江西同乡会馆，禹王宫作为湖北同乡会馆，四川人则以川主庙（祀李冰）作为同乡会馆，等等。

这些庙，可以作为离乡背井外出谋生或赴考的乡亲们联谊之所，也可以为他们提供力所能及的救助，供应膳食和住宿，帮助谋职，办子弟学塾，等等。客死异地的还能在庙里暂厝灵柩，它们甚至还附有义塚。有些庙宇香火田比较多，其他收入也丰厚，就办些慈善事业，如育幼堂、赡老所、义仓等等。山西省介休县绵山上的空王庙，过去便有规模不小的义仓，灾年开仓，活人不少。

庙宇也可以为村镇的商贸经济活动提供场所。如四川省合江县的福宝场，有一条六百米来长的商业街，街的东侧比肩有六座庙，每逢集市日，街上拥挤不堪，这些庙的院落就开放为专营市场：张飞庙是肉市，清源宫是粮市，五显宫里则摆满了小吃摊和赌摊，等等。这样，镇上所需商业场所的面积有了弹性，就大大方便了集市贸易。庙里的"香师"也可以借此得些收入。

清源宫里有一块道光年间（1821—1850）的碑，规定了每个借地的小贩应该付给香师的实物数额，不过实际上并不那么精确，无非是卖肉的切一刀肉，卖粮的抓几把粮。所以，农村的集市贸易又叫"庙会"。庙宇又是乡间文化娱乐的中心之一。

古时候农村文化娱乐最热闹、最重大、最欢畅的群众性活动是办庙会，其中最吸引人的项目是演戏，而演戏主要在庙宇里（南方各地有些宗祠里也有戏台，但演出比庙宇戏台少）。

中等规模的庙就可能有戏台。山西省介休县张壁村，很小，但它的可罕庙、关帝庙、二郎庙都有戏台，叫"乐楼"或"舞楼"。

山西省临县黄河边的碛口镇，水陆运输接转的码头，人口比较多，大约有三千人，而且商贾和船夫云集，镇里镇外几个庙，黑龙庙、关帝庙、河神庙、西云寺、观音庙，个个有戏台。

过年、过节、神诞、庙会、各种祈福禳灾的还愿等等都会演大戏，一演就是几天甚至十几天，碛口镇上几乎天天有戏，有些季节甚至有几台戏同时演出。这样的演戏盛况，对促进碛口镇的市面繁荣大有好处，甚至能把黄河西岸陕西的村民们都吸引过来，因此"社"、"会"都乐于承担，它们的费用由街市上的商家支持。

戏台多设在庙宇（或宗祠）里，也有历史原因。首先因为演戏起源于巫术，从傩戏演化出来。浙江省永嘉县的南戏，本来就是为了娱神的。唐代诗人顾况《永嘉》诗写道：东瓯传旧俗，风日江边好，何处乐神声，夷歌出烟岛。乐神的夷歌就是后来戏剧的源头。神是人根据自己的形象和性情造出来的，既然演戏能娱人，必定也能娱神，所以礼神的重要活动之一便是演戏。

春祈、秋报、神诞、开光、雩祭、迎神、还愿、新庙落成等各种场合都要办庙会演戏。山西省沁水县南瑶村玉皇庙有一块《致祭诸神圣诞条规》碑，记载了山神、土地、高禖、白龙、龙王、五瘟、河伯、马王、牛王、风王、关圣帝君、三蚕圣母等圣诞的日子、所需祭品和摊钱方式，其中"四月初三日致祭玉皇大帝圣诞"，要"戏三台，猪一口，依地亩摊钱"。

七月初三日又祭一次玉皇大帝，所需和摊钱与四月的相似，再加"蜜食一架，依随神摊钱"而已。半个月之后，"七月二十日致祭风王尊神圣诞，戏三台，猪一口，依烟户摊钱，又面一斤并水官……（有阙文）"。小小村子一年里一共演三次戏，一次三台。演戏的费用有的由宗祠出，有的由民间的"社"或"会"出，有的由行业或按地亩分摊，等等。

也有的可用"罚没款"，如在神庙里赌博，在神庙地界里放牧，买卖有欺诈，以及卖淫嫖娼等都要罚款。山西省泽州辛壁村成汤庙有一块民国二十二年（1933年）的《弹劾扣款自肥碑记》里面说到一个贪污公款的社首，"令其即行如数退出，……将退出之款演戏三天"。乡土社会里，对贪污腐败行为也是深恶痛绝而且严厉处分的。

江西省婺源县洪村也有类似的规矩：凡村民卖茶质量不好的，一经查出，就要罚出钱演戏。这规定刻石立碑，以保护本村茶叶的市场声誉。浙江省江山县清漾村毛氏宗谱里则规定，对外来商贩一定要诚信，否则也要罚戏。这又是泛神崇拜的庙宇在乡土社会中一个重要的功能作用，一个完全世俗化，生活化，人情化的作用。

大概因为善男信女们挤着看戏，不免"男女杂沓"，又加上各种演出多有"子不语"的怪、力、乱、神和人间情爱，因此惹起"儒者"们的非议，屡屡主张禁止。元代泰定二年（1325年）山西省高平县米山宣圣庙内的《米山宣圣庙记》碑一开头就感叹："泽潞里馆岁昵淫祀而嬉优伶，才乏俗浇，识者兴叹。

"明代初年，《大明律》中有"禁止搬做杂剧律令"，禁演一批剧目，而提倡一批宣扬忠孝节义的剧目。明末清初的大戏剧家李渔（1611—1680），竟被"世人腐儒"申斥"不为经国之大业，而为破道之小言"。稍晚几年的清初学者刘献廷（1648—1695）在所著《广阳杂记·卷二》里写道："余尝与韩图麟论今世之戏文小说，图老以为败坏人心，莫此为甚，最宜严禁者。余曰，先生莫作此说，戏文小说，乃明王转移世界之大枢机。

圣人复起，不能舍此而为治也。图麟大骇，余为之痛言其故，反复数千言。图麟拊掌掀髯，叹未曾有。"他的见解，见于《广阳杂记》中这一条之前的一条："余观世之小人，未有不好唱歌看戏者，此性天中之《诗》与《乐》也；未有不看小说、听说书者，此性天中之《书》与《春秋》也；未有不信占卜祀鬼神者，此性天中之《易》与《礼》也。圣人六经之教，原本人情，而后之儒者，乃不能因其势而利导之，百计禁止遏抑，务以成周之刍狗茅塞人心，是何异壅川使之不流，无怪其决裂溃败也。

"刘献廷很看不起这些"儒者"，反唇相讥道："夫今之儒者之心，为刍狗之所塞也久矣，而以天下大器使之为之，爰以图治，不亦难乎"？这种争论一直在朝廷和百姓之间进行着。因为"演戏酬神，例所不禁"，所以各地官方开放文人的苏腔北昆，称作"雅乐"，而排斥民间地方土戏，称之为"花部"，"土戏亵神，谋献苏腔"。大概"土戏"常有涉于"淫媒"的内容。

嘉庆三年（1798年）清仁宗下诏禁演"乱弹"，说它"声音既属淫靡，其所扮演者非狭邪媒亵即怪诞悖乱之事，于风俗人心殊有关系"，以至和梆子、弦索、秦腔等民间说唱艺术一起，"概不准再行演唱"。（见苏州《老郎庙碑记》）山西省蒲县柏山东岳庙里一块道光元年（1821年）的碑上说："旧规演乐，必须觅自外境"，就是觅"苏腔"。碑阴又说："正日不用乱弹，恐亵神也……用土戏暂补者，不得动用公钱。

"虽然不禁死"花部"，但不得不"遵旨"排抑"花部"。也常有些心眼儿被"刍狗"堵塞的地方官们，对演戏心怀不满。清代中叶道光、咸丰间永嘉县令汤成烈纂《县志》稿便说："报赛侈鬼神之会……士女游观，靓妆华服，阗城溢郭，有司莫之能禁。"不能禁而又心怀不满，不得已只好写在《县志》稿里，表个态，卸去心头负担、肩上责任。往下直到民间的宗族长老，也常常戒子弟不要耽溺于戏曲、小说。

永嘉县谢灵运后代聚居的第一个村子鹤垟的《谢氏宗谱》规定，在书院里要潜心读圣贤书，"小曲、淫辞、艳史等类，片纸不得留"。不过，演戏并不在禁止之列，原因就在演戏是演给祖先（宗祠戏台）和神灵（庙宇戏台）看的。

从鹤垟分房出去而建的蓬溪村，它的《谢氏宗谱》里写道，建于明代中叶的大宗祠于清初乾隆四十年（1775年）左右破败，便在残基上演戏，"道光初年，众修大宗，建前进，并建戏台，始在大宗演戏。春迎龙船山与关帝二庙神主至大宗，冬迎仙岩殿与陈十四圣母至大宗庆祝"。

宗祠演戏不但给祖先看，还要邀请外村神灵来一起看戏。祖先和神灵都喜欢看戏，还可以借看戏联络感情，这就是皇帝和儒者都不可能禁绝演戏的主要口实。这座蓬溪谢氏大宗祠的戏台建造的时间大约就是汤成烈当永嘉县令的时候，或者稍早几年。

永嘉县渠川村《叶氏宗谱》里有一篇《重修渠川叶氏大宗祠碑记》，它说道：原来造于康熙癸辛（原文有误）年间的大宗祠，到光绪甲辰（1904年）"旧建舞台倾圮，乃舍旧维新。越明年，乙巳（1905年），谋于众曰：台之改作，勿以戏观。族人致祭，岁时伏腊，团结一堂。

演剧开场，以古为鉴，伸忠孝节义之心，枨触而油然以生。"除了祖先和神灵爱看戏之外，演戏可以团结族众，可以伸张忠孝节义，这就是宗祠重建戏台演戏的最重要论据，便也是借口。

魏象枢在所著《庸言》（载《训俗遗规》卷三）里写道：看戏文的时候，"看得一个好人，好在何处，我当学他；看一个不好人，不好在何处，我不当学他"，不要糊涂到"终日笑花脸，自己当花脸"。看戏成了上品德课，那么就没有任何理由反对演戏了。

演戏既然首先为了娱乐神灵和祖先，必须在他们面前证明戏剧的内容是"健康的"，所以戏台必建在庙宇和宗祠里，至迟在北宋时候，北方庙宇里就有了"舞楼"。金、元两代更加普及，山西省芮城县元大德元年（1292年）《芮王庙记》碑里说："献有殿，舞有庭，戏有台"。

演戏为了酬神，最重要是正殿里坐着的"神"要看得清楚，所以戏台在殿前院子正中而面对正殿，正殿大多面南，因此也叫戏台为"南楼"。到了明代，舞楼就和山门结合，成了"倒座戏台"，从此大致在全国成为定制。

有的"倒座戏台"塞满整个庙门，人们出入在侧面设门。为方便出入，有的戏台后沿脱开庙门退一些距离。距离大小不等，最大的几乎全部从庙门脱出，但仍与庙门联成一体。贴近庙门的戏台，台面中央一溜台板是活的，不演戏时，可以卸下，成一条甬道，供人出入庙门。

乡民们不分男女都聚在正殿前的大院里看戏，有些庙宇，以院子两侧的廊下或楼上为观众席，当然是"贵宾席"。北方干旱少雨，大院没有遮盖。南方多雨，有些地方就在大院正中造"大亭子"，给观众遮雨。

浙江宁海和江西抚州都有极华丽的"大亭子"，前后两座或三座，连接戏台和正殿（堂），亭子天花上面前后列一串两、三个藻井，十分华丽。穷工极巧，都是小木作的最高级精品。在山西省，有些庙宇有二连台、三连台、品字台等等。

二连台和三连台就是完全相同的戏台并肩排列。品字台则是正面一个台，两侧厢房的中段各设一个台。二连台比较多，三连台有芮城县东吕村还存在的实例，万荣县后土祠则有品字台。也还有其他一些戏台作很特别的组合。

这种组合的"戏台群"，演的是"对台戏"，可见农村演戏，农民看的是热闹，并不很在乎戏的情节和演员的功夫。所以村里"戏社"的成员大多不脱离农业劳动，都是些"业余爱好者"。

有些地方戏则要求建特殊的戏台，例如"目连戏"的戏台，有上下两层甚至三层。上层是天堂，演出的角色是玉皇大帝之流，中层是人间，演的是庶人的事；再往下的台底是地狱，是鬼魅的表演场所。

士绅大户人家，重视礼数，为了严防"男女杂沓"，所以宗祠、庙宇，凡有戏台的，多于两厢建楼房，男子在左厢房的楼上看，妇女在右厢房的楼上看。山西省沁水县西文兴村，关帝庙右厢的楼梯设在庙外，大户人家妇女上下都不必经过男子汉拥挤着的院子，在院子里的人也上不了厢房的楼，加强了"男女之大防"。厢房楼下则是卖各色零食的挑子。

同治八年（1869年）十一月，曾经有一个"上谕"，"严禁五城等等寺院演剧招摇妇女入庙，以端风化"。有些宗族，也根本禁绝妇女看戏。如道光山西《灵石何氏族谱》卷七"家训"里规定，妇女不许"闲览小说杂传"，更不许参加"春游、聚谈、观剧、看灯"。

少数寺庙把戏台造在庙门前广场上另一侧，还是面对神灵，也便是面对庙门，如浙江省永嘉县岩头村的塔湖庙。这个庙前广场，左右两边都有狭长的湖面，演戏的时候，男子汉在广场上看，妇女只许在湖对岸远远地看个大概。

号称水乡的浙江省绍兴，有一种特殊的戏台布局，庙门和戏台面面相对，中间却隔着一条河，观众划船而来，在船上看戏，风味极佳。绍兴城北有十方土地庙，戏台全在水中，由四根石柱支承。台柱上有楹联，写的是："也弹流水也弹月，半入江风半入云。

"它的主演节目大约是"乱弹"，一种说唱。虽然防范严密，其实，看戏时候，不论楼上还是院心，都是相亲、定情的好场合。楼上的互相遥望，院心的面对面挤来挤去，常常会像戏台上一样演出些有趣的故事。陕西省东部，沿黄河岸边的村子，多在村南头有一个广场，场西一座关帝庙，朝东；场东一座戏台，朝西。

看戏的人们面对河东，看着"坐怀不乱"的关羽的老家，就不会心猿意马、乱了心思，所以不论什么风流的戏都可演可看，"百无禁忌"。乡民们不傻。庙宇就在实现它多种多样的用途时，来到人间，卸去神圣的光环，世俗化了，现实化了。这才是中国乡土社会中庙宇的真正气质。演戏不仅仅是庙里的事，它往往是一个盛大的迎神赛会的一部分节目。

演戏也不仅仅是一座庙宇、一个村落的事，它往往是许多村落共同参与的事。庙宇在这个场合成了一个相当大范围里的民俗文化狂欢中心，所以这种节日叫"庙会"。

山西省平定县元末至正十三年（1353年）的《蒲台山灵赡王庙碑》很生动地记录了这个场面：四月四日享庙上，前期一日迎神，六村之众具仪仗引导，幢、幡、宝盖、旌旗、金鼓与散乐、社火，层见叠出，名曰起神。明日牲牢酒醴香纸，既丰且腆，则吹箫击鼓，优伶奏技。

而各社各有社火，或骑或步，或为仙佛，或为鬼神，鱼龙虎豹，喧呼歌叫，如蜡祭之狂。日晡复起，名曰下神。神至之处，日夕供祀惟谨，岁以为常。就在山西省晋东南阳城县润城镇东岳庙里有一块乾隆三十六年（1771年）《润城社新制神伴仪仗记》的碑，碑文里说的是游行式的演出。迎神祈泽，则大起众庶，鼓钲竞响，伞扇麾幢之属夹道而前驰。

复有贝锦彩装，儿童杂剧，纷纭逐沓，填塞街衢，焜耀闾巷。而衣冠缙绅之族，亦往往相与揖让进退于其间。斯盖一时之盛也。说的是润城镇当年社庙庙会的盛况。从"众庶"到"缙绅"，从"儿童"到"衣冠"，都热热闹闹忘情地参与进去，很富有群众性。这种敬神大典，其实在各地普遍都有。

除了蒲台山和润城社这两块碑所描述的香火盛况之外，商贸活动也是庙会的重要内容。届时摊贩林立，出售各种生活用品，供应丰富多彩的小食品。庙会期间大多也免不了有各色赌博，放纵几天。山西省临县碛口镇，庙多庙会多，附近有些村民就以赶庙会做小买卖为生。

浙江省永康县方岩村的胡公（胡则）庙，一到秋收后、春耕前，几个月里庙会连绵不绝。不仅附近各县都有朝山进香的队伍来参加，甚至江西、安徽都有队伍过来。方岩山下因此形成了一条两三公里长的商业街，专门依靠庙会时的旅店业和香烛业的收入。浙江省建德县新叶村的三月三玉泉寺庙会，至今依然年年举行，也是商摊如云。

不过这个庙会没有正戏，戏剧场面的片段就在游行队伍中边走边演。农村生活艰辛、单调而闭塞，造就了乡民质朴淳厚的性格，但他们同样渴望欢乐、渴望宣泄。他们也有文化的创造，要求有一个展示他们才艺的机会。庙会是他们欢乐、宣泄和展示的场合。一种生命力冲破极端沉闷的生活环境喷薄而出，有点粗野、有点狂热，鞭炮火铳、锣鼓唢呐，震得四山回响。

山西省临县碛口镇黑龙庙里唱戏，黄河对岸的陕北小村都听得清清楚楚，乡人们一代又一代地记得这些，"河东唱戏河西听"，成为生活中鲜亮的一笔。作为泛神崇拜的祀神之所，小到古树下一个香案，悬崖边一个神龛，大到屋舍上百间、众神骈阗的宫观寺庙，是中国农耕时代乡土文化的博物馆。

这是一种综合性的博物馆，它展示着中国农民们对宇宙、对社会、对人生的认识，展示着他们对生活的态度，他们积极乐观的理想追求和无可奈何的落寞失望；庙宇也展示着他们的性格，他们的欢乐和焦虑，他们的忠厚和小心眼儿的狡狯；在庙宇里，也可以看到他们生老病死的痛苦和摆脱这种痛苦的努力。

乡土社会的庙宇里，没有玄奥的哲理，没有悲天悯人的说教，有的是乡民们最真实的现世生活。庙宇又是一座展示乡村艺人文化创作成就的代表作，它是乡土建筑中最丰富多彩的，规格高、技术精，艺术上也很成熟，还综合了雕塑、绘画、文学和书法等当地的最好作品。把建筑看作一部史书，宗教建筑是其中最丰富多彩的章节之一，也最叫人感动。

把庙宇看作一座博物馆，细细看去，人们可以从这里看到乡民们物质生活和精神生活的一个重要部分。

5.Public Functions of Temples The uses of temples are actually multifaceted—not only for worship or superstitious witchcraft activities.

Precisely because they have many public functions, they are often very secularized and very realistic.

The reasons for many temples in rural areas: first, China has never had religion in the true sense—what exists is utilitarian pragmatist nature-god and personality-god worship.

Every need and wish in production and life in agricultural society has a corresponding "responsive to every request" god in charge.This pantheistic god genealogy is very broad and open-ended, can be added at will.

Therefore, as long as there is spare money available, "licentious worship" increases more and more, and temples increase too.

Zhangbi Village in Jiexiu County, Shanxi—not large, about one hundred thirty households, but many in commerce—actually has twenty-two temples large and small.

Second, in rural areas, temples generally have public building functions—Jiexiu especially has this custom.

In Jiaqing's "Jiexiu County Gazetteer" volume 12 there is a "Record of New East Village Guanyin Hall" written by Ren (Wang Cong) in Yongzheng seventh year (1729), saying: "This hall is among a hundred houses—peasants can rest from summer fields, travelers can rest tired feet.

Moreover, on moonlit clear windy nights, village elders often discuss mulberry and hemp, talk of past and present here.If there are lawsuits, disputes can be resolved; if there are summons, meetings can be held.

Not only does evening chanting cleanse my worldly heart, morning bell provoke deep reflection.

" In "Jiexiu County Gazetteer" there is another more interesting "Record of Xintian Fort Jingming Temple" by Ma Shou, he says: "Now the poor grow daily destitute, the rich grow daily stingy—once hearing of blessed field benefits, they donate without persuasion, give without taking.

And widows, widowers, orphans, childless may get ordained to feed there, not dying of starvation—how does this contradict the policies of former kings?

…I think the establishment of Buddhist temples, though for enshrining Bodhi, we disciples often use them as places for singing and reciting—recalling former sages in the village, once lectured and discussed essays here and passed the highest exam, I also followed in succession… and the transmission of sages' ways is also maintained thereby.

If later there are sages like Han Yu, together promoting sage teachings—then this Buddha-selection field becomes like Ludong and Ehu academies, why not?

" Temples were treated as secular public cultural buildings—so building temples is a public welfare activity, temple buildings mostly have the character of public buildings, built inside and outside village gates, larger ones also have opera stages.

Yongjia County, Zhejiang has nearly two thousand "Three-Official Temples," built in fields, river docks, mountain roadsides.

They are actually pavilions for field workers to avoid rain and rest at noon—passersby can also cook rice, drink water, change straw sandals, drink summer heat-relieving herbal tea in the temples.

Those at village edges are even more paradise for the elderly and children.Some temples have spare courtyards and clean rooms for people to stay.

County officials going to the countryside on official business often lodge in these places—they become temporary government offices, trying cases and distributing grain can be handled here.

Passing merchants, official families, and exam-taking scholars also often live in temples.

In Yuan dynasty Wang Shifu's "Romance of the Western Chamber" zaju, first book "wedge," the old lady says: "After my late husband passed away, the old woman and girl carried the coffin to Boling for burial—due to road obstruction, could not go, came to Hezhong Prefecture, placed this coffin in Pujiu Temple.

This temple was built by my late husband the Prime Minister, it is Empress Wu Zetian's incense courtyard—moreover Elder Faben is a monk ordained by my husband, therefore we settled in a house under this Western Chamber.

" Second act, Zhang Sheng infatuated with Yingying, wants to move into Pujiu Temple, says to the elder: "Because I dislike the inn's noise and complexity, difficult to review classics morning and evening, wish to borrow a room, listen to lectures dawn and dusk, room rent by month, any amount.

" Elder answers: "A room in the Western Chamber beside the pagoda courtyard, quite elegant, just right for you sir.…This old monk prepares vegetarian food, come when your business is done.

" This story vividly describes one aspect of Pujiu Temple's construction, nature, and operation management.

Therefore, successive bureaucrats' "destroying licentious temples" were barbaric acts taken without any understanding of rural society.

Besides the various uses mentioned above, temples are also often used as hometown association halls—such as throughout the country, there are Tianhou Palaces (worshipping Mazu) as Fujian hometown association halls, Wanshou Palaces (worshipping Xu Jingyang Zhenren) as Jiangxi hometown association halls, Yuwang Palaces as Hubei hometown association halls, Sichuan people use Chuanzhu Temples (worshipping Li Bing) as hometown association halls, etc.

These temples can serve as gathering places for fellow villagers who left home to make a living or take exams, can also provide assistance within their ability—supply meals and lodging, help find jobs, run schools for children, etc.

Those who die away from home can temporarily place coffins in temples—they even have attached charity cemeteries.

Some temples with more incense fields and other丰厚 income run charitable causes—such as orphanages, old-age homes, charity granaries, etc.

The Empty King Temple on Mian Mountain in Jiexiu County, Shanxi, used to have a sizable charity granary—opening in disaster years, saving many lives.Temples can also provide venues for village and town commercial economic activities.

For example, Fubao Town in Hejiang County, Sichuan—has a commercial street about six hundred meters long, on the east side of the street six temples stand shoulder to shoulder—every market day, the street is unbearably crowded, these temple courtyards open as specialized markets: Zhangfei Temple is meat market, Qingyuan Palace is grain market, Wuxian Temple is full of snack stalls and gambling stalls, etc.

Thus, the area of commercial venues needed by the town has elasticity—greatly facilitating market trade.The temple's "incense master" can also earn some income this way.

In Qingyuan Palace there is a Daoguang era (1821–1850) stele, stipulating the physical amount each borrowing vendor should pay the incense master—though actually not so precise, nothing more than the meat seller cutting a slice of meat, the grain seller grabbing a few handfuls of grain.

Therefore, rural market trade is also called "temple fair." Temples are also one of the centers of rural cultural entertainment.

In ancient times, the most lively, significant, and joyous mass activity in rural cultural entertainment was holding temple fairs—the most attractive item was opera performance, and opera was mainly performed in temples (in some southern areas ancestral halls also have opera stages, but performances are fewer than temple stages).

Medium-scale temples may have opera stages.

Zhangbi Village in Jiexiu County, Shanxi—very small, but its Khan Temple, Guandi Temple, and Erlang Temple all have opera stages, called "music towers" or "dance towers.

" Qikou Town on the Yellow River in Linxian County, Shanxi—a land-water transport transfer dock, relatively large population, about three thousand people, with merchants and boatmen gathering—several temples inside and outside town: Black Dragon Temple, Guandi Temple, River God Temple, Xiyun Temple, Guanyin Temple—each has an opera stage.

New Year, festivals, god birthdays, temple fairs, various blessing and disaster-averting vow fulfillments—all perform grand opera, performing for days甚至 more than ten days—Qikou Town almost has opera every day, some seasons even several operas performing simultaneously.

Such opera grandeur greatly benefits Qikou Town's market prosperity, even attracting villagers from Shaanxi on the west bank of the Yellow River—therefore "associations" and "societies" are willing to undertake, their expenses supported by street merchants.

Opera stages are mostly set in temples (or ancestral halls), also for historical reasons.First, because opera originated from witchcraft, evolving from Nuo opera.

Nanxi opera in Yongjia County, Zhejiang—originally was for entertaining gods.

Tang dynasty poet Gu Kuang's "Yongjia" poem writes: Eastern Ou passes down old customs, wind and sun by the river are fine, where is the god-pleasing music, barbarian songs come from misty islands.

The god-pleasing barbarian songs are the source of later drama.

Gods are created by people according to their own image and temperament—since opera can entertain people, it must also entertain gods—so one of the important activities of honoring gods is opera performance.

Spring prayer, autumn thanksgiving, god birthday, consecration, rain sacrifice, welcoming gods, vow fulfillment, new temple completion—various occasions all hold temple fairs and perform opera.

Yuhuang Temple at Nanyao Village, Qinshui County, Shanxi—has a "Regulations for Sacrificing to Gods' Birthdays" stele, recording the birthday dates, required offerings, and money-sharing methods for Mountain God, Earth God, Gao Mei, White Dragon, Dragon King, Five Plagues, River God, Horse King, Cow King, Wind King, Guan Sheng Emperor, Three Silkworm Holy Mothers, etc.

—among them "April 3rd sacrifice to Jade Emperor birthday" requires "three opera stages, one pig, money shared by land acreage.

" July 3rd sacrifices to Jade Emperor again—requirements and money sharing similar to April, plus "one honey food stand, money shared by god followers.

" Half a month later, "July 20th sacrifice to Wind King Honorable God birthday, three opera stages, one pig, money shared by households, plus one jin of flour and Water Official… (text missing).

" A tiny village performs opera three times a year, three stages each time.Opera performance expenses—some paid by ancestral halls, some by folk "associations" or "societies," some by industries or shared by land acreage, etc.

Some can use "fines and confiscations"—such as gambling in temples, grazing in temple boundaries, fraudulent buying and selling, and prostitution—all require fines.

Chengtang Temple at Xinbi Village, Zezhou, Shanxi—has a Republic 22nd year (1933) "Stele Record of Impeaching and Deducted Money for Self-Enrichment"—speaking of an association head who embezzled public funds, "ordered him to immediately return the full amount, …use the returned money to perform opera for three days.

" In rural society, corruption is also deeply hated and severely punished.Hong Village in Wuyuan County, Jiangxi also has similar rules: any villager selling poor quality tea, once discovered, must be fined to perform opera.

This regulation was carved on stone stele to protect the market reputation of local tea.

In the Mao family genealogy of Qingyang Village, Jiangshan County, Zhejiang—it stipulates that foreign merchants must be honest, otherwise also fined opera.

This is another important functional role of pantheistic worship temples in rural society—a completely secularized, life-oriented, humanized role.

Probably because devout men and women crowd to watch opera, inevitably "men and women mingle," plus various performances often contain "what Confucius did not speak of"—strange, forceful, chaotic, supernatural, and human love—thus arousing criticism from "Confucian scholars," repeatedly advocating prohibition.

In Yuan Taiding second year (1325), the "Record of Mishan Xuansheng Temple" stele inside Mishan Xuansheng Temple in Gaoping County, Shanxi, begins with a sigh: "Zelu villages annually indulge in licentious worship and amuse themselves with actors—talent lacking, customs corrupt, those who understand sigh.

" In early Ming, "Great Ming Code" had "laws prohibiting performing zaju dramas," banning a batch of plays while promoting a batch of plays advocating loyalty, filial piety, chastity, and righteousness.

The great late-Ming early-Qing dramatist Li Yu (1611–1680) was actually reprimanded by "worldly pedantic Confucians" as "not undertaking the great enterprise of governing the nation, but making small words that break the Way.

" Slightly later, early Qing scholar Liu Xianting (1648–1695) wrote in his "Guangyang Miscellaneous Records, Volume 2": "I once discussed with Han Tulin the drama and fiction of our age—Old Han thought they corrupt people's hearts more than anything, most strictly prohibited.

I said, sir, do not say this—drama and fiction are the great pivot by which the enlightened king transforms the world.Even if a sage arose again, he could not govern without them.

Tulin was greatly shocked; I painstakingly explained the reasons, repeatedly thousands of words.Tulin clapped his hands and stroked his beard, sighing he had never heard such.

" His见解 appears in an earlier entry in "Guangyang Miscellaneous Records": "I observe the common people—none do not like singing and watching opera, this is the 'Book of Songs' and 'Book of Music' in their nature; none do not read fiction and listen to storytelling, this is the 'Book of Documents' and 'Spring and Autumn Annals' in their nature; none do not believe in divination and worship gods, this is the 'Book of Changes' and 'Book of Rites' in their nature.

The sages' six classics teachings originally derive from human feelings—but later Confucians cannot guide according to circumstances, using a hundred schemes to prohibit and suppress, determined to use Zhou dynasty straw dogs to block people's hearts—this is no different from damming a river to stop its flow, no wonder it breaks and collapses.

" Liu Xianting despised these "Confucian scholars," retorting: "The hearts of today's Confucians have long been blocked by straw dogs—and yet entrusting them with the great vessel of the world to govern, is it not difficult?

" This debate continued between court and common people.

Because "performing opera to repay gods is not prohibited by precedent," local officials opened literati's Su tone and Northern Kun, called "refined music," while排斥 folk local operas, called "flower section"—"local opera profanes gods, seek to present Su tone.

" Probably "local opera" often involved "licentious" content.

In Jiaqing third year (1798), Qing Renzong issued edict banning "luantan" performances, saying its "sound is licentious and decadent, what it performs is either obscene and seductive or bizarre and rebellious, greatly related to customs and people's hearts"—together with bangzi, xiansuo, qinqiang and other folk storytelling arts, "generally not allowed to perform again.

" (See Suzhou "Old Lang Temple Stele Record") A stele in Dongyue Temple at Baishan, Pu County, Shanxi, dated Daoguang first year (1821), says: "Old rule for performing music must seek from outside territory"—that is, seek "Su tone.

" The stele back says: "On the main day do not use luantan, fearing profaning gods… those using local opera as temporary supplement may not use public money.

" Although not completely banning "flower section," had to "comply with edict" to suppress "flower section." There were also local officials whose hearts were blocked by "straw dogs," dissatisfied with opera.

In mid-Qing Daoguang-Xianfeng era, Yongjia County Magistrate Tang Chenglie compiling "County Gazetteer" draft said: "Thanksgiving and god-worshipping gatherings… men and women sightseeing, in makeup and fine clothes, filling city and suburbs—officials cannot prohibit.

" Unable to prohibit yet dissatisfied, had no choice but to write in the "County Gazetteer" draft, making a statement, relieving heart burden and shoulder responsibility.

Down to folk clan elders, also often warned descendants not to indulge in drama and fiction.

The "Xie Family Genealogy" of Heyang Village—the first village where descendants of Xie Lingyun settled in Yongjia—stipulated that in the academy one must devote oneself to reading sage books, "little tunes, licentious words, romantic histories—no scrap of paper may remain.

" However, opera performance was not among prohibitions—the reason being opera is performed for ancestors (ancestral hall stages) and gods (temple stages).

Pengxi Village, built by a branch family from Heyang, its "Xie Family Genealogy" writes: the great ancestral hall built in mid-Ming fell into disrepair around early Qing Qianlong fortieth year (1775), so opera was performed on the ruined foundation—"Daoguang early years, all repaired the great ancestral hall, built front section, and built opera stage, began performing opera in the great ancestral hall.

In spring welcome the god tablets of Longchuanshan and Guandi temples to the great ancestral hall; in winter welcome Xianyan Hall and Chen Shisi Holy Mother to the great ancestral hall for celebration.

" Ancestral hall opera not only for ancestors to watch, but also invites outside village gods to watch together.

Ancestors and gods both like watching opera, and can use opera-watching to connect feelings—this is the main excuse that neither emperors nor Confucian scholars could completely ban opera.

The opera stage of this Pengxi Xie Great Ancestral Hall was built around the time Tang Chenglie was Yongjia County Magistrate, or a few years earlier.

In "Ye Family Genealogy" of Quchuan Village, Yongjia, there is a "Record of Rebuilding Quchuan Ye Great Ancestral Hall"—it says: the great ancestral hall originally built in Kangxi Guisi (text has error) year, by Guangxu Jiachen (1904) "the old built stage collapsed, thus abandoned old and renewed.

Next year, Yisi (1905), discussed with all: the stage reconstruction, not merely for opera viewing.Clan members offer sacrifices, at seasonal festivals, unite in one hall.

Opera opening, using ancient as mirror, extending hearts of loyalty, filial piety, chastity, righteousness—touched and naturally arising.

" Besides ancestors and gods loving opera, opera can unite clan members, can uphold loyalty filial piety chastity righteousness—this is the most important argument for ancestral halls rebuilding stages to perform opera, and also the excuse.

Wei Xiangshu wrote in his "Yongyan" (in "Xunsu Yigui" Volume 3): when watching opera, "see a good person, where is good, I should learn from him; see a bad person, where is bad, I should not learn from him"—do not be muddled to "laugh at painted face all day, become a painted face oneself.

" Watching opera becomes taking a moral education class—then there is no reason to oppose opera.

Since opera is first for entertaining gods and ancestors, must prove drama content is "healthy" before them—so opera stages must be built in temples and ancestral halls.

At the latest by Northern Song, northern temples already had "dance towers.

" Jin and Yuan dynasties more widespread—the "Ruiwang Temple Record" stele in Ruicheng County, Shanxi, dated Yuan Dade first year (1292), says: "offerings have halls, dance has courtyards, opera has stages.

" Performing opera to repay gods—most important is the "god" sitting in the main hall can see clearly—so the stage is in the center of the courtyard before the hall, facing the main hall; main halls mostly face south, so stages are also called "south towers.

" By Ming, dance towers combined with mountain gates, becoming "reverse-seat opera stages"—from then roughly became national standard.

Some "reverse-seat opera stages" fill the entire temple gate, people enter and exit through side doors.For convenience, some stage backs detach from the temple gate and retreat some distance.

Distance varies—the largest almost completely detaches from temple gate, but still connects as one body.

Stages close to temple gates have a central strip of removable stage boards—when not performing, can be removed, forming a corridor for people entering and exiting the temple gate.

Villagers, men and women alike, gather in the large courtyard before the main hall to watch opera; some temples use the corridors or upstairs on both sides of the courtyard as audience seats—of course "VIP seats.

" Northern dry and rainless, large courtyards have no cover.Southern rainy, some places build "great pavilions" in the center of large courtyards to shelter audiences from rain.

Both Ninghai, Zhejiang and Fuzhou, Jiangxi have extremely ornate "great pavilions"—two or three in a row front and back, connecting the opera stage and main hall; above the pavilion ceiling, front and back are a string of two or three caisson ceilings—very ornate.

Exquisitely crafted, they are the highest-grade fine woodwork masterpieces.In Shanxi Province, some temples have double stages, triple stages, character-pin stages, etc.

Double and triple stages are completely identical opera stages arranged side by side.Character-pin stage has one stage at front, and one stage each in the middle section of both side wings.

Double stages are more common; triple stages still exist as an example at Donglü Village, Ruicheng County; Houtu Temple at Wanrong County has a character-pin stage.There are also other very special stage combinations.

These combined "stage groups" perform "competing operas"—showing that in rural opera, farmers watch for excitement, not caring much about plot or actors' skill.

Therefore, members of village "opera societies" mostly do not leave agricultural labor—they are "amateur enthusiasts." Some local operas require building special stages—for example, "Mulian Opera" stages have two or even three stories.

Upper story is heaven, performing roles like Jade Emperor; middle story is human world, performing common people's affairs; below the stage bottom is hell, a performance venue for ghosts and spirits.

Gentry and wealthy families, valuing etiquette, to strictly prevent "men and women mingling," so ancestral halls and temples with stages mostly build two-story buildings in both wings—men watch from upstairs in the left wing, women watch from upstairs in the right wing.

At Xiwenxing Village, Qinshui County, Shanxi—the staircase of the right wing of Guandi Temple is set outside the temple—wealthy family women going up and down need not pass through the courtyard crowded with men, and people in the courtyard cannot go up to the wing building—strengthening "the great defense between men and women.

" Downstairs in the wings are stalls selling various snacks.In Tongzhi eighth year (1869) November, there was an "imperial edict," "strictly prohibiting temples in five cities etc.

from performing drama to lure women into temples, to rectify morals." Some clans also completely banned women from watching opera.

For example, Daoguang Shanxi "Lingshi He Family Genealogy" Volume 7 "Family Instructions" stipulates women may not "idly read novels and miscellaneous biographies," even less may participate in "spring outings, gatherings, watching drama, viewing lanterns.

" A few temples build stages on the other side of the square in front of the temple gate—still facing the gods, i.e.

, facing the temple gate—such as Tahu Temple at Yantou Village, Yongjia County, Zhejiang.

This temple-front square has long narrow lakes on both left and right sides—when performing opera, men watch in the square, women are only allowed to watch from across the lake at a distance.

Shaoxing, Zhejiang, known as water town—has a special stage layout: temple gate and stage face each other, separated by a river in between—audiences come by boat, watching opera from boats—excellent flavor.

North of Shaoxing city there is Shifang Tudi Temple—stage entirely in water, supported by four stone pillars.

On stage pillars there is a couplet: "Also playing flowing water also playing moon, half entering river wind half entering clouds." Its main performance program is probably "luantan," a kind of storytelling-singing.

Although precautions are strict, actually, when watching opera—whether upstairs or in courtyard center—are good occasions for matchmaking and romance.

Those upstairs gaze at each other from afar; those in courtyard center squeeze face to face—often interesting stories unfold like on stage.

In eastern Shaanxi, villages along the Yellow River bank—mostly have a square at the south end of village—west of square a Guandi Temple facing east; east of square an opera stage facing west.

People watching opera face east of the river, looking at the hometown of "sitting still without confusion" Guan Yu—so they won't be distracted or unsettled—therefore any romantic opera can be performed and watched, "nothing forbidden.

" Villagers are not stupid.Temples, in fulfilling their diverse uses, come to the human world, shedding their sacred halo—secularized, realized.This is the true temperament of temples in Chinese rural society.

Opera performance is not only a temple matter—it is often part of a grand god-welcoming festival.Opera is also not only one temple or one village matter—it is often something many villages participate in together.

Temples in this occasion become a folk culture carnival center over a fairly large area—so this festival is called "temple fair.

" The "Putai Mountain Lingdan King Temple Stele" from Pingding County, Shanxi, late Yuan Zhizheng thirteenth year (1353), vividly records this scene: On the fourth day of the fourth month at the temple, one day before welcoming the god, people of six villages prepare processions to guide—banners, pennants, treasure canopies, flags, gold drums and scattered music, community fire—layer upon layer appearing, called "raising god.

" Next day, sacrificial animals, wine, incense, paper—both abundant and generous—then playing flutes and beating drums, actors perform skills.

And each community has its own community fire—some on horseback some on foot, some as immortals and Buddhas, some as ghosts and gods, fish dragons tigers leopards—shouting and singing, like the madness of wax sacrifice.

At dusk rising again, called "lowering god." Wherever the god arrives, day and night worship respectfully, annual custom.

In Dongyue Temple at Runcheng Town, Yangcheng County, southeastern Shanxi—there is a stele from Qianlong thirty-sixth year (1771) "Record of Runcheng Community Newly Made God Companion Procession"—the inscription describes parade-style performances.

Welcoming gods and praying for rain—then great crowds arise, drums and gongs compete in sound, umbrellas, fans, banners and the like gallop along the roads.

Also there are brocade and colorful costumes, children's variety shows, bustling and crowded, filling streets and alleys, shining through neighborhoods.

And the gentry and official families, also often bow and advance and retreat among them.This was indeed the grandeur of the time.

This describes the grandeur of the community temple fair at Runcheng Town in those years.

From "common people" to "gentry," from "children" to "officials"—all enthusiastically and forgetfully participated, very mass-oriented.Such god-worshipping grand ceremonies are actually common everywhere.

Besides the incense grandeur described by the two steles at Putai Mountain and Runcheng Community, commercial activities are also important content of temple fairs.

At that time, stalls stand in great numbers, selling various daily necessities, supplying rich and colorful snacks.During temple fairs, mostly there is also various gambling, indulged for a few days.

Qikou Town in Linxian County, Shanxi—many temples and many temple fairs—some nearby villagers make a living by going to temple fairs to do small business.

Hugong (Hu Ze) Temple at Fangyan Village, Yongkang County, Zhejiang—from after autumn harvest to before spring plowing, for several months temple fairs continue endlessly.

Not only nearby counties have mountain-pilgrimage incense teams participating, even Jiangxi and Anhui have teams coming.

Below Fangyan Mountain thus formed a commercial street two or three kilometers long, relying specifically on income from inns and incense-candle businesses during temple fairs.

The March 3rd Yuquan Temple fair at Xinye Village, Jiande County, Zhejiang—still held annually today, also with stalls like clouds.

However this temple fair has no formal opera—fragments of dramatic scenes are performed while walking in the procession.

Rural life is hard, monotonous, and closed—creating villagers' simple and honest character—but they equally long for joy, long for release.They also have cultural creation, requiring an opportunity to showcase their talents.

Temple fairs are their occasions for joy, release, and display.

A kind of life force bursts forth breaking through the extremely dull living environment—somewhat wild, somewhat fanatical—firecrackers and muskets, gongs, drums, and suona horns—shaking the mountains with echoes.

Opera singing at the Black Dragon Temple in Qikou Town, Linxian County, Shanxi—can be heard clearly in small villages of northern Shaanxi across the Yellow River—villagers remember these generation after generation—"opera sung east of the river, heard west of the river"—becoming a bright stroke in life.

As places of worship for pantheistic worship—from a small incense table under an ancient tree, a shrine at a cliff edge, to palaces and temples with over a hundred rooms and crowds of gods—are museums of rural culture in China's agricultural era.

This is a comprehensive museum—it displays Chinese farmers' understanding of the universe, society, and life; displays their attitude toward life, their positive and optimistic ideal pursuits and helpless disappointment; temples also display their character, their joy and anxiety, their honesty and petty cunning; in temples, one can also see the pain of their birth, old age, illness, and death, and their efforts to escape this pain.

In rural society's temples, there is no abstruse philosophy, no compassionate preaching—what exists is villagers' most real worldly life.

Temples are also a representative work showcasing rural artisans' cultural creation achievements—they are the most colorful among rural architecture, with high specifications, refined technology, mature art, also integrating the best local works of sculpture, painting, literature, and calligraphy.

Regarding architecture as a history book—religious architecture is one of its most colorful chapters, also the most moving.

Regarding temples as a museum—looking carefully, people can see from here an important part of villagers' material and spiritual life.

关键术语 Key Terms (209)

其他建筑

Other Buildings
7
节
8.1 亭
Section 1

一、亭 乡土社会里有一些常见的公益性小建筑，其中比较重要的是亭子、桥（桥亭）、渡头，等等。

在浙江省永嘉县楠溪江两岸，在原徽州六邑的田野，还有江西和福建农村，处处都点缀着一些轻盈的、小巧的、形式活泼的小亭子供人休息。这些吴越稻作地区多雨，春雨缠绵，夏雨倏忽，在田间劳作的，在山路上赶脚的，在埠头待渡的，还有那些带着孩子挎着木盆在井边溪头浣洗衣服的妇女，都需要一个随时可以避雨的场所。于是，在这种地方就有了亭子。

亭子是村人们造的，作为一种公益活动，有独家捐钱的，有几家合伙的。有了点富余钱，就为乡亲们做点儿好事，这是农耕时代厚道的农人们的传统。有一些是出于许愿还愿，家里人病了，到庙里去烧香求菩萨，应允病人康复之后造一座亭子给大家。经济拮据的，只捐一根柱子钱也行。村里管事的会把钱存起来，待别家捐了，一凑齐了料就开工建造。

还有一种"孝子亭"，父母老了，做寿的时候，儿孙们造一座亭子给乡亲们遮风挡雨，一来为了祈福，二来为老人留下一份念想，永远受人敬重。这当然也是子孙们的体面。本来是纯功能的亭子，在社会中存在，便渐渐浸润了丰富的人文性。

路亭的公益性使它们成为田野间最富有人情味的场所。在农耕文明时代，路亭里一般备有茶水，炊具和柴草也都齐全。年年从端午到重阳还供应暑药。到亭子里歇脚的过客，自己取灶头葫芦舀一瓢山泉，倒进锅里，烧几根现成搁在灶边的山柴，解开随身带着的米袋，便可以煮一顿喷香的饭。吃饱喝足，翻起脚板看看，草鞋磨坏了，从容从柱子上解下一双新的穿上。

这一切都是免费的，用不着谢什么人，回家去照样做一点这类关心人的事就是了。亭子里的费用或者由村人分担，轮值砍柴、打草鞋，或者由宗族公田拨出一份，固定以所产供应亭子日常所需。楠溪江边岩头村南门口的乘风亭，正面柱子上的一副对联，刻的是：茶待多情客，饭留有义人。

殷勤的主人心地仁厚，把过路客叫做多情而有义的人，给离家外出晓行夜宿的人多少慰藉。这就是父老乡亲！富裕一点的人家，会花钱雇一个人在路亭里做些关照过客的服务工作，备下碗、筷、盆、碟供过客使用，略有一点做善事的味道了。这种功能比较多的路亭通常在明间加一小间房子，向后凸出。

有一些亭子造在水口、村口，那里除了过客多，还经常有老人们聚会，他们已经不再劳作而安享余年了。几十年风雨中共度艰难岁月的老哥儿们，整天坐在亭子里的栏杆椅上，议论着天气和庄稼，话儿不多，从缺了牙齿的嘴里吐出几个模糊不清的音来，就彼此都明白了。亭子给他们以生活的温暖，他们给村子的人们一种和谐安宁的气息。

夏季雨水倏忽，田间劳动的农人，在风雨突然袭来的时候，总能有亭子可以躲避。路亭的型制大体有两类，一类是穿心亭，多是三开间，三面或四面有墙，道路穿亭而过，从山墙进出。

亭里有大木架在柱子间，供人坐下休息。另一类是路边亭，小的一开间，大的三开间，正面贴路边而且通面阔敞开。也有少数四面完全敞开的，柱子间也有大木横架做坐凳。

亭子小，很朴素，但是按地方传统精心造来，封火山墙头曲线富有弹力，构架也用月梁。楠溪江中游山路、田畔和村头的亭子最多，曾经有过至少两千多座，至今保存下来的尚有二百七十四座。多用歇山式屋顶，飘逸洒脱的曲线屋面，中规中矩，风姿绰约。点缀得田野生趣盎然。

除了路亭，乡里的村落多有大大小小的公共园林，园林里大都有亭子。

再以楠溪江流域为例，如芙蓉村中心芙蓉池里的芙蓉亭、溪口村莲池里的水心亭、岩头村丽水湖南端的花亭、埭头村卧龙冈上大樟树下的清风亭以及水云村的赤水亭等等。这些亭子形式都很华丽，对村落有很强的装饰性，它们在赞美村子的安乐和文明。

水云村的赤水亭还附带着戏台。北半部面对道路，供人休息，南半部是戏台，面对远处的溪流。演出时北边一半便是后台，观众在溪流和戏台间的空地上看戏。台柱上的楹联是："为奸为忠昭然明鉴；入情入理莫作闲看。

"戏是教化人的，亭子也不忘教化。村子的"十景"、"八景"之类常常有以亭子为主题的，如楠溪江畔溪口村《南山十景诗》有"水心亭"一首："亭榭俯横塘，盈盈一水长，柳丝披拂处，惊起两鸳鸯。

"明代中叶，鹤垟村任职锦衣卫的谢廷循在村头溪边造了一座"临流亭"，他把亭子的图样上呈明宣宗御览，宣宗给他题了一首诗：临流亭馆净无尘，落涧泉声处处闻。半湿半干花上露，飞来飞去岭头云。翠迷洞口竹千个，白占林梢鹤一群。此地清幽人不到，唯留风月与平分。在楠溪江流域，各类亭子里大多都有神龛供奉三官大帝。

三官大帝是天、地、水三位帝君，他们掌管着农业生产的绝对命脉，尤其在稻作地区。楠溪江古属崇巫尚鬼的瓯越，所以既然乡野间、村门边有个亭子，就不妨顺例祭祀上三官大帝。那些亭子很朴素，但神坛却十分精美甚至华丽。

花坦村东门内一座这样的亭子，或者可以说是三官大帝庙，不但神坛精美华丽，天花上的藻井也十分精美华丽，竟是建筑艺术的上品。乡村里也有另外一种感情的亭子。

前徽州六邑之一黟县西武乡关麓村，是徽商的村子，北靠西武岭，半山上有一座穿心的三开间路亭被当作山神庙，有神像和祭坛。附近村里的孩子，跟徽州朝奉的子弟一样，一到"十二三岁"，便随父兄出去学做生意了。

十七八岁，回乡娶亲，然后每年回来度一个月的假，假期满了，便穿一双草鞋，背一只包袱，提一把雨伞，再出去谋生。妻子从粉靥胜花到白发如霜，年年送丈夫到山神庙，怅惘地望着他一步步踏着崎岖的石板路走进密林中。在等待的一年里，她们每逢初一、十五，都会到山神庙来烧香、磕头，祈求丈夫平安，祈求明年还能顺利迎来丈夫。

一代又一代的妻子们一年又一年的香火把山神庙的四壁都熏成了黑色。当年同为徽州六邑之一的婺源，有一个豸峰村，村外古道边也有一座"望夫亭"，讲着同样的故事。

其实，这故事几乎在所有村落的下水口亭子里都在演出，只不过并不都叫它们"望夫亭"罢了。乡土生活并不是单有"农家乐"式的恬静单纯，它也有自己的波澜。不但有个人的生老病死和躲避不了的天灾人祸，更重要的是有些波澜会和宗族兴衰社会治乱发生关系，以致引起祠堂和衙门的关注。

于是，一种常见的教化方式是建造作为扬善惩恶之处的亭子，它们多造在村落中心，来往人多的地方，官定的正式功能性名称是"申明亭"。本来，一般村子都会有一座或几座人们休息时候闲坐聊天的场所，大多是街亭，它们自然也渐渐成为舆论中心。

湖南省会同县高椅村就有几座这样的亭子，其中有一座叫"世德亭"，亭内中柱上挂一对木板，用墨汁分别写着一首诗的上下阙：不作长亭构短亭，乘凉多半属颓龄；好将忠孝谈遗迹，嘱咐儿曹仔细听。

这种习俗由来已久，渐渐形成规矩，政府就顺势规定宗族或"社"把它们当做官方的"申明亭"。清代道光年间（1821—1850）的《徽州府志》说："凡民有作奸犯科者，书其罪，揭于亭中，以寓惩恶。"另在城里县衙门附近则造"旌善亭"，这大概是因为当官的喜欢扬善，以表示自己政通人和的治绩。

江西省婺源县李坑村中心三岔路口有一座拱桥叫通济桥，桥边就有一座申明亭，大约五米见方，重檐。浙江省龙游县三门源村也存下了一座申明亭，也在村中心的一座拱桥边上。

桥头，长夏清凉，一般都是村人们喜欢会聚交谊的地方，自然成了村子的舆论中心。后来，大约因为只惩恶不大光彩，慢慢地，申明亭里就既惩恶也扬善了。

惩恶扬善本是宗族的分内事，所以，凡宗族关系薄弱的地方，这种申明亭就很不成样子了，例如山西省阳城县郭峪村是个杂姓村，它中心的三岔路口，一处号称申明亭的，竟是贴宅墙半腰的一溜窄窄的瓦檐，像个布告栏，勉强能给"揭单"挡一下小雨而已。虽然如此，历史上的这一件措施还是很有意义的。

1.

Pavilions In rural society there are some common public welfare small buildings, among which the more important are pavilions, bridges (bridge pavilions), ferry landings, etc.

On both banks of the Nanxi River in Yongjia County, Zhejiang, in the fields of the former six Huizhou counties, and in the countryside of Jiangxi and Fujian—everywhere are dotted with light, small, lively-form pavilions for people to rest.

These Wu-Yue rice-growing regions are rainy—spring rain lingering, summer rain sudden—those working in fields, those traveling on mountain roads, those waiting for ferries at docks, and those women with children carrying wooden basins to wash clothes at wells and streams—all need a place to take shelter from rain at any time.

Thus, in such places there are pavilions.Pavilions are built by villagers—as a kind of public welfare activity—some donated by a single family, some by several families pooling money.

Having some spare money, doing a little good for fellow villagers is the tradition of honest farmers in the agricultural era.

Some are out of vow fulfillment—when a family member is ill, they go to the temple to burn incense and pray to Bodhisattva, promising to build a pavilion for everyone after the patient recovers.

Those financially strained can donate just the money for one pillar.The village manager saves the money, waiting for other families to donate—once materials are gathered, construction begins.

There is also a kind of "filial son pavilion"—when parents are old and celebrating birthdays, descendants build a pavilion to shelter fellow villagers from wind and rain—firstly for blessing, secondly to leave a memory for the elderly, forever respected by people.

This is of course also the descendants' honor.Originally purely functional pavilions, existing in society, gradually become infused with rich humanistic qualities.

The public welfare nature of road pavilions makes them the most humane places in the fields.

In the agricultural civilization era, road pavilions generally have tea water prepared, cooking utensils and firewood all complete.

From Dragon Boat Festival to Double Ninth Festival every year, summer heat-relief medicine is also supplied.

Travelers resting in the pavilion—take the gourd ladle from the stove to scoop a dipper of mountain spring water, pour into the pot, burn a few pieces of mountain firewood already placed by the stove, untie the rice bag carried with them—and can cook a fragrant meal.

After eating and drinking enough, turn up the soles of feet to check—if straw sandals are worn out, calmly untie a new pair from the pillar and put them on.

All this is free, no need to thank anyone—when going home, just do a little of this kind of caring thing yourself.

Pavilion expenses are either shared by villagers—taking turns chopping firewood, making straw sandals—or allocated from clan public fields, with produce fixed to supply daily pavilion needs.

At Chengfeng Pavilion at the south gate of Yantou Village by the Nanxi River, a couplet on the front pillars is carved: Tea awaits affectionate guests, rice is kept for righteous people.

The diligent host has a kind and generous heart—calling passersby affectionate and righteous people—giving some comfort to those who leave home to travel by day and night.These are the elders and fellow villagers!

Wealthier families will spend money hiring someone to do service work caring for travelers in the road pavilion—preparing bowls, chopsticks, basins, plates for travelers' use—slightly having the flavor of doing good deeds.

Such multi-functional road pavilions usually add a small room in the central bay, protruding backward.

Some pavilions are built at water mouths and village entrances—where besides many travelers, there are also frequent gatherings of elderly people who no longer work and enjoy their remaining years.

Old brothers who spent difficult years together through decades of wind and rain—sit all day on the railing chairs in the pavilion, discussing weather and crops—not many words, a few indistinct sounds from toothless mouths—and they all understand each other.

The pavilion gives them warmth of life; they give the village people a harmonious and peaceful atmosphere.

Summer rain is sudden—farmers working in fields, when wind and rain suddenly strike, can always find a pavilion to take shelter.

Road pavilion forms are generally of two types—one is the through-pavilion, mostly three bays, with walls on three or four sides, the road passes through the pavilion, entering and exiting from the gable walls.

Inside the pavilion there are large wooden frames between pillars for people to sit and rest.

The other type is roadside pavilion—small one-bay, large three-bay—front facing the roadside and fully open across the width.

There are also a few completely open on all four sides, with large horizontal wooden frames between pillars as benches.

Pavilions are small and simple, but carefully built according to local traditions—the fire-sealing gable wall head curves with elasticity, and the framework also uses crescent beams.

Pavilions are most numerous on mountain roads, field edges, and village heads in the middle reaches of the Nanxi River—there were once at least over two thousand, and 274 still survive today.

Most use hip-and-gable roofs—elegant and free curved roof surfaces, proper and regular, graceful in bearing.Dotted to make the fields full of vitality.

Besides road pavilions, rural villages mostly have public gardens of various sizes, and gardens mostly have pavilions.

Taking the Nanxi River basin as an example—such as the Furong Pavilion in the center of Furong Pool at Furong Village, the Water Heart Pavilion in the Lotus Pond at Xikou Village, the Flower Pavilion at the south end of Lishui Lake at Yantou Village, the Cool Breeze Pavilion under the large camphor tree on Wolong Ridge at Daitou Village, and the Red Water Pavilion at Shuiyun Village, etc.

These pavilions are all very ornate in form, with strong decorative value for the village—they praise the village's peace and civilization.The Red Water Pavilion at Shuiyun Village also has an attached opera stage.

The northern half faces the road for people to rest; the southern half is the opera stage, facing the distant stream.

During performances, the northern half becomes the backstage—audiences watch opera on the open ground between the stream and the stage.

The couplet on the stage pillars is: "Whether treacherous or loyal, clearly mirrored; whether reasonable or not, do not watch idly." Opera is for moral education, and pavilions also do not forget moral education.

Village "Ten Scenes," "Eight Scenes" and the like often have pavilions as themes—such as the "Nanshan Ten Scenes Poetry" at Xikou Village by the Nanxi River has a "Water Heart Pavilion" poem: "Pavilion overlooking the horizontal pond, clear water stretches long; where willow branches brush, two mandarin ducks are startled to rise.

" In mid-Ming, Xie Tingxun of Heyang Village, who served in the Imperial Guard, built a "Linliu Pavilion" by the stream at the village head—he presented the pavilion's drawing to Emperor Xuanzong for review, and the emperor wrote him a poem: Linliu pavilion pure without dust, falling stream spring sounds heard everywhere.

Half wet half dry dew on flowers, flying back and forth clouds over ridges.Green confuses cave mouth with thousand bamboos, white occupies treetops with a flock of cranes.

This place is quiet and people don't come, only leaving wind and moon to share equally.In the Nanxi River basin, various pavilions mostly have shrines enshrining the Three Great Officials.

The Three Great Officials are the Heavenly, Earthly, and Water Sovereigns—they control the absolute lifeline of agricultural production, especially in rice-growing regions.

The Nanxi River anciently belonged to Ou-Yue, which worshipped witches and ghosts—so since there is a pavilion in the countryside or by the village gate, it is convenient to conventionally worship the Three Great Officials.

Those pavilions are very simple, but the altars are very exquisite甚至 ornate.

One such pavilion inside the east gate of Huatan Village—or it can be called the Three Great Officials Temple—not only has an exquisite and ornate altar, but the caisson ceiling on the ceiling is also very exquisite and ornate—actually a top-grade work of architectural art.

There is also another kind of emotional pavilion in the countryside.

Guanlu Village in Xiwu Township, Yi County—one of the former six Huizhou counties—is a Huizhou merchant village, backed by Xiwu Ridge to the north.

On the mountainside there is a through three-bay road pavilion used as a Mountain God Temple, with god statues and altars.

Children in nearby villages, like the children of Huizhou shopkeepers, at "twelve or thirteen years old" go out with fathers and brothers to learn business.

At seventeen or eighteen, they return home to marry, then come back for one month's vacation every year—when vacation ends, they put on a pair of straw sandals, carry a bundle, hold an umbrella, and go out again to make a living.

Wives—from rosy cheeks better than flowers to white hair like frost—year after year send husbands to the Mountain God Temple, wistfully watching him step by step along the rugged stone road into the dense forest.

During the year of waiting, every first and fifteenth of the lunar month, they come to the Mountain God Temple to burn incense and kowtow—praying for husband's safety, praying to smoothly welcome husband next year.

Generation after generation of wives' year after year of incense smoke blackened the four walls of the Mountain God Temple.

In Wuyuan, also one of the six Huizhou counties, there is a Zhifeng Village—by the ancient road outside the village there is also a "Wangfu Pavilion" (Husband-Watching Pavilion), telling the same story.

In fact, this story is performed in almost all villages' lower water-mouth pavilions—just not all called "Wangfu Pavilion." Rural life is not merely the tranquil simplicity of "happy farmhouse"—it also has its own waves.

Not only personal birth, old age, illness, death and unavoidable natural and man-made disasters—more importantly, some waves relate to clan rise and fall, social order and chaos—even attracting attention from ancestral halls and government offices.

Thus, a common method of moral education is building pavilions as places to praise good and punish evil—they are mostly built in the village center where many people pass—the official formal functional name is "Shenming Pavilion" (Declaration Pavilion).

Originally, ordinary villages would have one or several places for people to rest and chat—mostly street pavilions—which naturally gradually become public opinion centers.

Gaoyi Village in Huitong County, Hunan has several such pavilions—one called "Shide Pavilion"—on the central pillars inside hangs a pair of wooden boards, written in ink with the upper and lower stanzas of a poem: Not building long pavilions but short pavilions, those enjoying cool are mostly elderly; good to talk of loyalty and filial piety's traces, instructing children to listen carefully.

This custom has a long history, gradually forming rules—the government then took the opportunity to stipulate that clans or "associations" treat them as official "Shenming Pavilions.

" The "Huizhou Prefecture Gazetteer" from Qing Daoguang era (1821–1850) says: "Any people who commit crimes, write their crimes, post in the pavilion, to contain punishment of evil.

" Additionally, near the county government office in cities, "Jingshan Pavilions" (Praise-Good Pavilions) are built—probably because officials like to praise good, to show their governance of smooth politics and harmonious people.

At the center of Likeng Village, Wuyuan County, Jiangxi, at a three-way intersection there is an arch bridge called Tongji Bridge—beside the bridge there is a Shenming Pavilion, about five meters square, double-eaved.

Sanmenyuan Village in Longyou County, Zhejiang also preserves a Shenming Pavilion—also beside an arch bridge in the village center.

Bridgeheads, cool in long summer—are generally places villagers like to gather and socialize—naturally becoming the village's public opinion center.

Later, probably because only punishing evil is not very glorious—gradually, Shenming Pavilions both punish evil and praise good.

Punishing evil and praising good is originally the clan's duty—so where clan relations are weak, such Shenming Pavilions are very shabby.

For example, Guoyu Village in Yangcheng County, Shanxi is a mixed-surname village—at its central three-way intersection, a so-called Shenming Pavilion is actually a narrow strip of tile eaves halfway up a residential wall—like a bulletin board—barely able to shield the "posted notice" from light rain.

Nevertheless, this historical measure is still very meaningful.

8.2 牌坊
Section 2

二、牌坊 表彰性的和炫耀性的牌坊，在南北各地都很常见，尤其在东南部各个经济和文化都比较先进的省里。它们是一个村子的骄傲。凡建牌坊都要经朝廷审批，所以牌坊上部正中都有一块不大的竖匾，刻着"圣旨"、"敕建"或者"钦旌"等字样，表示确系"奉旨兴建"，是正宗的牌坊。

最常见的是为科名、宦绩、寿考、义举、女德等而建造的，它们有单间的，也有三间的，都跨着街路。但表彰女德的牌坊，大都侧向造在路边，中跨还要用矮墙挡住。经过破坏性极强的"文化大革命"，许多村落里大量建造过的文教类建筑在"破四旧"运动中遭到严重的破坏，但还有少数村落侥幸地保存了一些，其中就有江西省乐安县的流坑村。流坑村本来就是文化水平比较高的村落，宋代就"户户弦诵"。

据道光庚寅年（1830年）族谱记载，当时流坑董氏有八十三座大小宗祠，二十八所书院。据1989年《乐安县志》，董氏有著作三十余种刻板问世。村里的曾姓也创办了书院。董氏和曾氏都有著作收入《四库全书》。

流坑村民于宋代在科举上成绩斐然，北宋时，流坑董氏有进士十五人，南宋时董氏有进士十一人，且有一位中了状元。和科名大振相应，流坑村建造了不少文化建筑，其中有董德元中了状元之后造的一座状元楼。

这以后，流坑村居民转而以水运木材为主业，收入大增，但科考成绩大落，元、明、清三代只有明代出了一位进士（成化二十年，即1484年）。读书人转向实用，以医术和阴阳堪舆之术闻名。但这时期仍有牌坊等兴建，不过所旌表的多为寿考、贞节之类。流坑《孕昂公房谱》中记录了全村四十八座牌坊。

其中有：一为科名类：状元坊，纪念八世祖董德元于绍兴十八年廷试第一；五桂坊，为宋景祐元年洙公等父子、兄弟、叔侄同登进士榜；奕叶天香坊，为进士四十人立。二为封爵类：累朝师保坊，为太子太保、太子太傅等立；子男封爵坊。

三为贤德类：郡邑乡贤坊；七朝耆德坊，为明御史时望公立；丛桂流芳坊，为十六世祖季敏公立。四为学识类：道学源流坊，为祀乡贤仲修公立；文献世族坊；理学名贤坊，为二十二世祖燧公立。五为寿考类：齐泰坊，为二十世祖志杰公立；百岁坊，为二十二世祖光武公立。六为伦理类：慈孝坊二，贞节坊二。

但经过近年的大破坏，从上述近五十座牌坊中保存至今的只有"高明广大坊"、"应宿第坊"、"双寿坊"和"节孝坊"等几座了。状元楼，现有的是村子的西门，上下两层，下层为拱券过道，上层有一座大厅，三开间，柱上悬联："南宫策士文章贵；北阙传胪姓字先"。

村子的东门为"翰林门"，东门口有对联"数封天子诏，当代帝王师"。门楣上有"少司成第"匾额，落款为："内阁大学士杨士奇为国子司业前翰林院编修董琰立"。门侧有金幼孜书联：国史总裁望重一时锁闼；英才乐育名高天下宗师。

女德，主要是贞、节、慈、孝，特殊情况下有"烈"。明初洪武元年（1368年）诏曰："民间寡妇，三十以前夫亡守制、五十以后不改节者，旌表门闾"。丈夫去世时还不到三十岁的妇女，在不幸寡居后，敬老抚幼，含辛茹苦，维持了一个安定的家庭，最后使"老有所终，幼有所长，废疾者皆有所养"，她自己正常死亡后，宗族可以向官方申请旌表，建造一座纪念物，这就是节孝牌坊。

在当时的社会经济历史条件下，这样辛劳的妇女，确实应该受到尊重，得到表彰，她们维护了社会的安定。节孝牌坊和科名牌坊之类的形式是相同的，以三间三檐的居多。

不过节孝牌坊有一个特殊的要求，便是牌坊之下不可以容人穿行。因此，它或者在开间中设矮墙、铁栅等障碍，或者背靠甚至紧贴在一座建筑物的墙壁上，所以它们都顺街巷道路沿边而造。

有一些地方的贞节牌坊为了防人在它下面穿行，做了更加严格的防范措施。江西省乐安县流坑村有两座贞节牌坊，呈浮雕式，镶嵌在住宅山墙的上半截，而且位置很高，人们伸手也不能触及。为了减轻牌坊的重量，它们的体形尺寸比较小，而且很薄。

可惜因为保护太差，坊上原有的刻字已经漫漶不清了。它们所表彰的女子的事迹，全村也已经没有人说得清楚了，倒真正是"质本洁来还洁去"。在贞节或节孝牌坊明间的大小额枋之间，有一块石板，镌刻着"节凛冰霜"、"劲节可风"之类的褒词，也有略述苦节的。总之，多少也能表示对艰难的守节生活的同情和对抚老育幼的辛苦的尊敬和感谢。

在某些特殊的历史条件下，妇女所受的摧残很痛苦。例如，皖南和苏南，太平天国战乱时期妇女遭难的很多，因此应该建造的贞节牌坊便很多，就只好建"节孝总坊"。

清道光二十二年（1842年）朱骏声为安徽黟县的总坊写了一篇《疏》，说："《县志》所载，未旌孝节贞烈妇女共千九百十五，又新增采访已故贞节烈妇七百十九，现存孝节烈妇千三百二十三，共三千九百五十七"（见《黟县志》）。

苏州也在清道光年间（1821—1850）造了一座总节孝祠，旌表吴郡三邑"应"受旌表的贞、节、烈、孝妇女三千四百多人。苏州知府李璋煜为总节孝祠题了一副楹联，说：节烈阐孤寒，补五百年吴中阙典；春秋崇享祀，慰三千人泉下贞魂。关于这两地的"总祠"，长官们在诗与联中都提到"贞"、"节"与"烈"，可见当时妇女所遭的压迫、束缚、摧残之重。

又有一种旌表性的牌坊，多是纪念"功宗德祖"或各种杰出人物的。例如，浙江省宁海县县衙门口的方孝孺纪念坊。方孝孺是明代初年的一位大学者和一位杰出的大臣。他在朱氏皇族的内斗中因为坚贞不屈于暴力淫威而惨遭杀害，甚至牵累了"十族"。在当时的历史文化条件下他持正不屈的精神也是应该受到尊重并且世代纪念的。这座牌坊是木构的，三开间，额间特别用十分珍贵的柏木板做了一块大匾，匾上刻的是"天地正气"四个字。

这四个字源自文天祥（1236—1283）《正气歌》首句："天地有正气，沛乎塞沧溟。"不料，1964年，竟为了拆掉旧县衙门造新的办公楼而把这座几百年来受人敬崇的牌坊一起拆掉了，"破了四旧"。浙江省永嘉县芙蓉村旁有一座陡峭且高的芙蓉峰，峰下有一座坟墓，是陈虞之的。陈虞之是宋代晚年的进士，他响应文天祥的号召，带领芙蓉村的青壮年在芙蓉峰上扎营抗元，死守山头。后来，抗元失败，他跃马跳岩死节。

几百年来，村人都保护着他的坟墓，近年，这坟墓却因为无人照料而毁掉了。一座家祠，一堆孤坟，它们都可能有历史的和文化的信息，有善恶的和是非的判断，把它们保护住，本来也是应该做的事。旌表性的牌坊，在村子里常常建造在一起，或者相近的位置上，以求得更强的效果。

例如，浙江省永嘉县花坦村，大宗祠前的横街上前前后后排了八座牌坊，木石兼用，各有不同的旌表主题。安徽省歙县棠樾村的东门外，沿着有点弯曲的田间石板路，前后建造了七座石坊，受旌表的竟都是管理两淮盐务的鲍氏家族的。

它们是鲍家贤尚书坊（明天启二年，即1622年建，乾隆六十年重修）；鲍逢昌孝子坊（清嘉庆二年，即1797年建）；吴氏节孝坊（清乾隆三十二年，即1767年建）；"乐善好施"坊（清嘉庆二十五年，即1820年建）；汪氏节孝坊（清乾隆四十一年，即1776年建）；慈孝里坊（建于明初，清乾隆1777年重修）；鲍灿孝行坊（明嘉靖年间，即1522—1566年建），另外还有一座骢步亭（1736—1820年间建）。

这七座牌坊都是纯石构，四柱三檐，其中有五座为通天柱式。它们相距不远，道路又有弯曲，所以显得疏密十分适宜，尺度也很和谐。个体牌坊中最特殊的一座是安徽省歙县的许国石坊。它建于万历十二年（1584年）。

许国是"少保兼太子太保礼部尚书武英殿大学士"，地位很高。牌坊造在进城门第一个十字路口，竟采用了一种很特殊的构造：四面牌坊。它南北正面是两座牌坊，每座三间，两个侧面是两座单间牌坊。

四座牌坊组合成一座四面围栏式的牌坊。它位于距南城门不远的十字路口，阔面朝南北，窄面朝东西。这种四面坊极少见，安徽歙县丰口还有一座，得名为四面坊，每面只有一开间，共四根柱子。它四面都没有路，立在荒野的、狭窄的河边陡岸上。它的存在使对许国石坊型制的解释更加困难了。

2.Memorial Archways Commemorative and boastful memorial archways are common throughout north and south, especially in the economically and culturally advanced southeastern provinces.They are a village's pride.

Building a memorial archway requires imperial court approval—so in the upper center of every archway there is a small vertical plaque, engraved with "Imperial Edict," "Built by Imperial Command," or "Imperially Commended" etc.

—indicating it was indeed "built by imperial order," an authentic archway.The most common are built for scholarly honors, official achievements, longevity, charitable deeds, female virtue, etc.

—they have single-bay and three-bay types, all spanning streets.But archways commemorating female virtue are mostly built sideways along roads, with the central span blocked by low walls.

After the extremely destructive "Cultural Revolution," many educational and cultural buildings built in villages were severely damaged in the "Destroy the Four Olds" movement—but a few villages luckily preserved some, including Liukeng Village in Le'an County, Jiangxi.

Liukeng Village was originally a village with relatively high cultural level—in Song dynasty "every household had stringed instruments and recitations.

" According to the 1830 (Daoguang Gengyin) genealogy record, at that time the Dong clan of Liukeng had eighty-three ancestral halls large and small, twenty-eight academies.

According to the 1989 "Le'an County Gazetteer," the Dong clan had over thirty works published.The Zeng surname in the village also founded an academy.

Both Dong and Zeng clans had works included in the "Complete Library in Four Sections.

" Liukeng villagers had outstanding imperial examination results in Song dynasty—Northern Song: Dong clan had fifteen jinshi; Southern Song: Dong clan had eleven jinshi, and one became zhuangyuan (top scholar).

Corresponding to the scholarly glory, Liukeng Village built many cultural buildings—including a Zhuangyuan Tower built after Dong Deyuan became zhuangyuan.

After that, Liukeng villagers turned to water transport of timber as main business—income greatly increased—but examination results declined greatly—Yuan, Ming, Qing dynasties only produced one jinshi in Ming (Chenghua twentieth year, 1484).

Scholars turned to practical skills—known for medicine and yin-yang feng-shui.But this period still had archways built—though mostly commemorating longevity, chastity, etc.

Liukeng's "Yun'ang Branch Genealogy" records forty-eight memorial archways in the village.

Among them: First, scholarly honor type: Zhuangyuan Archway, commemorating eighth ancestor Dong Deyuan who ranked first in the palace examination of Shaoxing eighteenth year; Wugui Archway, for Zhu Gong and others—father, son, brothers, uncles, nephews—all passing jinshi in the same year of Jingyou first year; Yiye Tianxiang Archway, for forty jinshi.

Second, noble title type: Leichao Shibao Archway, for Crown Prince Tutor, Crown Prince Grand Tutor, etc.; Zinan Fengjue Archway.

Third, virtuous type: Junyi Xiangxian Archway; Qichao Qide Archway, for Ming censor Shi Wanggong; Conggui Liufang Archway, for sixteenth ancestor Jimin Gong.

Fourth, learning type: Daoxue Yuanliu Archway, for enshrining village sage Zhongxiu Gong; Wenxian Shizu Archway; Lixue Mingxian Archway, for twenty-second ancestor Sui Gong.

Fifth, longevity type: Qitai Archway, for twentieth ancestor Zhijie Gong; Baisui Archway, for twenty-second ancestor Guangwu Gong.Sixth, ethical type: Cixiao Archway two, Zhenjie Archway two.

But after recent great destruction, of the above nearly fifty archways, only "Gaoming Guangda Archway," "Yingsudi Archway," "Shuangshou Archway," and "Jiexiao Archway" etc.survive today.

Zhuangyuan Tower—the existing one is the village's west gate, two stories—lower level is arched passage, upper level has a large hall, three bays, with couplet on pillars: "Southern Palace selects scholars, literature precious; Northern Palace announces names, surname first.

" The village's east gate is "Hanlin Gate"—east gate entrance has couplet "Several imperial edicts, contemporary emperor's teacher.

" On the lintel there is "Shaosicheng Di" plaque, inscribed: "Grand Secretary Yang Shiqi established for National Academy Director, former Hanlin Academy Compiler Dong Yan.

" By the gate there is Jin Youzi's calligraphy couplet: National history president, prestige heavy for a time; talents joyfully educated, fame high as world's master.

Female virtue—mainly chastity, fidelity, kindness, filial piety—special cases include "martyrdom.

" Early Ming Hongwu first year (1368) edict: "Civilian widows, who remain chaste after husband's death before age thirty and do not remarry after age fifty—commemorate at their gate.

" Women whose husbands died before they reached thirty—after unfortunate widowhood, respecting elders and raising children, enduring hardships, maintaining a stable family—finally enabling "the old have their end, the young have their growth, the disabled have their care"—after her normal death, the clan can apply to officials for commemoration, building a memorial—this is the chastity-filial archway.

Under the social-economic-historical conditions of the time, such hardworking women indeed deserved respect and commendation—they maintained social stability.

Chastity-filial archways and scholarly honor archways have the same form—mostly three bays three eaves.But chastity-filial archways have a special requirement: people may not pass through under the archway.

Therefore, they either set low walls, iron grilles and other obstacles in the bays—or back against or even cling to a building's wall—so they are all built along streets and roads.

In some places, chastity archways took stricter preventive measures to prevent people passing underneath.

Liukeng Village, Le'an County, Jiangxi has two chastity archways—in relief form, inlaid in the upper half of residential gable walls, and positioned very high—people cannot reach even by stretching hands.

To reduce the archway's weight, their dimensions are relatively small and very thin.Unfortunately due to poor protection, the original inscriptions on the archways have become illegible.

The deeds of the women they commemorate—no one in the village can explain clearly anymore—truly "pure came, pure went.

" Between the large and small architraves of the central bay of chastity or chastity-filial archways, there is a stone slab engraved with praise words like "Chastity as severe as frost and ice," "Strong chastity worthy of emulation" etc.

—some briefly describe the bitter fidelity.In any case, it somewhat expresses sympathy for the difficult chaste life and respect and gratitude for the hardship of caring for elders and raising children.

Under certain special historical conditions, the oppression women suffered was very painful.

For example, in southern Anhui and southern Jiangsu—during the Taiping Rebellion war many women suffered—so many chastity archways should have been built—they had to build "Chastity-Filial General Archways.

" In Qing Daoguang twenty-second year (1842), Zhu Junsheng wrote a "Memorial" for the general archway in Yi County, Anhui: "The County Gazetteer records: uncommemorated chaste-filial-virtuous-martyr women total 1,915; plus newly investigated deceased chaste-virtuous-martyr women 719; existing chaste-filial-virtuous women 1,323—total 3,957" (see "Yi County Gazetteer").

Suzhou also built a General Chastity-Filial Shrine in Qing Daoguang era (1821–1850), commemorating over 3,400 chaste, filial, virtuous, martyr women of three Wu prefectures who "should" be commemorated.

Suzhou Prefect Li Zhangyu wrote a couplet for the General Chastity-Filial Shrine: Chastity and martyrdom illuminate the lonely and poor, supplementing five hundred years of missing classics in Wu; Spring and autumn revered sacrifices, comforting three thousand people's chaste souls beneath the springs.

Regarding these two places' "general shrines"—officials mentioned "chastity," "fidelity," and "martyrdom" in both poems and couplets—showing how heavy the oppression, bondage, and destruction women suffered at that time.

Another type of commemorative archway—mostly commemorating "meritorious ancestors and virtuous forebears" or various outstanding figures.

For example, the Fang Xiaoru Memorial Archway at the county government gate in Ninghai County, Zhejiang.Fang Xiaoru was a great scholar and outstanding minister in early Ming.

In the Zhu imperial family's internal strife—because he remained steadfast and unyielding to violent tyranny—he was tragically killed, even牵连 "ten clans.

" Under the historical-cultural conditions of the time, his spirit of uprightness and unyieldingness should also be respected and commemorated for generations.

This archway is wooden, three bays—between the architraves specially used very precious cypress wood boards to make a large plaque, engraved with "Heaven and Earth Righteous Qi" four characters.

These four characters derive from Wen Tianxiang's (1236–1283) "Song of Righteous Qi" first line: "Heaven and earth have righteous qi, filling the vast sea.

" Unexpectedly, in 1964—just to demolish the old county government and build a new office building—this archway respected for hundreds of years was demolished together, "destroying the four olds.

" Beside Furong Village in Yongjia County, Zhejiang there is a steep and high Furong Peak—below the peak there is a grave, belonging to Chen Yuzhi.

Chen Yuzhi was a late Song dynasty jinshi—he responded to Wen Tianxiang's call, leading Furong Village's young and strong to camp on Furong Peak to resist the Yuan, defending the mountain top.

Later, after resistance failed, he leaped on horseback off the cliff to die for his principles.For hundreds of years, villagers protected his grave—recently, this grave was destroyed due to lack of care.

A family shrine, a pile of lonely graves—they may all have historical and cultural information, judgments of good and evil, right and wrong—protecting them is originally something that should be done.

Commemorative archways in villages are often built together or in nearby positions to achieve stronger effect.

For example, at Huatan Village in Yongjia County, Zhejiang—on the horizontal street in front of the great ancestral hall, eight archways were arranged front and back—wood and stone combined, each with different commemorative themes.

Outside the east gate of Tangyue Village in She County, Anhui—along a slightly winding field stone road—seven stone archways were built front and back—all commemorating the Bao clan family who managed Lianghuai salt administration.

They are: Bao Jiaxian Shangshu Archway (Ming Tianqi second year, 1622 built, Qianlong sixtieth year rebuilt); Bao Fengchang Xiaozi Archway (Qing Jiaqing second year, 1797 built); Wu Shi Jiexiao Archway (Qing Qianlong thirty-second year, 1767 built); "Happy in Good Deeds" Archway (Qing Jiaqing twenty-fifth year, 1820 built); Wang Shi Jiexiao Archway (Qing Qianlong forty-first year, 1776 built); Cixiaoli Archway (built early Ming, Qing Qianlong 1777 rebuilt); Bao Can Xiaoxing Archway (Ming Jiajing era, 1522–1566 built)—plus a Congbu Pavilion (built 1736–1820).

These seven archways are all pure stone structure, four pillars three eaves—five of them are through-pillar type.They are not far apart, and the road has curves—so the density appears very appropriate, scale also very harmonious.

The most special individual archway is the Xu Guo Stone Archway in She County, Anhui.Built in Wanli twelfth year (1584).

Xu Guo was "Junior Guardian plus Crown Prince Grand Tutor, Minister of Rites, Wuying Palace Grand Secretary"—very high status.

The archway was built at the first crossroads after entering the city gate—actually adopting a very special structure: four-sided archway.

Its north-south front faces are two archways, each three bays; the two side faces are two single-bay archways.Four archways combine into one four-sided enclosed archway.

It is located at the crossroads not far from the south city gate—wide face facing north-south, narrow face facing east-west.

This kind of four-sided archway is extremely rare—there is another one at Fengkou in She County, Anhui, named Four-Sided Archway—each face only one bay, total four pillars.

It has no roads on all four sides, standing on a wild, narrow steep riverbank.Its existence makes the explanation of Xu Guo Stone Archway's form even more difficult.
